GUILTY GEAR XX ACCENT CORE PLUS R is the definitive version of Arc System Works’ classic 2D fighting game. It refines over a decade of Guilty Gear mechanics into a fast, aggressive, and technically demanding experience. This version stands as both a celebration of traditional fighting design and a showcase of mastery-level gameplay depth.

Combat is the centerpiece—complex, stylish, and highly expressive. Every character has unique movement options, special cancels, and combo structures. Systems like Roman Cancels, Faultless Defense, and Burst give advanced players enormous control over tempo and momentum. The execution ceiling is high, but so is the satisfaction of mastery.

The roster is large and balanced, with over 20 fighters, each with distinct mechanics and personalities. Characters like Sol Badguy, Ky Kiske, and Millia Rage retain their iconic styles, while niche fighters like Zappa and Venom introduce experimental playstyles. The diversity ensures replayability and encourages players to find their preferred rhythm.

Visually, the hand-drawn sprite art remains striking. Despite its age, Accent Core Plus R still looks dynamic thanks to fluid animation and impactful visual effects. The character portraits, effects, and backgrounds embody the raw energy of early-2000s anime fighting design. The soundtrack—guitar-heavy and intense—remains one of the most recognizable in the genre.

The single-player content includes arcade, survival, mission, and story modes, providing plenty of offline options. The story is chaotic but entertaining, with the signature Guilty Gear mix of heavy metal, philosophy, and absurd humor. Still, the game’s focus is competitive play, not narrative cohesion.

Online functionality was revitalized with rollback netcode, drastically improving stability and responsiveness. This update breathed new life into the title, making it a viable competitive platform even years after release. Matches now feel smooth, and the active community keeps it relevant in modern fighting circles.

Overall, GUILTY GEAR XX ACCENT CORE PLUS R is a refined, fast, and brutally technical fighter that rewards dedication. It bridges classic arcade design with modern competitive standards. For newcomers, it’s intimidating; for veterans, it’s a masterpiece of precision and style. Even in the era of Strive, this version remains one of the purest expressions of what Guilty Gear stands for—speed, aggression, and absolute flair.

Esse é um dos meus jogos favoritos de vida, desde que joguei pela primeira vez com um amigo em Split Screen lá no Xbox 360 eu acabei por gostar muito desse game e gosto bastante até hoje.

Acho mó massa o estilo "realista" do game, com a câmera tremida (ah quem prefira tirar ela nas opções do menu, mas acho a tremedeira um dos charmes do game) e ela parecendo que tá sendo segurada por alguém, como se os protagonistas estivessem sendo filmados (os efeitos da lente da câmera na iluminação também são interessantes, o contraste da imagem, a direção de arte faz muito bonito aqui, mesmo ele não tendo as melhores texturas, tem uma bela construção de cenários, simplesmente amo representações das cidades Chinesas ou Japonesas nos jogos).

O estilo realista se estende na jogabilidade também, onde os nossos tiros são por vezes imprecisos (menos das shotguns, por algum motivo elas são quase uma sniper nesse jogo kkkkk), por vezes caímos no chão, podemos atirar sem olhar, usamos galões do cenário como explosivos, tipo "usa o que tiver mesmo porque o negócio tá louco" (apesar que ainda sinto uma leve falta das granadas convencionais, mas nada que necessariamente atrapalhe, os inimigos não usam).

A história é pura confusão (no bom sentido), os protagonistas se ferram toda hora, ficou um baita gancho pra um Kane & Lynch 3, espero um dia poder ver esse jogo existir.

A inteligencia artificial do nosso parceiro é até razoável, volta e meia vejo ele matando alguns inimigos.

Há quem reclame de alguns pontos que citei aqui, mas não acho ruim, os que acho realmente ruim é o cover impreciso (você aperta o botão e o ele pega cover no lugar errado, fora os lugares que nem dão pra pegar cover), a mecânica de fazer um inimigo de escudo humano é praticamente inútil e não funciona direito e nosso personagem morre bem rápido (se por um lado contribui com o realismo, por outro é um saco porque tem vezes que um ou dois tiros já são o suficiente pra nos matar, mesmo na dificuldade normal), fora um bug ou outro no posicionamento dos inimigos ou dos outros personagens do cenário.

A trilha sonora desse jogo é uma relíquia que toca em momentos bem pontuais, façam questão de pesquisar por "Kane & Lynch 2: Dog Days OST/SOUNDTRACK", vale a pena demais.

Faltou jogar mais os modos arcade/multiplayer e zerar a campanha na maior dificuldade.

Come back when it's fully released and read some reviews then. The game's in a ridiculous state right now. Much of the game's content is gated behind a tedious looting and crafting mechanic. You frequently lose 1/2 hour or more of progress due to mechanics you didn't know about, or lethal bugs. Many of the games mechanics are cryptic or misleading. I don't think of the game as Nintendo Hard, I think it's on Sadistic Difficulty. For every good thing I can name, there's a more severe corresponding negative. Ultimately, you're not playing a game, evading and fighting against enemies. You're fighting the game itself.

The devs recently added a 'tunnels' update. The tunnel areas themselves look nice and add to the atmosphere of being a scavenger in the ruins of a futuristic metropolis. BUT. Someone on the dev team decided to add parkour sections. There are gaps you need to jump across in order to advance, thin pipes/cables you need to walk on, and at least one drop-down platform that leads to nothing and you cannot return from (without a special equipped item - pneumatic jump, which most players don't normally equip). The controls, and the camera, were not made for parkour. I don't think there's anything in the main areas that requires parkour. This is not a platforming game. They had to patch out a vertical pipe that was blocking one of the jumps, because it was pushing so many people off course and causing them to fall. The large pipes you traverse have no clear indication of the boundary where you'll start to fall off the side. The triple pipe/cable sections have invisible collision that will push you off to the side, and into a bottomless pit. These sections are also thematically misaligned, given there are lot of areas of scaffolding in the main maps that specifically prevent you from needing to make perilous jumps. So, they added new areas that add to the atmosphere, but someone on the dev team inserted sections that conflict with the base game.

Also, with these tunnels, they're functionally gating the rest of the interesting content. Previously, you could deploy to any map at any time. Now You can deploy to 'Tunnels A' for free. 2 other areas cost an in-game resource - water. The other 8 maps (and 3 other tunnels) cost hefty amounts of water, and a fast travel drone, in order to directly access them. These drones can each take hours of scavenging just to build one of them. The alternative is to go through multiple maps in succession in order to reach later maps. The problem is with the inherent difficulty of the game, various terrain bugs, and spontaneous memory access crashes, getting to further areas is mostly a gamble, with no meaningful benefit right now.

They added a personal quarters and shooting range. Those are pretty good. There are a lot of weapons, sights, handguards, and other parts, that will affect how your firearms behave. A shooting range is a great way to test them out. Unfortunately, these basic features are locked behind looting and crafting requirements. Some of the game's vendors are also gated behind loot walls - you need 16 water to trade with one of them, 6 for another. Water's easy to come by in the later game, but only after you've already unlocked these vendors. So, a lot of useful stuff is arbitrarily gated behind looting random drops. This would be like if Pokemon required you to beat the local gym leader before you were allowed to use a Pokecenter. In fact, I've beaten Pokemon Blue or Yellow without using a Pokecenter. Unlocking these vendors and starting areas is much more tedious.

Things will kill you, that you often can't avoid! There's a floating drone that spawns high in the sky. It floats down to low altitude. If it sees you and aggroes you, it can grab you and do an instant-kill animation before you know it's there. There's an invincible large dog-like machine that will do an instant-kill animation if you're below 2000 hp (most characters' max health is below 2000 hp). It runs obscenely fast, I think it's the fastest unit in the game by a large margin. If it sees you, you're already dead, with a few exceptions. When the unit (Euruskan Grabber/Stalker) is on the field, the game changes genres, to become like Alien: Isolation. There are other one-shot enemies, but only these 2 are the nearly-impossible-to-avoid type. You'll also die, or have to exit the game because: your character got stuck in the looting animation, stuck in the falling animation, stuck in the knocked down animation, got stuck below the ground. There are some memory management issues that will sometimes cause the game to crash after 40 minutes.

There are a lot of really cryptic game mechanics. Many weapons' displayed damage-per-shot is incorrect in-game. Certain weapon modifications are known to simply not work. These errors have persisted for months without basic fixes. There are a few thrown grenades in the game. As far as I know, nobody knows how much damage thrown grenades do. Grenade launchers have an unstated 10k damage explosion - the weapon itself does 1k damge on contact with an enemy. There are speculated features of the threat mechanic: where players who successfully defeat enemies and/or extract from maps will experience more aggressive enemies on further missions. This threat level is reset on player death. As far as I know, the devs have not confirmed the mechanic behaves this way, but many players have noticed strong enemy behavior changes. The exception would be The Girl, a character explicitly mentioned to not attract as much enemy attention. Levelling up is similarly cryptic. Characters' walk speed and health will increase when you increase your prestige level. I don't believe the values are given in-game. In fact, I don't think there's a way to see your max health if you're not deployed in combat.

The faction AIs are very anti-player. I observe battles where I believe units were firing at nothing. Some enemies won't even aggro against each other - notably cyborgs won't aggro against an Exo suit unit. The Exo will smash them all and they will neither try to fight back nor flee. If a player and an NPC both shoot the same target, that target will typically aggro preferentially against the player. Sometimes, all units of one faction will aggro the player in response to gunfire. They will ignore the other faction completely. In some situations, players have noted it seems like both warring factions have signed a temporary truce in order to hunt the player. The level of aggression can be difficult to predict. There are allied NPCs you can hire (once you have enough water, of course). These allies are generally a net negative. They tend fire aggressively against non-hostile mechs and tanks, attracting their wrath. At the same time, they will never engage melee units actively punching them, unless you give them a specific command 'defend the designated spot'. They also tend to get between the player and the melee enemy, actively preventing the player from protecting them.

The only genuine positives I have are the lore and the graphics. They're at least reasonably consistent, and add depth to the game. The 3 factions' feel distinct - the mostly traditional Europan military, aided by AIs in some of their machiens; the larger, biologically augmented Euruskans, and the fully cyberized Eurasians.

Amazing concept, Awesome art design, good game play loop. All consistently ruined by bad decisions.

First it was water being a mobile game mechanic that was tied to real time that hurt people with jobs or busy lives. 

Then  they added a stamina system which could have been fine if it were balanced right, but NOPE it only lets you run for about 5 seconds when it should be more like 20 seconds AT BASE! consistently the devs find ways to take a good thing and make it into a slog.

The recent update with the tunnels shows this best, The tunnels should be a level you only have to play once to unlock unlock fast travel points and each location should be up to 3 water at the most with the tunnels and by proxy the starting locations being entirely free as they once were  (Ashen Mesa/Scorched Enclave/Elephant Mausoleum). Fast travel drones are stupid and should instead be a way to pay for travel that does not use water but nope now they are incredibly expensive. And the high tier areas loot simply is not rewarding enough in its current state to ever justify spending the time or resources to get there. And for a looting game the amount you can carry is hampered by item weight making no sense, why the hell does one random sight weigh more than an entire box of ammo? It should either be removed or reevaluated to be more logical.

Besides these misguided decisions they also have the issue of ui that's to big and lacks customization for size and scale, or gigantic arcade like "good kill" nonsense when you take out a target, which goes against the entire theme of being the rat surviving hell. This game focuses on being cool to the detriment of literally everything else, and small decisions like this need to be changed.

This game has SO MUCH POTENTIAL but until it realizes it, I can not recommend it at this time. I'll update this review if they fix it.

I'm on Observation Duty 6 is a horror hidden object game where you look for anomalies in various environments and try to survive the night. Like 5, this was an excellent game to play with friends filled with sometimes subtle and sometimes ridiculous differences that always kept us on our toes. The maps are exciting, memorable, and perfectly creepy, and none of them ever felt like too much or too unfair. Hard mode makes for a great challenge, and even when you know most of the anomalies, it can still be difficult to notice them right away. The use of generative AI is frustrating and disappointing, but that's my only complaint about this game. I do love this series, and this makes for a great addition to it, so I would still recommend it, especially for those who need a fun and spooky game to play with some friends.

I almost want to recommend *Faceminer*, but the question isn’t “can you play it” so much as “should you?” Up front, it has an interesting premise and a bit of charm. The retro interface feels authentic and gives the impression the game might develop into something deeper. But the gameplay automates almost immediately and never evolves, creating an incremental idler that plateaus within an hour. The story tries to build mystery around who wants these faces mined and why, but it never really pays off that curiosity in either answers or impulse.

*Universal Paperclips* is the closest comparison: both games are about destroying the world through automating a single mindless task. Beyond that, the difference is obvious. *Paperclips* begins with a single button and keeps evolving—each new stage shifts the goalposts until you sit atop your throne of paperclips and realize how far you’ve gone in destroying everything to achieve it. *Faceminer* wants to tell a similar story about obsession and exploitation, but it gives away the moral upfront and never lets the mechanics mirror that descent. You’re told mining faces is bad from the start, so there’s no arc—just repetition. And mining faces isn’t fun to begin with, so why is anyone doing it?

The result is a game that looks clever but feels hollow. Its metaphor for crypto and AI collapses under its own contradictions, asking you to balance progress with environmental guilt in a system that insists you stop. Once you understand the point—and you will, because it’s endlessly repeated—there’s nothing left to play for. It’s a neat idea trapped in a loop that proves its own message: not playing really is the winning move.  And so, can I really recommend a game that actively insists you don't play it?

This was my first Atelier game I ever played, and a great introduction to the series for me. I absolutly loved it.

The characters and writing are all fantastic. The whole game feels like a really well made slice of life story in a fantasy setting, with some occasional serious stakes and personal goal seeking around the main plot and a couple character side storys.

The ost is also all around fantastic. Occasional art cg's are also very well made.
I personaly found the protagonist very likable as well. She was an adorable gem, and I had a lot of fun watching her interactions with other characters and how she managed through her own personal journey.

The game is fairly easy overall, but there are some late game difficulty spikes that really require you to properly learn the alchemy system to make progress. Don't be afraid to look up some advice on how mechanics work on that if you need to.

There is also a time limit mechanic, but I personaly did not find it a problem at all. I was able to get praticaly every side story and ending requirment done by the end of a single run, with time to spare, and that's with me being late to make certain items that would have reduced my travel time even more. Don't let the time limit stress you out too much.

Dude, Stop, developed and published by Team HalfBeard, is a mischievous and self-aware puzzle game that flips the concept of player obedience on its head. Instead of guiding you toward order and logic, it encourages chaos, disobedience, and playful defiance. The premise is deceptively simple: you are presented with a series of small puzzles and tasks that seem straightforward—stack boxes, arrange items correctly, or follow common-sense directions. But the true objective isn’t to play by the rules; it’s to break them. Each time you refuse to cooperate or find a creative way to mess things up, the game rewards you not with progress in the conventional sense, but with laughter, sarcastic commentary, and the exasperation of an unseen narrator who desperately wants you to behave. This concept alone turns a set of otherwise mundane microgames into a hilarious tug-of-war between player and developer, one that becomes more absurd the longer you play.

The game’s brilliance lies in how it manipulates expectations. Every scenario feels familiar at first, echoing the design of traditional puzzle games or point-and-click challenges. Yet, each one hides an opportunity to do something wrong in a way that feels right. You might be asked to sort books in a specific order but find that tossing them on the floor instead provokes the best reaction. The narrator—an unseen but constantly present voice—serves as both guide and antagonist. He praises you when you behave, scolds you when you misbehave, and slowly unravels as you continue to ignore his demands. His growing frustration and desperation to regain control give the experience its humor and pacing. Every puzzle becomes less about what you’re doing on screen and more about the emotional sparring match between you and the narrator. The writing is sharp and comedic, packed with fourth-wall breaks and meta-commentary on game design, player freedom, and the illusion of control.

The structure of Dude, Stop is divided into several chapters, each composed of multiple micro-puzzles that can be completed in different ways. The game tracks your actions and rewards both “good” and “bad” behavior, but it’s the latter that truly shines. Breaking the rules unlocks secret endings, new jokes, and alternative paths that make each playthrough unpredictable. What’s especially clever is how the game keeps a record of your moral alignment, poking fun at you whether you’re the obedient type or the chaotic one. Despite its simplicity, the design is tight—each puzzle lasts only a few seconds, but the way they build on one another gives the experience momentum. Like WarioWare for anarchists, it thrives on speed and absurdity, ensuring that even failures feel rewarding because they generate genuine laughter.

Visually, Dude, Stop embraces minimalism. Its art style is clean and colorful, using sharp contrasts and simple geometry to keep your attention on the interactions rather than spectacle. There’s a playful charm in its simplicity—the mundane tasks it presents, like stacking papers or plugging in USB drives, feel almost therapeutic until the narrator starts losing his mind over your deliberate sabotage. The sound design complements this perfectly, with crisp effects and an expressive narrator performance that steals the show. His tone swings wildly from polite encouragement to sarcastic fury, and the delivery carries a surprising amount of personality. It’s his voice that gives life to the otherwise simple visuals and mechanics, transforming what could have been a modest puzzle compilation into a fully realized comedy experience.

In terms of pacing, Dude, Stop never overstays its welcome. The campaign is relatively short, lasting only a couple of hours for most players, but every minute is packed with creative surprises. It’s a game built on novelty and humor rather than long-term depth, and it knows exactly when to end before the joke wears thin. Some players might find this brevity disappointing, especially if they’re looking for something with more mechanical complexity or replay value beyond hunting for every hidden outcome. Yet, its conciseness is part of its charm. The writing remains sharp throughout, and the short runtime ensures that the humor never grows stale. The balance between playful challenge and comedic reward keeps the experience fresh from start to finish.

Dude, Stop succeeds because it feels like a conversation between player and developer—a game about games, about how people interact with systems, and about what happens when you give players freedom and then scold them for using it. It’s a satire of puzzle design, but also a love letter to it, celebrating the joy of discovery in both following and breaking the rules. Its humor is clever without being mean-spirited, its design is deceptively thoughtful beneath the chaos, and its execution proves that even the simplest mechanics can be unforgettable when paired with personality and wit. It’s not a long or complex experience, but it is a memorable one—an interactive comedy that invites you to rebel, to experiment, and, above all, to have fun doing everything wrong.

Rating: 8/10

Newcomers can start with this one, it is a great entry point!

The Room 4 incorporates the best from all previous parts and greatly improves on any shortcomings.
While Room 1 played out in a single room dealing with a single multi-layered puzzle artifact, Room 2 gave huge rooms containing multiple puzzles that could either be solved on their own or provide/require items from other puzzles in that same room. Room 3 gave a huge mansion that overwhelmed the player with multiple large rooms like in the 2nd game, but instead gave them to us all at once. The puzzles now were connected between all rooms and required a lot of backtracking and frustrating travel animations.
Room 4 instead plays out in a single room, dealing with one artifact in the center, the dollhouse. (Just like in Room 1).
It alone is a huge puzzle you can rotate and solve from various angles. Once you unlock individual rooms, you can easily enter/exit them which removes the annoying traveling introduced in Room 3.

Regarding the puzzles, they are as usually ingenious but not impossible.
The graphics and visuals are amazing. No drowning in shadows like Room 2 did.


In my opinion, this is the best game of the series.

The Room 4: Old Sins marks another remarkable evolution in Fireproof Games’ series, expanding both scale and ambition while retaining the intimate puzzle experience that made the franchise legendary. From the very first step into the mysteriously abandoned mansion, the game immerses you in a world brimming with intricate mechanisms, hidden compartments and subtle narrative clues that demand attention and curiosity.

Mechanically, Old Sins is flawless. The tactile satisfaction of interacting with each device remains at the heart of the experience. The visual and audio design elevate the game beyond mere puzzles. Every room, every object and every shadow is carefully rendered, creating atmosphere and subtle guidance without overt hand holding. The mansion feels alive, with hidden passages and secret mechanisms encouraging exploration, while the audio (ambient creaks, distant footsteps and nuanced environmental cues) enhances tension and focus.

The puzzles themselves are a masterclass in balance. They range from elegantly subtle to devilishly complex, requiring keen observation, critical thinking and patience. The narrative unfolds gradually through letters, journals and devices, weaving a mysterious and engaging story without ever overshadowing the core puzzle gameplay.

The Room 4: Old Sins is not just a continuation, it is a culmination of everything the series has perfected: tactile engagement, atmospheric design and intelligent, rewarding puzzles. It is a game that invites careful attention and repeated exploration, offering both challenge and satisfaction at every turn. 

For fans of the series and newcomers alike, Old Sins is an essential, meticulously crafted puzzle experience that reaffirms Fireproof Games’ artistry in the genre.

补票童年。想起小学时，假期父母上班，我便被“寄存”在奶奶家。写完作业后，就窝在那台卡顿的老式台式机前瞎捣鼓。
直到有一天，我遇见了《粘粘世界》（当然是盗版）。在那个年代，这样独特的游戏远比4399上的小游戏更让我着迷。于是，一个人，一个下午，一场又一场歪歪扭扭的搭建。许多关卡当时怎么也过不去，绞尽脑汁，办法用尽，最后只能悻悻跳关。那时读不懂游戏背后的深意，但那古怪又忧伤的画风，却深深烙在了记忆里。
十几年后，在商店里与它重逢。我买了票，重新走进那个熟悉又陌生的世界。如今闯关已变得轻车熟路，当年不解的隐喻，如今也一一了然。只是，那个在屏幕前无忧无虑、为一个难题耗上一整个下午的孩子，却再也回不来了。
好的游戏像一本耐读的书，在不同年纪翻阅，会读出不同的滋味。谢谢你，《粘粘世界》，曾那样温柔地填满了我的一段童年。

This might just be the 10 years since launch, or my actual experience with computers, but the gameplay loop feels a bit off (pun not intended) for me. If you are into looking at hacker-looking interfaces and typing the same half a dozen commands over and over (tab complete and up key for history available), you will enjoy it. If you want anything that is anymore puzzling than following clear instructions, look elsewhere.

Basically: 1- open an email, 2- click email attachments for a target IP and maybe add a mission summary note to the screen, 3- click a button to connect to said IP and click another button to Probe the system, 4- run the same 2-5 commands on the same list of ports, 5- browse the filesystem to either find or place a file at mostly the same folders, 6- erase all logs and disconnect, 7- repeat. That's it. The game has a simplified terminal emulator missing a few basic features but fine, you can mostly use it to get things done instead of the GUI except when emailing (mostly). There are no puzzles, the exploits are literal executables you run and wait, the only variability is whether the target machine has proxies or a firewall then you gotta login into a bunch of places you already hacked first and run a shell overload (run and wait) then run a firewall analyzer to unscramble a keyword (run and read). Sometimes you gotta disconnect before a tracing timer runs out, which is never an issue until a single mission has like a 3 seconds timer but same difference. If you do *somehow* get traced, you might need to do the one different thing and change your IP address by... following steps 1 through 6! Or just reboot. Yeah, that's it: steps 1-7, sprinkle disconnects according to timer and if something fails just reboot and resume as usual is the whole game. There are two routes if you accept an optional mission but rest assured, same gameplay eveywhere.

It's a great game. It's Mario Party on PC with some magic dust.

A few downsides:

Some of the minigames are huge misses (e.g. Arty Smarty which is just an art history quiz).

Player 1 is at a disadvantage in many of the games, where each person takes a turn in sequence. Every other player can watch and learn from every run before them. They should really randomise the order, or force the leading player to go first.

There are no post-game awards. An award ceremony seems pointless when everyone knows the result, sometimes a few turns before the end.

I mean, what can I say? It's modern Mario party but better in many ways. 

Mario party has changed over the years and I don't dislike the latest version, but there are many QOL improvements in this game that make me want to play this far more than that. 

Pros:
*The mini games are all very well crafted, they're engaging and you never feel like there is luck or chance screwing you over. 
*There is just enough "mess with your friends" abilities on the board without it being too disruptive.
*Visually the game is extremely engaging. The animations, colors, themes etc are all clearly made with love and attention
*Character customization is insane, you can have so much fun creating great characters to play as
*The boards allow for a lot of changes through "Construction zones" meaning every time you play, it will feel different enough
*Cross platform works perfectly, and even on my PC with people playing on both PS5 and xbox controllers, the game correctly showed the relevant buttons for each person which was really great and I've never seen before.
*The gameshow hosts work so well, I thought it would be kinda cringey but it didn't get old or annoying at all and I'm sure for younger people it will be very funny for much longer.
*It's fun

Cons:
*A friend described the game as "Subway surfers Mario Party" meaning, there's a lot going on. A lot of the game feels very manic so I wouldn't recommend playing this with really young kids (My 5 year old loves how it looks, but struggles to keep up)
*There are only a handful of boards. This is true of the latest mario party as well and may not be a big deal to most, but hopefully there is room for more in the future.
*The higher amount of Studs and Golden bricks (Coins and stars equivalents) you get means they feel a little less special, but overall not a huge deal.
*At no point did any of us feel like we were screwed over by chance or things out of our control (with some exceptions, but those are board specific and clearly communicated)

Mixed feedback from my friends:
*No online matchmaking. I don't personally care about this as I will only ever play with people I know, but I know this matters to some.
*No bonus bricks (stars). Again, not something that bothered me, but is a common feedback and the developers have said they are looking into it with their own "Flavor"


Overall, if you like mario party, and even if you don't care about Lego as a whole or know what Ninjago is, this is an easy buy.

One of few EA title that I'm willing to commit some cash. For reference, this is a perspective from player who clocked thousands of hours in Arma 3 and few hundreds in Zero Sievert. So there will be bias/ preference towards certain model of PvE and gunfight. Additionally, most of the defects mentioned here was either already addressed or mentioned in passing by devs.

- Gunplay "felt" good. Both recoil and sound felt satisfying. Dev is smart enough not to follow Hollywood trope of "silencer" and instead made suppressed shot sounds natural. Unfortunately, all that got nullified due to lack of realistic ballistic. It will be immediately apparent once you attach laser to a 9mm pistol and one-shot every light in Military Base from nearby hill simply by playing cat.

- Gun customization is fun. But some customization either didn't really affect main stats or currently not shown properly. E.g I felt there's no penalty or change in ballistic properties when going all-in in CQB and cut my barrel length by half (apart from recoil). The only exception is SCAR-H, which didn't allow barrel replacement at all.

- Movement design and map traversal felt unfocused. There's clear bias towards fast-paced FPS with verticality of movements and map design itself. But there's barely any need for it since its both PvE and have no mission timer. For now, I'll wait and see until additional movement types is implemented. IMO it would be beneficial if there's a nudge towards slower-paced gameplay, with alternative actions to allow our PMC to go firm and dig in.

- Graphic is pretty, but that's about it. Much has been said about UE's cookie-cutter graphical feel, and past experience with UE-based game (e.g State of Decay) already biased my expectation. With a 3060, I can run all epic + lumen, but that doesn't stop lamps from popping, rather than fading, beyond certain distance. Having 4x or 6x scope barely matter since distant enemy is barely recognizable due to pixelation and jaggy movement. I do hope dev able to optimize it further before EA phase ends.

- AI behavior is hit-and-miss. Partly due to how it currently implemented; partly due to how it interact with the game world (i.e how they show and/ or react to aural and visual cues). Compounding the issue is limited vocab. You'll hear them scream about "enemy at the ridge" deep inside underground bunker. or "pretend" to find a dead body when their peers was shot in front of them.

- Some negative reviews mentioned "misdirected sound" issue. I found that toning down reverb setting from default 100 to ~20-25 fixed some of the issue.

With all that said. This is still one of the best, if not the only, "realistic" PvE extraction shooter in the market right now. I can play the game, pause for half a day to play IRL with my kids, and continue playing later at night. Pretty nice.

自分が一番好きな狩猟アクションゲーム。
PS4版でトロフィーコンプ済ですが、またやりたくなったので一からやっていきます。
自分よりも大きいモンスターというかこのゲームでは鬼を討伐していきますが、
武器毎のアクションやスタイルに合わせたスキル（タマフリ）、ゲージを貯めて使う必殺技の様な強攻撃、
ダッシュでの移動の高速化、鬼への飛び掛かりでの快適な戦闘機動が面白いゲームです。
使える武器は「太刀 / 双刀 / 槍 / 手甲 / 鎖鎌 / 弓 / 金砕棒 / 薙刀 / 銃 / 盾剣 / 仕込鞭」の11種類。
そこにタマフリというそれぞれ特徴のある能力セットが「繰 / 攻 / 防 / 迅 / 癒 / 魂 / 隠 / 空 / 賭 / 献 / 壊」の11種。
タマフリは武器と防具、それに今作から登場しためっちゃ便利な鬼ノ手という道具合わせて３か所付けられるので、
武器11種×タマフリが武器11×防具11×鬼の手11種の組み合わせが出来、ビルドの幅がめっちゃ広いです。
それにタマフリにつかう英霊ごとにミタマスキルが９つあり、そこから各ミタマ３つのスキルを選んで発動できます。
その組み合わせによってはめちゃくちゃ強くなります。
例えば瀕死時に攻撃力が上がるスキル持ったミタマで揃え、防具タマフリ（ニギタマフリ）で一定時間戦闘不能無効とかにする、さらに瀕死になった直後に武器タマフリで攻撃力や会心率上昇などを発動すれば超高DPSが出せたり、
連撃武器で攻撃速度を上げるスキルを揃えれば、気持ちいいくらいの怒涛の連撃になったりします。
他にも、というかこれが最強感ありますが属性武器を使って属性攻撃時に体力気力を回復するスキルを揃えるとか。（これでマルチ含む最高難易度までソロでクリアできます。）高速攻撃で手数を増やし各種ゲージを早く貯めてスキルで強化した強攻撃を叩き込むか等々色々出来ます。
強化としては武器や防具の製造や強化はもちろん、ミタマも関係のある人物で揃える組み合わせ次第で専用スキルが追加で発動したり、料理で発動するスキルや、拠点で禊を行うことで発動するスキルもあります。
アクションが苦手な人でも自分の使いやすい武器やスタイルで揃えて、各スキルを発動すれば簡単になると思います。
強化が色々出来るし、鬼もそこまで複雑な行動はしないので初心者でも楽しく遊べる狩猟アクションゲームだと思います。
あと、図鑑が充実していてモンスターの特徴や弱点、討伐数、落とした素材の種類などが分かるし、発動したスキル一覧が見れたりするので埋めていく楽しさもあります。各ミタマのスキルも条件を満たしながら使用すれば成長するし、やり込み要素としても十分なものがあります。
ストーリーも自分は結構好きなのでおすすめのゲームです。

Игру рекомендую, но авансом. Пока есть вопросики.

Итак - плюсы:
1. Геймплей - помесь Homewolrd со строилкой станций\кораблей. Вертикальные манёвры, сенсоры, туманности, огонь всем бортом - вот это вот всё.
2. Графика - приятна глазу, хороший визуальный дизайн кораблей, эффекты взрывов, лозеры пиу-пиу, пушки бадыщь, рокеты ба-бах, всё как положено.
3. Музыка - приятный спейс эмбиэнт, в бой переключается на более бравурные марши, опять таки приятные звуки стрельбы орудий разного плана. "Combat chatter" (фоновые переговоры в бою и нет) присутствует, но как-то громковаты, как и фоновый шум "сенсорной карты" - аж уши режет. Советую разрабам пристальнее присмотреться к Deserts of Kharak, там это было шикарно исполнено.

Внезапно, по плюсам всё. Минусы:
1. Геймплей. Реиграбельность. Её нет. По сути своей весь контент игры в данный момент можно пройти за одну катку. Этот "скирмиш", по сути не будет иметь никакой разницы - на какой карте или в какой режим не играй. Противник не будет стоить корабли-базы, не будет пытаться во фланговые маневры - он просто будет посылать на вас по прямой волну за волной все более злые корабли, пока вы до него не доберётесь сами. Финита ля комедия. Можно позалипать в песочнице-стоилке - но тоже такое, если не на ком опробовать очередной шушпанцер то и фана кратно меньше.
2. Контент и баланс. Кораблей откровенно мало. Зачем нужны истребители и корветы откровенно не понял - варшипы на голову лучше в плане цена\эффективность, а стоить их можно практически со старта. Никаких ранних рашей бомберами компуктер не делает. оглядываемся на homeworld - ни кораблей-ремонтников, миноукладчиков, стелс-торпедастов, захватчиков-абордажников, корветов ПВО! (а ракеты-торпеды здесь злые). У пушек есть условная эффективность урона по легкой\средней\тяжелой броне - но сухих цифр ДПСа, угловой скорости, дальности нет. Сколько дамажит тяжелая кинетическая батарея, а сколько тяжелая ионная? Ну, одна делает пышь-пышь, другая бзюююююм! С абсолютно одинаковой по цифрам эффективностью и дальностью...

Крч, игры выглядит как что-то хорошее, но контента тут - стопы замочить. Вроде и океан прямо перед тобой, иди да плавай, но нет, в невидимую стену упираешься.

[b]This review applies to both games in L4D series[/b]
[h1]Left 4 Dead is the only co-op game that perfectly combines story, gameplay, teamwork, emotional voice acting, the vocalizer, workshop mods, and pure fun — all in one package. I would even dare to call it the ultimate co-op game. [/h1]

[b]Games that come close to L4D’s greatness, in my opinion, are Earth Defense Force 4, SWAT4 and Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker.[/b]
But what sets L4D apart from every other game is its ability to make every session feel unique and fresh. Thanks to the AI Director, which constantly adjusts the gameplay as you progress, the game feels dynamic in a way no other co-op title can replicate — not even EDF 4 or Peace Walker.

And with the right custom maps, the fun can become limitless.

L4D features fast, simple gameplay that’s still tactical in many aspects. You can’t just run around carelessly, especially on Advanced difficulty or higher; it’s a team-based game — [b]but the good kind, where one or two skilled players can still carry the team. Unlike most modern team-based games, L4D never feels punishing or artificial.[/b]

Sometimes, the Director might spawn enemies unfairly, but those moments are rare — and because the core gameplay is so solid, you can forgive and forget. Even on Expert, the game feels fair if you understand its rhythm: how enemies behave, how positioning matters, and how to flow with the Director’s pacing.

L4D has impressive depth. You can learn tricks, like how to kill Witches in one shot, or find creative ways to deal with each type of infected. Once you think you’ve mastered everything, you realize there are still hidden layers to uncover.

The story is simple yet elegant — told through environmental storytelling, the classic “show, don’t tell” approach.

But what truly elevates L4D is its [b]voice acting[/b]. The actors bring the characters to life with such energy and emotion that it’s impossible not to get immersed. Their dialogue reminds me of EDF 4’s charm — full of personality and spirit. With the right mods, you can even use hilarious custom voice lines that create spontaneous, funny conversations in-game. No other title offers such an experience, especially with how many unique lines each character has. Francis’s grumpiness and Ellis’s absurd stories never get old — just like the gameplay itself.

I’m amazed not only by how perfect L4D is but also by how no one — and I mean no one — has ever recreated its level of quality. Not necessarily its gameplay or genre, but its essence.

Game quality began to decline after the early 2010s, with only a few exceptions. It’s depressing how co-op games continue to be neglected. Many developers try to capture what made L4D great, but they miss its fundamentals — the deep design philosophy that can’t be easily explained in a review. You have to play many games, good and bad, to understand what makes L4D legendary.

Sadly, mediocrity defines most games, and especially co-op games even today.

If your gaming experience is limited, you might not fully grasp how extraordinary L4D truly is. But this is a game everyone should keep installed — ready to play at any time.

I long for games with dynamic gameplay, alive characters, and soulful design — [h2]but sadly, it feels like we’ll never see something like L4D again[/h2]

Age of Wonders: Planetfall is a turn-based strategy game that brings the classic Age of Wonders formula into a sci-fi setting, combining empire management, tactical battles, and faction-driven storytelling. Its shift from fantasy to science fiction allows for varied unit designs, technological themes, and a broader strategic palette while maintaining the series’ core strengths.

Factions are the game’s standout feature. Each group offers distinct aesthetics, unit types, and strategic mechanics—from bio-engineered amazons to militarized space dwarves and cybernetic collectives. Their differences shape both diplomacy and combat, encouraging experimentation and replayability. The game reinforces this diversity through tech trees and mod systems that allow units to be customized extensively.

Combat takes place on tactical maps where positioning, cover, abilities, and unit synergies determine success. Battles flow quickly but offer meaningful choices, balancing accessibility with depth. The emphasis on flanking, status effects, and ability combos creates a dynamic battlefield that rewards planning without becoming overly complex.

Strategic gameplay involves colony development, resource management, exploration, and diplomacy. Maps are filled with neutral factions, landmarks, and hazards that guide expansion and create early friction. The economic model is clear and structured, though players who prefer lighter management may find the number of resources and systems initially dense.

Narrative campaigns extend the setting by focusing on multiple factions and perspectives across a fragmented galactic landscape. Story arcs introduce faction philosophies and conflicts while offering varied mission structures. Though the narrative delivery is functional rather than cinematic, it provides enough context to support long-term motivation.

Presentation is strong, with detailed unit models, colorful biomes, and clean interface design. Music and sound effects reinforce the sci-fi tone, giving battles and exploration a sense of scale. The visual identity is coherent across factions and environments, helping the world feel distinct.

Overall, Age of Wonders: Planetfall delivers a robust blend of tactical combat and strategic management strengthened by deep faction variety and strong customization. It is suited for players who enjoy layered turn-based systems, flexible playstyles, and long-form strategy rather than streamlined or minimalist design.

TLDR: While I do recommend the game, I do so simply because it's a solid game, not because I enjoyed the ride. The game mostly consists of a giant map with hundreds of points of interest that are mobs, collectibles and side quests. This should be a good thing, but it doesn't feel like one after a short while, it gets redundant and boring as it doesn't manage to keep the player hooked, or at the very least this player.

Story: Shunned at birth, meet outcast Aloy, brought up by another outcast named Rost. Set out on a journey that will reveal what happened to the world to end up having dinobots everywhere and why everyone is acting like neanderthals. The plot is pretty decent, at least the one regarding the main reasoning of why there's... dinobots (I mean I can't help it, those are freakin' dinobots, I don't care what they're called). However it tends to be a bit hard to care for it as the game feels more like a map dotted with repetitive tasks rather than a map you will enjoy travelling to and from with different story bits. Don't get me wrong, it's a big nice map, it's just... oddly unsatisfying. I think the 2 biggest moments for me were in the DLC, which is completely optional, and holograms of past events. That should not be a thing.

Gameplay: Definitely one of the stronger aspect of the game, though some enemies can be a handful.
You will have a decent selection of weapons to choose from, and up to 4 to equip at a time, each with modifications slots (stats, mostly) with more powerful variants.
Your arsenal will mostly be old fashioned weapons ranging from bows, traps and slings. It sounds a lot worse than it really is as many types of ammo can be crafted, ranging from elements to effects like tearing; which deals no damage but removes armor, which who would've guessed it, robots wear.
Each mobs have weaknesses that are important to consider, you can brute force things but it's a lot more efficient, and funner tbh, to play the game as intended. Removing a giant gun from a giant T-Rex looking robot and firing it back at it while making it catch on fire is much better than flinging puny arrows at it for 20 minutes straight because it's bouncing off armor that you're too stubborn to remove.
There is a decent amount of stealth in the game, none of which is necessary but it works well and is of a big advantage to the player.
Each removed components from enemies and kills each award XP (with bonuses if they're on fire, or killed from stealth, for instance), allowing you to level up, up to lv 60.
Each lv gives a skill point, as do some missions, allowing you to put much needed skills in your skill tree. The skills range from being able to execute bigger enemies to slowing down time while aiming. They are useful, but not necessarily game changing. 
You can craft ammo pouches, provided you've gathered all the required mats. Sadly, many mats are a little random (killing a mob does not guarantee the right mat as rarer mats are, uh, rarer).
You can craft every type of ammo yourself, and you easily do it within your weapon selection wheel, it's easy and fast.
You can craft potions and traps too, but they weren't as useful as I thought they were gonna be.
Dialogue choices can sometimes be made, though they will often do very little to impact the story. Unless it's obvious... Like, usually, killing someone instead of sparing do lessen your chances of meeting them later down the road, just saying.
Oh, and get the gold fast travel pack from a vendor as soon as you can, unless you want to always hope you have enough fast ravel packs.

Graphics: Surprisingly good, even by today's standards. While the base game has some off putting facial animation at times, the environments are good, the characters look good, and the chosen art style just works. The DLC's animations are plain better.

Audio: While I found the tracks lacking, the general audio of the game was fine. Aloy can be a bit too chatty at times, but it was probably just because I couldn't help but loot every single plant I saw. Cuz they're ''hardy little plants'', they'll be ''useful later''. ''Wind's howling'', no wait... That's a different game.

It's also worth mentioning that the game crashed quite a few times for no real apparent reason and there hasn't been a fix for this. I would also like to state that the Frozen Wilds DLC is a huge leap in difficulty, but totally worth it.

A história é contada de forma simples, mas com um charme especial — cada cliente que entra no café traz consigo emoções, dúvidas e sonhos, o que faz o jogador refletir sobre as relações humanas e o poder da escuta.

Para mim, Coffee Talk tem sido uma experiência extremamente relaxante e distrativa. Sua atmosfera calma, unida ao enredo envolvente, cria um espaço onde é possível desacelerar e apenas aproveitar o momento, como se cada diálogo fosse um gole quente de café em uma noite fria

Phantom Brave wasn't perfect and neither is The Lost Hero. There is both good and bad; there are things the sequel does better and other things that the original did better. It doesn't detract from it being a great game. 

The Juice Bar and the different Ship Types were my favorite new additions in The Lost Hero. The ability to go solo as Marona and divy up XP makes leveling and organizing units SO much easier than before. If you're like me you'll only ever use the EXP and BOR Ship to keep raking in those gains. It is a massive improvement that I absolutely adore. Creating a new unit and getting it into fighting shape is the easiest it has EVER been! Oh and Confriend as a new mechanic is really cool. Having infinite SP to use Giga Fire over and over never gets old. I'll admit there are stages I have only cleared because of being able to Confriend and get a huge power boost.

The biggest detractor for me is the story - though this is easily sped through as if they understand not everyone is here for the story. There are moments I see that get me to stop and pay attention, but soon enough I'm skipping scenes again. I am incredibly grateful to have the option to skip and not button mash through endless text - completely nullifying the problem for me. Oh and the English dub sounds off. I started with English, but Ash and Marona sounded weird to me. It's the same actress for Marona, but she doesn't sound right. Thankfully, the Japanese dub option allows me to avoid that prejudice of what I remember Marona sounding like. Once again, the problem I had is effectively nullified.

Ultimately, this is a good game regardless of whether its better than the original or not. I wish more people would play and enjoy it for what it is. I'm just thrilled that a beloved classic of mine like Phantom Brave got a sequel! I hope we'll see a third before I'm the Old Man in the game.

В XXI веке, когда доступ к информации неограничен, продолжать тиражировать эту замшелую ошибку переводчиков XIX века - просто дурной тон. 

Дворфы (Dwarves) или цверги (Zwerge) - это существа из древнего германо-скандинавского фольклора. Они - коренной мифологический народ, такой же, как чудь или турианцы. Это коренастые, бородатые обитатели гор и подземелий, непревзойдённые кузнецы и ювелиры. Именно этот образ могучих подземных мастеров взял за основу филолог-германист Дж. Р. Р. Толкин для создания своих дворфов.

Гномы (Gnomes), в свою очередь, - это "новодел" эпохи Возрождения. Их образ был введён в XVI веке алхимиком Парацельсом, который описал их как сверхъестественных, невидимых элементалей земли - по сути, переизобрёл полтергейста или домового. Позже этот образ развивался в литературе, постепенно материализуясь в маленьких человечков, которых стали ассоциировать с народцем фей (fairies). Из этой концепции и родились современные садовые гномики - духи-хранители участка.

Путаница началась с того, что ранние издатели, стремясь адаптировать немецкие сказки для русского читателя, пошли по пути наименьшего сопротивления. Вместо того чтобы познакомить аудиторию с концепцией цвергов, они совершили поступок, равносильный переименованию Facebook в "Одноклассники" или Twitter во "ВКонтакте" - просто заменили незнакомое слово на уже известное в литературных кругах - "гном". Этот чисто коммерческий ход, рассчитанный на лучшие продажи, создал опасный прецедент. Последующие поколения переводчиков, включая тех, кто работал над "Властелином Колец", уже не стали разбираться в первоисточниках и просто пошли по проторенной дорожке, закрепив ошибку и превратив её в псевдо-"традицию".

Дело дошло до откровенных извращений, когда любители этой ошибочной традиции, чтобы выкрутиться и продолжить называть дворфов гномами, стали называть gnomes "гнумами" или даже "полуросликами", полностью игнорируя существование halflings.

В русском языке слова гном, дворф и цверг - это заимствования, кальки, так как в нашей мифологии подобных народов не существовало. Поэтому нет никакого оправдания тому, чтобы подменять одно заимствование другим, искажая первоисточник и демонстрируя полное непонимание культурного и мифологического контекста. Это пережиток прошлого, от которого давно пора отказаться.

Empty Shell, developed by CC ARTS and published by Hyperstrange, is a top-down roguelite horror shooter that manages to blend the oppressive tension of classic survival horror with the unpredictability of procedural generation. Set within a decaying research facility on a remote Japanese island, the game puts players in the role of nameless “volunteers” sent on a mysterious recovery operation. The facility, of course, hides something far more sinister than anyone anticipates. Each descent into its labyrinthine corridors becomes a descent into madness and death, as you scavenge for weapons, face grotesque enemies, and try to survive long enough to uncover fragments of the truth. The premise immediately evokes the aesthetics of old-school horror—dark corridors illuminated by failing lights, grainy textures, and unsettling silence broken only by mechanical hums or distant screams. It is a world designed to keep you tense, uncertain, and constantly aware of how fragile you are.

The game’s structure thrives on repetition and dread. Each time you die, a new volunteer is sent into the facility, generating a new layout, enemy placement, and loot distribution. This procedural generation ensures that no two runs feel exactly the same, reinforcing the sense of unpredictability and danger that defines the experience. Death is not simply a failure but a part of the game’s rhythm, a recurring motif that reminds you that every trip into the abyss is fleeting. This roguelite loop is complemented by the game’s deliberate pacing—resources are scarce, ammunition must be conserved, and light is as precious as health. Even in its top-down perspective, Empty Shell successfully conveys claustrophobia; hallways feel suffocating, and every door you open carries the risk of something waiting on the other side. The minimalism of the interface helps sustain immersion, removing clutter so that every sound and flicker of movement commands your attention.

Combat in Empty Shell walks a careful balance between methodical survival and frantic improvisation. It uses a twin-stick control system, allowing players to move and aim independently while dealing with limited stamina and tight spaces. You can equip a variety of weapons—pistols, shotguns, rifles, and improvised melee tools—but each has drawbacks tied to recoil, ammunition scarcity, or slow reloads. The decision to engage an enemy or retreat becomes a constant mental calculation, especially when health kits are rare and every shot fired may attract more creatures. The design intentionally makes you feel vulnerable rather than empowered. Unlike many action-heavy roguelites, Empty Shell demands patience, awareness, and respect for its enemies. Every encounter feels dangerous, not because of flashy mechanics, but because the game enforces discipline—poor decisions lead to quick deaths, and each death resets your progress, forcing you to adapt and rethink your approach.

Visually, Empty Shell embraces a gritty, industrial aesthetic that suits its themes perfectly. The environments are rendered in muted tones, drenched in shadow, with the occasional burst of flickering fluorescent light to remind you of the world’s decay. The art direction captures a sense of hopelessness and mechanical coldness reminiscent of 1980s and 1990s Japanese horror cinema, where the mundane and the monstrous coexist. The sound design amplifies this atmosphere—footsteps echo unnervingly in the dark, mechanical whirs pulse in the distance, and distorted ambient noises create a sense of unseen presence even when nothing is around. The sparse use of music accentuates the silence, making every new area feel unpredictable. It’s a style of horror that doesn’t rely on jump scares but instead builds a psychological unease, the kind that grows heavier with every floor you descend. You begin to dread what’s behind the next door long before it opens.

The roguelite progression system ties this experience together by providing a sense of forward motion amidst the repetition. Salvage collected during runs can be spent on upgrades, new weapons, and improved stats, giving players a tangible sense of growth even when they die. The upgrades feel meaningful without undermining the game’s tension, allowing a slightly smoother start in subsequent runs without eliminating the underlying danger. This creates a satisfying rhythm between runs—a blend of short-term failure and long-term accomplishment that keeps you coming back. The story, delivered through scattered notes and cryptic logs, is intentionally fragmented, adding to the sense of mystery rather than spelling out the narrative outright. Each discovery deepens your understanding of what the facility once was and what it has become, but the unanswered questions linger, maintaining the game’s bleak and oppressive mood.

Still, Empty Shell is not without flaws. The same procedural generation that keeps each run fresh can also create uneven pacing, occasionally placing you in unwinnable situations with poor weapon drops or overwhelming enemy spawns. The control precision can feel slightly stiff in tight corners, and the twin-stick aiming, while functional, demands patience to master. Some players may find the minimalist narrative too detached or cryptic, preferring more concrete storytelling. Yet these imperfections do little to detract from the overall experience, as they align with the game’s philosophy of tension and vulnerability. Empty Shell is not about fairness or comfort—it’s about surviving in spite of those missing comforts, about enduring the unpredictable cruelty of a place that feels alive and hostile.

Ultimately, Empty Shell stands as a distinctive entry in the modern indie horror landscape. It borrows inspiration from survival classics while incorporating roguelite unpredictability and minimalist design sensibilities. The result is an experience that feels both familiar and refreshingly different—a game that respects the player’s intelligence and patience, prioritizing atmosphere and dread over spectacle. It’s a brutal, haunting, and strangely addictive descent into darkness, where each death feels like a lesson and each new run like another chance to defy the inevitable. For players who appreciate deliberate pacing, tension-driven design, and horror that thrives on atmosphere rather than cheap thrills, Empty Shell offers a deeply satisfying, nerve-wracking journey into the heart of human fragility and fear.

I haven't finished the game yet, but I'm already completely satisfied with what I've enjoyed thus far.

It has more inventiveness and interest in its pinky toe than the sum total of the hundreds of cosmetic solitaire re-skins that are sold ad nauseam for twice its price (and looks and sounds just as good). But, it's unlikely to be nearly as financially successful as those, precisely because it offers not the comforting familiarity of a staid pastime, but a novel, non-trivial, genre-bending challenge.

On the other hand, the die-hard puzzlers out there who don't particularly enjoy the semi-mindless mystique of shuffling cards about the tableau may find the basic game play here tiresome before and after the singular "aha" moments, and feel short-changed at the fact that there are fundamentally only seven "puzzles" to solve (although more variations are coming with an update). After the high of "solving" for the hidden rule, these people will likely see no point in returning to play a handful of what still amount to enjoyable solitaire variants, and will dismiss the notion that these could be enjoyed for their own sake.

If you can avoid these extremes of attitude and thereby thoroughly enjoy this unique and excellent game, I'll offer you the following bit of advice for beginners:

Beyond avoiding spoilers at all costs, try to play each deal of a new ritual to completion, if possible. It may not be obvious initially, but getting all four coins is not the only win condition; there are three "endings" for each ritual: winning with 0 coins, some coins, or all coins. If you are a completionist, this means that spamming the redeal button every time you lose a coin is actually a mistake, as it will make it more likely you'll just have to return to rituals you've already solved and "fail" them a couple of times to get the alternate endings you skipped (or even prevent you from deducing the rule). Rather, these partial wins would ideally be completed in ascending order as part of the solving process. So, always play each deal to the end, if you are still eligible for an ending you haven't got.

Receiver 2 is an in-depth gun simulator with a seemingly basic gameplay loop that surprises with hidden depth and secrets throughout and most surprisingly, some genuine, positive messages that show its heart is in the right place.

After an apocalyptic, reality-shattering event, you (and your gun) are left in an uninhabited, liminal reality full of kill-drones to clean up any survivors - meaning you. Funny that this should happen, since the conspiracy cult that you're a member of has been predicting this very thing, what are the odds! So you are primed for this scenario, but not fully prepared. Through listening to collectible cassette tapes, you'll hopefully "receive" the full teachings that will ultimately allow you to ascend past this fake, dreamlike reality of endlessly looping rooms.

And the game really tries to create the best version of this premise - and succeeds! The tapes you listen to are much more than a means of progression but a in-world guide on how to mentally overcome the challenges you're up against. And they're genuinely good lessons relating to awareness, mindfulness, breathing and meditation that encourage you to lock in and reach a sort of flow state. Literally improving the player from the inside instead of dishing out upgrades. No wonder since your fellow "receivers" have been focusing on resisting media-induced threats to the psyche, rather than pure physical skills.

There is of course the gun simulation aspect that receiver 2 is so well known for. Every action must be manually performed with a different keybind which sounds more crazy than it actually plays. You don't need to be a gun lover to play this, the game kind of assumes you are not. Even if you know the correct steps to ready a gun for firing, the game steps it up by really emphasizing the importance of caution and pre-caution. 
DO seat your mag by giving it an extra tap to prevent feed issues.
DO check the chamber after racking the slide to ensure proper feeding.
DON'T hastily jam a primed and loaded gun into your pocket without at least engaging the safety.
DON'T step into a new room without being fully mentally present and aware of possible dangers.
NEVER point a gun at anything you don't want destroyed.
ALWAYS assume a gun is loaded unless you've personally confirmed it's not.

It's one thing to memorize these things in training, but when a shock drone comes barreling towards your face flashing red and taser crackling, will you remember to draw your loaded .50 cal hand cannon in a smooth, controlled manner or will you claw at your holster in a panic, resulting in self-inflicted foot removal? There's many ways to die and you die quickly. Every bullet kills unless you get a lucky grazing shot. Falling glass will kill you. Jumping from heights will very nearly kill you and at the very least have you recover for a few precious seconds that you might need to react to something wherever you just landed.

On the flipside, you can get away with a surprising amount of parcours and the developers might have anticipated you reaching some areas that might seem out-of-bounds. You can scrounge absolutely silly nooks and crannies for much needed supplies and the more you play, the more traversal opportunities you'll start to see. Turret on the left, drone on the right, no bullets? Maybe you can juuuust about shimmy past on a narrow ledge outside.

Content-wise, the game seems very anemic, but everything is implemented with almost the same depth and care as the famous guns, of which there are a good variety. The drones themselves are also made of different parts that get individually hit instead of depleting health points. You can take careful aim and make a single bullet count or just hope for the best. Note that a turret with a busted magazine can still have one last round in the chamber! No bullets? Try hacking! Out of options? Bait a turret to deplete it's ammo. The cassette tapes full of positive messages towards enlightenment? Some are cursed with suicidal ramblings instead. Best scramble to render your firearm completely and utterly safe, who knows where it'll end up pointing late into a night of shut-in home-drinking with a picture of the ex. While there are no perks and bonuses, there's little twists and details about almost every aspect, allowing for a great variety of creative problems and solutions emerging organically during gameplay.

Then there's also a training compound you can project in your mind, which is one of my absolutely favorite version of the "secret filled hub". It's a huge place that opens up gradually as you explore and find new areas and activities and secrets. The shooting challenges are genuinely tough and I've never played a video game gun range that felt so authentic to the experience of target shooting.

All in all, a game that offers much more than it seems at first but really demands your full attention and concentration. The only downside is that the setback from a loss can be genuinely disheartening, that is to say, I've ragequit many times, only to start the game right back up, this time without a podcast in the background.

This is a strangely relaxing game (unless you plan reaching the final level, in which case - good luck). The voice on the tapes is very soothing. And I actually learned more about guns from a few hours here, which is a nice bonus!

I'm so glad that I sent all the negative reviews about the game to hell, of which there were just a ton. And from serious studios, whose opinions I could listen to, and from typical haters who feel bad about everything, and from players with reviews like "I played for 30 minutes, the game is bad, I give one star." Half of the negative reviews are based on "Poor optimization" and the other half on "This is not Dead Space". Oh, well, you know how serious these arguments are to vilify the game. Okay, let's take a closer look at the aspects of the game.:
PLOT: The game takes place in the Black Tin prison, where it is not clear why the main character Jacob, an ordinary courier who carries goods from point A to point B. After a while, a catastrophe occurs in the prison, people turn into incomprehensible creatures who want only one thing - to kill people. During the game, we got answers to most of the questions that the game throws at us at the very beginning.: What kind of creatures are these? Why did they break out? Who is to blame? What should I do next? During the game, we collect the history of the prison bit by bit by searching for recordings of dictaphones of former correctional officers. If you don't do this, the picture may not seem complete, and closer to the finale, they dump the whole story on us and send us to a meeting with the final boss. In my opinion, the narrative lacked some balance, because most of the plot was given to us in the last hour of the game, and before that, the first 9 (I completed the game in 10 hours) the presentation was ragged. The plot is good, solid, unpredictable, thoughtful and slightly absurd.

 The graphics are amazing. The emotions of the main characters, the painted drops of sweat that roll down their faces, the world around them and attention to detail. And what a view of space opens up to us, beauty. As far as I know, the optimization has now been fixed with patches, perhaps you shouldn't mess up the game so much because it came out raw in terms of hardware operation.
COMBAT SYSTEM: At the disposal of the main character: a crowbar (after replacing it with a police baton), a pistol of 2 types, a shotgun of 2 types, a semi-automatic machine, a kinetic glove. Each type of weapon can be upgraded for local currency, improving its characteristics and adding new features to the 3D printer. At the same time, at the beginning of the game we only have a crowbar, we will discover everything else as we progress. Any duel, with any opponent, is like a dance: left, right, left, right. If you do it twice to the left, you'll get hit in the head. And if it's not so difficult in a duel with one opponent, then when there are already two of them, problems begin. On the one hand, everything is very simple, but opponents sometimes hit twice and then you have a window for a counter attack, and sometimes three, and sometimes one. It wasn't uncommon for me to die in a one-on-one duel. Nobody forbids using firearms, but there are very few cartridges, and you always save them for more difficult moments.
DIFFICULTY LEVEL: passed the "maximum protection level". And yes, it's real hardcore. The world around us is not friendly at all. Everything wants to kill you, there aren't enough ammo for weapons, there are even fewer first-aid kits, the cat cried for the local currency (for the full passage I pumped only the pistol to the maximum, the rest by a couple of points). You die with two or three blows, and given the low number of first-aid kits, you always have to act very slowly, slowly making your way through the corridors, turning around at every noise, and even in a 1-on-1 duel, you have to think of ways to retreat. There are 2 bosses in the game, which is very frustrating. In this case, the first boss repeats 4 times. The boss battles weren't difficult, partly because I knew when the enemy would appear and saved shotgun shells for him. It would be very difficult to kill him with a club. The most difficult moment in the game is when I reached one of the locations, with 2 rounds and 15% health, and there was just a moment where I was facing 6 mobs that become invisible. And every time I died, I started with a checkpoint where I have 15% health and 2 bullets. I closed the final boss with 7-8 kills, which is generally fast enough considering the difficulty level.
THE ATMOSPHERE AND THE GENRE ITSELF: Now, actually, about why I liked this game. Horror gripped me from the very first minutes. I was afraid to move around the location, danger could be waiting for me around every corner. The grinding of iron, some kind of munching, the sounds of a swarm of insects, roars, screams, light music, the play of shadows, rustles, some movements that you notice out of the corner of your eye, turn around - and there's nothing. Stunning graphics - all this creates an indescribable atmosphere of hopelessness, into which our hero was dragged. You worry about him and you're scared with Jacob. There is no place in the game where I can feel safe, the enemy can fall right on my head anywhere. Because of this, moving around the world was slow, unhurried, and very careful. I don't know if it would be so intense if I played at the easiest level, maybe not. Therefore, I recommend only the "maximum security level" to everyone.
BOTTOM LINE: The game is just great for its genre, a real horror with excellent graphics. And what are the finishing scenes? When you're literally being torn apart. I don't understand the criticism and constant comparison with dead space. I went through Dead Space, I liked the game, but I went through Calisto with no less pleasure, and as for me, the game is definitely not worse. It's a pity that there won't be a sequel, because the game is a real financial failure, I think partly because of a lot of negative reviews, and many players didn't want to draw their own conclusions, but simply followed the general opinion. It's a pity that such games won't get a sequel. I give the game a solid five and recommend it to everyone.

Imagine Bloodborne mixed with Symphony of the Night, then drenched in thick Lovecraftian horror that’s Source of Madness. It’s a roguelite with RPG elements, wrapped in beautiful pixel art and backed by a haunting soundtrack that absolutely nails the cosmic horror vibe. The monsters are genuinely unsettling, constantly shifting into new grotesque shapes that keep every run feeling strange and unpredictable. But for all the style and ambition, the game struggles with consistency. Character personalization is pretty limited, and the combat while flashy feels floaty and imprecise. Aiming is especially unreliable, which turns fights into chaotic flailing more often than deliberate skill. Procedural generation can also be hit or miss some runs feel varied and exciting, others repetitive or unbalanced. Performance hiccups and frame drops show up during busier moments, adding to the already wobbly combat feel. And while the progression system works, it doesn’t meaningfully change your playstyle, making long-term runs feel a bit samey. There’s a genuinely great idea here, and the atmosphere is spot on. With more polish and tighter mechanics, this could be something incredible. As it stands, it’s a unique, eerie experience but one that needs refinement before it reaches its full potential.

O que me atraiu em [b]Source of Madness[/b] foi a ambientação lovecraftiana. Acabei pegando gosto por "horror cósmico" depois que eu fiquei um velho cínico e meio fuleiro.

Source of Madness é um metroidvania de fantasia sombria com elementos de roguelite e soulslike, permeado por uma linda direção de arte. Essa combinação tem sido o arroz com feijão para a produção de bons indies. Contudo, fica nítido que a desenvolvedora Carry Castle poderia ter dedicado um pouco mais de atenção à gameplay.

Como todo soulslike que se preze, o enredo é confuso. A história se passa em um mundo conhecido como "Terra Argilosa", assolado por uma invasão de grotescas criaturas extradimensionais. Os personagens que controlamos são membros de uma seita dedicada a estudar e combater essas entidades e (quem sabe) erradicar as forças sinistras por trás da invasão. Essas informações, e uma ou outra coisa a mais, você só vai descobrir jogando até o terceiro ato, ao ler os resumos dos capítulos em um poste nos arredores do templo. No início eu fiquei bem perdido e desanimado com a forma como a narrativa foi apresentada. O que me manteve no jogo foi a satisfação de atirar raios e bolas de fogo nas crias do Belzebu.

A gameplay de Source of Madness poderia ser ótima, mas opta por ser apenas boa. Cada vez que o seu personagem vai de F, aquele cultista já era de vez, e você assume o controle de outro cultista, com a possibilidade de uma nova build. Okay, isso é bem legal e trabalha com a proposta narrativa (o mundo está em ruínas, meu amigo. Nada de ego e nada de se apegar ao personagem. Você não é ninguém. A Ordem está acima de tudo). O problema está no sistema de evolução das builds. Com exceção da habilidade de esquiva (que varia de acordo com a build), todas as demais habilidades vêm de anéis e colares.

Você começa a run com dois anéis fracos, um específico da sua build (que você pode desbloquear com pontos de sangue, adquiridos matando inimigos) e outro generalista. Os demais anéis precisam ser dropados de mobs e bosses, encontrados em baús ou comprados de catálogos limitados dos vendedores que você encontra. Até aqui... Okay, nada comprometedor.  O problema é que todos os anéis desbloqueados do jogo podem aparecer durante a gameplay; não há como restringir os drops para favorecer as jóias que combinam com sua build, nem priorizar os da sua escolha. Ou seja, imagine que você queira montar um mago do gelo para cantar Let It Go na cara do Cthulhu. Se você não tiver sorte, ainda que escolha a build de criomante, pode acabar nem encontrando anéis de gelo ao longo da run.

O resultado disso é que o jogador não se sente incentivado a experimentar todas as builds, por mais que os combates sejam visualmente belos e agradáveis. Os confrontos contra criaturas gigantes, por exemplo, são especialmente prazerosos, principalmente pelo deslocamento gasoso dos personagens e pela arte das magias.

No fim, Source of Madness foi uma ideia interessante. A arte é impecável. O enredo fragmentado (em uma dose exagerada ao meu ver) e os personagens descartáveis casaram bem com a proposta de insignificância do indivíduo frente ao caos cósmico. É como estar em um pesadelo vívido (ou estar com dengue e pegar um trem em horário de pico). O maior erro aqui foi não refinar o sistema de builds rotativas e manter um sistema de loot aleatório sem qualquer afinidade com a build escolhida pelo jogador. Um erro que reduz drasticamente a vida útil do jogo.

Знаете, вот игра сразу цепляет своим внешним видом. Интригующий рисованный мир с классными для этого анимациями (я так понимаю, использовали технологию, где для 3D-модели рисуют 2D-спрайт в каждом нужном повороте, от того и получается такая плавная картинка). Саундтрек просто ахуительно подходящий — меланхоличный, а музыкальная тема из города долго будет звучать в моих наушниках от Сяоми.
Боёвка классная, но вот что немного разочаровало — все способности, которые даются, фильтруются игроком по параметру "как мне нравится", а не "как под босса подходит". Я хоть и пытался использовать разные тактики, но рывок на врага, получаемый в начале игры, — мой фаворит (использовал его везде). Боссы ну интересные, кроме стартового (логично, почему), твари в бездне, потому что это превращается в несколкоминутный дроч уклонений, пяти рыцарей, потому что комбинирование способностей начинается только с третьего рыцаря (и то 3–4 удара).
Кроме боссов тут есть ловушки, сделаны довольно неплохо, под игру, в меру сложные. Из минусов — пустоватый мир. Не критично для игры с боссами, но побегушки от одного к другому будут занимать минут 15. Отдельную похвалу могу дать за кооп-режим по сети и по локальной сети, поэтому с другом думаю можно кайфануть.
Сюжет высосан из пальца, притом из ноги. Всё довольно прямо и логично, хотя для короткой игры большего и не надо.
**Общий итог:**
*   **Стилистика:** 7/10 — мне зашло, но на любителя.
*   **Музыка:** 9/10 — моё почтение, но запоминающейся мало.
*   **Геймплей:** 6/10 — Сыро, хотелось бы немного ситуативности на боссах, кроме тех, где тупо даже отковырять не надо, тупо берёшь перки на уклонение.
*   **Цена:** 3/10 — Реально дохуя, 350 даже по скидке за 10 часов геймплея.
*   **Реиграбельность:** 2/10 — Босс-раш и всё, фармить достижения — это хуйня затея.
Берите игру только если хуй на графику стоит и вы любите шпагу точить на сосалики, остальным не советую.
