After a couple thousand hours and several years on this game, I finally broke. I've always had a soft spot in my heart for this game and have always wanted it to succeed. I've even went as far as to practice PvP combat extensively at a point in time. However, time and time again I am left immensely disappointed by several issues with the game itself and the developers working on it.

- This game is NOT beginner friendly. You must grow for several hours, and depending on which species, can be around 6-9 hours assuming you know how to achieve the ideal growth bonuses(which new players will not) and one mistake(or cheater) will reset you to square one in an instant. In its current state there are no tutorials, virtually no hints at what you are to do as a new player, and has one of the most toxic and petty communities I've personally ever seen in gaming. In this game, there are players who will group up with you, chat with you, sometimes for several hours and then betray you on a dime when you least expect it. You basically need to hide from your own species. You can trust nobody. The solo experience is absolutely miserable in it's current state. Mixpacking(herbivores and carnivores teaming up, usually in huge clans of 6 or more individuals) will absolutely mercilessly witch hunt any solo player they find, and often will arrange teams of dinosaurs to intentionally have a tactical setup as if they are playing Valorant. Pachys and Raptors to slow down the enemy, Ceratos, Tenos and Carnos to apply pressure so you can't turn around to fight back and some sort of apex to catch up and finish the job. I would personally not ever recommend this game to any new player who plans to play solo unless you plan to play on one of the limited unofficial community servers which tend to be heavily ruled and much of the time ran by some questionable individuals.

- Cheating. As many of the other reviews have expressed by now, cheating is absolutely RAMPANT in this game!! I'm not even sure why this is, as there is nothing to gain from paying extra cash for cheats other than solely wanting to ruin the experience. There is a disproportionate amount of cheaters running around on the official servers with ESP(wallhacks), many of the time also in the huge mixpacking clans mentioned above. The cheaters also get unbelievably creative in this game. This has to be the first game I've ever seen a cheater be able to fling entire servers of dinosaurs into the sky and watch them all die to fall damage. This has been patched recently, but don't worry, I'm sure they will come up with something else as they do every Tuesday. New hacks appear on this game as quickly as wildfire spreads. It is absolutely atrocious and unfortunately will always be a huge issue as there are not enough programmers to catch it in a timely manner.

- Mixpacking. I've already mentioned this earlier. It is very, very hard to play on officials without being in a large group that can protect you. Even then, there's a 50/50 their group is larger than yours. It is also becoming more common. Not quite on par with day of dragon clans yet, but oh boy we're getting there. A solution is in the works, but I have doubts it will deter them much.

- Bugs. There are several persistent and annoying bugs in this game that have not been patched for nearly 4 years, such as when grabbing a piece of meat it will get stuck on your face with no way to get rid of it and you will not be able to eat or drink until it rots and falls off.  A lot of the time other players will be able to smell it. Bodies will literally fall through the ground with no way to get them back. The raptor's entire kit is basically a bug. Playing the game is basically the same as running naked through a forest. As fast as you run you will not escape the never-ending bugs

- Balancing. There are some dinosaurs in this game that have the most insane balancing decisions being made behind their kits I've ever seen. The Ceratosaurus for instance has an ability in which he can simply hold right click to get a stun reduction and deal around 345 damage instantaneously, make your dinosaur vomit(soft stun) and do incredible bleed with no stamina cost and virtually no punishment to missing whatsoever. The community has been expressing issues with this for several months as it mows through the rest of the roster rampantly with ease and the developers responded by buffing it several more times and then adding more even more broken dinosaurs with the most unengaging abilities you've ever seen. Pins, which are basically free-win buttons where you basically watch your dinosaur die after the opponent presses right click at you are becoming very prominent in the balance of the game recently. Not to mention many dinosaur abilities are being shifted away from skill and more towards easy to land devastating abilities which require little effort and outrageous reward. The combat is becoming rather stale with a large margin of the dinosaurs having insta-win abilities such as long knockdowns and pins in a singular mouse click.

- Desync. Desync in this game is hands down the worst I've ever seen. It has been like this for years. You will be several meters away from abilities and get hit, knocked down or even oneshot by them. Small playables are incredibly frustrating because of this due to the low healthpool. Hitboxes are also insane as a whole.


- Developers. The developers in this game really do not seem to be very receptive to community feedback, or rather they cherry pick which feedback to take. Very often the community will warn against something or beg for change in areas where it is plain unfun or unnecessary and the developers will clap back by arguing with individuals in their discord or flat out ignoring the feedback and power through with whatever they want. The discord is a whole other can of worms. No, early access isn't an excuse after almost 10 years. Smaller dev teams have accomplished more with less funding faster.
The man who owns this game has an absolutely atrocious attitude and demeans his community actively and openly dislikes a large margin of the community that doesn't agree with his changes and has publicly went on tangents calling his audience "brainless zombies" etc on stream. The overwhelmingly negative attitude and public disdain for his community is outrageously unprofessional.


Overall, it's definitely... an experience, but honestly it does break my heart how much potential this game has yet fails time and time again to seize. It's fun sometimes, but that high wears off quickly after you lose several hours to bugs, desync, or straight up cheating. If this game ever improves in a meaningful way, I will be the first to remove this review and praise it. But for now, I implore you to spend your time and money on games that will value and appreciate your contribution and feedback to their product!!

Это буквальная визуализация тезиса вульгарного материализма «человек есть то, что он ест», или «тонкий» веганский месседж, или размышление об опасностях греха чревоугодия? К концу игры все нпс, которым, по идее, мы должны хотеть помочь, превращаются в сборище гротескных уродов, на которых смотреть противно.

Местами в игре проскальзывает неплохая социальная сатира, но всё портит проклятая повестка. Настолько навязчивой и тошнотворной репрезентации ЛГБТ я не видела уже давно. В игре две нетрадиционных пары, которые только и говорят о своих отношениях, переживаниях, влечениях и т.д. ЛГБТ-персонажи показаны максимально карикатурно: ботан и тупой кочка + две «сильные-независимые» истерички. В показанной традиционной паре муж-реднек изменяет жене с кактусом (!). Самое смешное, что одиозная тема половых отношений никак не влияет на основной сюжет, её можно было бы убрать, от чего история только выиграла бы.

В итоге, игра оставляет двойственное, в большей степени, неприятное впечатление. Непонятно, для кого она сделана. Если для детей, то в ней затрагиваются слишком взрослые темы, присутствует неуместная повестка. Если для взрослых – то сюжет слишком прямолинеен, а геймплей и стилистика просты. После прохождения остался какой-то мерзкий осадок на душе.

É muito fácil gostar de [b]Hollow Knight: Silksong[/b]. Embora possa assustar os desavisados com a dificuldade dos cenários ou chefes, tudo aqui já era de certa forma esperado para quem se aventurou pelos melancólicos corredores de Hallownest anos atrás.  Ou melhor, tudo, menos a própria esperança que acompanha o enredo.

Enquanto o primeiro jogo nos transportava para um cenário pós-apocalíptico, permeado por decadência, nostalgia e trevas, Silksong é uma história de fé e ascensão. Não que o nosso intrépido [b]Cavaleiro[/b] não fosse corajoso, mas o protagonista do primeiro jogo era movido muito mais por uma essência estoica do que pelo heroísmo propriamente dito. Pelo menos, essa é a impressão que o nosso pequeno herói calado nos passava. 

Já a princesa [b]Hornet[/b], também conhecida como a "Filha das Três Rainhas", além de uma guerreira letal também é uma heroína casca-grossa, com um espírito tão livre quanto nobre, na sua matéria-prima mais pura. Enquanto o carisma do Cavaleiro era representado pelo seu silêncio e obstinação frente a um mundo despedaçado que o tratava com desprezo e hostilidade, o carisma da Hornet em Silksong advém de respostas firmes, da total falta de resignação frente às circunstâncias, de não se curvar ao legado de tornar-se aquilo que ela combate e de não arredar o pé para ajudar os necessitados, eliminar inimigos, salvar a própria vida, afastar os inconvenientes beijoqueiros e enfrentar a escuridão, mesmo que o mundo insista em sugerir que ela desista. 

Ambos precisaram provar o seu valor, contudo a Hornet não é um experimento "fracassado" de receptáculo, ela foi forjada desde sua pré-concepção para ser "a maior", e para não se curvar às insanas exigências da vida que ela herdou.

O contraste entre as essências dos protagonistas também pode ser observado nos cenários. Pharloom tem seus graves problemas, mas nem de perto é uma terra morta e sem futuro como Hollownest. Isso é perceptível inclusive pela quantidade de NPCs com quem interagimos no segundo jogo, a maioria deles peregrinos, subindo por perigosas terras em busca da salvação. O próprio cenário da Cidadela é absurdamente belo e imponente quando comparado com a taciturna Cidade das Lágrimas (ainda que a primeira utilize mão de obra semiescrava e careça de saneamento básico, produzindo o cenário mais maldito da franquia: Bilebrejo).

Assim como ocorre com o primeiro Hollow Knight, Silksong tem uma linearidade bastante maleável. É possível chegar a diversos lugares por diferentes caminhos e diferentes momentos, enfrentar bosses nas ordens mais variadas e sair explorando Pharloom até onde suas habilidades permitirem. Repetindo a fórmula do primeiro jogo, não há um propósito claro aqui (apenas um direcionamento vago), há poucas explicações e mesmo os mapas inicialmente serão escuros, levando o jogador a facilmente se perder e morrer. É como se aquele universo fosse completamente indiferente aos personagens (e jogadores).

Ainda que essa premissa niilista seja menos melancólica aqui do que no jogo anterior, e até ofereça uns pequenos sinais de alento, a sensação que fica é que as duas obras se parecem com fases diferentes de uma depressão. O primeiro jogo te obriga a levantar e caminhar no escuro, não importa as dúvidas e perigos que te cerquem (o Cavaleiro quer acabar com a fonte da infecção, mesmo que já não haja mais nada a ser salvo). Já o segundo jogo te mostra que, agora que você está de pé, é possível voltar a sonhar e lutar por dias melhores (a Hornet quer libertar o povo de Pharloom da influência da Grande Mãe Seda e restabelecer um mínimo de normalidade).

A jogabilidade dessa continuação continua impecável, especialmente na maneira como ela treina o jogador de forma quase inconsciente. É gratificante perceber nossa própria melhoria ao longo da jornada, e isso não se deve apenas ao aprimoramento da arma ou das ferramentas, mas sim à memória motora que passamos a assimilar, permitindo-nos responder aos desafios com reflexos cada vez mais rápidos e precisos (claro, dentro das nossas limitações individuais...). 

Os banquinhos de salvamento continuam representando aquele breve momento de alívio e contemplação, entre diversas batalhas e perigos. Até mesmo nossos bravos insetinhos precisam descansar, mesmo diante do fim do mundo.

As trilhas sonoras mantêm o sublime padrão do primeiro jogo, sendo as minhas preferidas as dos bosses Carmelita, Seth, Phantom e Primeira Pecadora, além da própria trilha da Cidadela. É lindo como as músicas conversam com o jogador e participam da história que está sendo contada. 

Por fim, se possível [b]não espere uma promoção para comprar[/b] este jogo. O que a Team Cherry fez aqui, e COMO ela fez, é um farol de esperança para a indústria de jogos, e isso deve ser valorizado! Silksong é um ato de resistência, além uma prova de amor e de respeito da Team Cherry não só para com o seu produto, mas também para uma legião de fãs que há quase uma década aguardavam por essa continuação.

[b][i]"Mas acima de tudo, criança, sou filha de Hollownest. E o vazio que espreita sob todas as coisas, essa escuridão, não a temerei mais..."[/i][/b]

Achilles: Legends Untold оставила у меня смешанные впечатления. С одной стороны, видно, что разработчики старались — атмосфера древней Греции, общий визуал и идея сделать souls-like в изометрии выглядят любопытно. Местами игра даже затягивает своим спокойным ритмом и чувством приключения.

Но в целом, восторга не возникло. Боевка кажется неуклюжей и часто теряет динамику. Система прокачки и улучшения оружия ощущается скорее формальностью — вкладываешь очки, но по факту разница минимальна. Сюжет подаётся слабо, катсцены напоминают игры из начала 2000-х — они не вовлекают и лишь сбивают темп.

В итоге — игра не плохая, но и не выдающаяся. Проходится без раздражения, но и без особого удовольствия. Это — вариант «на один раз».

Achilles: Legends Untold is placed exactly between Titan Quest and Dark Souls without falling in any of these two genres. The game stands on its own but if you like both titles, you will probably enjoy it. While it's shallow and simple compared to its inspirational sources, the precise gameplay and the production quality make for a very entertaining journey worth a buy. Fun for a quick grab and play, especially on a handheld.

リリース時セールが終わる前に、ファーストインプレッションを残しておきます。

リリースから5日経過し、公式Discordでは毎日凄い勢いでバグレポートや改善提案が上がり続けているので、早期アクセスとしては理想的な状況だと思います。私の環境では進行不能になるような致命的な問題は出ていないので、UIが解り難くて混乱したり、小バグに戸惑いながらも遊べる状態です。

前作(Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes)から変更があった部分について、気付いた点を以下に記載しておきます。

ゲーム開始が指導者ユニット一体のみになった。補佐するユニットは都市で生産する必要があり、施設建設と並列処理はできないので、どちらを優先するか？というところで戦略的な選択肢が生まれています。

これと対になるのが、どんなユニットにも武器や鎧、アクセサリーといった強化アイテムを装備することができるようになった事です。クエストで仲間になる少し癖のある非英雄ユニットはもちろん、都市で生産した一般兵も、後から入手したアイテムを装備させる事ができるのです。これによりすべてのユニットがプレイヤーによって個性を与えられる存在になりました。このゲームには最早「一般兵」は存在しない、と言っても過言ではないかもしれません。

更に本作の大きな新システムとして、収集した素材を使ったアイテムクラフトがある為、ユニットの更なる個性強化に繋がって行く事が想像できます。こういった変更を踏まえると、ユニットは一体一体意識して追加していった方が面白いので、指導者一人スタート化は必然だったのだと、おおいに納得できました。

グラフィックの強化については、ユニットのポートレイトや戦闘画面はやや綺麗になった印象を受けました。戦略マップについては地形などは変わり映えしないものの、都市の描写が向上しています。とはいえ、最新ゲームと比べられると古臭さは否めず、かなり厳しいと言わざるを得ません。だだし、私は元々ビジュアル面にそこまで過度な期待はしていないので、ゲーム性の方で頑張ってくれればそれで良いです。

今後のロードマップとして、王朝（指導者が子を残し世代を繋いで行く）という大きな要素の追加が予定されており、更に現状からの品質アップにかかる工数を想像すると、12月目処とされる公式日本語サポートまで手がまわるのか心配になります。言語サポートよりも品質アップが優先されるのは当然だと思うので、遅延を想定しておいた方が良いかもしれません。

遊べる状態ではあるので、日本語はいつか？いつか？とヤキモキするくらいなら、もう買って遊び始めてしまって良いかもしれません。このゲームで英語に苦労する場面は、ほぼフレーバーと言えるクエストログだけなので、それほど重要ではありません。しっかり追いかけたい人は WindowTranslator を使うことで機械翻訳しながらの遊びもかなり快適になります。

People calling it Sesame Street meets Resident Evil are right. My Friendly Neighborhood is a survival horror game that isn't trying to be horror too much, but a Resident Evil that is rated E for Everyone. It's purely SH from a gameplay standpoint only completely by design and it works. Level design and flow is top notch. Story wise it tackles a few surprisingly mature themes, but it isn't hamfisted about it.

What some people might not like is the fact that, aside from a few rooms, muppets respawn instantly if not taped. They also constantly yap about everything and nothing, even if you immobilize them with tape. Additionally, FoV above 65-70 has negative impact on firearm accuracy, and increases player melee and enemy grab ranges to absurd degrees. It makes it hard to determine effective distance between you and the muppets. All of this due to a fish-eye effect at barely above 70. I dropped it from 90 to 80 FoV, since at 90 it was barely playable, and was able to compensate for the differences, but I was still considering dropping it further, even though this low FoV can cause nausea for myself. I have no idea how almost nobody is mentioning this massive technical issue.

In general My Friendly Neighborhood is a passion project and clearly a lot of love went into its production. Actors noticeably had fun voicing the puppets and the credits theme song is the cherry on top. Worth checking out.

Sesame Street goes Resident Evil. 
A true homage to the survival horror genre. 
10 out of 10!

SCP: Fragmented Minds begins with a familiar but effective premise: you awaken from cryosleep inside Mars Site-113, a once-thriving SCP Foundation facility now reduced to a silent, malfunctioning tomb. The moment you step out of the cryo pod, the game establishes its commitment to loneliness and decay. Flickering lights cast long shadows through rusted corridors, alarms echo faintly in the distance, and broken machinery hums with unstable energy. Fragmented Minds leans heavily into atmosphere, and it succeeds—its world feels oppressive, derelict, and full of unanswered questions. As Agent Kovich, your task is not only to survive but to piece together the events that led to the collapse of the outpost, and in doing so uncover the greater threat still lurking within.

Exploration forms the backbone of the experience. Much of the early progression is spent moving methodically through the sprawling facility, reading logs, listening to audio messages, and uncovering fragments of a catastrophe that swallowed the site whole. This slow build gives the environment time to breathe and creates a sense of mounting dread. Every new sector feels like a piece of a larger, fractured puzzle—cryo labs, containment chambers, engineering bays, and dark maintenance tunnels all carry their own tone and history. The environmental storytelling is subtle but consistent, giving you the impression that Site-113 wasn’t merely abandoned; it was overtaken by something unnatural, and its traces linger like smudges on a cracked surface.

Mechanically, the game combines stealth, survival, light puzzle solving, and sparse combat. In its early access form, Fragmented Minds favors avoidance over confrontation. Resources are scarce, your arsenal is limited, and even your first weapon—an improvised melee tool—reinforces the idea that you are not a prepared soldier but a survivor improvising moment to moment. Puzzles are spread throughout the facility in the form of locked doors, energy rerouting, simple hacking tasks, and environmental obstacles. While none are deeply complex, they help keep the pacing varied and force you to engage with the space rather than sprint through it. The limited combat encounters also contribute to tension, though some of the early enemies—particularly SCP-3199’s unsettling but somewhat awkward creatures—strike a strange tonal balance between eerie and unintentionally humorous.

Where the game shines brightest is in its presentation. For an early access title, the visual polish is surprisingly strong. Lighting and shadow are used effectively, giving the abandoned facility a grimy industrial ambiance that feels both authentic and cinematic. Rooms flicker between darkness and emergency lighting, and volumetric fog in certain areas makes traversal feel genuinely tense. The audio design reinforces the mood with distant metallic creaks, low machinery rumbles, and abrupt audio cues that keep the player guessing—and sometimes jumping. Even when nothing is happening, the soundscape makes it feel like something is always about to.

There are, however, elements that feel rough around the edges. The pacing sometimes slows to a crawl, with long stretches of exploration that lack escalating threats or revelations. Enemy variety is limited in the current build, and the few anomalies you do encounter appear repeatedly without new mechanics or behavioral twists. Some technical issues—occasional stutters, inconsistent animations, and infrequent crashes—remind you that the game is still in development. While none of these shortcomings break the experience, they do highlight areas where future chapters will need refinement to maintain momentum and deepen the gameplay loop.

Despite its early-access limitations, SCP: Fragmented Minds shows strong potential. Its foundation—a moody, atmospheric sci-fi horror adventure with SCP-themed mysteries—already resonates with fans of the universe. The developers’ roadmap suggests a significant expansion of content, including additional chapters, co-op functionality, and a PvP mode, signaling ambition beyond the initial release. For players drawn to exploration-heavy horror, unreliable facilities, and stories built around containment breaches gone wrong, the game offers a compelling first taste of what could become a standout entry in the SCP gaming catalog.

As it stands now, SCP: Fragmented Minds excels at creating a tense, immersive atmosphere and a sense of narrative curiosity. It may be slow-paced and still forming its identity, but the groundwork is solid, and the experience is already engaging for those who appreciate methodical sci-fi horror. With further development and the planned expansion of its systems and threats, it has the potential to evolve into a fully realized, gripping adventure that honors the mysterious and dangerous world of the SCP Foundation.

Half-Life (1998) – Not a Game, but a Mental Experience

Half-Life has never been just an FPS for me. It has been a mind laboratory running since 1998. Every time I replay it, I discover a different version of myself. Gordon Freeman may be silent, but everything around him speaks; even in that silence there is a kind of mathematics. In every corridor, in every echo of every sound, you can feel a spirit pushing against the hardware limits of its time.

Half-Life was the first game to say, “Don’t lock storytelling inside cutscenes. The player is inside the story itself.” With its scripted events, AI behavior, and that incredible atmosphere, it was the best thing ever created up to that point. In the classic sense, it tests your FPS reflexes, but it also trains your mind. To play Half-Life well is not just to aim; it is to read the map, feel the physics, and anticipate the AI.

Its physics system is so organic that the game teaches you how to dance with the engine’s code without you even noticing. Years passed, graphics cards changed, resolutions hit 4K, yet every time I hear that rusty door sound in Black Mesa, I still get goosebumps. Because Half-Life is not merely a game; it is a milestone etched into the DNA of gaming itself.

If a game leaves its mark on history, that means it is not only enjoyable in the era it was released, but it can still be played with the same joy even twenty years later. Only then is it truly immortal.

10/10 – A game that wrote the code of an era.

Diese Rezension wird sich in 9 Kategorien gliedern.
Ich hoffe, dass sie euch bei der Kaufentscheidung hilft.

Grafik:
Die Grafik ist okay, aber man kann bildtechnisch so gut wie nichts verändern. Es bewegt sich auch nur das Haustier und der Kopf des Menschen. Ziemlich eintönig meiner Meinung nach. Dafür startet man das Game aber nicht sondern aus anderen Gründen. Also spielt die Grafik nicht so eine große Rolle. 

Performance:
Ich hatte überhaupt keine Probleme mit dem Spiel. 

Preis:
Das Spiel ist kostenlos. Man kann also nichts falsch machen. 

Spielzeit:
Ich habe 102,5h in dem Spiel verbracht, aber grundsätzlich kann man es endlos spielen. 

Vergleich zum Vorgänger:
Es gibt keinen Vorgänger. Es gibt nur ähnliche Spiele wie zum Beispiel Chill Corner. 

Errungenschaften:
Insgesamt gibt es 8 Errungenschaften und diese hat man in genau 100h erreicht. Es dauert also ein wenig, aber dafür muss man eigentlich fast nichts machen. Es eignet sich perfekt als Idler. Die Errungenschaften zählen und von daher ist es schon empfehlenswert für geduldige Sammler. Eines muss ich nur anmerken: Wenn man das Game auf mehreren Geräten installiert, dann wird die Spielzeit auf jedem Gerät eigens berechnet. Wenn man also am Laptop 40h in dem Spiel hat und am Standrechner 60h dann bekommt man die Errungenschaft mit den 100h nicht. Man muss auf einem Gerät 100h erreichen. Man kann nachsehen wie weit man ist indem man auf P drückt. Dadurch hab ich nämlich herausgefunden als ich es am Laptop installiert hatte und ich die 8h-Errungenschaft nicht bekam, dass die Zeit am Laptop bei 0 los ging. Deswegen habe ich 2,5h mehr als man braucht. 

Story:
Die gibt es nicht. 

Gameplay:
Das ist sehr simpel. Man kann das Wetter und die Geräusche einstellen. Die Beleuchtung richtet sich nach der Tageszeit bei einem zuhause und es gibt durch die DLCs einiges an Liedern zum Anhören. Ich habe mir alle angehört und kam auf ca 2 oder 3h. Wenn es einem nur um die Errungenschaften geht, dann startet man es und lässt es einfach laufen bis man 100h hat. 

Fazit:
Ich brauche solche Software zwar nicht um mich zu fokussieren und zu datieren wann ich was gemacht habe, aber für mich als Idlespieler ist das einfach ein Idlegame mit fast keinen Funktionen was ich nicht negativ meine. Ich sammle liebend gerne 100%-Spiele und das ist jetzt eines davon. Da ich den Entwicklern dafür auch was zurückgeben möchte, habe ich die DLCs auch gekauft und kurz rezensiert. Ich kann es also nur positiv bewerten.

Ich wünsche euch noch viel Spaß beim Zocken und bis zur nächsten Rezension.

[h1] 瑕不掩瑜的良好塔防作品 [/h1]  

今天最高难度全部打完了，[b]仅代表最高难度的游戏体验[/b] 

[h3] 首先说缺点[/h3] 
策略性很明显的不足，出怪很不科学，就是一味的堆怪没什么逻辑，尤其是抗性设置的莫名其妙，后期大部分怪都是同时有双抗，如果一个怪有50的物抗和法抗，那么为什么不直接把他的血量翻倍？抗性的意义何在？boss也是双抗拉满叠数值，最后搞得物伤和法伤根本毫无意义就只要一味的灌伤害把对面打死就完了

防御塔的平衡也不是很好，有些塔完全用不上，有些塔的技能就是纯凑数的，尤其是到了后期怪物的数值膨胀的离谱，后期小怪的学都能跟前期的boss相提并论，但是防御塔并没有很大的数值提升，因此到了后期非常依赖单体高伤塔，猎魔修女和红钻几乎承包了所有输出，到了最后一章，小怪都有几千血，大怪人均上万的血，还有高抗性，导致传统炮塔几乎没有发挥空间

另一个很明显的问题就是塔位。由于本作全部为直线道路，并非王国保卫战那样的曲线道路，防御塔又是非常的手短，因此塔位非常糟糕，必须要在十字路口或者转弯的地方才能有像样的集火点，有些关卡因为有大量的长直线路径几乎没有合适的集火点。

英雄不平衡是一个很容易察觉的问题，而且已经到了非常严重的程度，埃及猫的强度极高，而部分英雄强度极低。其实星际要塞是一个很有意思的英雄，但是因为开局强度过低需要投入大量资金而显得极为无用。把英雄做成防御塔是一个很有意思的创意，然而地面上的英雄就做的不好了，移动需要冷却，也没有快捷键供我快速选中英雄。因此地面上的英雄玩起来非常不顺手。

Это не просто игра, это настоящее погружение в психологический триллер, где вы не просто наблюдатель, а главный герой сбивчивого, пугающего романа.

С первых же минут городок Брайт-Фоллс, туман и хвойные леса создают невероятное чувство тревоги и одиночества. Вы идёте по тёмному лесу, а в руках у вас лишь фонарик и пистолет. И это не просто "пришёл и пострелял". Главная фишка в том, что врагов, "охваченных Тьмой", сначала нужно ослепить светом, чтобы сделать уязвимыми. Это простая механика заставляет по-новому смотреть на любой источник света. Уличный фонарь становится островком безопасности, а внезапно включившиеся прожекторы - спасением. От этого геймплей становится очень напряжённым - постоянно считаешь патроны и батарейки, ищешь свет и боишься темноты.

Игру часто сравнивают с сериалом "Твин Пикс" и книгами Стивена Кинга, и это сравнение абсолютно оправдано. Вы - писатель, приехавший в этот тихий городок с женой, и вот она пропадает. А вы начинаете находить страницы рукописи романа, который, как вы уверены, никогда не писали. И самое ужасное - события из этих страниц начинают сбываться вокруг вас. Подача в виде сериала с эпиграфами "ранее в Alan Wake..." и кадрами под рок-музыку в конце каждой главы - это прекрасно. Чувствуешь себя не игроком, а зрителем захватывающего сериала, где вы и есть главный актёр.

Игра не идеальна. К концу геймплей может показаться немного монотонным: ослепил-выстрелил, побежал дальше. Враги не сильно разнообразятся. А ещё Алан - чемпион по марафону только на бумаге, на деле же он запыхается после двадцатисекундного спринта. Иногда это бесит.

Несмотря на небольшие шероховатости, Alan Wake - это уникальный опыт. Это история, которая затягивает с первой же минуты и не отпускает даже после финальных титров. Это атмосфера. Это не хоррор в классическом понимание, где тебя пугают скримерами, а интеллектуальный триллер, который играет на твоих страхах перед неизвестностью и безумием.


The Signal.

Если основная история была странным, но более-менее логичным кошмаром, то это DLC - это уже настоящая горячка, путешествие в самое сердце безумия Алана.

"Сигнал" - это не отдельная история, а прямое продолжение, которое начинается сразу после событий последней главы основной игры. Никакого покоя! Ты снова оказываешься в кромешной тьме, и твоя задача - поймать таинственный сигнал, который, возможно, является ключом к спасению.

Ещё более сюрреалистично и страшно. Основная игра пугала в лесах и на улицах Брайт-Фоллса. Здесь же разработчики дали волю фантазии. Локации начинают "ломаться" - дороги уходят в небо, дома возникают из ниоткуда и рассыпаются, как карточные домики. Это настоящий трип по подсознанию писателя. Атмосфера сюрреалистичного ужаса зашкаливает.

Здесь в полной мере раскрывается механика управления светом. Появляются новые виды "световых головоломок". Это добавляет приятного разнообразия и заставляет по-новому взаимодействовать с окружением.

Врагов стало, на мой взгляд, ещё больше, и действовать приходится ещё агрессивнее. 

DLC довольно короткое. Его можно пройти часа за два. И по большей части ты просто бежишь по новым коридорам, отбиваясь от полчищ врагов. Глубины сюжета, как в основной кампании, тут нет. Это скорее интенсивная доза того же геймплея, но с новыми декорациями.

Если вы после основной игры надеялись на ответы, то тут вас ждёт разочарование. "Сигнал" не проясняет картину, а наоборот, забрасывает новыми вопросами и метафорами. Это может немного утомлять, потому что хочется хоть какого-то понимания, а тебе его не дают.

Это дополнение стопроцентно порадует тех, кто обожал основную игру. Оно не даст ответов, но углубит ваше погружение в безумие главного героя. Это качественное, хоть и короткое, продолжение, которое усиливает самые сильные стороны оригинала - атмосферу сюрреалистичного ужаса и уникальный геймплей со светом.

Но если основная игра вам показалась немного затянутой и однообразной, то "Сигнал" вас не переубедит. Это такое же, только сконцентрированное и усиленное, варево из тьмы, паники и света фонарика.


The Writer.

Если "The Signal", был интенсивной поездкой по сумасшедшим американским горкам, то "The Writer" - это финальный, самый безумный и одновременно катарсический акт этого кошмара. После прохождения осталось странное чувство - смесь опустошения, легкого недоумения и восторга.

"Писатель" - это прямое продолжение "Сигнала". Алан продолжает свой путь через разум, пытаясь найти выход и наконец-то закончить эту историю, обуздав собственное творчество.

Безумие на максимум. Думали, в "Сигнале" было сюрреалистично? Здесь разработчики совсем оторвались. Локации - это чистый сон наяву. Ты идёшь по гигантской пишущей машинке, парящей в космосе; слова из рукописи становятся физическими преградами; целые пейзажи переворачиваются и складываются, как страницы книги. Это невероятно визуально и с головой погружает в идею о том, что всё вокруг - творение Алана.

Механика со светом достигла своего апогея. Здесь нужно не просто перенаправлять лучи, а буквально "переписывать реальность". Например, осветив определённое слово, ты меняешь окружающее пространство, открывая новый путь. Это гениально вписывается в концепцию и заставляет чувствовать себя настоящим творцом, пусть и в западне собственного измышления.

Это DLC даёт гораздо больше понимания (ну, насколько это вообще возможно в Alan Wake) внутреннего состояния главного героя. Здесь меньше бесконечных боёв и больше размышлений, метафор и попыток разобраться в себе. Финальная сцена... Она одновременно и пронзительная, и оставляет огромное пространство для домыслов. Это был тот самый горьковатый, но идеальный финал для всей этой истории.

Ощущение прощания. Это звучит странно как недостаток, но после прохождения осталось чувство, что это действительно конец. И как после любой сильной истории, немного грустно, что она закончилась.

"The Writer" - это идеальная точка в саге (на тот момент).
Оно не даёт всех ответов - игра бы потеряла всё свое очарование, если бы дала. Но оно даёт нечто более важное - понимание и катарсис. Ты реально чувствуешь, что Алан сделал огромный шаг вперёд в своей борьбе, пусть битва ещё и не выиграна.

Это DLC — обязательно к прохождению после основной игры и "The Signal". Оно собирает все впечатления в единый, мощный эмоциональный удар.

I first played Caesar 3 in 1999 and I was instantly drawn to it. It was one of those games that could pull you in completely. When I saw it on Steam after so many years, I grabbed it right away because this is one of those classics that deserves to be revisited.

Caesar 3 stands out because of how well it blends city building, management and strategy. You are not just placing buildings. You are creating a functioning Roman city where every decision matters. Roads, walkers, service coverage, desirability and production chains all interact in a way that feels organic and challenging. The game does not guide you with modern conveniences. Your planning and layout decide everything, which is exactly what makes it so satisfying.

The walker system is still brilliant. Watching citizens move around delivering food, pottery, entertainment, education and other services gives the city a very real sense of life. When your road layout is efficient, the whole city flows beautifully. When it is not, the problems start piling up and the game quickly teaches you how to fix them. That learning curve is part of the fun.

The graphics may be old, but the art style has aged very well. The visuals are clear, colourful and full of personality. The animations are simple but charming. The music is unforgettable and still creates a calm and immersive atmosphere while you build and expand your city.

The missions are excellent. Each scenario has a different focus and pushes you to master a new aspect of city building. Some missions test your economy. Others challenge your military or cultural development. No two maps feel the same, and you always have to adapt your strategy instead of repeating a formula.

The difficulty progression is well balanced. The early missions ease you in, but the later ones demand proper planning and good instinct. Balancing resources, population needs, industry chains and security keeps you fully engaged from start to finish. Building a stable, thriving Roman city feels genuinely rewarding.

Even today, Caesar 3 remains one of the best city building games ever made. Many newer games look more modern, but very few have this level of depth, personality and charm. If you enjoy classic strategy or city building games, this is an easy recommendation.

It is a timeless title that still delivers a great experience, even decades later.

Review — Haven: A Journey About Love, Freedom, and Connection

Haven isn’t just a game — it’s a quiet, intimate story about love and the desire to live freely, away from the systems that try to define who we are. From the moment I started it, I could feel how personal and emotional this experience was meant to be. The combination of gentle sci-fi worldbuilding and deeply human storytelling creates something that feels both cozy and thought-provoking at the same time.

The art direction is absolutely stunning. The world of Source feels alive with color — soft pastels, glowing lights, and calm skies that perfectly match the mood of the story. Flying across the planet’s surface with those trails of Flow behind you is both relaxing and meditative. There’s something almost hypnotic about gliding hand-in-hand with your partner, watching the world come back to life as you cleanse the rust.

The music deserves special mention. DANGER’s soundtrack is pure magic — a mix of ambient electronic beats and emotional melodies that never stop resonating. Sometimes I just stopped moving, only to listen to the music while watching the landscape. It perfectly captures the balance between peace and tension that defines the whole experience.

What really makes Haven unforgettable, though, are Yu and Kay. I absolutely fell in love with these two — their personalities, their voices, their chemistry, everything. Every conversation between them felt natural, sweet, and incredibly human. They joke, they argue, they tease each other, and they have those soft moments that feel so real you can’t help but smile.
Some of their scenes together were so cute and heartwarming that I honestly felt a little lonely while playing — like I was witnessing something beautiful that I didn’t want to end. The way they look out for each other, the way they talk about small everyday things, it all makes you believe in the kind of love that feels peaceful, safe, and real.

I also really appreciated that the game lets you choose a lesbian couple. It’s a small detail, but it means a lot — it shows that love in Haven isn’t defined by gender, it’s defined by connection and care.

If I had to point out flaws, I’d say the combat is one of them. It’s not bad, but it can feel a bit clunky or repetitive after a while — though honestly, part of that might be on me for losing focus sometimes. Exploring the map could also become slightly tedious, especially when you’re backtracking or trying to find those last few flow bridges or ship parts. The navigation sometimes breaks the calm rhythm the game builds so well.

And then there’s the ending — or rather, the endings. Without spoiling anything, I’ll just say that I felt they could have been a bit more impactful. The choices you make toward the end are meaningful, but the emotional payoff doesn’t fully match the strength of the bond you build with these characters throughout the game. Still, even if it didn’t hit as hard as I hoped, it left me thinking about the themes of sacrifice and freedom for a long time.

What I love most about Haven is how it treats love — not as a reward, not as a subplot, but as the core mechanic of the experience. Every system in the game, from exploration to combat to cooking, is designed around cooperation, care, and emotional connection. It’s not about power or progress — it’s about staying together, even when everything around you falls apart.

By the time I finished, I didn’t just feel like I had completed a game; I felt like I had shared a journey. A quiet, warm, sometimes frustrating, but always meaningful journey.

If you’re looking for a high-action adventure, Haven probably isn’t for you. But if you want something slow, sincere, and deeply human — something that reminds you how love can be both simple and revolutionary — then this game is absolutely worth your time.

It may not be perfect, but it’s honest. And that’s what makes it so beautiful. 🌌💖

광부는 자동으로 광석을 채굴하며 저장량을 채우면 트레일러로 가져갑니다.
플레이어는 클리커방식으로 채굴이 가능하며, 화면을 클릭하거나 꾹 누르고 있으면 자동으로 거리에 상관없이 흙을 파내고 광석을 수집하죠.

흙은 체력이 존재하며 0이 되면 제거됩니다.
기본적으로 골드를 지급하며, 석탄이나 철 등의 광석들을 얻을 수 있죠.
골드는 업그레이드에 소모하며, 채굴력이나 탭 대미지 증가 등이 있고 지정된 층에 도달함에 따라서 새로운 항목들이 등장합니다.

광석은 공장으로 가져가서 가공이 가능하며, 여기서 보유한 광석들을 가공할 수 있죠.
예로 석탄과 구리를 단조하여 구리 광석을 얻을 수 있으며, 이렇게 가공한 광석들로 다른 광석 단조에 사용하거나 골드처럼 업그레이드에 사용할 수 있습니다.
추가로, 각 주괴들을 연관된 단조에 재료로 소모해 업그레이드하여 한 번에 진행할 수 있는 수량과 속도 등을 상승시킬 수 있죠.

또한, 광부들을 활성화하는 대에도 광석들을 사용하고 그들을 업그레이드하는대에도 소모됩니다.
광부들은 제일 처음 친구 외에는 이종족이라거나 샷건...을 쓰는 광부 등 다양한 컨셉을 가지고 있습니다.
그런대 그에 따른 뭔가 패시브라거나 액티브 능력 같은건 없는 듯?
외에도 스킨을 언락해 장착시킬 수도 있으며, 최대 5명까지 팀을 구성하여 채굴 작업을 시킬 수 있습니다.

해당 층의 모든 광석을 제거하면 클리어를 하고 다음 층으로 이동합니다.
5층마다 보스층이 등장하며, 주어지는 모든 땅을 제한 시간 내에 모두 제거하면 다음 층으로 이동할 수 있죠.
당연히 제한 시간을 초과하면 이전 층으로 이동하며 성장하기 전까지는 계속 반복하게 됩니다.

25층에 도달하면 현재 코인/층/골드 업그레이드를 초기화하고 초기층으로 돌아가는 기능이 활성화됩니다.
쉽게 다른 방치형 게임의 환생이며, 이를 통해 광부 영혼을 획득하여 소울 업그레이드를 진행할 수 있죠.
참고로, 환생 후 보스층을 어느정도 빠르게 클리어하면 바로 다음 보스층으로 워프하게 됩니다.

또한, 일정 층에 도달하면 다른 광산들이 언락되어 이동할 수 있습니다.
광산의 종류에 따라서 주요하게 획득하는 광석의 종류가 다르며, 고유한 광산으로 처리됩니다.
그렇기에 광산마다 진행한 층과 골드, 광부 영혼이 구분되어 있죠.
쉽게 A광산의 층과 골드, 광부 영혼은 B광산에 갈때 같이 가지 않고 해당 광산에서 얻은 경우에만 사용 가능합니다.
다행히 광산을 이동해도 이전 광산의 층과 재화들은 그대로 유지되어 있기에 다시 돌아오면 유지되어 있더군요.

외에도 채굴을 진행하는 화면 상단에는 임무가 있으며 임무를 수행하면 보상을 획득합니다.
클릭 하기, 파괴하기, 골드 벌기 등이 반복되며 가끔 새 잡기나 특정 층 클리어 등이 주어지죠.
해당 임무들을 완료하면 보상으로 보석을 얻을 수 있습니다.
또, 가끔 새가 날아오고 새를 잡으면 보상을 얻을 수 있죠.
이건 일일 제한이 있는 듯?

I really wanted to like Capcom Arcade Stadium — the idea of having a collection of classic arcade titles all in one place sounds great on paper. Unfortunately, the execution leaves a lot to be desired.

The emulation feels off, with noticeable input lag and inconsistent performance across different games. Even on solid hardware, frame pacing and slowdown issues pop up far too often. The CRT scan line filters are also underwhelming — even at 1440p, they look artificial and don’t capture the authentic arcade look.

It honestly comes across as another quick cash grab rather than a carefully crafted preservation effort. I’ve built PCs with better emulation setups in the past that run these same games smoother and with more accurate visuals.

Not worth my time here. Sorry, Capcom — this one just doesn’t hold up.

Just wrapped it up, and overall I’d say the game is good but feels more like a beta — there’s a solid foundation here, but it’s still missing a lot of depth and polish. The story starts off strong, but it fades a bit as you go, and some areas of the ship are just empty rooms, which makes things feel unfinished.

I was expecting something more exploration and resource-driven, like visiting randomly generated planets to gather materials for ship and gear upgrades — for example, needing copper or iron for better tools, or unlocking new, more profitable (and more dangerous) destinations. That kind of system would’ve added longevity and replayability, especially if areas could reset or randomize over time while keeping story zones persistent.

A few small issues stood out too:
- The vacuum feels weak — would love an upgrade path for its suction power.
- Energy drains way too fast, even at max level.
- And seriously, let us buy bombs! Would’ve added a lot of fun and chaos to planetary runs.

Despite the rough edges, I do like the core gameplay and the potential here. If the devs keep updating it and flesh out the story and systems, this could turn into something really special. For now, it’s an interesting but incomplete experience that I hope continues to grow.

Joe Danger 2: The Movie, developed and published by Hello Games, is a gleefully over-the-top sequel that expands on everything that made the original Joe Danger a cult favorite. Instead of simply repeating its predecessor’s formula, this follow-up transforms the stunt-racing gameplay into a cinematic adventure where every level feels like a Hollywood action set piece. The premise is as ridiculous as it is fun: Joe is now a movie stuntman performing death-defying acts for an eccentric director. Each “film” you participate in becomes a sequence of challenges where you leap through explosions, dodge missiles, escape from boulders, and perform impossible tricks, all while racing toward the perfect take. The result is a game that blends platforming precision, arcade thrills, and the joyous spirit of creativity that defined Hello Games’ early work.

From its opening moments, Joe Danger 2 bursts with color and energy. The environments are vibrant and cartoonishly exaggerated, ranging from Western canyons and sci-fi laboratories to minecart-filled caves and futuristic cities. Every level is framed as part of a fictional movie, which allows the developers to constantly switch themes, vehicles, and objectives. One moment you’re riding a motorbike through laser traps; the next, you’re piloting a jetpack or steering a minecart through collapsing tunnels. This constant variation keeps the gameplay fresh, ensuring that each scene feels distinct from the last. The animation and art direction give the game a bouncy, Saturday-morning-cartoon quality, matching the tone of its lighthearted humor and slapstick stunt chaos.

Mechanically, the game retains the tight and satisfying controls that made the original such a success. Every jump, flip, and boost feels responsive, rewarding players who master timing and rhythm. The scoring system encourages chaining tricks and maintaining combos, adding a layer of depth that keeps the player engaged beyond simple level completion. The physics engine strikes a balance between realistic momentum and arcade-style exaggeration, allowing for both precision and spontaneity. Levels often feature multiple objectives—collecting stars, hitting targets, or finishing under strict time limits—inviting replayability and experimentation. For players who enjoy perfectionist challenges, achieving every goal in a level provides an addictive sense of accomplishment.

One of Joe Danger 2’s standout features is its level variety and the sheer amount of content on offer. There are over a hundred stages spanning the main campaign, “Deleted Scenes,” and bonus challenges, each packed with obstacles and secrets to uncover. The game also includes a robust level editor that lets players create, customize, and share their own stunt courses, dramatically extending replay value. The inclusion of Steam Workshop support on PC opens the door to an endless stream of community-made levels, allowing creativity to thrive long after the main story is complete. Local multiplayer further enhances the fun, letting friends compete for high scores or simply crash into each other in chaotic fashion.

Technically, the game runs smoothly and maintains the clean, colorful visual style of the original. The character animations are fluid, and the exaggerated physics give every crash and jump a slapstick charm. The soundtrack fits perfectly with the game’s high-energy aesthetic, with upbeat tunes that heighten the sense of speed and adventure. Small touches, like the film director shouting cues or the crowd cheering during big jumps, add personality and immersion. The user interface is simple and intuitive, giving players quick access to missions, replays, and customization options. Despite being a few years old, the game’s visual design has aged gracefully thanks to its stylized approach rather than reliance on realism.

However, Joe Danger 2 isn’t without flaws. The decision to expand the game’s scope sometimes results in a lack of focus. Certain levels feel overstuffed with mechanics, making them more chaotic than satisfying. The shift between vehicles—while entertaining—can occasionally disrupt the pacing, and some of the late-game challenges verge on frustrating due to punishing difficulty spikes and sparse checkpoints. Players looking for a smoother, more forgiving experience might find themselves repeating sections multiple times before finally succeeding. Additionally, the camera can occasionally obscure important obstacles, and while the controls are generally tight, precision can suffer in a few of the more complex sequences. These issues don’t ruin the experience, but they can break the flow in moments that should feel seamless.

Despite these shortcomings, Joe Danger 2: The Movie succeeds in capturing the spirit of joyful creativity and kinetic fun that defined its predecessor. It is packed with personality, variety, and polish, offering hours of fast-paced stunt-racing excitement wrapped in a whimsical presentation. The inclusion of a level editor and community features ensures it has lasting appeal, while the humor and visual charm make it approachable for players of all ages. Whether you’re chasing perfect scores or simply enjoying the absurd spectacle of Joe’s cinematic exploits, the game’s sense of fun is infectious.

Ultimately, Joe Danger 2: The Movie is a love letter to arcade-style gaming—a celebration of speed, skill, and spectacle. It may occasionally stumble under its own ambition, but its heart and creativity shine through every level. Hello Games once again proves its ability to craft experiences that blend technical precision with pure, unfiltered joy. For fans of the original or newcomers seeking a lighthearted and endlessly replayable stunt adventure, Joe Danger 2 delivers an energetic and thoroughly entertaining ride worthy of its big-screen aspirations.

Mundaun is a good example of folk horror.

The game opens with you on a bus heading back to your childhood home deep in the mountains after getting word of your grandfathers death. Things take a turn REAL QUICK. Not going to get in story spoilers, but the stakes are established real quick and you're given sufficient "Hey this is a problem I need to SOLVE" motivation.

How it plays is you walking around in first person solving puzzles and occasionally hiding from something that wants to hurt you. You have tools to make them stop, but its not permanent. In terms of difficulty I didn't really have a hard time, the game isn't a stickler when it comes to giving you what you need. There's more than one way to get some puzzle items, and you can have already have what you need to defend yourself when a threat shows up if you made a point to explore and look around.

The real star of the show is the art. Everything is hand penciled. EVERYTHING. There's a point where you can see the actual texture sheets for characters and it's all pencil (it makes sense in context). It's a great example of style carrying a game. Something about the mood it brings helps enhance the plot, and makes the game in general way more memorable than if everything was regular textures instead.

Not too long, multiple endings, secrets to find, goats to pet, this games might be what you're looking for if you're looking for something for spooky season that isn't TOO intense while still managing to be unnerving. I give Mundaun a "nefarious contents of an abandoned roadside shack" out of "Man, that old man sucks", would recommend.

Mage and Monsters II” isn’t a roguelike autobattler — it’s Dragon’s Lair (1983) disguised as one.

You pick a hero, juggle gold versus upgrades, and push as far as possible — but that’s it. On the surface it looks like an autobattler, but it doesn’t feel like one.

A true autobattler is about reacting in real time, countering enemy builds, and winning through clever unit composition and adaptation. This game strips all of that away. You just pick one upgrade path (“chunk”) and mindlessly buy whatever fits it. There’s no strategy, no improvisation, there is nothing.

Every run is the same 30 preset waves. The supposed “roguelike randomness” is a façade. The actual gameplay loop is pure trial and error:
1. Pick a hero
2. Push until you hit a wave you can’t beat
3. Die
4. Adjust your build order
5. Repeat until you memorize the “correct” sequence

There is single optimal solution to every wave, and you’re just bashing your head against the wall to discover it. This is just a game about memorization. 

The "random" draft system is equally deceptive. You pick 1 of 3 units from a “random” pool, but the pool itself is so tiny (5–6 units total) that rerolling is meaningless. You’re effectively just paying an extra 2 gold to buy what you wanted anyway. Same goes for upgrades: dull numerical boosts like “+10% damage” or “+10% health.” Nothing creative, nothing exciting — just stats going up, and reroll being meaningless because you can pick whatever you want. 

And because of how scaling works (attack speed × base damage × attack speed again = cubic growth), the game actively punishes diverse armies. You’re forced to commit to one upgrade aspect if you want to survive. Variety is a trap.

Meta progression? Nonexistent.
You unlock a new hero by winning with another hero. After about ten runs, you’ve seen everything. No permanent upgrades, no unlockables, no evolving strategy — just a new round of memorization for each new hero you play.

In reality, this isn’t a roguelike. It’s a deterministic memory game masquerading as one. You “win” by writing down the correct build order for every hero and difficulty, and executing it perfectly. Once solved, it’s dead. There’s no replay value, no tension, no creativity.

The game feels like a tech demo, not a finished title.
To actually become a game worth playing, it would need:
- Real meta progression (permanent upgrades, meaningful unlocks)
- True randomness and build diversity
- Interesting, creative upgrades
- Strategic freedom, not rigid solutions

As it stands, it’s hollow. The only thing you can do for fun is test which hero gets furthest in endless mode — but even that feels empty, since the optimal build for each hero is basically predetermined.

Yes, it’s an indie project. But it’s not complete. It feels like an early access prototype pretending to be a finished release.

After (almost) completing Celeste, I feel compelled to write a review about this piece.

First of all let me say that Celeste has managed to move my heart. This doesn't happen often and it is remarkable for a game, which prides itself as a difficult platformer.
I'm not a platforming gamer, not at all. Many of the finetunings of the genre escape me yet Celeste managed to keep me enticed through it's style, story and gameplay loop and I can't give it enough praise for such an accomplishment.
Regarding the gameplay: Yes, this is a difficult game. I won't fault you for not finishing it. I didn't either. 
(I did manage to beat chapter 8 but that's it)
 
Many a times, I had the thought: Fuck this game, I don't need to invest time in this!!!
It is brutally difficult, especially for people who are not accustomed to platformers. Yet it is also forgiving and well designed. There is an assist mode if it's too hard you. The deaths are plentiful but throws you quickly back into the action.
The story is neatly written, fits into the gameplay and doesn't shy away from exploring difficult, psychological topics. If I'd have to give it any faults, it'd be that there's a little too much perfect harmony going on between perfectly likeable characters without too much widespread conflict but I'm totally okay with it.

In a sense, Celeste is everything what a game should be: An experience, an eye-opener, a challenge to what one presumably took for granted, a reminder that there is more out there than you would dare to imagine.

I hope I didn't do Celeste any Injustice by voicing my rambling thoughts here and remain faithful that many more strangers on the internet will feel themselves encouraged to give this a try :)

Helldivers 2 is without a doubt one of the greatest video games ever made. It's exactly what I think every video game should strive to be: easy to get into but complex under the surface, a sandbox of creating your own story and "cinematic" moments but with enough guidance to never feel lost, and most importantly gives you the satisfaction of overcoming what appears to be impossible odds and come out on the other side of a challenge with your heart racing. Unfiltered dopamine, for real. When the games systems come together to help the player create all of these moments, it's legitimately video game perfection. I have countless images etched into my brain of the horizon lighting up with hellfire from orbital strikes while triumphant fanfare plays over the silhouette of Pelican 1 landing in front of me. This aspect of the game is brilliant, it legitimately feels like every mission is its own war movie playing out in front of me, and I’m the main character.

But who is this character I’m playing? Well, if you see the kind of things we’re able to pull off as The Helldivers, you’d assume we’re some kind of elite special forces, trained like some kind of sci-fi Navy Seals to be sent in to do the bidding of Super Earth in the galactic war. Each life you live, once you become good enough, you’ll end up racking up hundreds of kills before you go down in a blaze of glory by your own foolishness or bravado. Given that you’re essentially going 200-1 against an entire alien army, I’d say it’s pretty much confirmed that the Helldivers are not simply a bunch of meat shield infantry being sent to their horrific deaths in the name of democracy. 

But the developers of this game do not believe that is the case. Over the past two years, they have slowly but surely altered the balance of this game to ensure that the horde shooter they apparently accidentally made is being shifted back on track towards what they really wanted it to be: a tactical shooter with a “Soulslike” approach to enemy design. In other words, the developers of Helldivers 2 clearly do not like that this game is popular with players who enjoy it for its horde shooter gameplay. Over the past two years, they have lowered the number of enemy spawns by half, updated the enemy AI to be more “responsive” so that you are being attacked more often, and (most devastatingly) added multiple new enemies to this game that limit your movement and agency by ragdolling you constantly (effectively a 3-5 second stun), kill you instantly, require extensive DPS checks, ammo sinks, and stim taxes, and limit loadout diversity to a sliver of the available arsenal. 

These problems are the most apparent on the hardest difficulty. But the things I’m describing are not what I would ever call “difficult” or “challenging”. What they are is “not fun”. It is not fun to be shot at by a practically invisible bunker turret and get knocked over for 3-5 seconds in addition to losing 80% of your health and having to spam the stim button while praying it doesn’t decide to aimbot you again for the follow up kill that you had zero agency in preventing besides simply not being there. It is not fun to drop into a mission with a loadout that looks fun, only to be met with an enemy that you literally cannot damage being spawned in groups of 4 in every patrol and at every outpost, having no way of knowing beforehand whether it was going to show up at all. It is not fun to fight a faction (the Illuminate) that are designed around popping shields and mowing down zombies, only to find yourself emptying all of your magazines into a DPS check meatball enemy that spawns (again) in groups of 4 in every patrol and at every outpost. Loadout diversity has been straight up killed by these enemy designs. Either you bring anti-tank and explosives, or get hard countered by a single (common) enemy type and spend half the mission running away. Those are your options. 

And the thing is, the developers want the game to be this way. I have no other way of explaining their decision-making. They’ve had almost an entire year to respond to the unrelenting complaints about these enemies and at most (even very recently) they add one or two half-baked changes that will look satisfactory on the patch notes, but ultimately still adhere to their endgame design philosophy of discouraging players from bringing the guns they want to play with and subjecting them to unfun mechanics and enemy attacks that have the goal of unfairly killing the player as often as possible. The way they have decided to do this is to make sure there are always enemies in this game that will force you into situations that you cannot escape from. The idea of their “grunt fantasy” does not work if you do not die often, so they intentionally add things that will remove player agency and railroad them into inevitable and unpreventable deaths. That’s the story they want your Helldiver to experience, and becoming skilled enough to avoid death by kiting, taking cover, and landing precision shots is unacceptable in their eyes.

And this is where I feel the game has lost the plot. It becomes more and more apparent with every content update and balance patch that Helldivers 2 is being steered in a direction that I did not fall in love with. I have always loved the cinematic horde shooter with awesome guns and expensive bombs that you get to call down from a massive star destroyer to nuke a small family of insects. What they’re adamant about turning it into (aka stubbornly yanking it back towards its rightful vision) is a tactical shooter that they want Gamers to call “The Dark Souls of Extraction PvE”. I think this vision is not only a game I don’t want to play, it is the cringiest version of this game it could possibly be. It is the most unfun version. It is not fun to have my skill expression and agency stripped away from me in the name of difficulty. It is not fun to die to random bullshit I do not have control over. This kind of game design caters towards people who are like… idk, roleplaying as a no-name character in Starship Troopers who gets skewered by a giant bug and screams? Sure, that’s fun for a couple missions early on. But literally who wants to do that for 1000 hours? I know I certainly did not end up doing that for 1000 hours, I actually tried to get good at the game, to theory craft loadouts and experiment with strategems, but it was all met with more balance changes and content that railroads me into the narrative that they want to lay out for you in service of some dumb film trope.

The potential this game has was there, and I stuck around as long as I did because they’ve done a very good job in the past with producing hype content updates on a thematic level (the Super Earth invasion for example) but under the surface, if you pay attention as much as I have, they have been - and continue to - course correct this game in a direction I do not enjoy. I wish these devs would get their egos in check and accept that they accidentally made the greatest horde shooter of all time (a good thing). But even with their backs against the wall, during the lowest point in their favor with players, they still cannot and will not back down from this idiotic tactical shooter soulslike grunt fantasy concept, even when their playerbase is begging them to stop. 

I wrote this review out of love and appreciation for Helldivers 2, it’s genuinely one of the best games I’ve ever played. But I just can’t afford to waste my good will and hope on the actions of Arrowhead Studios anymore. Reading the patch notes, booting up the game to see if it’s not an awful experience trying to branch out and try something new… it’s actually become a waste of my time. I have officially lost all faith in these devs seeing the light and chasing after the core of what actually makes this game continue to be popular with players beyond the first few chaotic dives. So disappointing.

Came for simplicity, stayed just long enough for the analysis paralysis of a lifetime.

In all seriousness, it’s a pretty neat textbook approach to a tower defense game — almost reductionist in its design; a bare-bones skeleton of what constitutes the genre. All the pieces are there though — it’s just very low fidelity and unapologetic. Still, Gnomes is actually very refreshing and fun thanks to its snappy pacing. I love the roulette of powers and items that refresh every run, ensuring each game comes with its own restrictions and loopholes to play around with.

Once the complexity ramps up, though, it turns into a nightmare of pathing logic and vector chaos as the game visualizes every possible route the enemies can take to screw you over. It starts to feel less like a game and more like a math equation — like trying to decipher hieroglyphics while constantly repositioning your [i]gnomies[/i], aligning your crops, and building trees to slow the enemy down. You know how it is.

Anyway, it’s fun and all — just don’t kid yourself.

Recommended.

As a lover of the XCOM franchise I  enjoyed this game and would suggest anyone who likes the franchise to check it out. It is a nice hold over while we wait for XCOM 3 or whatever Firaxis is cooking up.

-The format becomes repetitive, Breach, Sweep, Repeat.
-The story is interesting, but completely undeveloped.
-The tactical depth is not what XCOM enthusiast would find challenging

Likes:
-The breach mechanic is actually pretty cool. It just shouldnt be the lynch pin of the entire game.
-The line art from the loading screens is awesome. (They should have used that style accross the board.

Thats actually about it. It's XCOM lite, I probably won't replay it. XCOM2 war of the chosen has so much more depth. Chimera Squad definitely felt like a proof of concept.

The game would have been infinitely cooler as a "Post War City Management" game, with needing to staff each regions police department, guarantee food/water/shelter for citizens, and unravel the different crime syndicates with the help of Chimera Squad. But what do I know?

Even if you are a big fan of the XCOM franchise and the Firaxcom remakes, this game is probably not worth the trouble. What I kind of feel from this game is an increasing lack of confidence from the developers in the XCOM formula. First there was Firaxcom 1, a janky prototype that tried to put a modern cinematic spin on the original with some light horror leanings. Then there was Firaxcom 2, more polished, going a bit more into the hero side of things rather than the tactical commander fighting an unwinnable war, smaller scale with light stealth mechanics, but still unmistakably XCOM. And then we get Chimaera squad. If you didn't have XCOM in the name I would not draw any ascociation, permadeath is gone, we are now full into the "hero" paradigm where your soldiers are no longer expendable, they have personalities and thoughts that they will unload on you, you are no longer fighting a war where sacrifices have to be made and things are tough, you are making sure the mission succeeds without a hitch so that the heroes can go home and digest it for you. Its a very different vibe and it is not XCOM whether you measure based on the original or even Firaxcom 2. 

But alright, clearly we went off in this new direction with the quippy dialogue and the interpersonal banter because it was just so compelling right? We get to see how all these wacky alien races from the previous games can learn to coexist and the troubles that brings. No. That should have been the angle given the game direction but the dialogue is kinda tone deaf, there is no real grit to any of it, it all reads like an office drama. Unfortunately I think the game kinda went woke and tore down everything to accomodate. Arguably the only compelling character in the whole roster is torque, and even then its kind of a little too reminescent of a bitter young person lashing out at society. The aliens don't feel like aliens at all, but stereotypes of people, and the humans, of which there are way too many for a game called chimaera squad are just as pointless. Godmother is just a hardass girlboss, I could not tell you a thing about her. Terminal is basically zoomer Shen from XCOM2 but oh no, she is also deeply traumatized. Shelter is some kind of frightened child stuck inside the body of an adult male. Patchwork I almost forgot was in the game, I guess she is also shen from Xcom 2 leaning more into the tech nerd side. Claymore is some kind of quirky indian foodie? Blueblood is just... regular cop guy who is too kool for skool? Let me remind everyone, this is supposed to be like the elite responder team, not a mental healthcare support group. These are meant to be soldiers who fought an unwinnable war against an unknown, supernatural enemy yet half of them come off as spirited housewives and the other half as regular people with some mental health struggles, except for blueblood he's just a cool guy that shoots good. What was so compelling in this lineup that it warranted destroying the pre-existing identity of XCOM? These characters don't do anything, they don't change or grow, they are just bantering for the whole game. And let's not forget, its not like firaxis doesn't have it in them to make cool characters. Remember Dragunova? Mox? Volk, Betos, the chosen? These people felt like hardened super soldiers while still having a human side (especially the chosen, but who could forget the dragunova Mox cutscene), we wanted to learn more about them as players and they fit right in narratively. I mean sure, this is a spinoff, but it is so out of sync with both the main series and the series roots that it should not carry the name XCOM. So anyway, the fact that this is kind of the core of the game now should already be a massive red flag.

Gameplay-wise the maps are even smaller and more bitesized. What started as an attempt to simulate a battlefield has turned into something of a turn based puzzle game. You have so many unique abilities, many of whom minimize the effects of chance which is another staple of XCOM. It just becomes a game of puzzling out how to use your abilities and win the encounter cleanly. To be perfectly fair, I don't think there is anything wrong with that on a conceptual level, to some degree it is fun to puzzle out the turns, but everything is so much more simple and streamlined. The character skill trees only have 2 or 1 choices per tier (1 meaning no choice, you just get a predetermined ability). There isn't that much to think about whether it be on the loadout screen or in combat. There isn't any danger since you either beat the mission or you try again. The meta-game is also simpler, it was a bit too simple in the main game already and now even more so. If the franchise continued in this direction the only place chimeara squad 2 could be released would be as a mobile game. This is no longer XCOM, this is a story campaign with some light turn based puzzle combat. And the game is small, I played through 1.8 ish campaigns (didn't finish the last one cause I just got bored), and that took me around 30 hours. Compare that to XCOM2 where I have somewhere in the ballpark of 1000+ hours (not for 1 campaign of course, a big chunk of that is due to long war).

In one word, the game just feels kind of dissapointing. The ambition is too small, it doesn't seem to understand the franchise it belongs to and the "innovations" it makes are arguably just regressions.

Rating: ★★★★☆☆☆☆☆☆ (4/10)

Watch Dogs Legion is the most disappointing entry in the Watch Dogs series a game that tries to innovate but ends up feeling empty, soulless, and directionless. After completing the story and all achievements, it’s clear that while the idea was ambitious, the execution completely missed what made the first two games special.

Story Mode
Set in a futuristic version of London, Legion tells a story about rebellion against surveillance and corruption. It sounds like classic Watch Dogs material, but the story completely lacks emotion, focus, and motivation.
There’s no main character to drive the narrative forward, and without a main character, it becomes impossible to care about what’s happening. The plot feels disconnected and not really interesting, the pacing is uneven, and the writing often feels like it’s just there to fill space rather than make you think or feel anything.

Play as anyone
The biggest selling point the ability to recruit and play as anyone is both the most creative and most damaging part of the game. On paper, it’s revolutionary. In practice, it’s shallow, repetitive, and emotionless.
All characters feel identical, just with different voices, faces, and accents. The dialogues are dull and robotic, clearly limited by the fact that recording real, unique lines for hundreds of random characters was impossible.
What could’ve been an immersive system turns into a hollow gimmick that completely destroys storytelling and connection.

Gameplay
Gameplay is still functional, but compared to Watch Dogs 2, it’s a major step back. The hacking system has lost many of its deeper features, leaving behind a simplified version that feels repetitive and uninspired.
Most hacks are single button actions that quickly lose their charm.
Combat and stealth are serviceable but repetitive, and missions lack the variety or flexibility that made the previous games so satisfying to replay.

Open World
The one thing Legion does right is graphics and visual atmosphere. London looks stunning from rainy neon lit streets to the detailed landmarks and reflections, it’s easily one of Ubisoft’s best looking worlds.
However, once you look past the lighting and effects, the city feels lifeless. Character models are stiff, animations are outdated, and NPCs behave mechanically. For a 2020 game, it looks good technically but feels outdated in everything else.

DLC Bloodline 
The Bloodline DLC is the only part of Legion worth playing. Bringing back Aiden Pearce and Wrench from the previous games gives the story focus, emotion, and identity all the things missing from the main campaign.
It’s well written, full of callbacks, and actually feels like a proper Watch Dogs story. Honestly, Bloodline should have been the main game.

Achievements 100% 
Finishing all achievements isn’t hard, but it’s not rewarding either it takes time and a lot of useless grind. The side content is repetitive, and without interesting characters or strong motivation, going for 100% feels more like a checklist than an accomplishment.

Conclusion
Watch Dogs Legion is a flashy but hollow sequel a game with great visuals and big ambitions that collapse under the weight of poor storytelling and shallow design. The “play as anyone” mechanic sounds good, but it removes the emotional connection that made the first two games special.
The story is dull, the dialogue is lifeless, and the gameplay is limited. Only the graphics and the Bloodline DLC stand out as positives.
It’s not unplayable, but it’s far from what Watch Dogs used to be. A beautiful city wasted on an empty experience.
