I'm not someone that particularly cares for remakes and remasters (Ports always available on all systems is fine for me) but these remasters are the definitive way to play the original Tomb Raiders, and has made the games available on all modern systems. You can play with the original graphics and switch to the remastered graphics at any time, moves from the newer classic era games were ported back into the original 3 (Jump twist in Tomb Raider 1, forward roll out of a crawl space in Tomb Raider 3 as a couple examples), the option to switch between 2 control types based on preference and more. 

A couple things could be better though. The frame pacing is a bit scuffed in the classic graphics mode so the 30 fps can feel a bit lower at times and there should be a 60 fps toggle for people who care about that. There should also be an option to add a bilinear filter to emulate the original pc versions. It would be great if they could back port some features for the 4-6 remastered collection to the first collection.

Bounty Star is flawed but compelling, an interesting blend of mech action game and farming sim, and as someone who doesn't play farming sims, it's not an unwelcome component. While my background in 90s-era mech sims such as Mechwarrior 2, Heavy Gear and Starsiege naturally led me to look into this title, the combat actually has more in common with so called "character action games" or "spectacle fighters" like Devil May Cry or God of War, with which I am also familiar. In that way it is quite different from either the aformentioned western mech simulators or eastern boost-spamming games like Armored Core: For Answer or Daemon x Machina. 

You play as Clementine McKinney, or just "Clem", as she prefers. Once a captain in a regional militia and protector, a mercenary attack leaves her to bury most of the people she knew and drove her far from home, to retreat into booze and smokes to try and escape that night. But as Clem herself says, ghosts don't care how far you ride. And now she's back in what's known as the Red Expanse, and with the help of an old friend is trying to set herself up as a bounty hunter. That's where you come in.

At Clem's disposal is a refurbished MKII Desert Raptor, a small but fierce combat mech and a relic of an age of war now centuries past, as well as a once-abandoned garage and farmstead to support it and herself. From here, the player can take bounties, grow and harvest crops, and purchase items and blueprints to increase Clem's ability to do both. 

The game loop is simple.  Buy some food on the market or seeds to grow your own (later you can keep chickens to generate meat and eggs, you can also pet them). Cook yourself a meal to increase your stats for the next job, customize the mech with different melee weapons, guns, active and passive subsystems and paintjobs, change the music on the jukebox, and even plink bottles with your sidearm. Then take a job, fight some bad guys, robots and giant bugs (and also dinosaurs, its complicated) and get paid in cash and crafting materials. Then you do it again. Along the way you can find some collectibles and readables to learn about the game world, and listen to Clem's narration as she keeps a journal and tries to put her mind and life back in working order.

There is some nuance to the combat. Guns have to be aimed before they can be fired, and melee weapons have a normal attack chain as well as jump attacks and dash attacks. There is a heat management mechanic as in many mech games- get too hot, and your mech will shut down briefly and reboot.  But uniquely, it is also possible for your mech to get too cold and shut down as well! Some weapons and systems purge heat instead of generating it, and running a setup with all cooling gear can be as inefficient as running too hot. However, running at high heat does increase your melee speed, and running cool does the same for your guns- so your loadout deserves careful consideration. There is a chain bolo launcher that you can use to capture targets for extra cash, "trick" systems that let you use timed inputs after melee attacks for a bonus such as a small heal, and an upgrade that lets you cancel melee attacks with gun attacks for a special "gun cancel" that differs based on the equipped gun- the shotgun lets you backflip, while the assault rifle lets you spin in the air and rain down shots, a la the "Rain Storm" attack in Devil May Cry. You can execute some fancier attack chains this way. Opposing mech enemies often have a  "stability" bar that needs to be depleted before they can be staggered by melee attacks, and some enemies can also perform a counter attack after taking too many melee hits, which is often a good time to use your gun cancel. Since first writing this review I have also obtained a shield item that is equipped as a subsystem, can block anything, does not affect your heat level and is capable of timed perfect guards to stagger enemies, including during their own counter attacks- very useful against the dangerous Driller Mech enemies, who have fast melee attacks and resist gun damage.

Originally it was intended for the player to be able to get out of the mech in-combat, as bad as an idea as that might sound, but according to the devs this was having a cascading effect on the encounter design that was detrimental to the overall development cycle.

I've seen some complaints about the combat and some of them are valid- the game was not entirely to my expectations as well. Dodging feels iffy, the camera is locked uniquely over the left shoulder of your mech, the revolver and the hammer feel a bit weak, the gun sounds are wimpy, and it's difficult to learn the timing of enemy attacks. But none of these little annoyances have derailed my progress. I haven't really been punished hard for being slow to learn the game's systems, which I appreciate. There's also some issues with sound mixing in the cutscenes. It doesn't feel like an amazing game to play, but it does feel like a pretty good one. There is passion that shows through in its execution. There is clearly a lot of depth to your mech's loadout, it has great music from the late Brother Dege, and the overall new-old-west vibe is very cool. Most of all, Clem's voice acting is excellent and her character elevates the game's appeal for me greatly. I fully intend to keep playing it. It reminds me of the vehicle-centric action games of the 90s in a good way and I'm happy games like that are still being made. In addition, the farming elements feel unobtrusive and well-integrated into the experience. Bounty Star has so far explained its systems very well. Some might call it "hand-holdy" in that regard, but those people are silly.

I first heard about Bounty Star some years ago and I was pleased to see it survive the so-called "Annapurnocalypse", wherin the entire games publishing staff of Annapurna walked off the job due to disagreements with their superiors. I'm sure that was a contributing factor in it's delay from an original planned release in 2023.

I've enjoyed my time with Bounty Star and if you enjoy character-action games and would be interested in trying one out that has a little more depth in the form of the farming elements, Bounty Star is worth a look.

ᅟᅠᅟ[h1]50小时，一周全成就（有特殊办法，要求在各个结局分支之前手动备份过）[/h1]
ᅟᅠᅟ先不说游戏，先说这个成就系统太坑，一周目可以全成就的，但是需要一点特殊办法和理解，很多人最后一个渊虚之羽（获得所有成就）的成就不跳，首先游戏按照正常来说是需要你达成4个结局，也就是说正常要4个周目才能达成，但是你可以通过增加文件夹的方式，把你之前手动保存的结局分支前的存档每个文件夹复制进去，然后改名字（具体可以看视频教程）然后进游戏把上面每个"周目"以不同结局通掉，这样基础工作大致完成，我是这样的，不排除有简单办法。
ᅟᅠᅟ接下来才是重点，这时候你可能成就还是不跳，为什么呢？原因可能是他检测你是否获得全成就是比较呆，类似于检测某些重要成就的完成要素你这个存档里是否有的暴力检测模式，如果发现没有，那么就算你四个周目都通了，也不跳最后一个成就，而我说的就是八斗之才这个成就，就是在第三个谜题门的时候，一般主流攻略都是先答对了开门做拿到八斗之才成就，再回档，故意答错打心魔走后面的结局，这时候你就发现了，你这4个存档里，没有一个是开了第三个门的，这就导致了他检测你是否全成就的时候不是卡在了结局上，是卡在了这个谜题门上。
ᅟᅠᅟ结局办法就是，建立第五个存档，由于这个地方你为了做成就备份有，那就复制进去，然后进游戏，进入你的第五“周目”答对谜题，开门，只要它检测到你所有的存档中有一个达成了这个八斗之才成就以后，就会一路往下检测检测，然后直到跳出成就 —— 渊虚之羽。
ᅟᅠᅟ（如果你删了就当我没说，做为一个合格成就党，一般都10几个压缩包保存着）

ᅟᅠᅟ另外说说游戏，刚玩上时节奏满天飞，被某些罕见当成武器使用，不好说，到底怎么样还是自己体验，个人觉得新娘这一关很喜欢，最后一关BOSS低级但是场景很高级，导致印象不深刻（参考只狼电闪雷鸣的芦苇地和苇名一心，黑猴的大圣残躯和一抹夕阳，法环的满天星辰和皮蛋）游戏的轮椅闪避也很体贴，但是制作人有特殊爱好，喜欢被做成罐子，虽然我也探索过这方面的东西，但是我也不喜欢这么正派的无常被这样弄吧（一码归一码噢），综合来说是非常值得一玩的，话说之前有个图是无常和月清疏的合照，真好看啊，诶嘿嘿。

Меня поразил невероятный реализм этой игры.
Чтобы заработать на свой первый караван в игре про караваны, действительно нужно потратить полжизни — и это восхитительно честно.

Экономика здесь продумана до мелочей: сразу видно, что только трудолюбивые и настойчивые смогут позволить себе транспорт и ночёвку в кемпинге. Всего-то — принести 276 бочек воды, продать их, проехать примерно вечность, и вот — у вас новый караван!
(Напоминаю, разработчик — соло!)

Отдельное уважение за реализм: чтобы сесть за руль, нужно пройти автошколу и получить права. Ответственность прежде всего!

А отсылки к Гарри Поттеру — просто восторг.
Невидимые мешки, летающие машины — всё это мгновенно возвращает в детство.
Спасибо, соло-разработчику, за тёплую ностальгию.

И карта… Это не просто карта, это континент!
Размеры сопоставимы с Forza Horizon, и это прекрасно. Ведь порой хочется просто ехать. Ехать час, два, в никуда. Смотреть на всепоглощающую пустоту и на камни, которые становятся самыми близкими друзьями.

Рыбалка — отдельный шедевр.
Реалистично, сложно, местами безнадёжно — как и в жизни.
Спасибо соло-разработчику, что передал всё это с такой точностью.

А ещё здесь можно почувствовать себя археологом, охотясь за метеоритами.
Это по-настоящему трудоёмкий процесс, и, возможно, вы никогда не найдёте ни одного. Но ведь в этом и смысл, правда?

Отдых в игре тоже заслуживает внимания:
ведь чтобы купить палатку и выбраться на природу, можно просто поработать на нефтяной вышке!
И снова — реализм и честность.

За удобный маркер на карте отдельное спасибо. Даже людям с топографическим кретинизмом теперь всё понятно.
Спасибо, соло-разработчику, за заботу.

Кастомизация фургона — просто праздник.
Губка Боб — мой любимый мультик, и увидеть его в такой игре было неописуемо приятно.

Да, и ещё: респект за то, как соло-разработчик контролирует дорожный трафик и оперативно удаляет лишние машины. Настоящий порядок на дорогах!

И, несмотря на то, что разработчик — соло, он не забыл о людях с друзьями.
Где бы ты ни находился, ты слышишь эмоции своего друга — и это по-настоящему трогательно.

Ну и, конечно, Башня Акдемира.
Кто-то скажет — самовлюблённо.
Но давайте будем честны: Башня Акдемира — это символ. Символ того, какая колоссальная работа проделана над этой игрой.
Ведь всё это сделал один человек. Соло
P.S. Don't smoke guys

Akif  ‘Just one more day, trust me bro’ Akdemir will serve as a case study for the video games industry for everything not to do when promoting and releasing a video game. Delayed games are no big issue in this day and age, in fact I would prefer a dev be transparent and delay a game rather than release a half- baked mess , but when you delay a game more than 5 times with each delay coming with a range of excuses from an earthquake, blaming Steam through to personal issues or simply because people are being mean to you, then people are going to start questioning what is actually going on with the game, you can’t consistently hype your fan base up for a release only to disappoint them when crunch time comes, and no being a solo dev does not excuse you from this. This is not to mention the games official Discord server, where power tripping mods and a cult like fan base full of immature and insolent teenage ghouls gaslight and shout down anyone for even asking a question about the game, it makes the place feel about as welcoming as a theme park based on fascism. You won’t survive long in the Discord server unless you conform and praise both the mods and the all glorious Akif. I was banned from both the Discord and the Steam discussion forums for simply quoting statements that the dev had made himself and asking a question regarding them. 


With all that being said there is no denying that Akif and PLEXUS GAME (the company that he founded according to his LinkedIn) do have a great idea for a game here, what is not to like about a game where you are free to explore and go camping in a massive open world environment with your friends, a world that promises diverse regions and biomes, a dynamic weather system, jobs and quests to earn money and a sustainable adventure in a huge world without boredom, sounds great right?

Except it is not actually great. The game boots up and the menus are in Turkish, great start! This leaves you fumbling around for 5 minutes trying to work out how to actually change the game into your preferred language, immersive gameplay!

 Graphically the game reminds me of the type of slop that frequently infiltrates the PlayStation store, this game should run on a potato but frequently brings an i5 10600k with 32 gig RAM and a 4070 to its knees. Frame stutters, frequent pop in, graphical artifacts in the sky, this game has it all. The settings menu doesn’t help either, you get a couple of graphical quality settings, and you are able to pick your resolution, that’s it, I suppose I should give out some props for the game having ultra-wide support, but there is no redeeming this mess.

The map itself is terribly designed to the point it looks like somebody typed ‘design me a map’ into chat GPT and just left it at that, sure the map is scattered with points of interest (assets bought off the UE store) but none of these are worth visiting, they are barren and empty, just like the soul of this game. It is actually more fun trying to get through all the invisible barriers placed on the map than it is to play the game as intended, make sure you take a swim as well, it is one of the more enjoyable parts of the game, you sink to the bottom like a stone and then come flying out of the water like a mentally challenged dolphin on some type of performance enhancing stimulant, riveting gameplay! Be sure to also check out the floating trees and graphical glitches that happen to the skybox as the map loads in for extra LOLZ.

Navigating the world itself is yet another exercise in frustration. the game handily includes a map, but does not show where you are located on it!  I am not sure whether this is because the dev didn't know how to ask Chat GPT to write the code for this or whether this is intentional by design, either way using the map is about as fun as being locked in a room and being forced to listen to K-POP all day, whilst also being made to crawl on broken glass, the glass is on fire too.

The menus and UI made me laugh harder than I have in years. It is as if the developer bought a few systems off UE marketplace and thought it would be a good idea to mash them all together in the same game. YOU CANNOT EVEN PRESS ESCAPE TO EXIT MENUS! Some menus you must exit via an arrow in the bottom left, others you must exit via a cross in the top right or by pressing the same button again, there is absolutely no cohesion in the design of this UI and trying to navigate it will leave you more frustrated than trying to navigate a maze with no exit, whilst blindfolded, and being set on fire..On one of the menus you can even type over the text that is already there and then have the pleasure of realising that you can now no longer get back out of that menu and that you  have to restart the game.

The sound is a mixture of absolute AI slop when it comes to voices, and  also sound packs purchased off the UE marketplace, all of them are mixed so sloppily that one minute you will be struggling to hear what is actually happening and then the next minute you will be reeling when a jet flies overhead and causes your ears to bleed profusely. You can also play acoustic guitar in the game and pick from a list of songs you wish to play, the first one is a nice little acoustic ditty, the second one is electric guitar accompanied by a full band, amazing, I laughed a lot.

The driving mechanics are some of the worst I have ever encountered in any game I have played, whatever you are driving will go from unresponsive to hyper-responsive in the blink of an eye, leaving you wobbling all over the road like an alcoholic driving home from his local bar.

If I was to list everything that is wrong with this game, I would unfortunately go over  Steams character limit for reviews. The game is an empty, soulless world full of AI slop, there is no redeeming gameplay loop here at all, unless you like picking up random objects such as trash and meteors and selling them, that’s it, that is what you do in this game, well you do also get rewarded with cash to buy cars and vans and upgrade them, I wouldn't consider that a reward though, as driving cars in this game is about as fun as being married to Lorena Bobbitt. Oh, you can urinate as well, when you do you will be presented with a cringey sound clip that goes “OH YEAAAAAH”, this pretty much shows the intelligence level of both who designed the game and those that enjoy it. The fact that the game costs 30 Australian Dollars should be a crime in itself, I am not about to tell you what to do with your money, but I would highly suggest that you don’t purchase this game, set your money on fire instead, it will be more entertaining.

This is the game that makes me want to have neutral rating option for steam reviews. The game's concept was immediate hook after I played the first part. The same game but with better graphics, space stuff and a bunch more belts and whistles - whether it would be good or not seemed like a no brainer. But the moment you get into the thick of it, pretty quickly you realize that unfortunately there's not that much meat on the bones as you'd expect. If I sum up my whole experience with the game most of the time it just felt like a labor.

Firstly, the game doesn't hide any progression from the player. From the moment you start and go through the tutorial, the game straight up lays in front of you everything you will unlock in your whole 60+ hours of playtime. Every shape, every goal, every task, every unlockable. I still cannot truly understand what were the devs thinking when they took this approach. In the previous game there were no bloated menus, it was simply "See this big cpu looking thing? Feed it the shape it shows in the center and see what happens next". Here you need to open the right menu, scroll through literally a dictionary of shapes and then choose the one you want to do. I assume that maybe the intention was to make shapes feel more important and add some 'attachment' to them. Well, they're not pokemon, and I don't feel attached to them, more so after the goal completion and even more after I tear down the factory I just spent my time working on. In this sence, the game progression and the UI are going complete opposite ways and I just can't shake off this awkward feeling, like I'm playing this game wrong.

The factory building in this part is more complex than in the previous one, and of course as a result there's much more tedium that comes with it, but I don't find it as big of an issue, it is to be expected.

The only other thing I can add is I liked the previous jazzy soundtrack much more, compared to the new ones that have this really annoying reverby mixing and get boring really fast.
So overall the game left me with mixed feelings, on one hand it has good graphics, performs decently well and I don't recall encountering any bugs, but it just feels like there's some fundamental flaw in it's design and the devs didn't make the game they would want to play themselves. Maybe upcoming new gamemode will make it more interesting.

The Jackbox Survey Scramble, developed and published by Jackbox Games, Inc., is a fresh twist on the studio’s long-running tradition of easy-to-learn, socially engaging party games. Rather than relying on humor-based prompts or creativity-driven answers like in Quiplash or Fibbage, this title builds its entire experience around real survey data collected from actual players. The goal isn’t to come up with the funniest response but to think like the crowd—to predict how people across the country responded to different questions. The result is a game that feels both familiar and refreshing, maintaining Jackbox’s signature accessibility while encouraging a different type of competition rooted in intuition and psychology.

At its heart, The Jackbox Survey Scramble is about reading the collective mind. Each round presents a survey question—something simple, open-ended, or occasionally absurd—and your task is to predict the most common answers or to rank them according to popularity. The real fun emerges from how well you can anticipate group behavior and human tendencies. The game features several distinct modes, including Hilo, Squares, Bounce, Dash, and Dares, each putting its own spin on the guessing mechanic. In one mode, players must determine whether an answer ranks higher or lower on a list; in another, you select squares on a board to reveal hidden answers. Each mode keeps the gameplay brisk and dynamic, ensuring that no two sessions feel quite the same. This modular design gives Survey Scramble a surprising amount of variety, despite all modes sharing the same central premise.

The presentation is classic Jackbox—clean, colorful, and designed for immediate social connection. It supports two to ten players directly, with room for massive audience participation that can reach thousands through mobile devices or browser links. As with other Jackbox games, there’s no need for controllers or complicated setup: players simply join via a unique room code, making it ideal for both in-person gatherings and remote play sessions. The interface is smooth and intuitive, with playful animations and a peppy soundtrack that keep the energy high throughout. This simplicity has always been a hallmark of Jackbox design, and Survey Scramble continues that tradition, ensuring that anyone, regardless of gaming experience, can jump in and start having fun within minutes.

One of the strengths of Survey Scramble is how it manages to tap into real-world psychology. Predicting how others responded to questions can be hilariously humbling—you might think your answer is obvious, only to discover that the crowd went in a completely different direction. This element of unpredictability makes for natural laughter and lively discussion as players debate why people answered the way they did. The variety of survey questions helps keep things interesting, covering everything from everyday topics to completely offbeat ideas. Jackbox’s clever writing ensures that even when the subject matter is simple, the way it’s presented adds humor and personality. The game encourages both quick thinking and a bit of self-reflection, as players realize just how differently people can perceive even the most mundane topics.

Still, the game’s single-concept foundation means that longevity may depend on how much new content is added over time. While the different modes offer a decent range of experiences, all of them ultimately rely on the same mechanic of ranking and guessing answers. After several sessions, especially with the same group, some players may begin to feel the repetition. A few modes are also more enjoyable than others—some reviewers have pointed out that the fast-paced “Bounce” mode, for instance, can feel chaotic or overly punishing compared to the more strategic modes. The quality of the survey data itself occasionally leads to inconsistencies, as wording variations or regional biases can skew the expected results. That said, these imperfections often become part of the fun, sparking playful arguments and laughter as players try to justify why their “obvious” answer didn’t make the list.

In terms of replayability and value, The Jackbox Survey Scramble fares well as a party game. It’s priced affordably and designed for repeated use across a wide range of social settings—family gatherings, online hangouts, or casual get-togethers. It’s particularly effective as an icebreaker, encouraging conversation and cooperation among players who might not know each other well. Its approachability makes it suitable for nearly any group size or dynamic, and because it relies on guessing collective human behavior rather than creative humor, it’s easy for anyone to feel competitive and engaged. While it may not reach the chaotic highs of Jackbox’s more comedic titles, it earns its place as a thoughtful and surprisingly strategic alternative that still delivers plenty of laughter.

Ultimately, The Jackbox Survey Scramble represents Jackbox Games at their most confident—streamlined, inventive, and grounded in social play. It takes a simple concept and polishes it to a mirror sheen, demonstrating the studio’s ability to create fun through human connection rather than mechanical complexity. Whether you’re the kind of player who loves to analyze patterns or someone who just enjoys laughing at how unpredictable people can be, this game provides a quick, smart, and entertaining experience that feels right at home in any party rotation. While it might not redefine the genre, it successfully captures what Jackbox does best: turning shared curiosity and conversation into a lively, memorable night of play.

Через неї можна вкотитися в боївку, щоб потім легше застрибнути в першу. Але якщо вам цінний сюжет та покликання, то краще, все ж, пройти спершу оригінал.

В даній грі ми потрапляємо в один з епізодів «Night Springs», де головний герой Алан написав розповідь, в якій опинився сам, і з якої він тепер намагається видозмінити розповідь, щоб змінити події і перервати часову петлю.  [spoiler]Або ж це все сниться Баррі[/spoiler]. Коротше, Remedy в усій красі із паралельними світами, часовими парадоксами, філософією тощо. 

Все, що могло дратувати гравців в першій частині, тут підправлено. Алан має більше стаміни і не задихається після кількох кроків у спринті. Темні сутності тепер не потребують просмажки ліхтарем тривалістю із сеанс у солярії: світло діє на них швидше, а отже відстріл стає динамічнішим і приємнішим. Зброї суттєво побільшало: додалася автоматична зброя, арбалет, цвяхомет, варіації пістолета і дробовика. На місці і апетитний імпакт з оригіналу, тож ця основа ігроладу приносить чимало задоволення.

Є і сюжет. Він не такий розмашистий, загадковий та багатошаровий як в оригіналі. Але і гра проходиться за втричі коротший час. Попри тривалість, він – хороший. Часто покликається на події оригіналу, розкриває долю персонажів, дає зв’язок із світом після подій фіналу. Тут є обов’язковий бектрекінг, який був люб’язно пом’якшений, тож кожне повернення до однієї з трьох базових локацій відчувається по-іншому і триває вже менше, ніж це було вперше.

Додали класних кіношник вставок із живими акторами. Власне, в більшості – із одним актором, котрий грає Алана і його альтер еґо. Грає, варто сказати, розкішно: настільки, що вам не захочеться бігти далі, доки не додивитеся його включення у телевізорі. Це неабияк додає до історії і загального вайбу.

У грі три локації – дуже камерні і затишні, особливо «мотель» і «кінотеатр під відкритим небом». В купі із ніччю, що не проходить, вони занурюють у класний настрій. «Алану Вейку» пасує ніч, попри всі мінуси, що нього з неї витікають.

Музика, а саме – ембіент на локаціях мені здалися кращими, ніж в оригіналі. Вони мені запам’яталися, крутилися в голові і викликали спалахи дежавю в купі з ностальгією. Коротше, якісна робота композиторів. 

Загалом, дана гра мені дуже зайшла, можливо, трішки більше за оригінал. Навіть вразила в дечому. Класна атмосфера і настрій, де письменник заточений в своєрідному потойбіччі, до якого доноситься луна звичного світу і в який він намагається повернутися. Особливо, коли чуєш по радіо голос Баррі чи дружини Еліс, стоячи посеред нічної пустелі. Якщо оригінал – це глибока історія, в якій вам доведеться жертвувати деякою «душністю» тут і там в плані ґеймплею, тут все збалансовано: хороша історія, прикольний ігролад, стильна подача і музика. І все це на два-три вечори за символічні гроші, особливо на розпродажі. Однозначно рекомендую.

In Stars and Time has affected me more profoundly than I could have ever imagined.

At first, the game was a genuine struggle. The core mechanic of replaying the same areas and fighting the same enemies over and over again felt like a tedious chore that quickly drained my motivation.

However, the longer I played, the more the repetition cracked open to reveal the game's true purpose. I began to see myself painfully reflected in the protagonist, Siffrin. His experience mirrors my own deepest struggles: the crushing belief that every connection, every thread of hope, and every friendship is undeserved, and that, ultimately, nothing matters.

This intense identification tapped into a profound emotional truth. I often found myself holding back tears and forced to stop playing because the emotional backlash was too familiar and intense. Yet, despite the pain, I couldn't put it down. I needed to see his journey through to the end.

The game's final chapters, where Siffrin’s self-doubt pushes him to the brink, were incredibly difficult and painful to experience. But by confronting that darkness, the narrative delivered a deeply meaningful and cathartic conclusion.

Now that I've finished, the immediate feeling is one of weariness and relief. There is still much to unpack and reflect on, but this is a game that is truly more than the sum of its parts. It's a mirror, and an unforgettable journey toward self worth.

Honestly, the idea behind the game is pretty cool, and I do want to like the game.

But frankly, it just gets way too tedious for my liking (which, again, I understand is kinda the whole point, but it's still exhausting and eventually frustrating).

Skipping dialogue you've already seen is both too slow (sometimes struggles to get going properly, though I imagine that might be a quirk of the game engine) and too fast (skipping over new variations of dialogue that I'd be interested in seeing), thus it feels like I'm missing out on something - ANYTHING - to look forward to, to actually pay attention to.

The music doesn't help, really; If anything, it adds to the frustration.

Mayhap there's some great payoff at the end to make it all worth it, some grand sense of catharsis/climax, but 11 hours in, I haven't found any real satisfaction to speak of.

9/10 - A proper collection with great games.

Mega Man Zero/ZX Collection is a great package. Not only does it contain all of the Zero and ZX games in a single place without splitting into two games, the challenge mode it has is actually quite enjoyable, being a nice addition to the collection, without overstaying its welcome.

The Zero series is amazing, it takes what it was good from the X series and dials it up to 11. Story wise, we actually have a narrative this time around, and it's well worth it. The ZX series takes it to a different place, while it still has a lot of the Zero DNA into it, it's very different, some of it is good, and some of it is also not so good.

If I had a nickel every time that in the Mega Man series they have dropped the titular character in order to push Axl as the new "protagonist", I'd have two nickels, which isn't a lot, but it's weird that it happened twice. That's Mega Man ZX Advent for you.

Talking about the games, the Zero series focuses around your performance, ranking you based on how well you play each mission. It may seem daunting at first, but it's actually very manageable and it ends up being very fun in the end.

Zero 1 does not change much around based on this, except some bosses show up with new skills if you have a good rank. Zero 2 and 3 on the other hand locks new skills based on the rank you have while doing the missions. This can be frustrating, but again, it's manageable. The worst part about this system in my opinion is that these skills don't seem all that important, only being "nice to haves", simply because they had to design the game to be beaten by someone without any of them, quite the opposite of the original X series. For Zero 4 they had a different way of unlocking skills altogether, based on how difficult you set the stages.

That being said, the games feel fluid and fast pace, like a deadly dance. You are given the tools to achieve a high rank and it feels awesome to learn the levels and actually perform well. And with the new Save Assist feature, which I definitely recommend you turning on, learning these levels and improving is actually much more fun.

The Zero series all have iterations on the "Elf System", which are collectible upgrades that you can use during your missions. All of them are one-time use only, some provide permanent upgrades, others just a in-the-moment aid. It's a decent system, but I think it sometimes hinders the game by being so limited.

To cap it off the Zero series, let's mention the story. It feels very refreshing. It takes place years after the last X game, and it is all about dealing with the consequences of the advancements of the technology in that world. Also, you're not just fighting against the same big bad guy in the end of all games and this alone is great. Sure, the story does have an overaching goal with all the games, but it feels escalating and fitting, not like the old "and Sigma was behind this all along" type of writing.

Then we have the ZX series. It takes place years after the original Zero series. I think a good way to describe how this series feels is like comparing Mega Man 6 to Mega Man 8, Both are good, but the shift in tone and just the atmosphere of the games is different.

ZX tries to merge Zero's gameplay with X's, hence the name. And it work at places, but not on everything. You have different forms than just Zero's and basically these forms are the new skills you get along the way. It can feel good, but I missed having a single base form where I can add new skills and attacks to shake up my combos.

ZX Advent takes a step further away. You are no longer playing as "Zero", but now you're playing as "Axl", and instead of gaining new proper forms or skills you just copy the bosses you fight. Some feel like actual forms, others are very gimmicky, but it all feels unpersonal. And the default Axl form is just terrible compared to the original Zero, or the ZX form.

Aside from that, the games are fun to play. They all have this new faux Metroidvania style that shakes things up for the better, and for a lot of times, the worst. The original Zero series had a little bit of this on the first game, but it was in no way near as this, and it quickly revolved back to the classic stage select formula.

The story for the ZX series is even more on the center stage, and it is quite fun I'd might say. This time is more of a rehash of the Zero series, but it is competent and very passible.

The only extra thing about this collection that I'd might add is that with each achievement we unlock, we get these cards, that were physical collectibles back in the day, and we can activate minor changes over on Zero 3. It is fun, but since we have achievements for every game, we need to either play Zero 3 out of order, or revisit it after beating all games and getting all achievements. Minor gripe I'd say

Overall, it is a good collection, with great games and also great added value. These games were released over on the GBA and the DS, with all its limits, and it shows. Comparing them to the original X series there's a clear hardware limitation taking place, yet they are equally amazing, I'd say Zero 3 might be the best Mega Man game out there. This collection is very worth it, especially if you like Mega Man X and even more if you loved playing as Zero in those games.

Here is an honest review from the perspective of someone who really enjoyed the first two. Well, the first one and then MOST of the second one.

I played the entire game with a friend and let's just start with the positives. 

1. The game is very pretty. Art style is dead on from the last ones and they definitely managed to continue that same dark gritty fairytale esque setting.

That's unfortunately kind of it for me in the positives. I honestly think that the dev team should have just let this franchise go and not attempted to resurrect it with a new team and the same IP. It's obvious playing through the game that there was none of the engagement or the depth that LN1 or LN2 had.

Here is the specifics:

Coop is honestly used really lightly here. This isn't really a coop game. This is a "you need two bodies to open doors" game. There are only maybe three times during the whole game that actually had a puzzle where people needed to either separate to complete a puzzle or actually interact in unique ways giving each player an important task to solving something. 

The game's biggest flaw though is just that it's extremely boring. Even though the game took us about 6 hours to play, almost 4 of those hours felt like we were just either moving through a transitional room (meaning a room that may have some set pieces in them but doesn't actually do anything for the player, like a hallway that maybe has a light in it and a desk, but there is nothing you need to do in said room) or moving through a tiny hallway crouched in order to get to another room or just to get to another door that just requires both players to open. We did run into bugs and some of the objectives were just insanely unclear on what to do to progress and those were frustrating, but truly the most frustrating thing was just not being able to have any mechanics in the game that were engaging in any meaningful way.

Also, there is no reason to collect any of the secret little dolls as they don't unlock any costumes and the costumes they do have are paid DLC (WHICH IS INSANE BTW FOR A GAME THAT COSTS 40$ AND IS HONESTLY JUST A DOOR SIMULATOR). 

It's just a bundle of issues that come together to make a once 10/10 series a 4/10 at BEST, and a 2/10 at WORST. There is also an end game boss chase sequence that was bugged for us and many players where if you don't crouch ????? while you break into a new room after a chase that the game will just kill your player. It's apparently a moderately well known bug. How this made it into the game is beyond me.

Lastly, and this is a point in the game's favor, the absolutely END of the game story... like I am talking the last 30 seconds of story that the game actually had before you go back to main menu.... it was really good. The game had a really questionable hogdepodge of a story throughout the game and you were just kind of guessing as to what was happening, but then the game hits you directly in the feelings and gives you an incredibly sad moment that kind of came out of nowhere. My only question is like, where was this storytelling and engagement the rest of the game??? 

tl;dr - Game is just incredibly boring. Play Reanimal instead as that 25 minute demo has more gameplay than the entirety of LN3.

Darkest Dungeon: Uma Obra-Prima que Extrai Beleza do Desespero

Deixe-me ser claro desde o início: Darkest Dungeon não é um jogo para todos. É uma experiência brutal, um teste de fogo para sua estratégia, sua paciência e, principalmente, para sua sanidade. Mas para aqueles que se dispõem a enfrentar as trevas, ele se revela um dos RPGs táticos mais recompensadores e únicos já criados.

A primeira coisa que salta aos olhos é a atmosfera. A arte gótica e cartoonizada, inspirada em H.P. Lovecraft e H.R. Giger é excepcional. Cada ambiente é sombrio, detalhado e sufocante, criando um mundo onde a decadência é palpável. Essa imersão é elevada a outro patamar pela narração soturna e épica, uma voz que comenta seus triunfos e fracassos de forma inesquecível, e por uma trilha sonora tensa que se adapta perfeitamente à sua situação, aumentando a ansiedade a cada passo em corredores escuros.

No coração de Darkest Dungeon está sua jogabilidade genial e impiedosa. Este não é um simples RPG de turno. É um jogo de gerenciamento de recursos, riscos e, acima de tudo, da saúde mental dos seus heróis. A mecânica de estresse é a alma do jogo. Conforme seus aventureiros enfrentam horrores indizíveis, falham ataques ou são pegos de surpresa, seu estresse aumenta. Chegando ao limite, eles podem surtar, desenvolvendo desde paranoia até masoquismo, sabotando o grupo e espalhando o pânico. Cuidar da mente dos seus heróis é tão crucial quanto curar seus ferimentos, uma camada de profundidade brilhante que poucos jogos ousaram explorar.

Aqui, a morte é permanente. Perder um herói de nível alto para um golpe crítico inesperado é uma facada no peito, e a sensação de perda é real. O jogo é notório por seu RNG (sistema de sorte), que pode ser brutal, mas, com o tempo, você percebe que a verdadeira maestria está em gerenciar esses riscos. A dificuldade não é injusta; é exigente. Ela força você a pensar taticamente, a montar composições de grupo sinérgicas entre as diversas classes e a saber a hora de recuar. Fugir de uma masmorra para salvar o que restou do grupo não é um fracasso, é uma estratégia de sobrevivência. E a sensação de superar um chefe após uma batalha tensa, muitas vezes à beira do extermínio total, é eufórica e incomparável.

No entanto, o jogo tem suas arestas. A repetição pode surgir no meio da campanha, durante o "grind" necessário para melhorar sua cidade e heróis. Algumas classes podem parecer menos úteis que outras, levando a composições mais "meta". E, é claro, a frustração é uma companheira constante: levar um crítico devastador de um inimigo insignificante ou ver seu personagem favorito enlouquecer no momento crucial pode testar o seu controle emocional.

As DLCs, como The Crimson Court, adicionam conteúdo valioso, mas aumentam significativamente a complexidade e a dificuldade, sendo recomendadas para uma segunda jogatina.

Darkest Dungeon é um jogo que te machuca, te estressa e, paradoxalmente, te faz voltar por mais. É uma lição de humildade e resiliência. Apesar dos momentos de pura agonia, a sensação de conquista é avassaladora. A combinação perfeita de uma jogabilidade profunda, uma atmosfera opressiva e imersiva e mecânicas inovadoras cria uma experiência que gruda em você. Se você tem estômago para o desafio e aprecia jogos que não seguram sua mão, Darkest Dungeon não é apenas uma recomendação; é uma obrigação. Mas lembre-se da lição mais importante: não se apegue aos heróis. Na masmorra mais escura, a luz da vitória brilha sobre os ossos de muitos que caíram no caminho.

先说优点：优秀的氛围塑造。简洁的美术设计，丰富的配音与真实可感的环境音效，在初次游玩体验中能够给担任接线员和调度员角色的玩家以很强的代入感。同时报警电话事件均取自现实案例，对话树中囊括了许多应急处置常识，富有教育意义。

再说缺点：事件池不够充足，后期重复度过高，点点点的操作新鲜劲过了就极其无聊，这类老生常谈的就不说了，说一下我个人的体验。这个游戏在细节打磨上是极其不到位的，甚至是反常识的，具体在以下几点：

[b]反人类的UI和操作设计。[/b]应急力量安排界面没有一键编队/乘员换装的快捷键也就罢了，甚至不能从载具/乘员的空栏位中点击打开乘员/装备列表再逐个选中，只能一个一个的手动拖到相应的栏位，非常浪费玩家时间，尤其对我这样的喜欢把同类载具编号在一起的强迫症来说极其不友好。到了游戏主要的城市执勤界面情况又反过来了，一如既往的不能悬停查看单位、事件详情，只能去左下右下挨个翻列表，事件好歹可以在地图上点击查看，单位连大地图点击查看都没做。同时相应单位分配到具体的事件只能通过点一下某个单位再点一下事件的方式来完成，这次怎么又不搞拖动分配了？连框定部分单位然后一键行动这种RTS的基础操作都做不到。怎么麻烦玩家怎么设计是吧。折腾玩家倒也罢了，最严重的问题是小图标扎堆，在火灾/地震剧情中更为明显，十多个紧急状况图标堆在一起甚至重叠，互相阻挡视野同时还无法选中，即使派人过去也未必选中正确的图标，甚至加剧了问题（因为单位图标同样会重叠），经常出现“你以为对应的单位分配了对应的事件，实际上单位都跑到一个事件去了/在很近的地方挂机，然后事件无人处理时限结束开始扣声誉”这类性质极其恶劣，严重影响游戏体验的问题，你还拿它没办法。

[b]AI的智力严重不足让人又气又急。[/b]警察空闲时默认随机画龙，导致许多时候前往案发地点需要多绕路；无法设计警察巡逻路线，警察有时无法自动参与处理近在咫尺的案件而是在不远处绕圈，有时又自动参与与其无关的消防和医疗事件且无法离开。

[b]世界观设计的割裂。[/b]事件设计极其不合理，部分紧急情况内容与世界观设定不符，大量的治安案件诸如车祸（无伤者）、超速、闯红灯、吸毒，酗酒，性交，裸奔，扰民派对、酒驾、路怒症、毒贩子，流浪汉，一般盗窃居然都要出动玩家操纵的精英警力去管（就那么几辆车不可能是一个地区的所有公职人员），甚至部分并无紧急处置需求的一般社会事件比如猫上树、盗版软件、精神病人、车锁损坏等居然都要出动应急力量处置，实在不合常情。这是游戏设计的缺陷： [u]对玩家作为接线员和调度员的角色认定不明确。[/u]要么玩家主管特警，处理极端情况排除无用事件；要么主管全体警察处理治安案件，开局就应该多给点警力和车辆，而不是两三辆车五六个人一头扎进大城市。该缺陷在火灾事件期间极其明显，剧情强制玩家无视居民着火的车库（需要优先救人）却必须完成随机刷新的一堆通马桶任务，实在是过于荒谬。
 
[b]对话树选项和内容不合常情。[/b]这方面的例子可太多了。球队打架事件不能及时中断对面的废话问出关键信息，火灾事件中的选项不能直接询问安全通道，发生抗议时无辜店主被袭击，不能首先询问他是否有足以自保的武器，等等。事件处理结果的评分标准，判定逻辑更是存在严重问题。有些要好声好气适当撒谎安抚当事人，有些要实话实说明确表明态度，具体问题具体分析倒是没什么，但游戏并没有给出明确的判定标准和即时反馈，玩家只能看着下降的声誉发懵；部分剧情事件设计更是逆天，玩家一边调度武力镇压抗议，一边不能在电话中公然批评对方报假警，音乐节时面对投诉语气平和，却被判定为没有控制好情绪；电子音乐噪音事件中明知刁民瞎打电话拒绝出警却喜提扣分，甚至扣的分数比无视事件还多；烟花仓库火灾事件中车库着火无人员伤亡，拒绝出警被判定态度恶劣；抗议事件最后在电话中表态对国民警卫队遵守命令后，通话在事实上结束，只剩事件在地图上的持续时间进度条还没有走完的时候，选择忽略对话提前完成事件，居然会扣声誉？？？这是严重的恶性BUG。（注：抗议事件最后国民警卫队会入场要求玩家的警察撤离。玩家遵守命令涨声誉，拒绝则扣声誉。但弱智的地方在于，即使你表态遵守命令，和国民警卫队通话完成，同时撤回警察的前提下，提前点掉通话的图标也会扣三百声誉（游戏判定为拒绝国民警卫队要求），搞笑的是这样扣声誉最后结算的时候不会显示，明显属于恶性bug。）
再叠加上国情差异，某些事件足以造成百分百初见杀，比如一个高楼失火的事件，楼梯充斥浓烟，火烧到防盗门外，按照我们接受的教育应当是躲进卫生间这类小空间湿毛巾堵门然后不停门框浇水等待救援，但事件没有这个选项，结果当事人躲在公寓里把自己烧死了。最后解决方案是通过窗户进入紧邻的另一栋房屋再下到楼底，我是不知道老美有多少这种窗户相隔近到可以直接跨过去的公寓楼，至少中国没有。还有一个烤面包机着火的事件，三个选项没一个是断电，都是直接上手救火（水/灭火器/湿毛巾），我只能默认已经断电了然后选一个对家居损害最小的灭火方式，最后当事人触电了。谁教你一上来不断电直接灭火的？哪怕用二氧化碳灭火器也要断电啊。
最后还有老美特供的集体抗议过程中对普通人的伤害，非法移民问题，动保因为狗被撞了就报警，必须以政治正确的态度处理，牺牲无辜普通人的利益，让人看着恶心。虽然代入感这一块是到位了，但还是令人难评。

[b]极差的难度平衡性。[/b]这里点名批评专家模式的难度设计，在开局只给玩家三辆车的情况下，几分钟内能疯狂爆出多达十几个需要联合处置的复合事件，而且时限要求很紧，掉事件是不可避免的，加上掉事件没有提示，玩家往往只能后知后觉地看着声誉狂掉，有心处理也无力应对。遇上暴风雪事件所有载具趴窝更是可以直接等死。这游戏是内置控制台可以修改数据的，难道制作组想鼓励玩家开启控制台？ [/spoiler]

说了这么多可以得出结论：[b]瑜不掩瑕。[/b]在优秀的美工、配音掩盖之下是极其失败的游戏性，这样的作品也只能当个模拟器玩玩。

这家公司总能把优秀的题材做成垃圾的成品，同系列的112在没有或很少优化这些问题的同时，有着平衡性极其失败的DLC设计，后续的无感染区是个半成品，更还有反恐模拟器这种做一半跑路导致玩家永远无法全成就的骗钱作品（事实上他们的大部分游戏都是这种换汤不换药的复刻圈钱作）。你问我最终结论是什么，结论就是[b]他妈的不推荐。[/b]

[h3] 差点忘了，最后补充一点：迈阿密音乐节的配乐真他妈好听，谁没听过谁就等于白玩这个游戏。[/h3]

I remember a Dead Cells devlog from years ago where they were talking about controls. How game should not only react to buttons pressed but read the mind of a player as much as possible to make the medium of controller and monitor as transparent as possible, immersing the player in the game world.

Here is an antithesis to this idea. A game where controls hate you. A game that pretends to behave and let you have fun, all while lying in wait as a venomous serpent, poised to strike when you are most vulnerable. 

Every corner, every railing, every stair is a potential deathtrap, waiting for you to dodge or sprint by so that it'd lock you in place for mobs to punish you for trying to play this abomination. And then there are environmental puzzles in acts 2 and 3... I can imagine the dev thought process to be something like:
"At last, I have perfected the laggiest, most unresponsive and unreliable control scheme in gaming! How should I utilize it to its full potential? Hmm. How about making half a game a platformer?!"

Simply diabolical.

Очень похоже на Resident Evil 2 Remake: такой же хоррор-сёрвайвл с двумя героями (за которых играют звезды Дэвид Харбор и Джуди Комер), мрачной атмосферой и ограниченными ресурсами.

Запутанный сюжет. Игра намеренно сбивает с толку. Чтобы понять, что происходит, нужно внимательно читать все записки и документы. История — это микс из детектива и лавкрафтовских ужасов.

Несколько концовок. Есть разные варианты финалов — от плохих до очень странных. Чтобы увидеть полную картину, нужно пройти игру за обоих персонажей.

Итог: Хороший хоррор для тех, кому зашёл RE2 и кто не против запутанного сюжета. Если любите простые и понятные истории — эта игра не для вас.

Every room is a gamble. Every enemy a small psychological battle. Every upgrade — a double-edged sword. The controls are deceptively simple, but the depth of strategy is staggering. You’ll die a hundred times, maybe a thousand, but each death teaches something new.
What makes Isaac legendary isn’t just its challenge, but its infinite replayability. With hundreds of items, synergies, and secret endings, it’s a labyrinth of discovery that can swallow hundreds — even thousands — of hours. No two runs are ever the same, and no run ever feels wasted.
It’s brutally hard, emotionally heavy, and unforgettable.

I've been putting off playing this game for awhile now and all my preconceived notions about The Binding of Isaac Rebirth have been completely wrong, easily one of the finest, most unique roguelike I’ve ever played. Don’t be fooled by its silly or innocent appearance the rabbit hole runs deep, and there’s far more to this gem than meets the eye. Let’s start with the gameplay. The core mechanics are simple, and while the game is challenging, it’s easy to understand at first. But before long, you’ll find your progress blocked by hidden secrets and mysterious mechanics you’ll have to uncover on your own. The RNG and the vast variety of items ensure that every run feels distinct, keeping the game fresh even after hundreds of hours. My only real complaint about The Binding of Isaac is that same randomness it’s both its greatest strength and its biggest frustration. Sometimes a run can be completely derailed by bad luck or a lack of essential items like keys or bombs. Still, that unpredictability is part of what makes it so compelling. There’s a wide roster of characters, each with their own challenges, abilities, and unlockables. On PC, that roster can grow even larger thanks to the community’s endless stream of modded characters and items. Now, onto what I think is Binding of Isaac’s greatest strength the story. What sets this game apart from other roguelikes isn’t just its addictive gameplay, but its mysterious, symbolic narrative. Beneath the grotesque humour and cartoonish style lies a deeply thematic story filled with religious symbolism and psychological undertones. Many fan theories attempt to piece together what truly happened to Isaac and his family, but the game ultimately leaves it open to interpretation. Whether it’s the haunting imagery, the cryptic storytelling, or the endlessly replayable gameplay loop, The Binding of Isaac Rebirth is a game that will stick with you.

The Haunted Carousel is the eighth Nancy Drew adventure game. In this game, Nancy has to investigate some strange incidents that have shut down a theme park. Despite the fact that the park is supposed to be "haunted," the "ghost" activity never feels at all supernatural and that aspect of the mystery isn't focused on very much. This is one of the shorter games in the series, even among the early games.

This game relies less on logic puzzles than some of the other games. Instead, you'll collect objects and interrogate suspects. There are also a couple of minigames, which were pretty easy and, unlike in some of the other games, not annoying. My biggest issue with this game was that some of the items and locations are pretty easy to miss. I needed help from a walkthrough a couple of times, and it was usually because I had missed something onscreen. It was usually pretty easy to figure out what to do with all the items after you find them. This game offers a task list, and unlike most of the later games you can still use it if you're playing on senior detective.

The mystery was fine but didn't really pull me in. The culprit wasn't obvious from the beginning and all the suspects had believable motives, and there was a sweet subplot about uncovering a character's past. All the parts of the story fit together and the answers weren't too obvious, it just didn't stand out for being interesting, unique, or particularly suspenseful. The setting also isn't particularly interesting or memorable.

Overall, The Haunted Carousel was an okay game with some minor flaws. I enjoyed playing it, but nothing about it stood out to me compared to the other games in the series. 6/10

Quiplash 2 InterLASHional, developed and published by Jackbox Games, Inc., represents one of the studio’s most refined and inclusive takes on the party game formula they helped popularize. Building upon the success of the original Quiplash and its sequel, this version adds a global twist—expanding the experience into multiple languages while maintaining the same sharp wit, fast-paced humor, and socially driven chaos that defines the series. It’s a celebration of creativity and comedic timing, built around the simple idea that laughter is universal, even if the punchlines are not always perfect across every culture. Designed for gatherings both in-person and online, Quiplash 2 InterLASHional aims to make anyone, anywhere, part of the fun.

At its core, the game’s premise remains disarmingly simple yet endlessly entertaining. Each round presents players with a series of prompts—sometimes absurd, sometimes clever, and occasionally bizarre—that they must complete with their own witty responses. Once everyone submits their answers, the group votes on which one is the funniest. The winner earns points, but the true reward comes in the form of shared laughter, playful teasing, and the unpredictability of group humor. Anyone with a smartphone, tablet, or laptop can join by entering a code into a web browser, making setup effortless and gameplay highly accessible. There are no complicated mechanics to learn and no skill barrier; all that matters is imagination, timing, and how well you can read the sense of humor in the room.

Where Quiplash 2 InterLASHional distinguishes itself from its predecessor is in its embrace of multilingual accessibility. The game supports English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish, each with its own set of culturally adapted prompts and jokes. This expansion makes it far more inclusive and ideal for international groups or multilingual households. The humor, of course, varies between languages—some jokes hit differently depending on cultural context—but the inclusion of unique prompts for each language demonstrates Jackbox’s genuine effort to make everyone feel included in the joke. It’s an especially welcome feature for families or friends who speak different native languages but still want to share the same experience. The humor may occasionally stumble in translation, but it often gains a new kind of charm when played among diverse groups, creating spontaneous moments of cross-cultural comedy.

The game’s presentation and design retain the signature Jackbox flair—colorful, cartoonish visuals, playful music, and smooth pacing that keeps the energy high throughout a session. The minimalist interface ensures that the jokes remain at the center of attention. It’s the players who create the content, not the game itself, which means that every round feels fresh and personal. Whether the humor is sharp satire, surreal nonsense, or unabashed immaturity, the unpredictability of human creativity keeps the experience alive. The host’s quips and reactions provide a layer of continuity, and even when a joke flops, the light-hearted tone prevents the atmosphere from ever turning dull.

Beyond the linguistic additions, Quiplash 2 InterLASHional doesn’t change the underlying mechanics of the series, and that’s both a strength and a limitation. For newcomers, it remains one of the most approachable and entertaining social games on the market. For returning players who already own Quiplash 2 or have access to it through the Jackbox Party Pack 3, this edition might feel familiar. The main differentiator is the broader accessibility and the slight refinement in prompt writing and interface polish. However, for those who regularly host game nights with international friends, language learners, or multicultural families, this expanded edition offers a level of inclusivity that justifies its existence. It transforms the party game from a strictly English-speaking affair into something more universal.

Quiplash 2 InterLASHional also thrives in online and streaming environments. Like other Jackbox titles, it supports an audience feature, allowing larger groups of spectators to vote and influence the results. This makes it perfect for live streams, remote gatherings, or community events where not everyone can directly participate. The simplicity of joining via browser means even casual players or less tech-savvy participants can join without hassle. The design philosophy here is elegant: reduce barriers, maximize fun, and let personality drive the entertainment. It’s a testament to Jackbox’s understanding of social dynamics that even years after its original release, Quiplash still feels fresh when played with the right group of people.

That said, the game’s success ultimately depends on the players themselves. Quiplash 2 InterLASHional is less about winning or losing and more about the energy shared between participants. With the right crowd, it becomes hysterical—a room full of people laughing uncontrollably at each other’s offbeat humor. With the wrong crowd, it can fall flat, as the game relies heavily on player engagement and creativity. The prompts are designed to encourage absurdity, but they only come alive when players embrace the silliness. It’s a game that thrives on personality, improvisation, and camaraderie, making it perfect for casual parties, family gatherings, or virtual hangouts.

In the end, Quiplash 2 InterLASHional succeeds because it understands that the essence of good humor transcends borders. It’s not about complex systems or visual spectacle—it’s about laughter, connection, and shared creativity. By expanding its linguistic reach, Jackbox Games has opened the door for even more people to participate in the chaos, proving that humor can bridge cultural gaps in ways few other games can. While it doesn’t reinvent the formula, it refines and expands it in meaningful ways. For anyone seeking a versatile, inclusive, and endlessly replayable party experience, Quiplash 2 InterLASHional is one of the best options available—a simple but brilliant reminder that the funniest thing in any room is still the people in it.

I tried to start a few times and always ended up finding something more interesting to do instead. Between attempts, I did a bunch of research, and I discovered that the game, while interesting, has a huge number of sharp corners that can result in an extremely unpleasant experience.

One dungeon at the end of the campaign in particular, The House on the Edge of Time, or something like that, is infamous for having many players drop their campaigns in it.

For such a massive game, the prospect of encountering these things is very discouraging. Especially since i'm sure a good portion of my time here would simply be padding.

Besides that, the very easy possibility of creating useless builds if you don't have a deep understanding of the system (because balancing a video game with this amount of variables is practically impossible) or being overwhelmed by a kingdom management system that even the game's most die-hard fans seem to hate tells me the game doesn't seem worth the time.

Still, with the little I've played, I've been able to recognize qualities that some players might appreciate, such as a high level of customization and role-playing opportunities (as long as it's within the game's simplistic tone), and the nearly inexhaustible replayability these factors offer.

The presentation in almost every way is excellent for a mid-budget game in this genre.

And for better or worse, at least they do a good job of covering the game with information everywhere, so as long as you have the patience for a tutorial format that requires a lot of effort and probably isn't all that worthwhile, it should work because the information will at least be there, in ample detail, even if not intuitively.

The writing, however, seems quite poor. Long paragraphs, full of redundant prose. No objectivity whatsoever. Flowery, but lacking eloquence or genuine emotion to color the text and simultaneously function as a conversation.

It doesn't take long, and right in the prologue, you'll see examples of diplomacy checks where the logic and arguments presented make no sense, and certain characters will accept very stupid and forced opposing arguments simply because you failed the checks.

People with completely nonsensical motivations who seem to have stepped out of a cartoon for very young children.

The characters seem like parodies straight out of the rulebooks.

The feeling I got was that a game designed to fit a niche of 10-year-olds who have a PhD.

Still, you might be one of those legendary kids, or you might be more tolerant of the writing than I am, and actually get to the meat of the story and find something interesting there, or you might simply enjoy the gameplay for its gargantuan complexity. So, since I didn't make it all the way to the end, I'll give it a thumbs up. Because I actually didn't find anything major wrong with the game so far, though I've resigned myself to not trying to play it again.

It seems like an ambitious project that could well benefit from being cut in half and having the rules and options streamlined to make it easier to join in on the fun, if it even exists.

The general recommendations I found were to ignore more than half of the content, which is always a bad sign.

P.S: There's a popular YouTuber who's made several very comprehensive and extensive video guides about this game and its sequel (to several RPGs, actually) called Mortismal Gaming.

If you have no idea what you're getting into, I recommend checking it out and watching a few things so you don't make unnecessary mistakes and waste your time restarting campaigns or reading irrelevant information.

Alternatively, another channel called MandaloreGaming has a video giving an overview of the game, without going into too much detail, more accessible for those who don't want to waste two hours watching the other guy.

[h1]良かった点[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]やりごたえがある[/b]
難易度が手頃かつ多様で、サクッとクリアできる爽快なステージがある一方、数個に一個は何回かやり直すほどの難しさが有ります。

各ステージのクリアには防腐剤軍団をカビで押し戻して殲滅する必要が有ります。カビはクリックで生成され、その後は自動で右に走っていくので、敵の出現位置に合わせて、有利に戦えるユニットを適量配置し数的有利を広げていく形です。配置するタイミングやカビの種類を間違えると簡単に壊滅して殺菌されてしまうので、注意深くカビを配置する必要が有ります。

ステージが進むと、異なる弱点を持った複数の敵が同時にでてきて弱点をつくのが難しくなります。片方のユニットには強いがもう片方には弱いといったことが頻繁に起こるため、こちらも複数のカビを駆使し配置するタイミングや順序を工夫することになります。

[*][b]キャラデザインがよい[/b]
韓国製のようなのですが、日本的な既視感のある属性デザインではなく、欧米のような異文化のセンスほどでもなく、適度に新鮮です。攻撃方法や耐性などの特徴も色々バリエーションがあり、キャラが良く立っていると思います。
[/list]

[h1]悪かった点[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]戦略の幅が少ない[/b]
配置を色々試すのは楽しいのですが、前進後退の指示や陣形地形を利用した戦略ではありません。上に書いたように、敵と味方の弱点の組み合わせを配置タイミングでうまくやりくりするケースばかりです。盾キャラと遠距離キャラの後方支援陣形ぐらいはできますが、そういった技術だけで打開できることは少なく、弱点の要素がメインです。カビをたくさん出せるボーナスタイムや、カビごとに異なる特殊能力の発動などもありますが、大きく戦況を左右する活用は難しく、やりようが少ない印象です。

[*][b]メニューの操作がわかりにくい[/b]
メニューのどこが操作できるのか、スティックをどう動かせばどこへ行くのかがわかりにくく、ストレスが溜まるレベルです。落ち着いて十字キーで一個ずつ動かすのが良いです。
[/list]

I think my current playtime speaks volumes for how much I enjoy this little game, but I'll ramble on.

Ropuka's Idle Island is a very very simple and basic idle game that sits anywhere on your desktop. It's very easy to resize Ropuka and his island and relocate it so that it won't get in the way of anything, and you can toggle it so that it can or can't take priority over other windows (sit on top). He's just a little frog guy who has a little island to take care of, he won't disrupt you! You can also turn off the music and ambience separately, meaning that I can mute the music but still keep the sounds of wind and birds to a "low hum" for relaxation.

I've seen some people deem this game "boring", and I get that. This is no action game, there isn't much you can do with Ropuka other than customise him and his island. But it's important to remember this game is intended to give you a little desktop friend who does his own thing whilst you also do your own thing. I personally like big numbers and seeing them rise, so I like leaving him for a few hours and coming back to see millions of grass trimmings. Plus, this game is very low-demand so you can easily run a different game or other programs alongside it!

Overall, I love the little chill vibes this game brings. And I love little Ropuka, too.

The main reason I installed this game was to have more dialogue with my daughter. Every night, she comes into my office and says, “Daddy, I want to see the frog.” And every day, I change his clothes and the setting so that each time she comes, there’s something new for her to talk to me about.

This game had some big shoes to fill after west of loathing came out, and it filled them Shadows over Loathing is a fantastic game thats a few times the length of a West of Loathing and an overall great time, with stunningly beautiful and dramatic music. 

However, I feel like SoL is the inferior product to WoL. The classes in my opinion are a big step back from how they were done in WoL, it sticks to the 3 M's (Muscle, Moxie, and Mysticality) but somehow makes them feel a lot less impactful. while there are a lot of Stat checks, there are far more elemental resistance checks, this is done because you cant spec into your M's directly, and have to purchase them alongside other upgrades on your character sheet.

Character progression in general feels like a step down from WoL, you can no longer spend XP to directly put a point into a stat. Instead you get 4 single tick boxesfor each stat, plus a few more general upgrades, that you can purchase for 1 point in the stat, and some other boost like more AP. This simplifies the system, but its more limiting. Previously in WoL, there was a large variety of things you could spend your XP on from the get-go, did you need to pass a skill check? grab the point in the main stat and do it, no sweat. Did you need to eat more food for a buff that would help you out? upgrade Grit, Glamour, or Gumption, and feast! Now you can spend points on the stat boxes, exactly 1 time, for a total of 5 in each stat once you have everything upgraded. and you can't even increase the amount of potions, liquor, or food you can intake for buffs, you can eat infinitely but only 1 buff in each category of consumable is active. Grinding is made semi-pointless unless you for some reason want to grind out all the sheet upgrades in chapter 1.

It's an RPG game, combat is one of the main focuses, and honestly Shadows does it pretty well, there's more strategy in West of Loathing since stacking up stuff that gives AP isn't viable anymore. For the most part Jazz Agent, and Cheese wizard (Moxie and Mysticality) are fine, they get combat abilities that relate to their theming, Jazz Agent plays instruments that adds more sounds to the battle music, and cheese wizard does stuff with cheese, but Pig Skinner, the muscle class, got the VERY short end of the stick, what you would expect, a skilled knifeworker who can skin whatever is in front of them, is instead a generic highschool bully giving people noogies and making them hit themselves. compared to the Seal Clubber, the Turtle tamer, and the Cow Puncher of games past, the Pig Skinner is really stripped of an identity, a better name would've been "Nerd Slapper" or something.

Ok look, Is Shadows over Loathing worth it? Absolutely 100%, if you loved West of Loathing, then you will love Shadows, there is a lot to be enjoyed, but there is also a lot to be envied , and a lot to be learned from the masterpiece that came before it. The years of development time were not wasted, the hundreds of hours of writing time to make the story work, incorporate gags, and more, these are all best experienced by playing the game, thanks for reading, it means a lot if you didn't skip to the end!

Duke Nukem 3D: 20th Anniversary World Tour is a polished re-release of the 1996 classic that keeps the original game’s attitude and action intact while adding small modern touches. It’s still the same fast, over-the-top shooter, but with a few updates to make it run and look better on today’s systems.

The core gameplay hasn’t changed—and that’s a good thing. You run, shoot, and blow everything up while searching for keycards and secrets. The levels remain open-ended and packed with hidden paths, traps, and explosive fun. It’s pure, old-school FPS design that rewards curiosity and aggression in equal measure.

The “World Tour” edition adds a brand-new episode called Alien World Order, created by members of the original development team. It’s a solid expansion with new locations, enemies, and weapons that blend perfectly with the old content. It feels like genuine 90s design, not a fan-made add-on.

Visually, the remaster adds dynamic lighting and smoother performance. It’s not a full remake—the sprites and geometry are still retro—but everything runs at high resolution and looks crisp. You can also switch between classic and updated lighting modes, which is a nice touch for purists.

Audio got some attention too. Jon St. John re-recorded Duke’s iconic voice lines, and the soundtrack includes new music from the original composer. There’s also a commentary mode that offers insight into the design of each level, adding a bit of historical depth for long-time fans.

Technically, the game is stable and runs well across platforms. Controls are tighter, aiming feels better with a mouse or controller, and level transitions are seamless. The simplicity of the design means it loads fast and plays smoothly even on low-end hardware.

Overall, Duke Nukem 3D: 20th Anniversary World Tour is exactly what it should be—a respectful, energetic remaster of a legendary shooter. It doesn’t try to modernize too much or change what worked. Instead, it celebrates what made Duke Nukem 3D iconic: fast gameplay, big explosions, and unapologetic attitude.

Rayman Legends is a great game. I've played it twice through now, once on Wii U and another time on Steam. The game feels a little bit more natural to play on Wii U because there are certain challenges that use the Wii U gamepad. However, the Steam version works fine. The game is colorful and interesting, and the music (especially the end of world music stages) is great. A nice quality of the game is that it includes many of the Rayman Origins stages in addition to the newer Rayman Legends stages. I think it's an overall good experience, and it's worth playing.

I think the main complaint I have with this game for both the Wii U and Steam editions is the end game grind for either max level or the final achievement. On Wii U and other consoles, there is a final level of "awesomeness" that is only acquired by continuing to play weekly challenges. The servers for these challenges are no longer in place, so this is no longer an attainable end game requirement. However, to unlock the final in-game costume and earn the final steam achievement, you need to acquire 1,000,000 Lums. By the end of the game, you will probably have around 450,000 to 500,000 Lums. Savvier folks will use a hex editor to edit their save to attain 1,000,000 lums. Less savvy folks, like myself, will grind Lums for a couple months, a little at a time.

I think it's an overall fun game and one that's easy to recommend for more casual players, but the completionist grind for the 11th level of awesomeness or 1,000,000 Lums detracts from the overall experience. 

For those with a Steam Deck, I found the game to work flawlessly at 4K 60 FPS on my television. Though, the game's colors really pop on the OLED screen of the Steam Deck.

Se nota muchísimo la inspiración en SH de este juego. Los escenarios en los que cada personaje está atrapado funcionan como un purgatorio personal, basado en algún hecho traumático u horrible de su pasado, de manera muy similar a lo que ocurre con James, Angela y Eddie en Silent Hill 2. 
La música, la ambientación, y el diseño tanto de los monstruos como de los personajes están muy bien logrados. No llegan a ser espectaculares, pero cumplen perfectamente con lo que buscan transmitir y consiguen crear un tono inquietante muy efectivo. Los puzzles son bastante buenos y no demasiado complicados. 
Como suele ocurrir en este tipo de títulos, el combate es el punto más flojo. Es tosco y poco satisfactorio, aunque los enemigos son lo suficientemente fáciles de derrotar como para que no llegue a convertirse en un problema serio. 
La cámara es fija, siguiendo el estilo de los survival horror clásicos, y ofrece planos muy cinematográficos al estilo del primer Silent Hill. La única excepción son las secciones de Carlos, donde la cámara pasa a primera persona. Esta decisión no termina de aportar algo significativo a la historia; quizá se buscaba ocultar la identidad del personaje, pero aun así no parece del todo justificada. Además, en algunos momentos la cámara fija de las secciones de Roman y Freya puede marear un poco debido a que no se comporta del todo con fluidez.
Las voces en ingles son bastante mal actuadas y hasta en ocasiones podrían resultar simpáticas, también no se porque el personaje de Roman dice palabras en Japones, como si se olvidaran de doblar esas partes.
Aun así, es un juego totalmente recomendable para disfrutarlo en unas pocas horas. Tiene una historia interesante, una atmósfera muy bien lograda y un fuerte toque nostálgico para los fans del género.

Review of Kingdom Rush 5: Alliance TD 6/10
Overall it has been a good experience to play this game. Personally I have been very hyped and excited for this installment and I did unfortunately not find that it lived up to my expectations.
The theme of an alliance of good and evil, and of having two heroes is unfortunately not explored very thoroughly.

If you are looking for a Kingdom Rush game this is it. If you are looking for THE Kingdom Rush game, this is not it.

Main campaign 6/10
The main campaign felt very short with only 3 areas, I would love for it to have had a 4th area or more.
The levels have been somewhat polarizing, some levels were awesome, requiring me to think about what I had to change about my strategy to complete it. On the other hand, some levels were just boring, and at times unpleasant to play.

The first area was very beautiful and well crafted, I liked the thematic and the difficulty.

Aesthetically the second area was only decent, however the difficulty was very fun! I had to spend time to adjust my strategy, and think about what towers and upgrades I wanted to bring to the battlefield.

Personally the last area was thematically uninteresting. The maps were annoying to play because of the ”eye” mechanic of the maps, healing and buffing the enemy units. It felt very uninteractive to play against since there was not much I could do to prevent it. On some maps there is an opportunity to fight the enemies before and after but it does not matter that much. Also the last 3 levels i just spammed the eldritch channeler and found it to be the most effective :(

Heroes 4/10
The heroes are for me mostly quite uninteresting. The whole idea behind having two heroes is for them to be strong and interact a lot with the levels. Yes, that did happen, but I only ever seemed to find myself using Raelyn + Someone else.

If you're a fan of Atelier games, you'll like this one. If you're not, this one won't do anything to garner your interest in the series. That being said it IS a step in the right direction from what Atelier Yumia was.

Atelier games have always been about two things. Cute Girls Doing Cute Things, and a deep, indepth alchemy system that starts simple and gradually gets more complex as you unlock more functionality, get access to more items/recipes and progress further into the game.

This has a little less of the CGDCT aspect due to the existence of Slade, but there's enough of it to scratch the itch. More importantly the Alchemy system, while still fairly simple, is a marked improvement over Yumia. Atelier Yumia fumbled their system so badly that by the 2nd (of like 5) areas you were already making items so powerful you could beat the rest of the game on Charismatic Difficulty (the hardest difficulty). Traits didn't matter. Item effects didn't matter. Nothing mattered. You just stacked so many stats on your items that you capped all your attributes at 999 and made your items do 1,000,000 damage. It made the alchemy system all but pointless in Yumia, destroying the core aspect of the game.

That's not the case here. You can get strong, early on, sure, but the best traits, items, and abilities are story gated and it's impossible to make OP items very early on. It's a return to form for Alchemy and that's a good thing. You feel 'rewarded' for using all the systems to the fullest and not it just being a waste of time because you go from 1-shotting + a million to 1-shotting + a billion.

The music isn't anything special (except the final boss) but it's not so offensive that you get tired of listening to it. The voice acting is really good and the facial expressions are REALLY good. I've never seen the Atelier girls this expressive before and I really enjoyed it.

Then there is the combat system. It's going back to the earlier games with its turn-based system and I prefer that to the Action combat of Ryza and yumia. Turn-based gives you time to think strategically and enjoy the battle. With the Action combat in Yumia/Ryza I couldn't enjoy the battle. I was just mashing buttons and watching cooldowns. I often didn't see much of what was actually going on.

That being said the game isn't perfect. There is a major, glaring flaw in it.

The Story, in particular a singular character.

Rias. She is the problem. The main female character. We've had main male characters before in Mana Khemia, so it's been done before, but I get why they're hesitant to make this game focus around one. That being said, Slade and the story are dragged down by Rias. Slade feels like a real person with a solid head on his shoulders who is unfortunately made to have his personality warped to Rias' stride. Rias also doesn't seem to serve any purpose in the story aside from being the Alchemy bot. Her eyes are what allowed her to do alchemy, not her own ability. And beyond that she was used for little else. All the plot revolved around Slade and what he brought to the table. Give Slade her eyes and there'd be no reason for her to be there aside from having a token cute mascot girl. 

Rias is at least cute, so I do give her a point for that.

The story itself is bare bones, but that's fairly typical for Atelier games. Only the Ryza and Dusk trilogies had truly deep, overarching stories that had genuine long-term implications and game-to-game connections. So I wasn't expecting too much. The story is often just a backdrop for the alchemy and CGDCT interactions.

So I'll get to what I consider to be the biggest flaw. Atelier games shouldn't have forced romance. Period. You can NOT introduce a half dozen amazing characters and then say 'only this one is canon'. There's a REASON past Atelier games had multiple endings that often paired the MC with the various interesting party members/characters you met in the story. It's to give the player the agency to CHOOSE the ending they wish to be canon. What makes this game especially egregious is that it felt like they were setting that up. Everyone had a journey they were going to set out on. Everyone asked the MC to join them. The MC had a good rapport with all of them.

But then the game is all like 'HAHA SYKE!'. If the game was leading into a sequel, ok sure, but this game very neatly wraps up everything and there's no room for a sequel.

Anyways, forced relationships is, I think, something Atelier shouldn't do. It hasn't been done well since the Atelier Iris games, but those games were structured more like your prototypical JRP game rather than an Atelier game which is what allowed them to get away with it.

Anyways, overall score? 7.5/10. My grip about the ending aside, it is a marked improvement over Yumia. We have an improved alchemy system (although it can still be better), an improved combat system, decent music and vastly improved character animations and graphics.

If you're an Atelier fan I do suggest getting this game. I genuinely feel it's a step back to form, and a step up from Atelier Yumia. A return to form as it were.
