The Castlevania Dominus Collection continues on Konami's actually commendable video game preservation methods, while providing great emulation features. Even if Konami just shovels all the work off to M2, who has been doing an amazing job at recreating or servicing these old, important Castlevania games. The Dominus Collection has great built-in rewind, save states, etc. for cheesing to your heart's content. 
Dawn of Sorrow, sequel to Aria of Sorrow, is the first game chronologically of this trio of great Metroidvanias. A truly beautiful pixel art game, held back somewhat by the anime art style for character portraits. Sadly both Dawn of Sorrow and Portrait of Ruin are somewhat marred by this choice, but I digress. Dawn of Sorrow's main character continues his adventure from Aria of Sorrow, still providing smooth control and a diverse play style with various weapon types and magics to supplement. It even features a handy two load-out equipment layout for easy testing. The setting is unique, like Aria of Sorrow, yet again, diverting from Dracula's Castle and being placed in a cultist base instead. Sadly, the level design isn't the pinnacle of Metroidvanias, as there are some repeating and mirrored rooms. But, overall, yet another fantastic addition to anyone's Metroidvania library.
Portrait of Ruin is a very hopeful experience at the beginning, implementing an incredibly interesting partner system. The main characters of the game are hot-swappable at any time, able to both be on the field at the same time with one as an NPC companion, and be used for puzzles in a handful of ways. Sadly, the game under utilizes this mechanic as it falls to the wayside about two hours in, and is only sparingly used throughout the rest of the game. But, both characters provide unique play styles and the new quest mechanic is fun to interact with. Although the castle provides an underwhelming padding experience in the latter half of the game with very little interesting backtracking, every Castlevania game has a great soundtrack to listen to as you wander so the exploration for 100% is still worth it.
Order of Ecclesia is my favorite Metroidvania in this pack, but I can certainly say that it suffers somewhat from the only mild backtracking and linear level-based world map. I personally love this aspect of the game. The game is difficult, journey across the map is hard-won, and the payoff of getting to a "real", large-scale Metroidvania map in the final section of the game is therefore satisfying. The weapon system in this game in particular works on a weakness system, so having now three load-outs to swap around allows you to stay strong against any particular enemy you fight. There is even a "proficiency" system, allowing you to increase the damage you do with types of damage, up to three times damage before enemy weaknesses are factored in. Fair warning, though, for "true" 100%, you will have to grind this out for a large chunk of time. Regardless, this game contains the titular "Dominus," and is at the forefront of the marketing for it's beautiful art style. This game alone makes this pack worth it.
Finally, Haunted Castle and Haunted Castle Revisited are part of the Dominus Collection. Haunted Castle and Revistied are Classicvanias, or in other words, linear, level-based games. Haunted Castle is a horrifically hard, super punishing arcade game from the past that, as with any Castlevania, has highly influential songs that sadly make the slog of save-state scumming through it worthwhile. Revisited is a modern, Dominus Collection-exclusive, faithful recreation of Haunted Castle. Revisited is a forgiving, hand crafted, pixel art masterpiece that only takes about an hour and a half at most to beat.

[b]Thronefall[/b] — це той випадок, коли очікуєш спокійну й вдумливу стратегію в мінімалістичному стилі, а отримуєш жвавий симулятор нічних оборон у жанрі «захисту веж». Ця гра під настрій і дарує різнобарвний потік емоцій: від цікавості та захоплення до дратування й навіть моменти нудьги. Водночас затишна, приємна на вигляд і часом зачаровує своєю простотою. [b]Thronefall[/b] цілком вписується в категорію так званих «вбивців часу» — легких, швидких ігрових розваг, які зараз особливо популярні серед сучасних гравців, а найбільше поширені на мобільних пристроях. Баланс місій нерівномірний: одні проходяться майже на автоматі, а інші перетворюються на справжню боротьбу з хвилями ворогів з різними модифікаторами. Візуальна частина тішить око: чисті лінії, м’які кольори та відчуття настільної мініатюри. Проте за цим мінімалізмом іноді ховається спрощеність, якій бракує стратегічної глибини. І все ж, попри певну монотонність, гра має дивну притягальність. У ній легко загубитися й провести доволі багато часу. [b]Played this as an actual drinking game last night - and it was a riot![/b] I have a group that plays [i]TowerFall[/i] and [i]SpeedRunners[/i] like twice a week. We will try anything that supports major local co-op action. This game was a no brainer.

What is cool about this title is that the game modes are randomized for each round. One round may be a race, one may be a deathmatch, and yet another may be an obstacle course. The variety is great. Everything stays lite and accessible for newish players yet there is still some cool difficulty for old-school gamers. Here is a great example of how they accomplish this: there is a room with lots of spike hazards, and it is a race to the end. If you can get to the end without touching a single one - you can win it in one go, BUT if you touch a spike, it is removed, essentially making the run easier. You keep respawning infinitely after death.

[b]Totally accessible game that is really fun for local co-op. I highly recommend.[/b]

原文：
首先提出总结：我对NBA2k的氪度肝度的容忍度最多就停留在2k25了，这代买了算我倒霉，下一代真不买了。我从2k9开始买光盘装机打，到这一代，16年了，2k这十几年的变化我看在眼里，我还一直很怀念十三四年前玩2K贴吧的时光，所以我对这个游戏系列基本很少提出批评，情怀一直在心里。

但是这一代我玩了一段时间了，有点忍不住，有很多话想说。

第一，如果游戏允许氪金，是不是能通过氪金来减少玩家的肝度呢，结果没有，一个玩的舒服的账号，你氪了能获得快速的能力增长，但是破冒器你就得通过肝了，没见过这种花了钱还得当牛马的，劳资TM平时上班当牛马，进了游戏还得当牛马，还是花钱当的。

第二，作为NBA系列的游戏，线上什么先发成就，终生成就基本上就是线上游戏获得的，你打NBA比赛获得了什么四双五双，历史最高分，三分王等等，都不算一个独立的成就。你想要通过成就得到破冒器，你不玩线上是不可能的，独狼玩线上想赢基本是不可能的，这里要点名几个欧服的锁闭素人，打公园不仅球不传，还开公麦扯着嗓子边打边唱歌，突出一个伪人，两天碰见三个了。

第三，2k如果你这么喜欢钱，这么喜欢搞篮球之城，这么喜欢搞线上茬架，你就不如弄个NBA2K线上版的，你到时候想搞什么RPG元素，抽卡元素都可以。

最后槽点，我看到很多人说什么不管挂壁，封刷成就的人，我觉得最严重的问题就是我花了两百多买了，进去还叫我花钱搞什么通行证，再就是游戏建模起点低，你光靠打线下基本得不到足够的VC去提升自己的模，他就是要暗搓搓地逼你充钱，不然游戏体验差到玩不下去，所以这种无孔不入的微交易逼氪才真的是该骂的，还有这一代更绝了，他除了要拿走我的钱，还要最大程度上拿走我的时间，那种专精获得的破冒器还有徽章+1 +2，你累死累活都拿到了，再建一个膜，专精的东西没了！你还得重新来。

Another neutral rating if Steam would allow me to select that. To preface - turned based combat really isn't my thing, but I've enjoyed a few games with it and wanted something a little Halloweeny that was a little relaxing.

I was initially pretty hooked on the game. A cozy town, beautiful pixel art, and a pretty interesting story. There were some minor annoyances though - forced to do certain tasks in the beginning with absolutely no freedom to explore and figure things out on your own. Still, I pushed through because it was still new and I was engaged. However, as the game progressed the newness wore off and I eventually found myself just wanting to reach the end - and I just stopped at that point.

Pros:
- It is a pretty cozy town.
- Really nice pixel art.
- Interesting story

Neutral:
- Combat seems to be pretty standard turn based stuff

Cons:
- Some mechanics I feel weren't explained well or traits not shown surrounding combat. I wish it was easier to see what switching demons will do to the available skills of your character. I did a large "upgrade"/switching of demons and ended up inadvertently losing some nicely balanced skills which was very annoying.
- Choices, puzzles, and story felt very on the rails.
- Subjective, but the combat music is just....awful. Like teeny bopper j/k-pop bad. Thank god they at least let you disable the lyrics.
- The town, while cozy, felt...fake maybe? NPCs zip by but really don't go anywhere or do anything. Everything was made to look filled out but it was very surface level. Named characters would almost always be standing in the same spot.

I feel this is worth getting on sale if you're a big fan of turn-based combat RPGs and wanting something a little Halloweeny, but otherwise I don't think you're really missing much by passing. Giving it a positive rating because I did get it on sale, it's an indie dev, and I did really enjoy about 1/2 my playtime with it.

Methodical, intentional, and tense gameplay that makes defense fun. This is one of the most underrated fighting games of the past ten years, only dismissed because it launched with poor delay-based netcode and no cross-play right before the pandemic—a time when fighting games lived or died by the netcode. Even then, everyone who played the game on launch had nothing but praise for its less mechanical/high-octane but more concise, taut, and deliberate approach. 

Now that the game is bolstered by rollback netcode and an incredibly fun roster, it’s an easy recommend if it looks remotely interesting to you. It's a game where many characters have a single button which can take 30%–90% of your health bar, but somehow is probably one of the best fighting games for beginners without introducing bad habits.

The graphics are actually a lot better in-game than what you see on video due to how extremely high-contrast/saturation art styles interact with bitrates. It’s a uniquely stylized and timeless aesthetic.

Shares many traits with all the other Yakuza games. Okay, but limited, combat and rpg type stat progress and excellent storytelling. The difference with this one is that it's clearly the developers having fun with the "history is cyclical" theme. Familiar characters in a completely different setting mean that Ishin somewhat relies on the "in-joke" of spotting anyone you know from the other games and perhaps wondering if they all have the same personality traits they do in previous iterations.

 As for the Like a Dragon labelled games in general I've not really seen how they are more or less RPG centric than any of the earlier games so I'm unclear what all the fuss was about.

This said, I feel the Yakuza series as a whole offers a high level of quality and entertainment value. Are they padded in places? Of course; but that's always been the nature of JRPGs and I don't really see anything negative in extending the gameplay of something if you are enjoying the experience - especially when it's entirely possible to skip through and just follow the main narrative if that's what you prefer. Are certain Yakuza games any better than others? They are but the production and narrative quality of them all is largely consistent. There isn't one I've played I'd call terrible.

If you ignore the character spotting aspect and take Ishin as a stand alone product then it's as good a place as any for newcomers to the franchise to start since it isnt otherwise chronologically connected to the series narrative. Personally I'd go with Yakuza 0 as a start though as it's one of the best of them and most likely to give you the impetus to put up with the (acceptable but not brilliant) graphics of the older games to immerse yourself in the series lore. A solid, if fanciful, entry to the cannon that is likely the most "stand alone" if you aren't all that interested in learning the WHOLE story. 8/10

I have to say, I can write a bloody book about just this fuckin game but I will try to keep it short(Edit- I failed to keep it short🤣) . FF12 is without a doubt the hardest and most hardcore Final Fantasy I have played to date. With some of the most exhausting superbosses in the series( Yiazmat 🖕, this boss alone has radicalized me dude fml) frustrating bosses in the series( Zodiark🖕, Ultima 🖕🖕) ragebait inducing dungeons that will make anyone go 2009 Randy Ortan on the developers( the entirety of the fucking Great Crystal and why you cant fight Omega until late game 🖕🖕 and AGAIN, YIAZMAT 🖕🖕🖕) some of the best game mechanics in the entire series( the gambit and job system❤️) stunning locations and OST(all the forest levels, erupt village and towns❤️) and the best superboss fight in the entire series( the 5 Judges on floor 100 of Trial mode❤️❤️❤️) 
As a casual game, its kinda mid ngl but it is a good entry into the franchise with its biggest downside being the story just being passable but the gameplay more than makes up for it. However since this is a Final Fantasy and a JRPG, it having just a passable story is what makes it a underrated entry into the series and the genre since story is the meat and potatoes of a JRPG. TLDR, 11/10 gameplay with a honestly 3/10 story that starts strong but ends ok.

Story 3/10
As I mentioned before, the story in this game fuckin sucks. It starts off strong, ends ok but the middle is just a blur for me. Of the main cast,  2 of the 6 in the game, Vaan and Penelope ADD NOTHING of value to the game and were only added to attract younger players( the devs admitted the latter in interviews). Your actual main characters are Ashe, Bathier, Fran and Basch. The tonal consistency of the game is kinda deaf too and IIRC its because the game changed directors midway from Yasumi Matsuno( biggest games made being FF Tactics and Vagrant Story) to  Hiroyuki Ito and Hiroshi Minagawa. This change in directors DID very much affect the game. Had the original director stayed, the story execution may have been better at least to the point that the game would be talked up more with casuals as the themes, as is common in the FF franchise, were rather complex but the execution was so lacking that it has unfortunately meme-ed as a poor mans Star Wars, specifically the original trilogy. Honestly as distasteful as it sounds, its really on the nose.

Gameplay  11/10
The gameplay in FF12 is pretty up there, to the extent I would say its almost GOATED. The game canonically inspired the battle system for the Dragon Age games and in more than 1 interview, the creators of Dragon Age have mentioned this when discussing Origins specifically. The job system addition later only made the game that much deeper. Tho before being ported to PC, there have been a lot of changes to the game for balancing purposes and to keep the players happy. The devs have prevented players from wondering off and getting some late game items 3-5hrs into the game BUT allowed players to abuse Trial mode to get late game gear, spells and technicks 🤷‍♂️. Some bosses like Omega had their HP reduced because they were already too kak strong compared to the OG PS2. I am greatful for the fanbase crying to the devs to release the game, allowing characters to equip 2 jobs as 1 job would have made the late game unplayable if you built your team wrong for fights with Yiazmat and the judges, making them MAD AIDS. 

But imma keep it real, this is 1 of the games I would encourage everyone to not play fair. The bosses and enemies can do so much bullshit that why should you lower yourself and play fair when they dont? Yiazmat alone radicalized me.  I had the best gear in the game, [b]IN THE FUCKIN GAME[/b] but it took me 5hrs to kill the son of a bitch and burning a ton of consummables compared to doing it closer to 1 had I known that making my melee characters fight on low health would increase the likely hood of them combo-ing attacks and that their dmg output was greater at low HP. 

Which leds me to my next point, the game does a poor job of explaining [b]"hidden"[/b] mechanics. I say [b]"hidden" [/b] because its not in the in-game item/battle description but rather stuff other players have documented in the WIKI. Certain items like white/dark robes boost holy/dark dmg by 50%. [b]THATS NOT MENTIONED IN THE FUCKIN INGAME DESCRIPTION[/b]. Also the ability to combo melee attacks is another can of worms. Melee weapons have a hidden combo probability to chain strikes. So for hardcore players, they will choose weapons with not per say the biggest DPS per strike but rather the biggest DPS potential over say 5 seconds because in those 5 seconds, my character chained 4-8 strikes. THIS SHIT IS NEVER EXPLAINED INGAME and is something only literal sweats will pick up on BECAUSE BLOODY CASUALS LIKELY JUST ONLY PLAYED THE MAIN STORY OR DROPPED IT BEFORE REACHING GIRUVEGAN, THE LOCATION AND HALF WAY MARK.

On that note, player retention is something to be fascinated by. From the 60% that own the game that made it 3hrs  into the main story and werent dismayed at its unique mechanics, only half of that playerbase made it to the  halfway mark. Then half of those remaining players actually finishing the game. So I think its sage to say that a lot of people who did play this game, were not a fan of the game's aesthetics and gameplay AND CERTAINLY the overwhelming majority of those players didnt know about the hidden stat systems in this game.

Dont even get me started on the side content. OMG dude, this game is like 20% main story, 80% side content but the game only keeps logs of the main story and the hunts, which make up roughly 50% of the game. The other 50% is so dense and there is so much going on, so many conditional boolean statements to unlock that you ABSOLUTELY need a guide to make your life easier but even then dude fml

Cuphead — это не просто игра, это искусство, замаскированное под пытку.
Она учит терпению, реакции и смирению перед безумием.
И да, когда вы пройдёте её — вы будете гордиться собой.
“Don’t deal with the Devil... unless you’re ready to rage in style.”

“Here’s a real high-class bout! - And begin!”

Was meant to write a review for Cuphead after beating the game and deciding whether or not to grab The Delicious Last Course. But it’ll probably take quite a while before I reach that point and you know what, that’s totally fine. It took me eight years just to finally start playing it. Plus, I’m not exactly in a situation right now where I can just summon the motivation to finish it no matter what, especially with plenty of other games catching my attention. Still, hope to finish it someday.

The difference between many masocore, soulslike or just games with a high difficulty and frustration level and Cuphead, is that this one really really grabs me, visually and musically. 
The whole look and sound hits something deep in me, and even though I’ve honestly thought about just watching a playthrough, I actually want to experience it myself. That old-school Betty Boop/Fleischer style just has something special, the way arms and legs move like rubber hoses, objects come to life, and everything feels a bit surreal. Of course, nostalgia also plays a big part.
Maybe I’m not telling anyone anything new here, but I was blown away when the soundtrack hit number one on the US Billboard Jazz Charts and even made it into the Guinness Book of World Records. Back then just like now, I really wanted that soundtrack on vinyl. But just like with games, there’s so much other great music out there. Still, I really hope that one day the OST will find its way onto my record shelf.

Cuphead is one of the most successful indie games of all time, with around six million copies sold. So yeah a lot of people bought it, played it and failed miserably. Well, not everyone, a few actually pushed through and someone out there has probably even mastered it. With Cuphead it’s not really you playing the game, it’s the game playing with you. It’s pretty fair for the most part, but it still wants to crush you. I’d love to be part of the nine percent who make it all the way to the end, and when I finally do, I’ll reward myself by watching a ton of reaction and fail videos. 
Then again, maybe I’ll fail spectacularly, throw my controller at the main monitor, bite off the corners of my Editors Keys - Designed for Ableton Live or just jump out the window. 
Still, let’s hope it doesn’t come to that.

[code][h1]Хороший ремейк, который нельзя было делить на три части.[/h1][/code]

На удивление, это, пожалуй, самый неожиданный игровой опыт за весь год. Это моя первая Final Fantasy, и я запускал её с простыми ожиданиями — думал, будет классическая jRPG, неспешная, с кучей диалогов, квестов и прокачкой. А получил бешеный экшен, где ролевые элементы соседствуют с киношной постановкой и зашкаливающим CINEMA на экране. Каждая вторая миссия тут выглядит как отдельный блокбастер: пролёты камеры, оркестровая музыка, эпик на каждом шагу.

Временами ловил те же мурашки, что когда-то от лучших миссий старых Call of Duty. Режиссура вообще на каком-то безумном уровне, всё снято, сыграно и поставлено с таким драйвом, что забываешь, что это jRPG. И при этом играется она как слешер с комбинацией jRPG. Миссии на байках — абсолютный угар, особенно в последней главе, это как сцена со снегоходами из MW2, только под спидами и с несколькими босс-файтами.

Когда я начал проходить Final Fantasy VII Remake, знал, что это не вся история, а только часть оригинала, но с изменёнными событиями и новыми сюжетными линиями. Поэтому первое, о чём я подумал — будет ли игра ощущаться законченной? Не хотелось снова дойти до титров и почувствовать, что передо мной лишь половина игры. Всё-таки я не играл в оригинал и не знал, чем это всё вообще должно закончиться, поэтому было важно, чтобы история сама по себе имела смысл и не зависела от знания прошлых версий.

[h1]Про самостоятельность и целостность:[/h1]
К сожалению, ремейк всё же оставляет ощущение незавершённости. Да и назвать его полностью самостоятельным тоже нельзя, но как отдельная часть он работает нормально. Это большая, насыщенная контентом экшен-jRPG, где всё движется к финальной точке, но обрывается на полуслове. Каждый персонаж постепенно получает развитие и следить за каждой аркой очень интересно, порой игра напоминает второй Масс Эффект по настроению. В конце Клауд и его команда сталкиваются с серьёзной угрозой, которая задаёт темп для последующих двух частей.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3598912359
Интереснее было другое — как разработчики превратили небольшой кусок оригинальной истории в отдельную игру. Как я и говорил, оригинал я не проходил, поэтому могу судить только по ремейку. Многие миссии тут явно искусственно растянуты и игрок вроде меня, не знакомый с оригиналом этого не заметит, некоторые миссии и загадки в них слишком выбиваются из общего геймплея, и становится очевидно, что именно в этих игровых сегментах игру искусственно растягивали. Но главная проблема ремейка оказалась в том, что ни одна из персональных арок не получает завершения. Злодеи остаются живы, корпорация «Син-Ра» продолжает творить своё, Сефирот появляется, но не раскрывается. Но как эффектный босс и задел на будущее он работает отлично.

Под конец ремейк начинает требовать знания оригинала, и мне приходилось искать нужную информацию уже в интернете. Если вы его не проходили как и я, финал может показаться непонятным или пустым. Я вот пошел и загуглил кто такой Зак, и жалею до сих пор, потому что я себе проспойлерил всю вторую часть ремейка парой строчек текста. Для ремейка это минус — новая версия должна работать сама по себе, без опоры на прошлое.

В итоге попытка превратить небольшой эпизод в самостоятельную игру сработала наполовину. Сюжет обрывается, линии не сходятся, а некоторые идеи не до конца раскрыты. Но при этом проект выглядит масштабно и богато: не особо длинная кампания, но она захватывающая, с хорошими боссами и эпичным финалом. После прохождения даже появляется желание пройти оригинал. Лично мне бы хотелось видеть ремейк, который действительно закрывает весь сюжет, а не только создаёт видимость законченности.

Персонажи являются главным украшением игры, они харизматичные, живые и вызывают симпатию. Первые часы игры слишком хороши и вызывают много положительных эмоций. I have been playing turn based strategy games since Civ III around 20-25 years ago. I've played Civs 3-7, Endless Legend, many total war games starting with the first Medieval one, GalCiv 3, Dominions 3-6, Shadow Empire, EU 2-4, CK2, Stellaris, Victoria 2-3, HOI 3-4. I think that this is probably the best one that I have played, at least to my tastes.

It is very clear that it is made by a small group of developers that have a deep love for the genre and are designing a game that they themselves want to play for years on end. When I play I feel that each decision I make is on average a lot more impactful than decisions in other strategy games and I think it is very intentional game design. There is a fair amount of random chance in the game that can be quite impactful, but the random events are frequent enough that they are unlikely to decide whether a game is won or lost in isolation. Rather, they provide an ever changing shifting set of circumstances that you have to learn to adapt and react to in order to be successful. This is not the kind of game where you can go in from the very beginning with a very specific long term strategy and expect to be able to execute it without deviations. Rather, this game really shines compared to its peers when you consider it as a game where you are trying to leverage the complex interplay between choice of nation, families, leader archetype, terrain, resources, other nations, etc to take advantage of whatever unexpected opportunities or challenges present themselves. You are the captain of your ship, but you must navigate in the context of greater forces.

My main complaint about the game is that there can be a lot of variance in single-player game difficulty depending on map generation. Under the same difficulty settings, you can have several easy games in a row and then several brutally difficult games in a row. This is because diplomacy and terrain are both quite powerful in this game, so that it is possible to protect one flank with diplomacy and the other flank with a convenient mountain range or sea. But if there are no natural barriers and the other nations are not amenable to diplomacy, then best of luck to you. But this kind of variance depends a lot on which map type that you choose so I would encourage experimentation.

This game is very focused on its vision, which is driving an American semi-trailer truck in space.  I think because it is so laser-focused on providing this specific experience, the game is arbitrarily limited by itself.

Your truck is the main character and you are stuck with it the entire game.  You can upgrade it, but there aren't different models you can get or anything like that.  It moves very sluggish, does not have vertical or lateral thrusters so positioning can be very tricky since you are in a 3D space.  Visibility in the truck is very poor, the entire bottom half of the screen is always obstructed by the hood of your truck.  There is no 3D radar to show relative position of objects around you.  Again, you're stuck with this the entire game.  It really wants you to feel like you're driving the space version of a big, sluggish semi truck.

The survival elements are honestly the coolest part of Star Trucker for me, but on default difficulty starting out it can feel oppressive, especially if you have issues with collisions (with the lack of visibility, you will).  Your truck/ship consists of several systems running at the same time (Gravity, Suit power, Mag lock, Core functions, Air filtering) and you have to maintain the parts to keep these systems running.  You will be purchasing lots of batteries to keep them powered and selling off used batteries, because there is no battery "recharging" in the game.  Rechargeable batteries do not exist in this game where people have colonized multiple systems in space.  There are also circuit boards that can degrade over time and need to be replaced, so just checking battery levels does not ensure everything will keep running smoothly.

Whenever you collide with an object, depending on your overall hull integrity, there is a chance you can get a hull breach on your truck/ship which then you'll need to park in the middle of space, walk to the back of your cabin and suit up, eject out the airlock and repair your ship from the outside.  I actually love this, I think this is awesome.  I also think it's funny that your suit has both vertical and lateral thrusters - the technology exists in this universe, but for some reason it's not on the vehicles.  Or maybe just your vehicle, that you're stuck with the whole game.

I don't think this is a bad game, but coming from my background of playing Truck Simulator games and stuff like Freelancer or Elite Dangerous, I can't recommend this over those.  I could only recommend this game to someone who specifically wanted a game where you fly a literal truck through space.

This is a really fantastic, addictive game, and I really recommend it if you enjoy narrative-style rpgs and political sims, but like, applied to a bigger scope. The framing of the story is that you will be slowly rebuilding your “dynasty”, after a nation-wide rebel invasion killed off most of your clan members and destroyed your estate: you start with one clan member, horrible stats and no money, progressively amassing power and influence—to the point you could easily stage a coup and supplant the Emperor (if you so choose). 
The game gives you a lot of freedom to try different playstyles and approaches to the problems you face: you can go for the military route, sending your characters to conquer the surrounding provinces, or have them enter public service via provincial examinations; although realistically you should be going for both to reach higher renown and such. (In theory, sending your characters to war should be a gamble, since they run the risk of dying in battle, but in practice none of my characters ever died because of it, even with low stats.) 
Since your interests are spread out over many different clan members, the game isn’t afraid of dishing out pretty realistic consequences for your actions, either. If you try and fail to assassinate a royal clan-member, the character who attempted assassination will be executed and your relationship with the royal family will take a hit, but it’s not like it’s a game-breaking thing. This way, mistakes and failures actually become a gateway for more content and interactions, and these unpredictable ups and downs make the story even more realistic and “alive”, if that makes sense. Events also happen at a time scale of generations, which gives a pretty organic feel to your progression through the ranks. 
What I loved the most is how interactive the game feels: there’s a lot of RNG events that can happen at key moments, which sometimes make or break the narrative you were building towards. Marriages are one of the easiest ways of building strong relationships with other clans, so you catch yourself thinking really pragmatically about it, almost like a C-Drama villain. 
(“You’re 18, Ge clan’s Huer Ge’s 18, they have a Chancellor in court, can I make it any more obvious?”)
Even so, while you can make plans for them, characters will sometimes get really interesting bursts of agency—ask to divorce from the Royal Family because life in the palace is making them miserable, fall in love with someone in a party they were invited and move in together, have an affair with their partner’s third cousin…. I think these are really neat, and I’m always positively surprised by these events. 
That being said, there are a lot of features that are still being implemented, so some parts of the gameplay will feel “missing”, or the late-game can feel a little still. Other problems are QOL, like multiple sub-menus, but the update roadmap shows there are on their way to being fixed. Personally, one thing that bothers me is that once they pass away, clan members go missing from the family tree, and all the connections they used to have disappear. This can make it even harder to track who is who, especially when the number of people in your clan reaches a hundred. I imagine this is made to avoid using up too much processing power (which is an admirable effort, the game runs pretty well on my 8yo laptop), but it would still be nice to have some way of keeping track of your complete family line, maybe with the portraits of deceased members greyed out?
All in all, I really enjoyed playing it so far, and I’m looking forward to the next updates!

"Orbital Gear" ist ein 2D-Multiplayer-Shooter, bei dem die Gravitation eine wesentliche Rolle spielt. 

Wir steuern einen Mech, der zwei verschiedene Angriffswaffen und eine Sonderfunktion wie etwa Minenlegen besitzt. Die abgegrenzte Spielfläche besteht aus Planeten mit geringem Durchmesser (und manchmal auch anderen Objekten), die alle ihre eigene Gravitation erzeugen. Ohne unseren Boost zu nutzen würden wir immer nur auf einem einzigen Planeten im Kreis laufen. Durch den Boost springen wir von Planet zu Planet und können auch auf dem Weg im freien Raum die Schwerkraft der Objekte nutzen, die merklich unsere Flugbahn beeinflußt.

An diese Gravitationsbedingungen muß man sich erstmal ein wenig gewöhnen, auch wenn sie inzwischen in mehreren Spielen ähnlich genutzt wurden. Hat man die erste Orientierungslosigkeit überwunden, ist der eigene Mech durchaus recht zielgenau zu steuern, was auch an der relativ präzisen Steuerung liegt. 

Die zu Verfügung stehenden Waffen sind abwechslungsreich, auch wenn es eigentlich nur 12 unterschiedliche sind. Dazu kommt dann noch eine Spezialfähigkeit wie Minen zu legen oder ein Turret aufzubauen. Bei den Waffen haben wir relativ normale Maschinenpistolen, aber auch Lenkraketen oder sogar ein Projektil, das die Oberfläche eines anderen Planeten kurzfristig entzündet. Auch ein Schutzschild steht uns zur Verfügung, das sich aber als nur wenig nützlich erweist. 

Es macht durchaus Spaß mit den Waffen herumzuexperimentieren. Das Tempo ist recht schnell und das Gameplay ist flüssig, wenn auch immer wieder ziemlich chaotisch. Manchmal gelingt es, den Gegner gezielt zu treffen, oft ist ein solcher HIt aber auch mehr Zufall als Können. Das geht aber in Ordnung, denn das Spiel ist merklich primär auf Fun und ein schnelles Spiel zwischendurch ausgelegt.

Das größte Problem, wie bei vielen älteren Multiplayer-Titeln: die Server sind praktisch leer. Man findet kaum Mitspieler. Zwar gibt es auch ein paar Single-Player-Herausforderungen, die sind aber kein adäquater Ersatz. Um wirklich Spaß mit dem Spiel zu haben, sollte man also unbedingt ein paar Freunde zur Hand haben.

I struggled a lot with this review, but eventually I just can't recommend this game. The concept of this game is great, but it fails in the execution. Here's why.
 
It's surprisingly fun in the start. The gameplay loop is engaging, gaining money by performing manual tasks to purchase tools and machines to automate the workflow. Also the package validation process is straight forward enough and doesn't feel as punishing as e.g. Papers, Please. Invalid packages are quite obvious most of the time, so you can focus on velocity without worrying too much about mistakes.

As time passes by, your system grows, you keep purchasing conveyor belts and new machines until you've finally managed to automate the whole process. Tada! It took me less than 10 hours to get there, and I really didn't try hard to speed run this game. But this is not the end, now is where the scaling starts: More packages, faster deliveries, more money, more improvements. The holy loop of automation efficiency.

It feels like I'm just entering the mid game phase, with so much more to do, so much more potential to unlock, however, this is where the game died for me.

Parcel Simulator wants to be an automation game, but it doesn't understand how automation games work. Automation games are about continuous improvement, endless refactoring and scaling, always trying to keep everything as efficient as possilbe. And most automation games understand this and make it easy to refactor, tell you production rates, and offer the necessary tools to make building and refactoring fun.

This is where Parcel Simulator fails. It doesn't give you any production rates, so you have to guess (or experiment to find out) whether you should spend 10k in another machine upgrade or scale horizontally with more machines. But more importantly, refactoring your system is a HUGE pain in the butt. It's extremely tedious to disassemble, rethink, reassamble a system. Every single conveyor belt needs to be placed individually. Need to pick it up again? Long-press E. Moving a conveyor line by one tile to the side should take seconds. In Parcel Simulator it can well take minutes, depending on the length. There are no blueprints to make this easier either.

Bottom line: In my opinion, Parcel Simulator offers a fun and engaging early game which transforms into a tedious grind after a single-digit number of hours. If you can get it cheap, it may be worth a try, as long as you understand and acknowledge its shortcomings.

Перед началом этого превью стоит сразу же отметить, что я пропустил оригинальную Wreckfest, но зато в свое время провел много времени в играх серии Flatout. Правда, играл я исключительно в одиночный режим, и это все равно было невероятно весело. Разные режимы, возможность превратить машину в клочок железки на колесах и, конечно же, великолепный саундтрек — все это делало игру незабываемой и заставляло проводить в ней десятки часов. Wreckfest 2 является своего рода духовной наследницей Flatout, призванной утолить жажду старых фанатов. Получилось ли у них — пока судить очень рано.
Wreckfest 2 сейчас находится в раннем доступе, но даже для этого этапа здесь весьма мало контента. Один режим, три трассы и четыре автомобиля — это, скорее, уровень альфы, куда пускают совсем небольшое количество игроков, чтобы отловить критические баги и собрать фидбек. По сути, так оно и есть, только для доступа вам еще нужно заплатить. Даже сами разработчики настоятельно просят не покупать игру и дождаться версии 1.0, если вы хотите получить полноценную и идеально оптимизированную игру с несколькими режимами, десятками трасс и автомобилей, а также расширенным режимом карьеры. Сейчас же мы имеем лишь фундамент, на котором будет строиться проект.

Впервые запустив Wreckfest 2, я выбрал одиночный режим с ботами — не столько для того, чтобы ознакомиться с основными механиками, сколько из-за привычки с Flatout. В начале меня ждало разочарование: 24 машины толпятся на мелкой трассе и особо не пытаются друг друга таранить. Более того, создается ощущение, что попытка разрушить вражеский автомобиль приносит больше вреда для тебя самого, чем пользы из-за чрезвычайно неповоротливого управления, поэтому все заезды превращаются в скучные гонки без какой-либо изюминки. Разработчикам определенно стоит сделать ботов более умными и агрессивными, чтобы удовлетворить потребности любителей синглплеера.

Of Guards and Thieves is a competitive multiplayer stealth game, and you don't really see a lot of those around. Plenty of cooperative stealth but rarely does a game put you against other players. In fact, the best comparison is the “Spies vs Mercs” mode on Splinter Cell: Blacklist. Basically, if you liked that mode but found it to be too severe on the Call of Duty spectrum of gaming, then I have news for you!

OGAT is the same idea but in a more indie/flash game type style. Makes sense, as many people who play it through Kongregate and aren’t even aware it’s on Steam.

The core mechanics are simple; The Guards tend to be better equipped with more health and assault weapons. The thieves have crossbows and silenced weapons, less health, but one major advantage; Night vision. They must navigate all the maps and turn off the lights while they steal a specific item that only they know about. The guards can find and patrol the multiple items but are not aware of which one it is, giving the less-equipped thieves a tactical advantage. Distraction is a major gameplay element here.

There are also other modes to mix this up, including a Team Deathmatch, Capture the Flag, Bomb Defusal, and more.

If I had to find a criticism, well... There’s two. They both overlap slightly.

The first is that the playerbase is incredibly small, usually peaking at 200 people and going down to 40-60 in off hours. While this is a fine core for the main game mode, I have found it very difficult to explore other game modes such as CTF, or that extra large map where you explore and loot (and what ever happened to Slender?!) I pretty much see 0/10 on all servers unless it’s private or just on a different gametype.

Due to the small base of players, there’s no matchmaking and games don’t always autoshuffle so sometimes it can feel like a team is outclassing another. If it does shuffle, there may be a couple of particularly experienced players crushing everyone who just downloaded and are giving it a try. I'm not the worst player but I have on a few occasions found myself in an endless loop of failure because one enemy was just crushing it. I have some friends who can barely play it for more than twenty minutes at a time and it’s a shame.

The flip side of this; There's no equipment or pay2win system here. If you play enough you can eventually learn the maps, figure out decent hiding patterns, and perform better yourself. 
(Protip: Guards can turn off their flashlights and hide in bushes themselves, which is hard to see even with night vision). That kind of thing.

Regardless, It’s a great, small game with a fair amount of replayability. The matches are quick and bite-sized, and you can usually get several games in just twenty minutes or so.

The content: PTTR started with some scenarios and some basic features and a map creator, and since then the scope of content added has been immense. The game has scenarios to get you started, it has a sandbox mode, it has a massive catalogue of user made levels some of which are genuinely beyond impressive and play better than the scenarios do. An arena challenge mode for veterans to test their skill, and a full story mode that takes the form of a roguelike RPG which is impressive enough to be it's own standalone game and what a good chunk of my hours are represented by. This game has almost infinite content and you can play for hundreds of hours and not get bored. 

The gameplay: The gameplay is also an incredibly strong element of this game, it takes the form of a brawler, the controls are simple enough to be considered intuitive to new players but also have a remarkable of mechanical depth and let you bludgeon, stab and dismember people in countless macabre and creative ways. The game has a vast array of weapons from a tape dispenser to a claymore to a fully automatic rifle. The game really let's the playr loose in an environment to create as much chaos as possible and the voxel physics add a feeling of further chaos to the game as people will literally explode into pieces. The game also has powers you can utilise as kill streaks that only enhance the carnage creating experiance. 

The map maker: I have never once used it as my passion lies in the work of almighty Khorne. However, I can say with absolute certainty that it seems incredibly detailed as some of the maps I have seen people make really defy expectations. Perhaps the best aspect of the map maker is the ability to share custom assets on the workshop or use them for yourself which means you won't be having to make skins and items from scratch. Maybe not to everyone's interest but certainly worth a look if you have that creative passion to make in game levels. 

Beneath: Beneath is a Roguelike mode that deserves it's own section really. It has all the hallmarks of a roguelike RPG, wide variety of monters and mobs, different classes, weapons, playstyles, and the ability to play co-op with others. Beneath is really it's own game that uses the vehicle of PTTR to create an incredibly enjoyable, addictive and satisfying experience. Anyone who likes games like Hades should definitely give this a try, its absolutely fantastic. 

Conclusion, this game is a masterpiece made by these devs who have prioritised player freedom, variety and gameplay while still giving the game it's own unique graphical charm. If you are on the fence about this one or you've just found it and somehow slogged through this review, I cannot recommend it enough. It's a minimal investment for a massive amount of content and the devs should be proud of what they have achieved here and the price makes it feel like it's stealing for what you are getting out of it.

As with every Naruto game, the character movesets and abilities are almost identical — there’s little originality beyond changes in graphics, text, or colors. A few new characters with some extra techniques were added, but that’s about it.

This game stands out because the story mode is experienced entirely through Naruto. There’s no interaction with other characters who might have their own missions or story battles. It’s an interesting approach, as Naruto’s missions introduce fresh elements through reactions, fights, and cutscenes.
Still, overall, it’s a fairly average game—good for passing the time.

Boruto, on the other hand, is a different story. The VR plot involving an evil Naruto and a mysterious woman of his age, possessing skills from a well-known clan, was truly intriguing. It’s a story you won’t see in the anime or manga, and it’s compelling enough that you want to keep discovering what happens next. I felt like I was genuinely playing and watching anime just like I did when I was younger. Fantastic entertainment worth the price.

The tournament battle system and character customization also left a very positive impression on me.

[h1] Yet Another AA Gem [/h1]

[b] EDIT: They fixed the combat. Ryn's movement feels more natural, animations are both weightier and faster, and I actually [i] want [/i] to parry now. We're not talking best-in-class; it's not suddenly a FromSoft game. But I don't think I would have dropped the difficulty if this had been the version I played, so it's an even heartier recommend from me now. [/b]

This game does have a lot of problems; movement feels floaty, combat lacks weight and enemy variety (I dropped the difficulty to Story and never looked back), collectibles are kind of meaningless, and it's heavier than it should be, even for the visuals they're offering. There are also gonna be bugs, from major (HDR turned my entire screen rainbow) to minor (the 'you last saved at XX:XX PM' clock was always wrong, and never seemed to correspond with any clock, timezone, or setting that made sense). In a very clear sense, this is "we have God of War 2018 at home".

So why am I recommending? Because the issues above, while meaningful, are functionally issues of presentation and resources. This is a small team, a young team, without a ton of money and time to polish and refine. Despite those limitations, the core of the game, the bones of it, are solid and rewarding. It's full of ideas, with clever puzzles and inventive combat techniques. Throwing people around in this game is more fun than in the Star Wars Jedi games, and there was always some new puzzle mechanic so the between-combat sections never overstayed their welcome. Additionally, the writing, if sometimes predictable, is solid, and the main performances are *excellent*, moving past the very stage-y quality of most video game voice acting to actually give the lines heft and subtlety. I'll be keeping an eye out for anything Aldís Amah Hamilton performs in next; she plays Ryn with an understatedness which so easily could have come off detached and annoying (see Aloy in HFW), but instead paints her as mature and morally serious. 

The core relationship between Ryn and Abram is wonderful, developing slowly and realistically over a bloatless runtime. The ups and downs of their relationship feel earned, both through writing and gameplay, which is too rare even in narrative-first Sony-type games like this one. Moreover, avoiding a huge pitfall of this genre, the game doesn't shove lore down your throat, instead letting you explore the world to the depth you want. And exploration is worth it, because the world the team has made is beautiful. There's definitely a few too many cave sections (and commenting on this in the dialogue doesn't absolve the sin). But there are vistas that'll impress, and impress even more once you realize you'll be moving through and climbing all over them. 

I've been playing a ton of really excellent indie games this year, and the closest comparisons I can come up with are games like Tainted Grail and Banishers: Ghosts of New Eden. It's been really rewarding, in a world of AAA slop, to see how new tech is enabling small teams to make solid AA games. We’ve seen that in Clair Obscur and Eriksholm and Hell Is Us, and this game belongs on that list. All of these games have jank, all of them make compromises, and all of them are absolutely, 100% worth your time and money. A rough diamond is still a diamond.

[h1]Great RTS, But the AI will make you uninstall[/h1]

This is probably the best RTS in its genre. The [b]attention to details[/b] is amazing, the [b]atmosphere[/b] and historical accuracy you feel like you're really there. It feels great to play, [i]up until[/i] it doesn't.

[h2]Why I'm so frustrated[/h2]

The game gets ruined by an [b]immense amount of AI spamming[/b] in some missions. It gets to the point where it's literally unplayable. Strategy doesn't matter when the enemy gets infinite units, as the game just turns into a meatgrinder where you focus on endlessly killing AI tanks and hoping yours survive.

To make things even worse, sometimes your own AI just picks a weird path and runs straight into the enemy for no reason. So you're fighting an enemy that's a perfect micromanager, while also trying to stop your own guys from getting themselves killed like idiots. It's frustrating as hell.

A lot of these missions are likely meant for co-op, but [b]you can't host your DLC missions for friends who don't own them[/b]. Since the game's missions are mostly locked behind DLCs, I was forced to play them alone. I can micromanage a few squads, but trying to defend a huge area against an overwhelming amount of AI attacking you (on a mission where you are the one supposed to attack) makes me uninstall this game.

And when the AI starts spamming, the performance starts to show some cracks. It all just becomes a huge, laggy mess.

[h1]Final verdict[/h1]

Basically a hit-and-miss game.

[b]BUY THIS FOR CO-OP[/b], if your friend has enough money to buy all the same DLCs.

[b]AVOID THIS FOR SINGLEPLAYER[/b], unless you're ready to waste hours battling an AI that's 100 times better at micromanaging crap than you are. I really liked this game, but I've got enough of AI spamming bullshit.

As a long time Atlus fan, this is the only game where I had stopped playing right at the start of the final dungeon, uninstalled the game, and was glad to never bother with it again. it's not a bad game by any means, but I find it baffling that it gets such an overwhelmingly positive reception, despite having plenty of flaws both in story and gameplay.

The main reason that I'm so disappointed by it, is because that this is a new IP, which meant that they could go wild and do whatever they wanted, crafted a well written and in depth story, explore new gameplay ideas, innovate on their formulas, but instead what we got is basically "Persona 5, medieval edition" with incredibly poor writing and stagnant gameplay. 

Generally speaking, Atlus games never did have the best writing in them, but they did tackle their themes and plots in a decent way that it didn't constantly bother me, so I could give them a pass and enjoy the gameplay and character moments in them, however, in M:R, the worldbuilding and plot are so poorly written that I couldn't take the story seriously at all at any point. The main theme the game tackles is Racism, a heavy, complex, and important theme, however, the way you are shown how racism is portrayed in this world is just throwing shallow stereotypes at you about the various races in the game, and that's it. And hilariously enough, in many cases, the stereotypes turn out to be completely correct, further undermining the point of the main theme. In many points in the plot, it felt to me that the writers think that race and culture are one and the same, meaning that if you're one race, no matter your upbringing or your personality, your race determines everything, which, again, undermines the main point of the plot.

The writing, beyond the main theme, is again, not very good. Your party members are one dimensional, most of the plot is your basic JRPG plot of "Kill the main villain with the power of friendship and save the day" and some of the "twists" if you can call them that, just made me roll my eyes, because they too, manage to undermine the main theme.
I had hoped that the game would go into depth about it's themes with the main party, with each person conveying a different point of view, having conflicts about different matters ,but most of the party feel really samey. They are all nice, agreeable and get along just fine, which is really nice if it was real life, but in a story that's pretty boring. The last two characters that get added to your party are the exception, but even they aren't particularly outstanding or have too much time to shine, unfortunately.

The gameplay side of things isn't much better, which isn't to say that the gameplay is bad, far from it, it's just that if you played any of the recent Atlus titles, you won't be too amazed by the gameplay, and considering that this is a new IP, one would imagine that they would want to innovate instead of retreading old ground, and unfortunately, they didn't really innovate. The main difference in M:R between other Atlus games is Archtypes.

The Archetype system, which is essentially your "job" system in this game, is pretty okay, nothing too mind blowing. You can freely set your party members to different Archtypes based on the situation and try out different strategies, such as warrior, mage, healer etc, which is pretty nice, however, the amount of menuing you have to do every time you decide to change between Archtypes and their gear is pretty annoying.
An additional annoyance that I found about the system, is that by the endgame, every party member has a a unique Archtype only they can use, and they require two specific Archtypes to be maxed before being unlocked, if you're like me, and you enjoy experimenting, and you might find, like I did, that you weren't close to getting the relevant Archtypes to max, and you'll feel like you were punished for experimenting by the game telling you "oh, you didn't level these specific two archtypes to max for character x? too bad, get to grinding if you want it". In the game's credit, you don't have to unlock them, the game isn't too difficult on its normal difficulty, but it does feel like it arbitrarily punished you for using the system as it was supposedly meant to be used.

Dungeons are pretty lackluster, both main story dungeons, and side dungeons. The main dungeons feel like they're big for no reason and don't really have any interesting gimmicks or mechanics to make the gameplay more varied, for example, in one dungeon you have 30 minutes before you die, in another, you have to hide occasionally from a difficult monster, not very unique or interesting in both ideas or execution.
The side dungeons are pretty bland, they look boring, mostly long brown or grey hallways sometimes broken up with a large empty room or a ladder to a different floor of bland brown or grey hallways and big empty rooms with nothing in them except enemies, sometimes it's caves, sometimes it's ruins, sometimes it's a big empty, flat forest. I have no idea if the side dungeons were randomly generated during development, but I won't be surprised if they were.

Many times during the game I had hoped that I will encounter unique situations that require you to really experiment with the Archtype system and really challange you in more than a "big damage number" or "HP bloat" type of way, but unfortunately, that isn't the case. Mobs are usually dealt the same way they are dealt in the persona games, which is to say, abuse elemental weakness, kill enemy, move on. Boss fights weren't particularly memorable to me, so I can't recall any interesting gimmicks if there were any at all, take it as you will.
I will say that there was one dungeon in the beginning of the game that if your party had a certain Archtype present during combat the common enemy type in the dungeon would enrage and could cause a wipe to your party, which meant that you had to change your Archtypes to deal with the situation, but that's literally the only dungeon I remember that happening, which is unfortunate,  because that kind of mechanic could be really interesting to explore and could provide much gameplay vareity and depth in my opinion.

In short, if I had to give the game a score, I'd give it a 5, it's not bad, it's not the worst game ever made, it's okay. If you're really interested in the game, or just want another JRPG to play and you think it needs to be this one, I would suggest to wait until a deep sale.

I really, really, REALLY love this kind of game. I'm the person who really enjoyed Cultist Simulator despite its insatiable grind that makes me so annoyed, who re-running depressing rounds of The Life of Suffering of Sir Brante to be an exercise in showing the absolute beauty of how life can persevere, who thinks that Roadwarden is a modern masterpiece of text-based resource management.

If you've ever heard of any of those games, you should instantly buy the Sultan's Game – but come in with an understanding that its themes are somehow even more brutal and sinister than the examples I just listed.

If you haven't – think of it as a board game where you have agents that you get to place, constantly, each turn. Except the spaces are constantly appearing and disappearing, and if you don't act quick enough, you can permanently miss opportunities. 

I read a negative review that described this game as basically "torture porn", as you're forced to murder the people that you love and do horrible things to those that are left over. I think if you were a completionist, that'd probably be the case – but I find myself playing the game in a very specific way: how can I be the most good? How can I overturn the corrupt system? How can I show my wife that I love her while being forced to do these terrible things? How can I use the cards that chain me into this system towards a better aim?

I think it means that I'll miss out on some absolutely crazy endings, but I'm fine with that. This game is unbelievably compelling to me, and feels like an evolution of all those original games I mentioned at the top of my review. If you have even a semblance of love for strategic, agent-based board games, or stories about trying to come from underneath a terrible system, this is a perfect game for you. 

And also, let's just say that not making this a real-time strategic card-placing game (like Cultist Simulator, where you are literally counting down seconds waiting for timers) is so much better!

One of the best experiences of this kind of "movie night" game, the remaster has done it wonders. An engaging and interesting story, well-defined characters that you grow to love (some more than others, sorry, Emily), and moments of genuine tension and fear for the lives of these characters.

However, I value these games primarily for their multiplayer aspect. The possibility of sitting down with friends, each choosing a character, and enjoying a "live your own adventure" horror night together is priceless to me. In this game... I don't see that as much. For instance, there is a very dangerous AI named Killer which kills sentient AI indiscriminately. You can choose to trap it or kill it. I get writing is tough, and by and large it's... decent. But for a game focused so heavily on story, feeling such a stark disconnect from your own character takes away a lot of the enjoyability for me.

It's always bittersweet to find a free game that you want more of. Such is the case with Mandagon, a 2D exploration game set in a Tibetan vision of limbo. You don't know why you're there or what you're doing or why you're a cheeful-looking stone head that can jump, but all will be revealed as you wander the serene temples and ruins of this magical place. There's no real puzzling to do, other than sussing out the story from the cryptic rhymes shared by ancient statues, but the exploration is more than enough to keep you engaged for as long as it lasts.

The heart of Mandagon's appeal is its environment and atmosphere, which would be remarkable even for a full-priced game. The graphics are finely-detailed pixel art, showing off every crack and bit of moss on stones and every groove in the pillars holding the place aloft. You'll start your adventure in a stony valley of pools and cliff dwellings, but soon your adventure will take you to etherial ruins floating in the sky, their banners and wind chimes tossing gently in the breeze. With no enemies to harangue you and no challenging platforming to speak of, the art turns Mandagon into a peaceful trek across a gorgeous and fantastic world.

It's not a big world, of course, and you should be able to see all its sights in 30 minutes or so. Your goal is to place six tablets back in their proper places, and there aren't a whole lot of places where they could be hidden. The arches where the tablets must be placed also serve as the fast travel points, making it easy to get back to where you need to be at any time. You won't find any abilities or upgrades, just shortcuts to activate and one special travel method high up in the ruins. There are a few little secrets tucked away that also build on the excellent atmosphere as well.

The story's not bad but it's told in terribly vague terms, so unless you want to really puzzle out the rhymes you'll just be here for the journey. And it's an absolutely lovely, imaginative journey for the short time it lasts, so there's no reason not to give it a go if you like exploring. This feels like a title for people who loved the Knytt games, because it definitely pushes a lot of the same buttons for me. Here's hoping Mandagon's creators are hard at work on a full game, because this little slice of heaven left me hungry for more.

220+ hours in. I’m still playing even with the population drop, so this is not a rage-quit review.

Gameplay / balance:
Moment-to-moment gameplay is actually really fun. Flying, spice runs, base building, sneaking supplies back without getting jumped — feels great and “Dune,” not generic survival. Combat and gear are in a way better place than launch. Early on you had rocket cheese, scouts sprinting around like anime ninjas, and PvP choke zones where day-1 no-lifers camped resources and bullied anyone trying to do quests. A lot of that was nerfed or reworked, and some protected areas got added so newer players can touch higher-tier mats without getting instantly farmed. Huge improvement.

PvP / griefing:
Still messy. People found ways to weaponize the game systems to grief (ex: dragging worms into “safe-ish” areas to nuke players and vehicles without technically flagging PvP). You still get the usual sweaty clans sitting on choke points and trash talking while they block progression routes. The game is also stuck between wanting to be PvP war politics vs PvE survival/base-building. Casual players keep asking for true PvE servers or at least clearer separation. Hardcore PvPers want open conflict everywhere. That split is a big reason people leave.

Population:
You can feel the drop. Launch numbers were huge, then it fell off fast. Now during off-hours you’ll see fewer players in the world and you start recognizing the same names. The devs keep talking long-term (multi-year plan, new regions, eventually even off-world content), which sounds great, but a lot of people are like: fix the current problems first.

Economy (big problem):
The in-game market is basically player-run, and right now that means price gouging nonstop. You can farm certain items and relist them for insane money because nothing stops you from scalping newer players. There’s no price history, no “average sale,” no cap, nothing warning someone “you’re about to get ripped off.” Since gear and base upgrades depend on money, this turns progression into “who scams hardest” instead of who plays smart. Calling that “emergent economy” is cute, but let’s be real: it’s just legal scamming unless they add controls or at least transparency.

Family Sharing / value for money:
At release you could use Steam Family Sharing. A lot of people (me included) factored that in — like “cool, my kid/partner can play on their own profile without buying 2-3 full copies for one house.” Then the devs disabled Family Sharing because cheaters were abusing shared accounts to dodge bans and exploit. I get WHY they did it. I still think how they did it feels bad.

Here’s why players are mad:

We bought with that feature in mind.

Game hasn’t really been discounted.

Now the “solution” is basically “just buy another copy.”

If you’re going to turn off something that was part of the value people paid for, give a real timeline to turn it back on, offer a household license/bundle, or compensate in some way. Right now it just feels like legit players got punished for cheaters.

Stability / patches:
I’ll give the devs credit: they are fast to hotfix when something is on fire. They’ve pushed bans, patched exploits, and even publicly admitted when a bad patch ruined people’s bases and promised to reimburse. That honesty is good.

But… almost every big patch also breaks something else. You log in after work and find PvE zones accidentally turned PvP, or gear gone, or some new exploit popping off. People get tired of rebuilding after “oops.”

Where I’m at:

Core loop is fun.

Visuals and world feel perfect for Dune.

Combat/balance is way better than launch.

The economy is predatory toward new players.

PvP vs PvE identity is still not solved.

Family Sharing being disabled without a real replacement feels like a bait-and-switch for households.

Player drop is real and you can feel it.

Should you buy right now?
If you like survival crafting, politics, ambush PvP, and you’ve got a group to play with, you’ll have a blast.

If you’re mostly solo/PvE, hate getting camped by 5-stacks, hate market scams, and planned on using Family Sharing so your household could try it without buying multiple copies — I’d wait.

The foundation is honestly sick. This could become something legendary if they fix cheating, fix the market, and commit to fair access for casual players. But you can definitely see the cracks right now.

If we want to look back in history at Madden, very little has been done to improve it over the last 5 years that is of note. We are getting a fresh taste of different, and we should absolutely be excited about the potential it has. The customization is off the charts, and the flow isn’t terrible. The announcers are basic, but if you play a game “in the stands”, it’s much better. Personally, it’s an exciting time for football fans with Maximum. The beginning is only the beginning, the polish is coming.

Full disclosure I was on a playtest team for the game and have been playing since the beta test so I may have some positive bias here.

I know people don't like long reviews so I'll just say... I like it so far. It obviously has the bugs and glitches that you would expect for an early release. No play action passes yet? No pro/franchise yet? Yeah, it's coming.

I'd suggest that since the base game is free, just try it out and play it, the game play is actually very nice and it's a visually great game. I do want to address the elephant in the room, and that is how people are upset about the pricing tiers and in-game purchases when it was marketed as a "free to play" game. On some extent I can understand and don't think it was a good idea to market the game as free when obviously there would have to be paid items and not being clear what those things would be. But on the other hand, was anyone expecting that a game of this sophistication would be COMPLETELY free? Come on, really. Yes there is paid DLC. But considering you can do a lot for free and most of the big modes require no more than the $20 tier which is pretty cheap for a game like this, all this stuff has to be paid for somehow, right? We're in the Internet Youtube age where everyone expects to have everything for free and without making societal comment, there are too many people who just don't grasp that things they like cost money.

As for features, I have not yet tried the dynasty mode since pre-release, but as I said the game plays well. The MPL mode that's the card-based team building online play, I had some doubts about it at first but found it quite addictive I haven't even bothered to go into franchise yet.  

Of course there are some genuine negatives I find, beyond the obvious growing pains of bugs and glitches. 
One thing that disappoints me is the lack of difficulty settings. I'm not very good at playing games like this and the game does move fast. The passing game has to be worked out yet, receivers don't go for the ball well, and interceptions, turnovers and blocked kicks are too frequent. Kicking is more  challenging than it should be. The developers are against putting in sliders but I wish we had SOME difficulty control.

I could write a book about all the good and bad things but come on, try it for yourself. Play a few games, collect a few cards, get in a few online matches (those are in the free version) and you can even earn a few dynasty seasons just from challenges. What have you got to lose? You've got hundreds of hours of good football play to gain.

I honestly, and yes this is my bias again, think that many of the bad reviews are people pissed off that the entire game isn't free. Oh we love Youtube but get annoyed that it has to be paid for by ads. Seriously? Try it you'll be glad you did. It's far from perfect but just by downloading and playing you're showing your support and the developers are truly dedicated to making this a top-quality game which is more than I can say about certain AAA studios out there.

This is a fantastic game that never fully got the attention it deserved. You can very clearly see how bad the game almost was; the home base sections are riddled with currencies and unlockables, which screams "we built this game to be a microtransaction hell". Thankfully "The Avengers" live service game from the previous year tanked, and it looks like the monetization mechanics were scrapped. This game should've got an award just for that. On top of that, the devs patched out the 2k launcher so you don't have to worry about your PC being scanned.

What's left is a fantastic RPG story starring you as an OC, surrounded by a cast of popular Marvel heroes. Gameplay loop is walking around the Abbey, finding collectables and talking to, upgrading and customizing heroes. I liken these sections to a more engaging version of hanging out in the Normandy in Mass Effect, except imagine if the Normandy was bigger and had more stuff to do. Once done for the day, you queue up a combat mission with 3 heroes and do a 5-15 minute turned based tactics battle. The combat is determined by an upgradable card deck, but all the action the cards cause is fully animated so it doesn't "feel" like a card game.

Highly recommend you mod the game to increase resource gain. It's not necessary, but since it was initially designed to make you grind (or pay) you'll enjoy the customization aspects more if you're drowning in currencies. Doesn't really take away from the combat difficulty.

Very niche game, but I'm enjoying it. To enjoy it, you can't be in a hurry. The pacing is incredibly slow. At the time of writing, I've done 14 battles in 17 hours. There is a huuuuuge amount of exposition at the beginning, so it feels like you don't get to 'play the game' for a while. The strongest part of the game is the voice acting and writing. There's a lot of it, and not everything hits, but I've laughed out loud after several of the jokes.

The game has 3 major parts: friendship sim, exploration, and turn based battle. You spend most of your time listening to dialogue, and if you opt into it, can do a chunk of exploring, then you get to do a battle. One dubious design choice: treasure respawns. So you spend a fair amount of time re-exploring the hub for motes of currency, re-reading books in the library for arcane xp, and re-exploring the grounds to re-open chests and unlock new areas. 

Battle is good. It is fun to combo enemies, the powers are thematic, and I've already found a few of the randomly generated battles pretty challenging, so I would say that the difficulty is very well tuned. The devs really worked hard to give players lots of ways to upgrade their hero card decks. Manor customization feels like wasted dev effort to me. I like customizing the superhero costume of the player's character. Most of the other cosmetics have not felt particularly rewarding.

If you've ever wanted to interview some superheroes, this is the game for you.

I have been highly sceptical of TTS for a long time.

I'm an avid IRL table top gamer and - having played a few board games online (web based) - I felt that clicking on a screen cannot compare in the slightest to sitting around a table moving cards, tokens, and rolling dice, hanging around with friends. "Thanks but no thanks!" I thought.

Boy, I was wrong.

Wen the corona crisis came and I was forced into TTS to keep playing with my mates, I realised how TTS is not what I thought it was. It is not a collection of games whose rules have been coded in an algorithm, it is a physics simulator for the top of a table. The fact you use that table to play games on it is almost incidental.

That means that playing in TTS feels a lot like playing IRL, you still get to roll dice, shuffle cards, moving tokens around... all while chatting merrily with your friends.

So, this brings me to the top 3 pros of this game for me:
1. It retains 83% of what makes a board games night with friends IRL a great experience.
2. The fact some games are scripted cuts down on the tedious tasks (e.g.: setup, cleanup, scoring...)
3. The availability of thousands of games allow you to get to know a lot more games than you'd discover if you had to purchase them IRL.

Moreover for the last point: I was worried that playing games for free online would have disincentivised me from buying the physical ones the game designers get their livelihood from.

I was wrong on that account too.

While I played some games that I did not like and would not buy IRL, I discovered many more games that I fell in love with and of which I have now ordered the physical copy (that I would have never bought of my own accord otherwise).

So I feel like to endorse TTS completely.

Despite looking like a game from Newgrounds, this is probably one of the closest games in feel to Final Fantasy Tactics mixed with an adventuring guild management system. You will not regret this game!

Genuinely one of the biggest surprises I've had in gaming in as long as I can remember.  Somehow a single guy made one of the best SRPGs in years.  This is the type of indie game that needs to be supported.

You play as a guild master of a simple adventurer's guild down on its luck, and try to reclaim your former glory while also finding out dark secrets regarding the former guild master's (and your best friend) mysterious death.  A pretty interesting story that keeps you interested throughout the game even if its a very simplistic "good vs evil" story.  The characters are also all entertaining and well fleshed out.

The gameplay is very deep.  There are essentially two major phases to the game, the "management sim" aspect where you manage your guild by caring for your adventurers.  This is setup as a list of menus around your base where you can hire/train/equip/heal and organize your adventurers.  You also unlock different features in the base throughout the game's story.  The game almost NEVER stops drip feeding you things to upgrade and unlock.  It's part of what makes it so great.  It doesn't run out of steam.

The adventurers themselves are basically your RPG party members.  They have a stat sheet that will remind a lot of people of fire emblem and each of those stats affects their functional battle stats in various different ways.  Each time they level up, there's a percentage chance that stat will increase.  This increase varies WILDLY between different adventurers based on what traits they have.  Each one is randomly generated in the hiring menu.  You'll never get sick of looking through the hiring menu whenever it refreshes with new adventurers looking for interesting combinations that can make very powerful characters.  This combination of randomly generated traits and the stat growth system make character building so interesting.  I should probably mention there's also a "class" or "job" system for all these characters.  Each class has very unique stats and skills that make none of them redundant - they all have a different purpose and fulfill them masterfully.  With the DLC release that added a couple extra classes there are a LOT of different character archetypes that you can mix and match now.  

The combination of different classes plus the limited character deployment in each mission requires you to have a wide variety of characters that do different things.  Each mission you do with adventurers also applies a mood debuff on them or injuries that penalize their max health if they took damage that force you to rotate through multiple characters and teams.  The teams themselves can even be customized to have unique relationships within themselves and with other teams.  The fun never stops!  

That's a tiny little view of the management aspect of the game, the other parts of the game don't slouch either.  Each mission you undertake is displayed almost like a board game where you move your "piece" (your adventurer party) around a grid through a small randomly generated dungeon.  You can interact with resources to collect things, and there are roaming monster parties that will hunt you down to initiate combat. You can also run into randomly generated events that can give your party members unique and powerful traits or curses.  Part of the fun of the game is rolling with the punches, I HIGHLY recommend playing with the iron man setting on so you can't save scum.

Combat takes place in a grid style turn based strategy RPG.  If you've played tactics ogre you'll be right at home here, it's very very similar from that aspect.  One of the biggest differences from tactics ogre is that every character in the combat has a chance to go each turn, the order is just separated by their speed or "initiative" value.  The gameplay here is pretty garden variety (more characters through cells to do things to the enemies), but has enough to chew on to keep you entertained.  The big payoff is seeing your adventurers growing and becoming strong to the point where they can do absurd things in combat like delete an entire enemy combat group alone in a single turn.  There's a lot to explore, and because the game continues to unlock new weapons, armor, items, classes, etc throughout the game you're continually unlocking new interesting things to do in combat.

About the only downside of the game, is the art style is kind of scuffed and the music and sound fx are generic.  The art style does grow on you a little.
