Jogo de tiro multiplayer que coloca os jogadores no papel de caçadores humanos ou dinossauros em uma batalha sangrenta de sobrevivência. Ao longo dos anos, o jogo manteve uma base de jogadores fiel, embora não tenha alcançado um grande público mainstream.

Pontos Fortes:
1. Variedade e Dinâmica de Jogo

A premissa de dividir os jogadores entre dinossauros e caçadores humanos cria uma dinâmica única e diversificada, que não é comum em muitos Jogos Multiplayer. As classes de personagens têm habilidades bem diferenciadas, o que adiciona uma camada estratégica a cada partida.

2. Comunitária Engajada

Embora Primal Carnage: Extinction não seja um título de grande sucesso comercial, ele possui uma comunidade sólida e engajada (pequena). A maioria dos jogadores ainda é entusiasta da ideia central do jogo, e a comunidade costuma ser ativa em servidores, com encontros e partidas regulares. Isso contribui para a manutenção do jogo, especialmente para aqueles que já apreciam o conceito e não se importam com a quantidade de novos jogadores.
Além disso, há uma presença contínua de atualizações e pequenos ajustes por parte dos desenvolvedores, o que mostra que há uma atenção dada ao jogo, mesmo que em menor escala.

Pontos Negativos:
1. Comunidade Pequena e Morta (em Algumas Regiões)

Embora o jogo ainda tenha uma base de jogadores leal, a comunidade não é grande o suficiente para garantir partidas rápidas o tempo todo, especialmente em horários de pico mais baixos ou para quem deseja jogar fora dos servidores oficiais.

2. Falta de Inovações e Atualizações

Após seu lançamento, o jogo recebeu algumas atualizações, mas nada que tenha realmente mudado ou aprimorado substancialmente a jogabilidade. Isso significa que o jogo permaneceu em grande parte estagnado, o que é uma desvantagem quando comparado a outros títulos do mesmo gênero, que continuam a receber novos conteúdos, mapas e mecânicas.

3. Desbalanceamento nas Partidas

Algumas classes de dinossauros ou caçadores podem se sentir desbalanceadas, o que afeta a experiência de jogo. Por exemplo, certos dinossauros, como o T. rex, podem ser extremamente poderosos, causando uma diferença significativa de habilidade entre jogadores novatos e veteranos. Da mesma forma, algumas armas ou estratégias podem parecer opressivas em determinadas situações, o que pode resultar em uma sensação de que o jogo favorece certos tipos de jogabilidade, deixando os outros em desvantagem.

Se você é fã de dinossauros e de combates intensos, Primal Carnage: Extinction pode ser uma experiência divertida, mas esteja ciente das limitações do jogo e da comunidade.

-Bug do save corrompido (Um slot de save sempre fica marcado como corrompido)-

1 - Desative o save na nuvem nas opções do jogo na Steam.
2 - Vá pra pasta do save do jogo na Steam (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Sunset\Saves\<Pasta com id do usuário>)
3 - Abra o arquivo steam_autocloud.vdf com o notepad e apague todo o conteúdo dele e salve.
4 - No arquivo steam_autocloud.vdf clique com o botão direito, propriedades e na caixinha lá embaixo, marque como "Somente leitura".
5 - Abra o jogo 
6 - Reabilite o salvamento em nuvem na Steam.

-Bug onde não é possível mudar a resolução-

1 - Abra a pasta do jogo.
2 - Clique com o botão direito no executável Sunset.exe e vá em Propriedades.
3 - Vá para a aba compatibilidade, e clique em "Alterar configurações de DPI alto"
4 - Lá em baixo clique em substituir o ajuste de DPI. e na caixa de seleção deixe selecionado como "Aplicativo".

It is a solid original MGS clone with procedurally generated missions between a few story missions. Not a fan of Rogue Games, but Spy Drops pulled me in, so a big plus, although I preferred linear story missions.
The story is heavily inspired by the first and third installments and is brief but right to the point without any unnecessary strayaways. Great cinematic-ish cutscenes and music.
After experiencing the gameplay, I would say I got quite eager to experience the original MGS if I had the possibility to play comfortably and not have a god awful Master Collection as the only legit way to play it.
Controls are great, so no issues anymore, although I wouldn't know what to compare to.

As for the situation around this game. Sadly, it is a great example of how marketing campaigns own the popularity. I clearly remember how everybody was praising the MG clone - Unmetal, and seeing how Spy Drops was immediately dropped (sorry for the pun), begs the question, do true indies really stand a chance in modern industry? To developers, if they read it, as your previous projects have shown, the PS1 stylistic is the best way to go on, and I hope you will stick to it, because it looks and feels really great and more unique than Mario-esque style.

And the last point about the so-called "scandal". I would say only that it is very easy to pick on small indie devs and not the multi-billion dollar corps like NVIDIA, Microsoft, Apple, or Google, who are the true promoters of AI and potential culprits behind the firing of hundreds of thousands of people and further mass unemployment. But the puny,  feeble, and intellectually weak people feel like the single-person (or a small team) game developer is the one who should be blamed and persecuted. It is easier that way. 
To finish the topic, I would be the devil's advocate in this sentence, and remind some people that Salvador Dali, or Bob Ross (for a more modern audience) haven't lost their jobs because of the creation of photography, opera singers and troubadours didn't lose their actuality because of the creation of sound recording, and so the game industry or art industry, as Kojima himself said, won't disappear due to usage of AI. Talented people will always be needed, but that cannot be said for mediocre artists or copy-pasters. This is absolutely valid.

My point, dear dev or devs, please don't take it personally and keep making your projects the best way you can. You did a great spy game and should be proud of it, you deserved it.

No, what this game cements to me is the disempowering feeling of an abusive relationship. Quickly you realize your job, your position as supervisor, just puts you closest to this giant man eater, lets you bond with her, have romantic moments sure, but only to immediately shutter in fear as you dare pick an imperfect option. 

Here being shrunken while literal magic, is more about having been made powerless, to feel small and threatened, not a partner in crime but a victim. Interactions are tests, honesty is for idiots, your only goal is appeasement. As one of the other little people often tell you, all moral reality has been stripped away, there is only the safety and peace found in Saeko’s joy, and the utter oblivion of her disapproval. 

The thing that really gets me is the way it captures abuse in how fast the turn can be. Were you a little too quick to speak? Maybe you thought things were going well, you made her blush, you made her happy so you told a well meaning joke. Then her eyes get cold. It's not got a clear internal logic, part of the fear, and a part of the real life horror is you can not make yourself perfect for your abuser, what is and isn’t acceptable is going to be arbitrary. It's a state of chaos that makes you more pliable, being unsure and afraid is the point. Anyone who's been in or seen an abusive relationship has seen it can identify it.

Stylistically the game captures it well too, the art style's sketchy look, the way the text seems to always be shaking with your character's panic. The music too and the subtle scares of seeing Saeko’s reflection on the phone screen looking at you with venom.

On the story side I also like the abuse themes that exist within Rin’s relationships among the little people as well. She, and I use she due to the story hints that suggest to me that Rin to be a closeted trans person which you can even admit to Saeko in one scene, is constantly being tricked and manipulated, and pressured into doing the same to others. She is sexually abused in a deeply sad if thankfully not at all graphic scene by a fellow little person early on, an older lady that routinely pressures you to be complicit in the cruelty of the place. Though you have the power of life and death in there, or the illusion of it, no one even remotely respects you. You’re just the favorite bug for now, for now.

In truth this continues into the games choices, frankly, there just isn’t many and on second playthroughs I was deeply disappointed with how many of the choices I did make that were illusory. This fits the themes but did make second playthroughs much more boring despite my initial interest in jumping back in. It was enough of a bummer I got to admit that I went from loving the game to just liking it. I would advise doing one blind playthrough and letting what happened be what happened. If I had done that I feel like I would have found it more resonant. 

While I focused on the themes of abuse, there are definitely other ideas churning in the game. Concepts like complicity, moral relativity, sexism, gender, and even everyone's old favorite capitalism. There is plenty in this game as is in my opinion. Though, ironically, I don’t think it's a very good dating sim for giantess fetishist lo.

112 Operator is the big cousin of 911 Operator, and as much as I liked the first game, this is a genuine improvement on all fronts. The main takeaway from this review is that 112 Operator is intentionally a very stressful and demanding game. Multiple times I caught myself thinking, “this is so bad,” as I tried to will the city not to crumble into disarray. That said, this is exactly the experience I was looking for, and I’m very happy with it. However, I would expect this level of stress from a “hard” difficulty, not medium. Still, a “crisis manager responder” game should be stressful and demanding by necessity.

The main improvement over the original is the addition of a campaign. In 911 Operator, the calls eventually started repeating, yet there were still many you never got to hear. The campaign solves this problem very elegantly.

My main complaints are mostly about everything outside the core gameplay. The game does a poor job of communicating which squads will be injured for the next duty or what equipment is actually useful. The weather tab feels overdesigned and provides little helpful information ahead of time. Emails are a mixed bag, ranging from highly immersive to trivial messages like a firefighter complaining about not having enough work.

Overall, 8.5/10. I’m very happy with my purchase, though I did get it on a good sale.

I’ve put around 3,500 hours into Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020, and honestly, it’s been a wild ride. When it first came out, it completely changed the game. The graphics, the detail, the realism... it blew everything else out of the water. Flying anywhere in the world feels so amazing.

But after five years, the excitement’s been replaced with frustration. The same core bugs from day one are still here. Things like autopilot acting up, broken ATC, weird flight models, and random performance drops. It’s crazy that this stuff still isn’t fixed after all this time.

The focus over the years has been all over the place. Instead of tightening up the core sim, they poured effort into world updates, marketplace content, and third-party partnerships. Looks great for marketing, but doesn’t fix the issues that actually affect flying day to day.

Those developer Q&As started out promising, but they turned into the same routine: big talk, nice words, little action. Month after month, the community raised the same concerns, and the answers never really changed.

And now with MSFS 2024, it’s hard not to feel like we’re being sold the same story again. It’s built on the same foundation, and many of the same problems seem to have carried over. After years of loyalty and patience, that’s a real letdown.

To be clear, MSFS 2020 is still an incredible simulator..... when it works. It looks stunning and can deliver truly amazing moments. But after 3,500 hours, I can say it’s been one of the most impressive yet frustrating sims I’ve ever used.

Man, this game is bloated. Don't get me wrong, it is not quite a bad thing. I like long games with meaningful content, but if they cut a third of it, it would be just perfect. 
- The crusade part is undercooked. It is like a Heroes of MM-like mini game, but there is not much space for experimentation with the troops or trying tactics. There are some basic units, but the upgrade for them feels random, and the mercenary units are many, but good luck recruiting many for cheap. You can skip it, but doing so will cause some achievements to fail and miss out on some cool gadgets.
- Fights are monotone after Act 4. Basically, you always fight against the same 4-5 types of enemies except bosses, you buff, you shoot some spells (mainly the same ones), chop-chop, and they die. I shouldn't play on core, it is so much fight... 
- Voice acting is more just for flair than really for immersion, sadly. Some DLC started to use a cinematic camera for some events. That looked cool. I wish there were more of them. It is like playing any old school CRPG.
- Some of the companions are undercooked, like Daeran, Seelah, or Nenio, compared to Wendulag or Arueshalae
- Movement is so slow. If you want to backtrack, have fun watching the map for minutes. There is an option to speed up the fights, but not the running around... I think 20% of my playtime is just running around. 
- There are no or just very few remarkable quests. The ending is mostly what sidequest you did for your companions. But in the end, it is quite a Mass Effect ending. You got a slide show based on what quest you did or not. Only the main story could be changed somewhat by choosing a different mystical path. But do I want to run around (slowly) another 50ish hours just to check the other paths and to read some different lines?
- Secret ending is insanely specific, and good luck finding it by yourself.
- DLCs: You should only buy Season Pass 2. That gives some nice things for the main game. I don't like DLCs that don't give anything to the main story. Also, A Dance of Masks didn't start for me somehow.
- Still, there are many bugs and frame drops with some crashes that killed Steam, too. It was interesting.

After all this whining, I still recommend it. It is a solid combat-heavy CRPG, but after playing this, I finally see how BG3 changed the CRPG scene forever.

As a photographer I wanted to love this game. It is a great concept. I really enjoyed all the manual camera controls, the photo missions to unlock more levels, etc. But this game gave me extreme motion sickness - dizziness, nausea, eyestrain, headache - even after applying the recommended settings as directed by the game instructions. I even tried again another day to see if it would improve and had to close the game within a few minutes. Not sure what the problem is as I have no issues with other realistic sim games. But the second I begin walking around the movement feels unnatural and dizzying.

The other nitpicky type issue I had is that the DOF settings do not seem totally true-to-life. Even stopped down all the way to 1.8 or even 1.2 I was still seeing a pretty large range of objects in focus. At these levels the DOF should be incredibly narrow. Additionally, I found the controls a little clunky. It was awkward to have to hold down E to "crouch" while also using the arrow keys for camera settings and the right mouse key for focusing.

The game has fantastic potential with some improvements but for now I do not recommend it, especially for those concerned about motion sickness.

[h1] Inspired by True Urban Legends of Sumida City! [/h1] 
I know that his VN's a bit tad wee expensive but it 100% approved by me that its worth the money! 
It's very interesting, with HOG mechanics, amazing music, great characterization and an amazing story inspired by a real city in Japan. Join the investigation of seven mysteries of Honjo by exploring the history, suspense and getting into a hunger game situation; a supernatural fight for your life! 

[b] Story: Amazing but Overpowering? [/b] 
I loved the story, its woven around these seven historical mysteries surrounding a city but the more you look into it the more you realize everything is just part of a big puzzle. You follow the life of an unremarkable guy named Shogo who meets Yuko and of course as unremarkable office guy he is, he was just looking for a girlfriend. Yuko has an immense fascination with the supernatural and is trying to find clues to a mystery in a park, but within one night everything changes in your life. You are given powers and a hunger game begins! Yes you direct this story or more like, sometimes even the 4th wall breaks, sometimes things happen that doesnt make any sense but will do later. You examine the story with so many characters POV, i think at least 5 characters stories and they get interconnected with each other. You are later introduced to a story board and you need to be very careful with choices here. Yes you can die easily, you can use powers too.  I really loved the fact that the artefacts are woven out of those seven mysteries and each has a unique story to boot, but are there only 7 mysteries are they? Join hands in hand in 90's Japan to address an incomplete mystery that was in Edo period through ancestral connections that will leave you desperate for more. And what I meant by overpowering is that I wonder if there is too much info thrown at the player in one moment, it did make me bewildered on why I was exposed to so much info at first. Yes yes but most of all did you know? That these seven mysteries WERE real urban legends? Read on to figure out more below! 

[b] Characters: Best Characterization [/b] 
Characters are amazing, they have their own backstories, trauma and somehow in the end you find out that everyone and everything is connected. With all of the 5 characters I think I like Yakko and Hajime's fiancee. You are given the power to destroy, but each character have their own selfish interests; The two funny police detectives, the mother who lost the child, the student who lost their bff, the fiancee who lost their partner, all have tragic situations but you get to see how they develop and progress to fight evil or embrace it. They could have released an Ayame Tono perspective too, but I don't complain. This amount of characters are enough. Some danganronpa feels here. 

[b] Gameplay: Unique! [/b] 
Yes it's a horror VN but the horror is only in the beginning however the story would also bring it out later. You have timed scenes, HOG scenarios, story board shifting so you dont have to replay the whole game to get achievements. You have a lot of dialogue options and I am so glad it did not end quickly. I did wish that we could have won the game without the alternative timeline, but it's still fascinating how the past makes sense to the future. You have also the inventory sometimes, and can read files, documents and an insane 15+ character database in detail. The amount of hard work put into this game is intense and showcases it appropriately with the amazing execution. There are some minor jumpscares here and there but its not over-staturated with them. You can also use the mouse and look around a 360 degree, which makes the suspense intense! 

[b] Art and Music: Great! [/b] 
This is an art style on its own, it does have chromatic aberration I think? which I did turn it off so its easier for me. I loved the main theme, it pumps blood into you amazing composition and I do wish that the characters were voiced. This deserves its own anime and voice over! I would have preferred an extra chapter like in Shironagasu island with this load of characters though. The backgrounds are drawn beautifully. 

[b] Achievements: Bold [/b] 
Some of them are straight forward and easy, you just unlock them while unlocking all character endings. You will tend to miss one with the mysterious story teller at the start so make a save there. The mocking bird stickers can be intense to find, the 4th sticker can be found clicking on the crazy detective several times repetitively at the candy shop. Took me 17 hours to beat while reading story. 

[b] Crimes and Historical Legends - Based on real urban legends!  [/b] 
According to Duncan Heaney's review on Square Enix website, the seven mysteries are based on real urban legends to the Honjo area. The Tourism office of Sumida City (where game is set to occur) has helped with game setting and locations. So i decided to investigate more; In a 2012 article by Zack Davisson titled "Honjo Nanafushigi" details the real urban legends related to Sumida City can be found. He says that Ryogoku performers back then narrated these legends during Edo period. It's a collection of legends in Honjo and popularized. You can search in Japanese Honjo Nanagushigi and you will get access to the real stories. I heard there is a tourist spot now but some say it had disappeared and you can read signs about the urban legends and buy sweets back then. 

[b] Historical Relevance - SEIMEI NO ABE!  [/b] 
Abe no semei the legendary onmyoji is mentioned here! He is my absolute fave so I do know some facts about it. It would be amazing if we had our own Shikigami lol, but the scrolls passing down from seimei's generation is still true to this day I heard, I am glad someone took note of that. It's a lesser known fact. Tsuchimikado family here is real and there is a temple dedicated to Seimei in Kyoto. The resurrection ritual in the game was known as Taizan Fuku no sai (Taizan ceremony) and was rumored at that time as a secret ritual to summon the dead.  Its a closely guarded secret and only the Abe clan has access (as rumored). The game also used a real city because I read in credits that they are giving thanks to Sumida office. 

[b] Overall [/b] 
Thank you Xeen studio for paying respect to Abe No Seimei and onmyodo, as well as honouring the Sumida City.  It was a fantastic execution using supernatural stories and creating a hunger games scenario where us the player can interact more in rather than just playing a visual novel. This was my go-to-go game for Halloween 2025 and I am not disappointed! Eagerly waiting a sequel so I can find about the mysterious story teller and such!

Хороша гра, схожа на XCOM, але вимагає більшої уваги - як настільна стратегія, для якої кількох годин після роботи буде замало. 

[h3]Геймплей[/h3]
На відміну від XCOM, де кожна місія - окрема висадка бійців, тут є щось на кшталт напіввідкритого світу. Разом із командою ти досліджуєш його сектори, збираєш матеріали, обмінюєш їх на зброю та витратні ресурси й вступаєш у бій - зазвичай тоді, коли сам вирішуєш.

Пряме зіткнення - майже завжди помилка: варто відкрити вогонь, і вороги збігаються з усієї карти. Через це більшість часу йде на підготовку - виманити когось поодинці, відокремити від групи, зібрати ресурси, підтягнути рівень зброї. Тут потрібні не поспіх, а терпіння й уважність.

[h3]Атмосфера[/h3]
Атмосфера апокаліпсису тут справді класна - навіть коли хтось проходив поруч з монітором, зупинявся й казав: «Вау, у тебе дуже атмосферно!»
І це правда: музика підібрана ідеально, персонажі відчуваються як справжні сталкери з досвідом - без американських соплів і героїзму. До подій ставишся серйозно, але водночас світ уміє розсмішити - хоч якимось кумедним скелетом, знайденим у кущах.

Але в якийсь момент ловиш себе на думці:  [b]«Щось тут не так...»[/b]
 - стиль будинків — частково фінський,
 - дороги — німецькі,
 - машини — радянські,
 - реклама — американська.

І стоїш, дивишся навколо й думаєш: [b]де ми взагалі? Що відбувається?[/b] 
Саме тут відкривається інша сторона гри.

[h3]Деталі[/h3]
По-перше, у гри був невеликий бюджет, тому розробники економили на всьому, на чому могли. Наявність радянських автомобілів - просто результат використання безкоштовних 3D-моделей із бібліотек.

По-друге, гра заснована на [b]шведській настільній грі[/b] вісімдесятих зі своїм особливим гумором. Це пояснює мутантів у стилі Даффі Дака - тоді взагалі було модно показувати, як радіація перетворює людей на тварин (привіт, Черепашки-ніндзя).

[h3]Враження[/h3]
У підсумку маємо поєднання серйозного бойового настрою та світу, який немов жартує з тебе. Це досить незвично, якщо звик до американських апокаліпсисів на кшталт Fallout або The Walking Dead. Може скластися враження, що всі тут тікали від зомбі, але їх просто немає - майже всі загинули від ядерного вибуху.

[h3]Підсумок[/h3]
Загалом я раджу цю гру. У неї справді цікаво грати, особливо якщо вам подобається XCOM. Просто приділіть їй трохи більше часу - і будьте готові, що всі ці «Волги» й «Жигулі» можуть трохи дратувати.

you'd think a simple roguelike like this would be boring or frustrating after 40 hours or so. but unlike other games where you've figured everything out by then... in nuclear throne, the endgame is where the real fun starts.

i rarely write negative reviews, but nuclear throne is truly one of my favorites. it's like a zen state. every run is so intense yet *so* relaxing. the first 20 hours are an unforgiving learning process, but this is a necessary sacrifice in order to truly appreciate what comes afterwards.

nuclear throne avoids the problems of many other roguelikes, where you're doomed if your items aren't good enough or you get swarmed by enemies in the wrong way. this game is fine-tuned so that you can ALWAYS theoretically win a run, if you know what you're doing. it is the epitome of tough but fair. it should be frustrating but it isn't, because at the end of the day, *every single mistake* is your fault. (okay, that was a lie, a few of the achievements are just brutal. but it's about the journey, not the destination!)

true, sometimes the deaths feel like BS, and sometimes they even are. but it's a learning process. for example, getting suddenly blown up for all of your health is pretty funny -- and more importantly, it's a lesson to respect the power of grenade launchers (and stage props!). even the most explicitly unfair obstacles, like certain boss attacks, can be avoided with practice or planning. the end result of this mountain of failures, is a very satisfying flow state that tests your reflexes and tactical planning.  this is doubly true of the "endgame" system, which is a lot of fun if you can pay attention to all of the chaos. even now I am finding dumb ways to die, some really dumb ways to die.

overall, it's awesome for 15- or 30-minute study breaks. definitely a unique and interesting vibe, maybe slightly annoying at times, but it's grown on me. for example, i wasn't a huge fan of the soundtrack but you can easily go in the game files and swap it out with, say, the hotline miami music. great time, solid recommend. it should be even better when they release the epilogue update with custom difficulty & more character-specific achievements.

Ys IX is a decent ARPG. All aspects range from "average" to "slightly above average." Story, combat, and music are all decent. It is not a miserable time, but it is not a stellar time either. If you have played Ys VIII: Lacrimosa of Dana, this will feel exceedingly familiar; they are cut from the same cloth. Ys IX inherits almost all the problems from Ys VIII, with some notable improvements and additional drawbacks. Ys IX effectively feels like they took Ys VIII and made a new game from its component parts. Don't go in expecting something fresh.

In this review, I'll mainly compare it to Ys VIII, as this is the only other Ys game I have played and they are so similar the comparison just feels inevitable. I'll note the key ways it differs in this review. 

[h1] Story [/h1]
The story is interesting but ends up being quite shallow. Adol is arrested in the city of Balduq. You find out there are many seemingly random arrests, and the mystery is all around this prison and the spooky "Grimwald Nox" world that occurs when the plot demands you do some wave-based enemy combat sections. There are some other hooks here [spoiler](like there being two Adols)[/spoiler]; largely, however, you're stuck with these "hooks" for the entire duration of the story. 

All the pay off, explanation, and any plot progression is basically entirely back loaded in the story. You only learn what is going on in the final 25% of the game, leading to it feeling very shallow plot-wise. The other 75% of the time, you're running in a very predictable loop. You do side-quests, fight a horde of enemies from Grimwald Nox (literally copy and pasted wave-based defence from Ys VIII), then you enter some dungeon that ends up always leading to prison, without fail. You even always have an extra side-quest to rescue some random person from the prison. All of it is exceedingly repetitive and predictable. Most of the story that goes on here describes political history and tension between Romn and Gllia (two countries).

However, in contrast to Ys VIII, the Scooby gang this time around actually has plot significance, and it feels a lot more cohesive why these characters are in the plot to begin with. Each character plays some role, minor or major, in the overall mystery you are presented with. Sadly, you only learn and see all these things at the end of the game. They could have done a far better job drip-feeding these details over the course of the story rather than dumping it at the end. This compounds yet again in it feeling too shallow, on top of the fact Adol is a silent protagonist. The story is held back from realising its potential for expanding on the plot points it has. Party members also lack many moments that show chemistry between them, but when there are moments, they are quite enjoyable. 

Overall, however, from a character perspective, it is a large improvement from Ys VIII, which had Dana as basically the only character and all the ship crew, which were literally just bodies to fill 50% of the game so they could tell Dana's story. Here, all the characters you "recruit" into the larger Scooby gang add quite nicely to world-building and contextualising all the political tension and history between Romn and Gllia. There are shallow, yet nice sub-stories here of people who are connected and side-quests related to these characters. I think the only character that doesn't add anything is literally a random dude you find at a lake, who decides he's just going to live in a pot in your basement now. 

Wrapping it all up, the story is decent. It won't keep you hooked, it won't surprise you, it won't feel crazily satisfying or shocking at the end, but it's okay.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
If you played Ys VIII, you pretty much know how the gameplay is. It has most of the same pros and cons, with some exceptions. Cons being, chest rewards are still boring (open chest, get two twigs, YAY), no i-frames, unintuitive hit boxes, etc. Pros being, combat is generally fun and feels satisfying, mildly interesting accessories, and mastery (when you get past the jank) feels good.

Ys IX has the same set-up as Ys VIII for combat. You have 4 attack abilities you can use that require SP, which recharges over time or with a charged attack, some ultimate move you can activate when a bar fills up, and you can equip 2 accessories, plus armor and a weapon, etc. 

Ys IX does improve on general exploration in comparison to Ys VIII. You get "Monstrum" abilities here, highlights of which are wall climbing and gliding. Wall climbing feels very nice and fast (though glitchy if you bump your head into a ceiling). For exploration, this means that horizontal maps are much more prevalent than in Ys VIII. Ys VIII is just filled with flat planes and the occasional hill; in Ys IX, you can explore roof tops, towers, all sorts. The drawback is a lot less map variety; you're stuck in Balduq and some generic grassy plains the entire game. Many collectibles are scattered around to encourage exploration; they end up being busywork but don't overstay their welcome *too much*. 

Weapons and armour are the same as in Ys VIII, that is, boring and linear. You have one line of weapons that get better linearly. Two sets of armor, one focused on evasion %, one on defence and HP, they linearly get better. Almost zero choices to make here.

Hit boxes seem tighter than in Ys VIII. They still have some issues with appearing delayed or unintuitive after an animation, but I didn't find the hitbox of an ant in Australia wiping out my entire team. This problem is replaced with another one, in that often there are just *too many* enemies simultaneously attacking at once; it is almost impossible to see what's coming. Some sort of arrow or mechanism is needed to show enemies off-screen readying to attack you.

Ys IX has flash guard and flash dodge; it works the same as in Ys VIII. I like this system, but it is critically flawed. Whenever you do certain special attacks, all enemies freeze on the screen for a time. This makes it almost impossible at times to actually time guards and dodges with enemy attacks. You have no idea if the enemy is going to randomly freeze, so you mistime the parry, then there's a cooldown window so you can't parry again, and thus, you get hit. There is also no feedback that your parry is on cooldown, so it ends up feeling like you missed the timing, even when you might not have; your parry is just on cooldown. Ys VIII had this problem to some extent, but it didn't feel nearly as bad there. 

Ys IX feels like it has far less enemy variety than in Ys VIII. Mostly, this is because a lot of enemies are of a samey design due to being Lemures (enemies in Grimwald Nox), so they end up feeling less distinct. There are some unique enemies in dungeons and outside Grimwald Nox, but it is a striking downgrade in variety from Ys VIII. Bosses are okay; it is the same as Ys VIII, entirely non-contextual. You walk into a sewer, find Lord of the Lizards: God of Destruction, you walked into his crib, he doesn't like it, so now you do battle. I found bosses in Ys VIII generally more enjoyable, though.

Ys IX rehashes the defence and elimination missions from Ys VIII, only this time there's no parrot [spoiler](a pro or a con, depending on your affinity for parrots or hearing "Adol, Adol, Squawk" every few seconds)[/spoiler]. As stated in the story section, you do these consistently each chapter, usually one required defence mission per the story and one optional elimination. They're mundane, not very interesting.

In summary, combat is better and worse than Ys VIII in nuanced ways, but it is still generally fun.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
You can't go too wrong with Ys IX. It's a solid mix of flaws and middle-of-the-road gameplay and story. It is the more well-rounded version of Ys VIII, though I'd prefer Ys VIII over this. If you liked Ys VIII and don't expect anything wildly different, you can't go wrong with this.

This game really wants to be Portal. And that isn't a bad thing, I really want to be Portal too, but if you really want to be Portal the first step is to bring something to the table.

The Entropy Centre tries to, and it is a commendable attempt. The concept is interesting; interesting enough to get me to buy the game and play it. But it falls far from the mark.

SOME PROS:

Game looks great and has a consistent art style, runs great as well.
Neat conceptual gimmick.
That's about it.

THE REST:

I did not finish this game. But, I got 10 chapters in, in 3 hours. Most people who have finished the game report around a 10 hour game time, and unless the last 5 chapters are 7 hours long, I have a feeling I was solving puzzles a bit ahead of schedule. I only bring this up because a large part of my complaint is how easy the puzzles are by design and conception, and I possibly have a biased perspective because they were easy for ME, and I apparently did them quicker than most. So just keep that in mind, I suppose.

The comparisons to Portal in this game's design are also so blatant that I am going to directly compare them in my review quite a lot. This game basically demands you think about Portal while you play, so I don't think its unfair to contrast them.

But, I digress, the puzzles were easy. In Portal, you have to get cubes onto buttons. How you do this is interesting, because you must utilize the limited space and your limited amount of portals to pilot the cubes where they need to go, then pilot yourself to the exit. By the time you have finished solving a puzzle in Portal, you are at the exit and moving on to the next section.

Ironically, for a game about reversing time, the structure of solving a puzzle in The Entropy Centre is also reversed. Where you solve the puzzle mentally, then go through 3 mins of walking to set up the solution in order to arrive at the exit. The fact that the puzzles involves the manipulation of the cubes rather than the manipulation of yourself (Like Portal) every puzzle is easily and instantly solved by knowing where the buttons are, where the cubes are, and what order each cube must go on each button. Every second after SEEING the puzzle, is tediously and slowly setting up the solution you immediately intuited. This is frustrating rather than satisfying. Any realization in The Entropy Centre was never 'AHA, THAT was the solution.' it was 'Oh... I forgot that button was there. Guess I'll redo the whole thing.' As the puzzle rooms got bigger, and more cubes were needed to solve the puzzles, this became tiring and eventually led to my quitting.

There is combat in this game. Why? I have no idea. It is not clever, it is not fun, it is not difficult, and it is not interesting, nor did it interact with the puzzle solving during my time playing. Portal had turrets, so maybe that's why, but the turrets in Portal were incorporated into the puzzles. The combat in this game is a separate obstacle that does not interact with the puzzle elements and is just an extra fail state to facilitate more restarting from zero.

The writing is also not great. Portal is renowned for the funny talking robots for one VERY simple and VERY hard truth... The writing was really fucking good. It was witty, and nuanced, and told jokes that are fairly high concept for a computer game at that time and felt oddly real and endearing. When it was made the whole 'corporate language used in dire, dystopian circumstances to juxtapose bureaucracy with societal collapse.' schtick was not tired and cliche, and even on top of that the themes of the story were deeper than that surface level observation. And even though I have a thousand good things to say about the writing in Portal, it was all secondary to the experience of solving the puzzles. You know why Portal (And first person games in general around that era) had a silent protagonist? Because WE are fucking already playing the game. Most humans do not need a person to affirm what they are seeing, a character to constantly react to every thing that happens, because we already do that innately. The Entropy Centre does not understand this. The Entropy Centre's main character's dialogue includes a lot of "What the heck?" "What's going on?" "What the sigma was that?" ass dialogue, and it is distracting and unnecessary.

I do wish there was a more neutral option, because although I did not enjoy this game, there is clear passion and direction that I think is worth a shot. Maybe it is for you, and maybe the puzzles will be interesting for you. I know I would suffer through far worse writing than what is present here if I got a good puzzle experience, and maybe you struggle with spatial reasoning and can enjoy The Entropy Centre. The sounds like a dig, but it is earnest. I would say its worth a shot if you are REALLY desperate for a puzzle game that's kind of like Portal...

But I'm not sure it meets that bar, at least for me it definitely didn't.

The Entropy Centre is a very good game. It is very similar to titles like Portal and The Talos Principle (especially the latter, in my opinion, including its environments and soundtrack), though it still stands out with its own distinctive features. The time reversal mechanic for objects is particularly interesting and very well implemented.

The only things that frustrated me were:

- The time limit for rewinding objects can be a bit of a hassle. Although it encourages you to move items more efficiently, it is not always clear while manipulating them whether the time limit will run out until it actually happens. Resetting the rewind timer by clearing an item helps, since it allows you to see if it will exceed the limit as you move it.

- Some sections require more platforming and precision skills than actual puzzle solving, such as puzzle 1404.

- There were a few bugs where objects disappeared. This was especially frustrating in puzzle 1405, where the large box fell near the base of the elevator, clipped through the ground, and vanished. This happened to me twice, and I had to restart the stage, going back to the previous room since there was no checkpoint in between.

- The lack of checkpoints in certain areas forces you to replay large sections, which becomes even more frustrating when bugs occur and forces me to do everything again (like explained in my previous point). This was particularly annoying in the first puzzle involving conveyor belts, where you need to rewind them from the second room. It took me a long time and many attempts to finish the first room, only to realize later that I could have rewound the conveyors. The game had not yet explained that mechanic. A short introductory puzzle requiring conveyor rewinding before that long one would have helped me discover it sooner and saved a lot of time.

That said, I greatly enjoyed the game overall. I completed all puzzles without looking up any solutions online, although in 2 of them I might have used unintended methods (1404 being one of them). The puzzles were creative, the ending was satisfying (although not extraordinary), and the story was engaging. The atmosphere was excellent, conveying a strong sense of mystery and desolation.

I highly recommend this game, especially if you enjoy puzzle experiences similar to Portal or The Talos Principle. I give it 9.2/10.

This is a game where one run as of 2025, with 4/7 episodes released, will take you maybe 3-5 hours. This is one run, with two traits and the annoying feeling that maybe something else could have happened if you played with a different pair. But you only played one run. You're curious about what might happen if you could just have stopped that bad thing in episode 3. You restart the game with two new traits. You play again. You see new dialogue, you experiment a bit, you try new things. You discover, to your delighted surprise, that certain characters are opening up to you more now than they did previously, and others are closing off. You're finding new substories. You're getting invested in the mystery. You start saving and reloading at certain junctures just to hear that one conversation that you've never been able to hear in any prior run. You go through the game again and again, each time with different pairs of traits and witnessing new outcomes at the end of every episode, and to your delight and horror, the game *just keeps branching*. They've accounted for every possible state a character might address you, every single way you might want to approach a situation has been added. You think you've seen everything, but you've joined the Discord and people just keep putting up screenshots of stuff you've never seen before. You dig into the code desperate to find out what sorcery has been made to craft this, and you realize that it really just is the dedication of an extremely small studio of two primary developers that simply Will Not Stop until they've made the "choices matter" game you've always dreamed of in your head but, after years of being burned by the likes of Telltale and Bioware, you thought could only go so far. It can go that far. It really can. And that's how a 3-5 hour experience becomes almost 100. And there is no way that won't continue going up.

Welcome home, cousin.

Originally, I was extremely skeptical of this entire game. I really liked slay the princess, probably the best narrative game I've ever played, and then pristine cut came out and that probably became a definitely. Slay the princess is the kind of narrative game that rewards replayability because you learn more and more about the world and the characters. Scarlet Hollow does the same thing, but better. The difference, is that in SH, you pick traits that unlock information, which you then have the potential to learn. StP was simpiler, but information felt less impactful because it is mechanically "cheaper".
I played through every path of StP, chose nearly every dialogue option, experienced every cutscene, image, soundtrack, and ending, at least I remember doing so (I dont have 100% achievements). That story helped me through some very difficult times.

I bought this title because I was desperate for some actual original, deep content. So caught up in the busy rush of college work and job hunting, family drama and existential stress, nothing was fun, and every experience I tried wasnt rewarding, or left me feeling worse for wasting time. It was tough times again, and so I came back to StP, but I had already experienced all it had to offer. I was reminded of this game afterwards, and had to try it based on my experiences with StP.

Scarlet Hollow is different, it is probably the deepest story I have experienced in my life, though im not sure what refrence I am for that (I have read very few books). I dont know where Black Tabby is taking this title, but there is nothing in the digital world I await more than the full release for this game, and thats coming from someone who has experienced practically everything the gaming world has to offer. 

Black Tabby does writing right. There are no jumpscares, everything is built up. Orchestrated into the most disturbing yet humanizing experiences I have ever seen. Their games allows you to take them lightly or seriously, mainly refering to comedic choices/dialogue options. The people in the world feel real, and perhaps it's just me, but almost all of them feel ridiculously relatable too, they feel human. For those who have forgot, it can remind you of what that means and feels like too, In a world so silent and blind as ours, I couldnt ask for anything better in any game I could play.

Their writing is impeccable, the illustrations express perfectly the tone of the world and the emotions of those within it, the pacing is slower than StP, but it is better for that. I have no doubt that when this title is finished, it will be the greatest visual novel that has ever existed. The only thing that can elevate this experience above 110% is voice acting. The immersion VA created in StP made everything hit harder and was one of the reasons it became so important to me, it helped me resonate with every message Black Tabby attempted to convey. I dont expect it to come to SH until the entire story is published, if it comes at all, but it is something I would love to see.

Tldr: Buy it, then buy it again as a gift, and then all the OST to support the best visual novel writers of our age

I was really hyped for this game but fell for it like a sucker. A warning to all prospective buyers, the author does not respect the player's agency, and the story of this game is as linear as can be. Any individual player choices in regards to dialogue are window-dressing at best, and very little of your choices actually even matter.

And where they aught to matter, your ability to choose to retry (in a timeloop game of all games), is simply taken away, because despite the fact that you get to usually choose how the character interprets events (through internal dialogue), these interpretations do not matter for the sake of the absolute railroad this game is on.

And then there's the writing, which has some quite charming characters, but then curtails whatever options or points of interaction you have with them. A timeloop plot is rich with the opportunity of "what if" scenarios that could occur, but almost all of the choices you make cannot be made again once you've made them once before.
And that is /if/ those alternate choices would actually lead anywhere, which, invariably they don't.

And then there's the matter of pacing. This game's pacing is utterly horrendous, thanks to a combination of the previously mentioned disregarding of the player's agency, but also the fact that you constantly have to go through unskippable cutscenes over and over again to figure out some of the puzzles, thanks to the 47 minute limit on each loop. (Which is neither internally consistent, based on your actions, nor real life progression of time.)

At least it did one thing that any piece of art is supposed to do, and that's the evoking of a feeling unto whoever experiences it. However my only reaction is a combination of frustration and disappointment.

Don't waste your money on this. 
And to the developers of this game, you aught to be ashamed of yourselves for wasting the opportunity to make something actually great, and should remove the "Choices Matter" tag from the steam page, cause that's a blatant lie. Just write a novel next time.

Games need to stop advertising themselves as “choices matter” simply because there are choices in them. The choices in this game are arbitrary and do not result in any real effects other than minor bits of flavor text. Simply put, they don’t *matter*. Some would argue the same for a game like Disco Elysium, but Disco Elysium has much, much more depth and reactivity to it. 

The writing is okay. It’s not bad but it’s not great. The dialogue tree is surprisingly limited. 

The art is beautiful but gameplay and writing should always take precedent over appearance, especially in what is essentially a visual novel. It seems like most of the budget went into designing the game rather than actually making it. I would have loved to leave a positive review for this game but it is absolutely not worth the $30 it costs.

I wasn’t expecting it to be as good as it is. As a long time Hitman fan, this was superb. I had never played the fourth entry before, though I went through the first three, which were solid but lacked the incredible environmental design found here. Some of these missions have the best layouts I’ve ever played, and the third mission genuinely stunned me. It hooked me the same way Hitman does making me want to revisit each location to explore it more thoroughly, since I usually don’t the first time around. The level layouts make sense, and the scale is absolutely impressive. The freedom to approach objectives in multiple ways really enhances the experience, making each mission unique which was awesome might I add and coming from the third game that surprised me.

The gunplay is excellent the sniping feels impactful, and the iconic kill cam is as satisfying as ever. Its just the medium range that lacks finesse so usually the best option is either close up or long range which suits the game and guns ablazing is possible but not without the right loadout. The ability to customize weapons is always appreciated and my god are there a lot of options available to you, even a testing range to try out your combinations, and you will want to replay missions to unlock new weapons since only a limited amount of armaments are available from the beginning. However, it’s not without flaws. The story is your usual fan fare and characters aren’t particularly strong they mostly serve as background for the gameplay. The AI can be inconsistent, sometimes reacting unrealistically, and there are moments where close quarters combat overshadows the sniping focus. All in all, it’s much better than I expected, and I’d wholeheartedly recommend everyone give it a try especially since it’s often available at a steep discount.

I'm an experienced TFT, Autochess etc. player and the tldr here is that it's an enjoyable experience that I played for 2 weeks and then just kinda ran out of content. I also think most people complaining about the balance are correct. However I think it's still worth the price tag if you like these sorts of games. 

More details
Presentation
- I think it's a very high quality game with charming visuals and satisfying looking fights. As played more runs I tended to speed up the battles and especially buffs but I think that's pretty normal for a game of this type. Some art is reused or similar but everything looks and acts differently enough that it doesn't bother me at all. One exception here are the blobs that are recolors and could really use some more distinguishing features since their effects vary a lot. Besides that I have no criticisms here for an indie game of this price this is some top tier visuals.

- Sounds are fine since it's not really important for games of this type but doesn't feel particularly satisfying either.

Performance
To preface this I want to mention that I primarily play on Steam Deck.

- I did run into a couple performance problems pretty consistently. They mostly show up deeper into runs but were never severe enough to stop the game from being enjoyable.

Balancing issues 

- As an experienced player in this genre I might have a different experience than someone who just picks this up on a whim. I think they actually put effort into easing players who are newer to auto battlers into the genre and have done so pretty successfully.

- Let me start of with my biggest gripe I have about the game. Splitting units into "squads". Most Units in the game come in a squad of multiple units. These squads take additional damage from AoE attacks and distribute the damage they deal across the different members of the squad. I feel like this mechanic is bad for multiple reasons. 

1) It makes the game needlessly difficult to read. Why is my 500/500 Squad losing to a 50/150 single unit? why is my 30/80 Dragon completely outperforming a 150/150 Zombie Squad?

2) It invalidates Squad unity from being tanks. Most of the bosses and elites apply AoE Damage. These are the challenges you are building your team up to in a stage. If you can buff up a squad to beat them you could have buffed up a mid sized unit for much more benefit. This even applies to smaller squads. 

3) On the same note it also invalidates melee squads from being effective damage dealers as they never deal full damage and don't effectively surround bigger enemies. 

This hurts especially Zombies since they have some support units attached to them that loose all viability because Zombies don't work as a tank or a damage dealer. Honestly I wish they would just remove the mechanic entirely. 

- My next point kinda intersects with the previous but too many units are unviable at higher difficulties. This is okay for units that are worse than others but can still perform since they will sometimes be your best option in the right situation. A number of units are only unviable because they are worse than other options at the same tier, not necessarily because they are bad themselves.(Mages, Towers, Salamander, Spellblade, Succubus). However a significant number of units just don't fulfill their role (Sentinels, Wardens, Zombies) and a couple also vastly overperform (Dragons,Sergeant, Dryads, King). This creates a formula for winning runs (build up dragons early, add in dryads, miners and sergeants, get an Ogre, add in King) that feels way too consistent. 

- I want to emphasize again that I still had fun figuring out the game and I still think it is worth a purchase.


- The above points combine to make the game a bit too easy.  I found some success pretty quickly on the normal and hard difficulty finishing both in just 1 run. That's fine of course as players should still be figuring out the quirks of the game. Insane difficulty was harder to beat but not in the way I expected. I just felt more funneled into the strategy mentioned above instead of using whatever units I had by the end of finishing all characters on insane I really felt like each game felt the same and whenever I tried branching out I got punished for it. 

- This unit balancing problem also makes most classes feel very similar and their unique units very rarely felt like worthwhile additions that made other strategies more viable.  

I hope they can improve the balance of the game and I will be very excited to try it out again when they do as I think the foundation they built is very solid and can become a truly great game.

Before we begin I have to mention this PC port is a travesty, it's basically broken from every aspect and requires patches to fix some of the issues. Some QTEs seem impossible on controller without this fix -
https://www.pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/Silent_Hill:_Homecoming
Without even considering the game it's a non recommendation even before we get to the game itself, but we'll dive into that below. 

Silent Hill Homecoming is considered by many to be the start of the end for the franchise, the first in the series made by a western dev (ok it was actually silent hill origins but that's often forgotten for being a psp game). The first game from newly formed double helix games a dev that has long since been absorbed into the amazon games machine and a dev that had potential, that killer instinct remake is an absolute classic. 

Homecoming is often considered a bad game, it's poor story, weird combat and reliance on popular SH iconography that diluted the game's own story and themes are often at the forefront of the conversation, with rushed development and many players distain towards the idea of an American developer, homecoming has had an up hill battle, but is it actually that bad? 

The short answer is yes, the longer answer is mostly yes but some no, I do think it's a bad silent hill game, I'd even go as far as saying it's a bad game, but it does have a few good things going for it but it's not enough to warrant you play it. I must admit that the bosses are actually really great, mostly fun to fight with fantastic designs and really showcase the design talent of double helix when they stop sucking off silent hill 2 and 3. 

Music as well is really fantastic, which isn't too surprising considering Akira Yamaoka composed the soundtrack. It's incredible with some truly fantastic tracks. Almost a shame it's been wasted on a game that is mostly hated. 

So the negatives, well it's hard to list them all but the big thing that's always bothered me in that this is essentially silent hill the movie the game. It borrows a lot from the film and also takes many things from SH2/3 whilst also not really understanding what made them special, it haphazardly throws nurses, pyramid head and robbie the rabbit at you without really spending the time to justify their inclusion. 

The story is also a weak retelling of silent hill 2, with a twist i find to be so undercooked that it just comes across as silly. That's not to say it's all worthless, the inclusion of Shepherd's Glen as an offshoot of silent hill which has it's own practices similar to that of silent hill itself, is an interesting take and exploring outside of the iconic town is a welcome change. I think for me the main character is so boring and uninteresting that it harms the story. 

I also really just don't like the combat, it's functional and is fun to a degree but it feels like I'm playing ocarina of time rather than a silent hill game. Alex throws himself around like he's Geralt of Riva and it's just so dumb. I also hate that you fight human enemies which is honestly a massive misunderstanding of the franchise in my opinion. The shift in focus on the cult is something I really dislike about silent hill and this game doubles down on it. 

It's also a misunderstanding of the source material when you can unlock the UFO ending on a first playthrough and it's not even difficult, so the idea of this being someone's first SH game AND they unlock the ufo ending must be one of the most confusing things ever.

Overall this is a pretty poor game, it's not completely worthless (well on pc it is) but the overabundance of film references and bizarre combat with a weak story make this the worst mainline games in the franchise. You can mod the game to make it playable but you can't mod it to make it good.

The Verdict: A Great Game, an "Okay" Remaster
Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition on PC is, at its core, an exceptional open-world crime drama that still holds up years after its initial release. However, the "Definitive Edition" itself is a bit of a mixed bag for existing PC players; it mostly just bundles all the DLC with a few minor visual tweaks and performance enhancements that the original PC version already largely offered. 

What Makes It a Must-Play (If You Haven't Already)
The real star here is the original game. The story, following undercover cop Wei Shen as he navigates the brutal Hong Kong Triads, is cinematic, engaging, and genuinely feels like a great action movie. The voice acting is top-notch, featuring a celebrity cast that brings depth to the characters.
 
The combat system is arguably the game's best feature. It's a fluid, Batman: Arkham-style free-flow martial arts system that is incredibly satisfying and brutal. Environmental takedowns—like tossing enemies into a wood chipper or an electric eel tank—never get old. This focus on hand-to-hand combat is a refreshing change from most other open-world games which rely heavily on gunplay. 

Hong Kong itself is a fantastic, dense, and vibrant open world. It's not as massive as a GTA map, but it's packed with detail and unique activities like cockfighting, karaoke, and illegal street races. The city has a wonderful atmosphere, especially at night in the rain when the neon signs light up the slick roads. 

Conclusion:
Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition on PC is a highly recommended purchase, particularly for newcomers to the game. It's a complete package of an already excellent title with a compelling story and satisfying combat. If you can find it at a discount (which is common on Steam), it's an absolute steal and easily one of the best open-world experiences available.

Terra Nil hates its players.

A new mechanic is introduced every map, and that mechanic often breaks the way that you have been taught to expect things to work, and for no obvious reason.

The new mechanic is inevitably poorly explained, and requires refined sequencing over time as you fill out the map. The specific details required to achieve acceptable sequencing are only revealed progressively, meaning that you can be a significant distance into the map before realising that you’ve done something that makes it impossible to hit an arbitrary target. The only solution at that point is to restart the map from scratch. For example, in the last level you are asked to recycle your buildings once the map appears completely finished, however doing so results in you deleting critical components required to power your space ship before you actually leave.

Every map requires you to achieve very specific ratios of different biomes to progress, and what biomes can go where often requires significant refinement. This can mean, for example, that you start flooding rivers and establishing vegetation on the banks, only to later discover that this has prevented you from setting up certain other conditions that require empty creek beds to achieve. At this point the only solution is normally to restart the level.

Each map is very finely balanced in terms of resource production, but this typically only comes to a head when you’re nearing one of the three interim transition goals within a map. This means that if you do too much of this and not enough of that you will only discover this after you've been happily building away for some time, unaware of the resource cliff that is approaching. At this point the only solution is to restart the level.

Accepting that this is a game, and there is a lot of suspension of disbelief involved due to the abstraction, but particularly jarring to me was that game routinely requires you to achieve ambient temperatures significantly exceeding what would normally be conducive to most animal and plant life. Honestly, just re-scaling the temperature range to something around half of what the game keeps requesting would be simple, and enough.

On any objective level Terra Nil fails as a game, but it looks pretty and the animations are relaxing, which in this case seems to be enough for me. As a result I am giving it a grudging thumbs up, however your tolerance for the game's very many rude hand gestures directed at the player may vary. I guess I must be a masochist.

10.25.又来i蓄力锤{已平衡}了，耗能技能增幅+普攻蓄力的左右脑互博的设计，走技能蓄力要吃能量增幅则要武器改造的+10秒cd，走技能增幅能找到一个方向非常不可控，生存和蓄力挨打坐一桌的低频3次转圈圈且被击中或者主动中断没有任何补偿，并且在付出5个资源点（技能/商店）满改造技能且舍弃武器改造收益且要接受技能cd制后的收益比不上走高暴击高频率完全不管技能或者单纯挂暴击buff的巨剑普攻。技能普攻蓄力和耗能增幅总要舍弃一堆，不论选择哪个不是蓄力挨打就是不可控挨打。花钱，技能改造，能量上限，能量恢复效率，到头来伤害还没有人家高频高爆普攻流高，命中率要降低自己的生存，挨的打要更多。

11.9.更新给蓄力锤普攻增加了范围方便前期真空期的清怪，让攻速能作用于蓄力速度，不过相比受击蓄力立马完成显然后者更直接，但是考虑到不一定能拿到这个模块这个效果对于下限有保底，我的建议是放到武器初级改动，满改门槛显然太高，它也没那么强，因为蓄力dps更多受限于技能cd而不是蓄力速度（毕竟普攻蓄力不吃技能增幅，更多服务于真空期和前期），或者把蓄力受击立马完成蓄力做成武器改效果也行，因为它非常核心。同时蓄力锤需要一点点身后判定和技能取消释放的部分cd+能量补偿，这涉及命中率，空蓄力导致的是恢复，cd，能量的清空，空技能有负反馈是应该的，但是面对高机动或者抓取技能不得不取消释放是常有的结果，给主动取消以部分补偿我觉得也很合理。关于狼博士，他的战斗场地大到boss能够离开玩家的视野范围外，并且他能够在视野外冲刺和释放远程攻击，可能是我平常没开声音可能有声音相关的反馈，但是我希望有高度相关的不同颜色的屏幕外感叹号告知玩家狼博士正在释放某个技能而不是等待他屏幕外的本体或者弹幕的高速突脸。最后给制作组点夸奖吧，做内容也要动力，言语支持虽然无实质性，但多少开心一下。单次大范围高伤我觉得还是很符合“原地蓄力”“受击反击”“带cd长真空期”的设计直觉，数值给到位之后就会有承受了上述要素后打出强大的一击的正反馈，不论是一击干掉大范围小怪还是一击给boss血条重创都是很爽的点，而打断进入眩晕状态增幅也算是给眩晕该有的收益，单纯的让boss一段毕竟短的时间当靶子实际上由于不能带来多少命中率或者dps上的提升所以原有的正反馈不明显，晕眩期加伤害就让晕眩更有用的同时不至于太强，因为晕眩时间所占的输出时间并不长，我用蓄力打出晕眩，并不一定能够在晕眩期再打出高伤技能蓄力，这需要用普攻蓄力进行前置，属于更有操作难度的部分。当然加眩晕时间让一些多动症安分点也是思路，给相对更灵活的，会主动躲避的怪/boss设计眩晕时间显著增长我觉得也是可以考虑的设计，就好像一巴掌拍停拍死了烦人的蚊子一样有爽快感。测试时期难免有一些预料之外的非常强的东西，直接削弱显然会导致反感，将其作为更特殊的，更稀有的强大变异则是让它到它该有的地方，也更符合收益越大获取难度越大的基本准则。总得来说改动还是挺不错的。

我目前还没解锁充能斧，就我个人感受对玩到的武器进行评价。
巨剑：围绕着暴击率和爆伤来做构筑的武器，凑到暴击相关的组合时就很舒服，没有也只是有点难受。
火焰刀：我的首通武器，构筑非常明确，只要围绕火焰方面构筑就可以了，持续作战伤害越打越高的类型。
电细剑：玩得我手疼的武器，可以往闪电或者是单纯的技能循环流构筑，纯闪电流只能说按技能按的手疼，闪电刚需层数，稳定多触发要多技能连携。无论是有延迟还是无延迟都需要多按技能达成高收益，前者需要叠层保证爆发时的收益，后者要保证稳定爆发的量。如果是纯技能循环就简单多了，只需要找准一个技能以这个技能为核心构筑就可以了，还不用废手。
武士刀：个人体感最爽的武器，围绕攻速和破坏力构筑，成型后只需要靠满配的初始技能就可以通关。难点在于前期刚需上状态手段，导致初始技能的爆发打不出来。
蓄力锤：整体围绕着蓄力、基础伤害和消耗能量上构筑的武器。蓄力有霸体，主打一个抗伤蓄力反击。主打一个放空大脑。
爆炸刀：最牢武器，围绕易伤作文章。但是易伤又很容易消耗，自身除了抓基础技能和连击技能外就只有初始技能带易伤，武器本身和易伤没有一点关系。但凡装满弹后打出的那一发带有粉碎效果也勉强可以接受。这一发前摇长也不带霸体，很容易被怪围殴时打不出来，手感很差，到了后期这个伤害完全不够看导致其性价比低。后期爆发完全要看能不能抓到核心的易伤爆发技能，通关后甚至不想用这个武器打第二遍。

Live A Live is a Top 10 game for me.  Each character's scenario in the 1st Act has unique elements overlaid on top of the common mechanics.  The 2nd Act twist is among the best I've even seen in any medium.  And the 3rd Act brings everything (and everyone) together in a mysterious sandbox where poking your nose into every corner yields big rewards.  The Remaster has great quality of life updates, charming retro-esque graphics, and a bit of rebalancing to make Masaru not useless and Sundown less OP.

This game is absolutely a great time that I highly recommend. The story structure of following different heroes across different eras of time gives some nice varied settings with a few chapters that could stand alone as their own amazing stories. It also is so satisfying when everything comes together in the end. The combat is also fun and strategic. I can't stop gushing about how much I love this game and would highly recommend all my friends to check it out.

[b]Rune Factory: Guardians of Azuma[/b] takes a western fantasy-inspired series eastwards in this new spinoff game. And since it’s a spinoff and not a proper numbered entry, that means the game gets to try things of its own. How does it fare?

The farming has been simplified, going for the bare minimum. That means there’s health or levels for soil among others. It’s clear the focus is not on farming on its own, but on the new village building mechanics. You can build houses and other establishments and have generic villagers do various jobs – tending to crops, working at shops, chopping wood, mining, etc. You also have to decorate the village to increase village level and gain various bonuses like stat boosts or improving areas of proficiency for villagers. You can make the villages autonomous, generating cash, so you don’t have to engage with it too deeply either. As a “city builder” type of game, it is competent, but that’s it. One problem is that you either want to make “aesthetic” villages or “functional” villages, since there’s just not enough space to have lots of décor and buildings and make it look adequate, most notably in summer and winter villages (it used to be worse for the former before the patch!!).

The combat has a better feel than that of [b]Rune Factory 5[/b], thanks to more open level design, but mechanically also simplified. In previous games, you could customize weapons during crafting or with upgrading, giving special properties or exploiting stat ailments, and there was consideration for trading off defense and offense for different weapon types, and you can’t throw bad stuff at enemies like Object X or failed dishes. That means the combat of this game boils down to choosing bigger numbers and abusing sacred treasures.

The visuals are very nice. I praised [b]Rune Factory 5[/b] for having a bright and colorful aesthetic, but this game triple downs on that, the visuals are even more vibrant, with nice stylish visuals. The modeling is great. There’s no 2D sprites for conversations, but the characters are expressive and well animated. The graphics are definitely one of the highlights of this game, especially since arguably none of the previous games were particularly impressive in this department.

I noted in my review of [b]Rune Factory 5[/b] that it lacked a jumping mechanic, which could’ve elevated the world exploration and combat. Look at that! Jumping! There’s now an element of platforming and verticality, and the traversal is more enjoyable with jumping, and you can attack in air as well. The world design in general is VASTLY improved, the exploration is much more enjoyable and detailed. I hope they’ll bring the jumping mechanic and these world design sensibilities into [b]Rune Factory 6[/b].

The music is different, this time handled by Noriyuki Asakura, notable for contributing to the soundtrack of [b]Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice[/b]. All previous games’ music was handled by Tomoko Morita, this time credited for sound design, with some similar jingles like sleeping and levelling up, but easternized. I think the soundtrack is okay, but I prefer the music of previous games. There aren’t many memorable and fun tunes, mostly atmospheric. It probably doesn’t help that with all sound settings being at max, the music is quiet relative to everything else. While not a big deal in villages, the sound effects and voice lines drown it during combat, which means you can barely hear combat or boss battle themes.

The story is good. I’ll admit, I wasn’t very invested in it initially, but it does become more interesting later on. First, you go rescue the 4 gods of seasons and their respective villages, and then some shenanigans happen. I like how both gender characters are present at the same time, instead of being a simple binary choice, and you duke it out in the intro. And there’s even one choice with actual consequences and some pretty good emotional moments. The voice acting also helps. Speaking of, the production values are improved substantially, the main story is almost fully voiced, as well as bond stories, and the cutscenes aren’t as stilted.

For a game that otherwise has some solid writing, it is disappointing to see the “Let’s Chat” option result in characters saying generic stuff, the chats were more enjoyable in previous games, it reminds me of those generic NPCs of [b]Rune Factory 5[/b] in a bad way. [b]Rune Factory 4[/b] is still the king in this regard. The addition of hanging out is a positive and I would like to have it in future games. Sure, the options are generic and typically result in a short cutscene, but it’s better than nothing. Bond is easier and more enjoyable to level up, with characters having preferences for different activities. I also like the bond stories, though they are only available for romance candidates, they do a decent job of fleshing out the characters and giving interesting stories to chew on. I also like dialogue when outside of villages, with some NPC combinations bouncing off each other.

Same-sex marriage integration has been improved. No longer is there confusion about how to get a child for couples of the same gender. Not only is it better mechanically, even lore-wise I like it more. For how hyped the feature was for [b]Rune Factory 5[/b], the way you get a kid was actually a let down. [spoiler]You pray to the tree and it just gives you babies. In this game you pray to the shrine, and plant a turnip and it grows into a kid. It feels more unique and natural for the series.[/spoiler]

There are a few changes that make the game lose a little bit of [b]Rune Factory[/b] identity in my eyes. RP is now a generic mana pool. In previous games, RP was both mana and your stamina, pretty much everything you did required RP, combat, farming, crafting, you name it. In this game, it’s only used for Sacred Treasures (expect for Plum Branch). While in combat, they act as powerful attacks or healing in case of Sacred Drum, which can be pretty useful. As for farming, only Sacred Drum and Sacred Sword are worthwhile, which is half of sacred treasures that can be used for farming.

They even renamed some items like flowers from unique names like Toyherb -> Daisy or Charm Blue -> Bluebell Flower, which makes the game (and the series if you haven’t played previous games) appear more generic. Feels like they didn’t have the creative juices to make up some new fantasy flowers/crops exclusive to Azuma.
 
The skill progression has been gamified. You gain All-Purpose EXP for doing general activities like farming, combat, shopping, etc, and then there’s specific EXP for stuff like different weapons or sacred treasures, crafting or social activities. All-Purpose EXP can be a substitute to specific EXP in case you don’t have enough. You use EXP to unlock stat boosts and some perks in various skill trees, like making sell prices better or unlocking new combat moves. This system feels a bit more generic in comparison to how your character growth was handled before. Also, it’s funny to imagine that you can unlock an ability to share a kiss with your loved one by fishing days long (that is a real unlock by the way).

Overall, while I am positive about [b]Rune Factory: Guardians of Azuma[/b], and it might be a better game than [b]Rune Factory 5[/b] if we take into account production values and polish... I prefer the gameplay of mainline entries. Some of the streamlined, simplified and removed elements mean there’s less engaging mechanics to occupy yourself with, there’s little satisfaction in doing general activities on their own, and there’s not as much stuff to do. I do think this game is a worthy addition, though maybe not $60. There’s some fun to be had, it has an interesting story, lovable characters, pretty visuals, and some elements worth bringing into future entries. I like to think of [b]Rune Factory: Guardians of Azuma[/b] as a distraction, a vacation of sorts. And everyone deserves a vacation.

[h1]割と何でもできる3DアクションRPG[/h1]
ルーンファクトリーシリーズ初です、難易度ノーマルで60時間ぐらいで本編をクリアしました。
基本的に、里の復興や内政、収穫を行う→フィールドに出て敵を倒したりしてストーリーを進行を繰り返すゲームです。
序盤の内は里の復興がメインになりますが、復興しきった後は本格的にストーリーが進んで問題解決に向かう感じです。
全体的にこういうので良いんだよこういうので！と感じて非常にプレイフィールが良かったです。
ただ、プレイ時間が長くなる分もうちょっとこうだったらな～～と思う点も結構ありました。

[h2]良いところ[/h2]
・NPCのアルゴリズムが良く出来ており、場面に合った挨拶や会話が細かく用意されています。
NPCの気分で色んな箇所に行ったり、普段と違う会話が聞けたりで「生きている」感じが凄かったです。
・アクションはややシンプルですが、操作感が良くて軽くアクションをやる分には丁度良かったです。
・NPCの数が多めで、半数程のNPCは恋愛→結婚も出来るし、同姓婚や人間x神の結婚もカバーされています。
個別のイベントやエンディングも用意されているので、お気に入りのキャラクターと何処までも仲良くなれます。
・導入やストーリーの指針がかなり丁寧に用意されているので、迷ったり困ったりする事はほぼありませんでした。
ゲーム初心者にもおススメできる優しさです。
・こういう系統のゲームには珍しく、敵モンスターを仲間にする牧場システムがあるので、
色んなモンスターを仲間にして、戦闘に使ったりアイテムを生産して貰ったりで面白かったです。
・結婚システムは神ですね。結婚すると同じ寝室で寝たり起きたり、朝出掛ける時に行ってらっしゃいを言ってもらえたり、
遠出して帰ってくると晩御飯作って待ってたりします、理想の嫁すぎる……！

[h2]悪いところ[/h2]
・カジュアル寄りに作った結果、アクションは頑張って敵の攻撃を避けなくても余裕で勝てるバランスになってます。
神器を連打するだけで最後まで勝てました。高いアクション性を求めている人には合わないと思います。
・NPCの作り込みは凄いのですが、半数のNPCは恋愛→結婚のイベントが無いので、
イベントが無い人が好きなキャラだと辛いかもです、そこは調べてから買った方が良いかも。
・弓で遠隔のケガレの花を狙い撃ちするところとか、舞いのデカ判定を利用してケガレの花を破壊するところはかなり分かりにくいです。
基本的に行き詰まったら弓か舞いで大体何とかなるので、詰まってる人は試してみてください。
・町の住民の並び替え機能が無いので、役職毎に並び替えしたいのですがゴチャゴチャしててかなり分かりづらい……。
最終的にスキル欄だけを見て何とか管理してますが、この辺はソート機能や並び替え機能が欲しかったですね。
・住民の農業作業で収穫→種植えまで勝手にやってくれるのですが、元の畑に植えていた作物と違う奴を植えたりするので、
畑がぐちゃぐちゃになって理想の形になりません。
結局自分が収穫するとスキルポイントもいっぱい貰えてお得なので、全部自分でやるのが一番楽で得でした。
（視点を切り替えると上からの視点で一気に作業できるので、チンタラ作業が終わるのを待つよりよっぽど早かった。）
この辺は「同じ種類の種を植える」的なAIもしくは行動パターンを選択できるようにして欲しかったですね。
・スキルツリーを取り切った後のポイントが勿体ない。
最初から片手剣をずっと使っていたのですが、後半はポイントが余り切って結構勿体ない事になりました。
スキルツリーが埋まっている場合は汎用ポイントに振り分けるなどの処置はちょっと欲しかったですね。
・冬の里だけ、やたら建物を建てる領域が狭いので置物を死ぬほど余らせました。
夏の里はアップデートでデカイ場所が増えたらしいのですが、冬の里も増やして欲しいですね。
・ストーリーは[spoiler]異性主人公[/spoiler]を助けるところあたりまではかなり良かったです。
そこから後半のストーリーは無理やり畳んだ感があって微妙でした、散々名前が挙がった[spoiler]カムロサキ[/spoiler]がほぼ小物扱いだったのが盛り上がりに欠ける…。

[h2]総評[/h2]
恋愛→結婚や、そんなに考えなくていいぐらいの戦闘、建物建ててNPCを管理したり、という全体的な色々をカジュアルに楽しめるゲームです。
この中では恋愛→結婚システムが抜けてよく出来ていると思います、キャラクターとイベントの出来も良いのでかなり楽しめました。
ただ、戦闘や内政に歯応えや遣り甲斐を感じている人には物足りないかもです。
個人的には、ちょっとセールが入ったら買うぐらいが丁度良いと思います。

This is my opinion upon playing an hour and a half.

Game is basically a porn version of an old anime called Mahōjin Guru Guru. 

It takes a lot from the series such as character design, overall plot and the running gags which was common in the anime. For people not familiarized with the anime, some of the jokes might not land, but still the game manages to keep the writing and characters feel funny and engaging. You don't need to know about the series it took "inspiration" from, but if you, you'll appreciate the nods, Game is your typical RPGMaker turn-based battles, but you can see that a lot of effort was put on the sprites and character portraits. Lots of original assets here.

Oh and this goes beyond saying, but there's like A LOT of shota on loli stuff, so if that's your thing, and you like the classic hero vs the demon lord tropes and tongue in-cheek humor, then you'll be right at home.

Regarding the spicy parts, they are surprisingly voiced and even animated to some extent. The high pitch voice of the witch girl gets annoying really fast but that's OK, at least the visuals are good and consistent.

Overall this is a welcomed surprise. Game has great presentation, good writing and great scenes and can't wait to get back at it and play some more, but as of now I'll give it a 9/10. Recommended.

It's an interesting experience revisiting Myst with a modern engine.
