With the modern graphics and full freedom of movement, the Ages of Myst end up feeling oddly small and under-detailed. The puzzles, too, were both less difficult than I expected, but also clunky in ways that modern puzzlers have mostly refined away from. There was an opportunity here to expand on the Ages and the puzzles in a way that could have explored the setting like we've never seen it before. And I mean everyone would have hated that (probably including me), but it's cool to think about.

That's not a complaint, though. The game looks great (aside from the CG character models) and runs smoothly. And the nostalgia trip was nice. I'd imagine it's very worth trying in VR if you have the rig for it.

銀河のどこかにある自然美しい星で、いつもと変わらない日常を謳歌していた人々に突如？突然？空から降ってきた機械軍団が襲い掛かり、主人公の姉が機械に攫われ、慌てた主人公は一心不乱に大切な人を攫った機械を追いかけていき、そして・・・という、美しい惑星の景色を見ながら右に左に駆け巡り機械軍団の謎を暴いていく、手順を踏む・パズルを解くのが主の一本道、まるで映画を一本見たかのような気分になれる２Dアクションパズルアドベンチャーゲームです。

面白かったです！相棒の黒猫のような生物「Mui」が可愛かったです！背景が凄く綺麗で合間合間に入る映画的な演出も迫力があって最高でした！言葉は通じなくても感情が伝わる作りになっていてプレイしていて気持ちが良かったです！楽しかったです！

基本一画面の中でパズルを解く・手順を踏んで先に進む系のアクションパズルがお好きなお方や、映画的な演出を楽しみつつ綺麗な風景を見ながらパズルを解いていくのがお好きなお方や、物語を想像、妄想しだしたら止まらないお方や、可愛い相棒(Mui)と共に冒険がしたいお方にお勧めです。

プレイ時間は全実績解除時点で１３時間程でした。
ただ私は美しい背景を隅から隅まで眺め、相棒のMuiをことあるたびに撫でながら、更に実績の「完璧(死亡せずにゲームをクリアする)」を取るために２周目にかなり慎重にプレイしていたのでこのぐらいかかっていますが、恐らく普通にプレイした場合は１０時間程で全実績解除できると思います。


「このゲームの良かったところ」

・背景が綺麗。
  青い空を背景に日の光を浴びて風に揺れる木々に草花、ごつごつとした岩肌に深い青色の海の水、底の知れない谷に砂埃舞う砂漠、そして無機質な機械達に星空に浮かぶ大きな月、一場面一場面記憶に残る綺麗な風景、背景を楽しませてもらいました。素敵です。
  
・Muiが可愛い、兎に角可愛い、ひたすら可愛い。
  相棒の黒猫のような生物「Mui」が可愛い、兎に角可愛い、ひたすらに可愛いです。
  このゲームの良いところの八割は「Mui」の可愛さだと言っても過言ではないと思います。
  「Mui」は好きなタイミングでいつでも撫でることができます。可愛いです。
  私は事あるたびに「Mui」を撫でまくっていました。最高です。
  
・パズル、進むための手順の難易度は丁度良い。
  先に進むための手順やパズルは簡単すぎず難しすぎずで丁度良い難易度だと思います。
  この手のゲームは大抵１箇所や２箇所ぐらいは「えええ？これってどうやって進めばいいの？」と画面の前で頭を抱えながら何度も何度も失敗し続けて尚「わからない～！ヒント見ようかどうしようか、う～む...」となる場面が出てくるというのが定番(私の察しが悪いというのもありますが)なのですが、このゲームではそういう場面はひとつもなかったです。
  少しだけ悩むことは数回ありましたが「どうしてもわからない！ヒント頂戴ヒント～！」と叫びそうになるパズルはなかったので難易度は丁度良いのではないかと思いました。

・即リトライができる。
  パズルに失敗して死亡したり奈落の底に落下しても失敗した直前から即座にやり直せる親切設計で助かりました。
  
・映画的演出が素晴らしい。
  合間合間に入る映画的演出が迫力があって素晴らしいです。
  ゲームをクリアした後スタッフロールを眺めながら、まるで映画を一本見た気分になっていました。
  その分ゲームとしては自由度は少なくて物語も完全に一本道なのですが、圧倒的演出と物語を盛り上げるBGMと各キャラクターにピタリとあったボイスが相まって、とても楽しかったです。
  
・色々と想像、妄想ができる物語。
  この惑星は何か？人間達と機械軍団の関係は？「Mui」は何者なのか？一本道の道すがら少しずつ謎が明らかになっていきます。
  そのたびに想像・妄想が広がってとても楽しかったです。
  

「このゲームの少し残念だったところ」

・ジャンプの操作が少し難しい。
  ジャンプの操作が少し難しいです。
  届く距離のはずなのに何故かジャンプしている途中でキャラクターが突然壁に当たったかのように垂直に落下する現象が数回起きました。
  そのせいで死ななくてもいい場面で数回死んでしまいました。
  
  この現象は私の操作が下手なのか、ゲームの仕様なのかはわからないのですが、もしゲーム側の問題でしたらこの部分を調べて修正していただけると嬉しいです。
  あと、できれば下に地面がある状態での落下死をなくしていただけると嬉しいです。
  下に地面がある状態で落下死してしまうのはジャンプ操作の難しさも相まって少し辛かったです。
  
・「完璧(死亡せずにゲームをクリアする)」の実績を解除するのは大変すぎる。
  操作に慣れて、パズルの解き方を全て覚えていても、１周するのに３時間ぐらいかかる道程を「一回も失敗せずにクリア」するのは辛すぎます。
  
  映像が綺麗で映画的演出が素晴らしく相棒の「Mui」がひたすらに可愛いこのゲームで何故こんなに辛くて苦しい実績を用意したのでしょうか？
  もうホントこの実績だけは意地悪としか思えません。
  せめて各章毎で死ななければ良し！ぐらいの難易度にして欲しかったです。
  
  特に上にも書きましたが、ジャンプ操作に少し難があるのでジャンプするたびに「お願い届いて～！」と緊張と祈りで凄く疲れました。
  本当に切に落下死だけは無くして欲しかったです。


言葉はなくとも感情が伝わり、風景は素晴らしく、映画的演出は迫力満点で、兎に角ひたすら相棒の「Mui」が可愛い、想像・妄想が広がる２Ｄパズルアクションゲームです。
パズルを解き、先に進むための手順を踏みながら進む系のゲームがお好きなお方や、風景が綺麗で迫力のある映画的演出を見ながらアクションパズルを楽しみたいお方や、物語の謎から想像と妄想を広げるのがお好きなお方にお勧めです。

完全不挂机，需要全程点击屏幕，挂一下午一点提升没有，居然连材料都需要手动捡，你管这叫挂机游戏

游戏评价：游戏本身作为一款像素风的放置挂机游戏，个人觉得美术不错，攻击特效，人物风格等等都挺好。但是，游戏玩法非常非常匮乏，现在更新后添加了一键拾取材料金币等等功能，比之前方便不少。但本质上长时间挂机所带来的正反馈及其的少，挂机数个小时可能只是升级某一项东西或者合成一次英雄，再购买两次。然后再接着挂机，这貌似比上班还无聊，还使人分心。
以下是带有个人喜好的一些建议：
1.英雄内容的扩充和消耗。在我心中这个游戏，龙崖和开罗冒险村物语是同类型中我特别喜欢的内容，两个游戏都有个特点可以组织养成的英雄下副本获取材料或者装备，高稀有度的掉落会带来一定的正反馈。但龙崖养成周期漫长，需要刷特定英雄的队伍这需要大量长期的挂机，而冒险村物语就是受限于其非常过时难用的UI界面等等。所以，我觉得摸鱼小镇可以在围绕养成的基础展开，添加一些可以使英雄职业组队消耗的一些游戏内容，现在英雄就单纯是高稀有度的耗材，混沌boss也是毫无掉落和正反馈。不如添加一些小型的地下城，可以挂机攻略，然后带回一些道具等等，甚至装备系统（简单的也可以，甚至只有饰品都可以），理想的场景就是我写完一段材料打开，可以进行收菜（装备，道具等等），高稀有度的道具和装备会带来一定的惊喜和满足感，而不是这些单纯堆砌数值的金币，然后一看发现还啥都买不起。
2.养成系统内容丰富。目前是34h的游玩体验，房屋道具等等实在是太少了，就是要时间堆砌攒金币解锁。例如，麦田会产生小麦，小麦可以用于增加英雄怒气，可是我有麦田的时候，根本无法马上解锁消耗麦田的建筑，这完全不合理。又会被金币或者等级卡住，虽然是个挂机放置摸鱼游戏，我希望道具还是可以丰富一些，小麦可以主动用来生产某些东西，可以是预选项放置生产，然后强化英雄或者之类的，还是围绕小镇上的英雄养成来展开，不然毫无正反馈。

总结：游戏美术底子很好，个人喜好是冒险，英雄，小队等元素的放置游戏，这款正好符合。现有的好评类游戏都是些牧场类的养殖养成，个人更喜欢这类题材，希望能越做越好，后面会改评价。

Ni no Kuni could be a perfect game but unfortunately it suffers from many bad dev choices:

- battle system is janky, you have almost no control over your party members behavior aside from very general preset patterns like "attack my target". The AI of your party is really bad and hardly any help except healing or tanking damage

- familiar catching is extremely grind heavy. Even with ability boost the chance of charming a monster is VERY low (10%) and even if you trigger the charm procedure there is a chance one of your party members uses an area attack, killing the monster in the process. And you have to catch 400 of them. AND they come with different stats so even if you catch one, you may need to keep trying to get a better one.

- most of the familiars are completely useless so you just grind to get the achievement but even if you decide to give it a pass the game still forces you to chatch batches of crappy familiars just to get progression points (stamps)

- some progression skills are totally useless but you still need to learn ALL of them to open next tier of skills

- tons of filler mechanichs. Kill quest within a fetch quest within another fetch quest. Every new town has those, making you scamper back and forth in an endless hampster wheel

- take heart - give heart mechanics is complete bollocks, most of the time the corresponding person is within the same town so you just run between people and watch the same unskippable casting cutscene happen like 100 times just to get some progression points (stamps) meaning you can't avoid this.

- you have a ton of spells in your grimoire that serve no other purpose than being cast once or twice during the entire game on a specific spot and then NEVER USED AGAIN. Also every time you need to use those the game force feeds you line like "you have to cast "REGROWTH" or "BRIDGE" or "TIME LEAP" here, killing any sense of wonder or problem solving.

- glacial pace of movement. Party movement whether in dungeons or towns is slow which wouldn't be that bad if the game didn't force you to walk everywhere and revisit multiple areas multiple times.

- the alchemy system works but it's utility is mostly negligible. All resources needed for better equipment are fully tied to your story progression and by the time you get enough of resources to craft let's say a better weapon, you're either able to buy one just slightly weaker or even stronger.

- familiar abilities are not properly explained, the affinity system is a mystery unless you read about it online. You have no idea whot any of the familiars you catch evolve to, what abilities they possibly learn, no way to gauge how good they are. Unless you like to torture yourself by trial and error you just google "best party lineup" and hunt for the best familiar you can get. It's DINOCEROS btw. After that it's OVER. You basically just one-shot everything till the endgame.

Final thoughts:
I loved the GHIBLI graphics, I liked the story and most of it's protagonists. I adored the music written by Joe Hisaishi (Spirited away, Mononoke) performed by Tokyo philharmonic orchestra and the professional character voice-over. 

I felt that EVERY piece of the puzzle for a great game was at the devs fingertips yet somehow they managed to make a mediocre game out of it. I would LOVE to recomend the game but I can't. That notion died by thousand cuts of bad game design choices. If I knew this before I've sunk 30 hours into the game I would have never bought it and I've completed it just because I'm a stubborn nerd. You were warned.

This game feels promising, so I am going to try to leave feedback that is as detailed as possible. 

The first few missions felt reaaaaallly slow. This may have been in part due to the length of the tutorial. In the labyrinth and battery tutorials you spend longer than necessary pushing heavy objects and just waiting for them to move, and in the spare parts tutorials, it takes way too long for the little repair drones to do their jobs. In the weapon tutorial, leaving your weapons on auto-fire leads to you running out of energy before the end, and turning off auto fire leads to getting destroyed by the big enemy before you have time to react. I feel like there should be an easy way to turn on auto-fire for all weapons or to manually fire multiple weapons at once in case of a sudden emergency, but that could also cause problems as sometimes my weapons seemed to hit my own ship, which seemed like a poorly explained mechanic. 

Prologue Mission
It feels very unpolished that the scrap pushers just despawn at the end of their track. It's clearly supposed to be an obstacle that traps you at the end, so it should look good at the end. In my opinion, several objects are too dark and seem like they could be background objects when they actually have collision (ex. the repeater towers). Crashing into one of the repeater towers and killing Shrub right before passing through a save point actually managed to softlock the game because I couldn't reactivate the station without a living human and the save happened after he had died. There were a lot of little secrets, but none of them really felt worthwhile to pick up, and it felt like stopping to explore them just made the mission take even longer with no real benefits. I was even more annoying when I decided to gather extra modules for my ship and they just ended up slamming into my ship while being pulled toward an airlock. I feel like the pulling mechanic should never pull an object with enough force to damage the object or your ship. 

This stuff may seem super nitpicky, but the tutorials and prologue are going to be most players' first experience with this game, so they really need to be a stronger starting point. I made it into the first real mission already feeling bored/burnt out, which is not a good sign. I think the prologue and tutorials could probably be condensed into one mission and streamlined to teach you the basic mechanics and story introduction more quickly, which could improve the issue of the  slow start. 

Some of the more mechanical issues I brought up could use some polish, but the idea and mechanics seems like a solid base to build off of. I will be keeping an eye on this game as it develops, and may update this review as things change. 

To the devs: Feel free to reach out if somehow this feedback wasn't already severely over-detailed, and you want even more.

[h1]A game that is way ahead in combat mechanics and animations[/h1]

Though I had completed the game way back, after having got into the hype train back at the end of 2024, I could not find the time to write down a review of the game despite having enjoyed it greatly. As I remember, playing Black Myth Wukong felt great - to witness the never before seen superior combat animations together with great graphics, while also keeping one eye on the GPU temperature. Going into the game it felt like stepping into Chinese mythology - one created by the sheer hype the game brought back then and to be honest, the game's atmosphere and gameplay does not disappoint and still stands tall even today. From the fog-covered mountains, twisted forests and ancient temples it was clear this game was crafted with care - especially the gameplay part of it. 

Coming to the story - the storytelling, however, is more abstract. The game avoids traditional exposition or lengthy cutscenes. Instead, it communicates through silence, imagery, the atmosphere of each encounter, all explained in a journal or in one immaculate video presentation at the end of each chapter. The game trusts you to piece things together. While this approach adds mystery, it also leaves many narrative elements underexplained, especially for those unfamiliar with Journey to the West. The lore is rich - but only if you're willing to dig for it.  

Though the game lacked proper narrative presentation, the focus was more on the gameplay here. What stands out most is the combat. It’s not just good — it’s exceptional. Fast, fluid and full of depth, with transformation mechanics that make each encounter feel unique and personal. You can play in whatever combination of stance or transformation that pleases you. Boss fights are the heart of the game, and they are designed to test your reflexes and adaptability. Many are cinematic and unforgettable, and there’s a real sense of accomplishment when you bring one down. Black Myth doesn’t just challenge your skills - it respects them and makes you strive for perfection.

The game also delivers in sound design. The traditional Chinese music, blended with modern orchestration, sets the mood perfectly - whether you're exploring a quiet shrine or locked in an epic battle with celestial beings. The ambient sounds, voice acting and especially the score in the final act are simply phenomenal.

[b]PERSONAL REFLECTION[/b]

The final section of the game was easily my favorite - visually stunning, emotionally intense, and featuring some of the best boss fights in the game, including battles against heavenly gods. The music during these moments elevated everything. Honestly, I wish the entire game had matched the brilliance of that final stretch. Still, what Black Myth: Wukong does best i.e., combat - it does incredibly well. As a boss-centric action RPG, it delivers where it matters most.

If it had offered stronger narrative clarity from the start, it could have easily entered “modern classic” territory. But even with its storytelling flaws, it remains an unforgettable journey — and one of the most mechanically impressive games I’ve played in years.

Cleaned up version of Sonic Generations with a short but sweet Shadow add on. It's just as fun as the original and Shadow's stages add some neat new mechanics into the mix. Great score for any Sonic fan!

[b]Sonic X Shadow Generations[/b] is two games in one: A slightly enhanced port of [b]Sonic Generations[/b] (originally released 2011) and [b]Shadow Generations[/b], a brand new entry starring everyone's favorite spiky anti-hero.

Sonic Generations is the same great game that it was back when it was released; a mix of exciting 2D and 3D gameplay celebrating Sonic's history, featuring recreations of fan favorite stages from previous games, and numerous challenges. Other than re-recorded dialogue (the story is an excuse plot anyway), the Drop Dash, some improved textures, and the inclusion of Chao as additional things to find, it's otherwise almost identical to the original release. Missed opportunity to improve the somewhat clunky Classic Sonic controls or add an extra stage or two, but still the game that Sonic fans loved back in 2011. As such, my gripes with the stiff 2D controls and the game's short length remain, but the rest is otherwise very good stuff overall. Also worth nothing that you can't unlock the original Sonic the Hedgehog like you could in the original Generations.

Shadow Generations uses a similar 2D/3D hybrid style for gameplay. Shadow's got his own arsenal of moves, some being iconic while others are all-new. To compensate for Shadow having less iconic levels to pull from compared to Sonic, his game contains a sizable hub area loaded with challenges and optional items to search for. It truly feels like you're Shadow himself when you're going around freezing time and warping from one enemy to another. Boss battles are few but memorable, all requiring a drastically different strategy to defeat. The serviceable (albeit not great) story, tight level design, incredible graphics & soundtrack, improved controls compared to Sonic Frontiers, and tons of collectibles all come together to make Shadow Generations an excellent game and well deserving of its hype. I just wish we had a little more of it; why no stages from Shadow the Hedgehog?

Overall, SxS is a great package with two of the best Sonic games to date. Definitely worth grabbing if you're into Sonic or platformers in general, and haven't played either. Even if you have played Sonic Generations previously like I have, it's worth it for Shadow Generations alone, and the former still holds up well.

Vampire Survivors-vari ortalama bir oyun diyebilirim. Build seçenekleri kısıtlı. Karakter sayısı ve ana silah seçenekleri yeterli olsa da savaş içerisinde hep aynı güçlendirmelere tıklayınca bir süre sonra sıkabiliyor. Görsel olarak çok basit, müzikler de öyle keza. Düşük bütçeli bağımsız bir yapım olduğu için çok önemsemedim. Bu kadar yapabilmiş olsa gerek. 

Tüm başarımları toplayana kadar oynadım, aslında daha erken bırakabilirdim. Başarımların çoğunu Darkness 15 seviyesinde açılacak şekilde ayarlamışlar. Sorun şu 15. zorluğa gelene kadar oyunun tüm içeriğini tüketiyorsun zaten. O yüzden 15. zorluktaki başarım tamamlama mücadelem ekstra sıkıcı oldu. O noktaya gelene kadar oyundaki her şeyi görmüştüm. 20 dakikalık savaş süresi bunaltıcı olmaya başladı o yüzden. 10 dakikalık hiper modu da var aslında oyunun ama nedense hangi mantıkla düşündüyseler bu modda başarım açamıyorsun. Ben de 20 dakikalık modda yazılım kullanarak oyunu %75 hızlandırdım. Biraz daha zor oldu oyun tabii çünkü düşmanlardan kaçması bayağı refleks meselesine dönüştü o noktada ama yine de hallettim çünkü sabit oynadığım build'im bayağı güçlüydü.

5 dolarlık fiyatı varmış şu an. Yeeeani pek de değmez gibi. Ben 20-30 lira gibi bir şeye almıştım. Tüm başarımları almaya zorlamayacaksanız 15-20 saat oyalanmak için oynayabilirsiniz. Oynamadıysanız Türk yapımı Swarm Grinder'ı öneririm bunun yerine. Çok çok daha kaliteli bir oyundur.

Devam oyunu daha güzel görünüyor, çıkması için bekliyorum.

By some miracle, developers from the old Marble Blast (Ultra, Gold) projects created Marble It Up, with full PC support, and Steam Workshop support... and you also are given the old, delisted version once purchasing Ultra. Really great stuff here, super happy to see it. Played a lot of Marble Blast Ultra back in the day!

Look at my total playtime. If we round down a bit to account for my pausing and walking off, it wouldn't surprise me if I spent a solid week exclusively playing Marble it Up.

[i] I don't even like marble rollers most of the time. [/i]

Controls in this game are incredibly tight. Driving the thumbstick is less about making the marble go a certain direction and more what sort of spin you put on it, but with enough friction to make ground control feel responsive and satisfying. Powerups like the super jump or dash are cumulative to your current momentum allowing for all sorts of wild physics play. Weekly challenges shuffle up the mechanics if you want a change of pace. Even the multiplayer is varied, interesting, and snappy. While I was grinding out the last achievement I would go back to the campaign levels to beat my times that were already diamond rank just because I was having fun doing it.

So yeah, I recommend Marble it Up to anyone even slightly interested in it. I sank what could very possibly be upwards of seven full days of my life into it and every second was a great time.

I did two runs and was already bored.
I loved the concept and idea, was looking forward to it.
Im not saying its a bad game, i just found it, for me, to be too boring and not how i imagined it to be.
I assumed this to be a bit slower in pace and packed with more actual combat action.
You know, Vampire Survivors but wall of death scrolling slowly up.

But i found combat to be unsatisfying and rather badly executed.
Tough to describe, but its a big package of stuff i didnt like about it.
Starts with sounds being totally overtuned in some places (especially projectiles hitting or a bag of gold collected) to enemies running around as if they were on crack.

The Reaper got stuck several times, i exploited that.
But later this turned into a problem, because the Reaper became unreliable and unpredictable in his movement.
He was stuck between two trees, then suddenly unstuck, then stuck again, then suddenly unstuck and killing me one shot.

You can pick up cards but i dont really get it. I mean i understand that there are passives you can pick up, like a gold magnet.
You have limited charges for these pickups, they overwrite themselves if you pick up another of the same type.

However:
I had a hard time at first to see any difference on what i am going to pick up.
Sure theres a symbol on that card, but often you dont have the time and they look too samey so i ended up running around and picking up whatever layed around.

In the heat of playing while trying to keep track of gold and not getting stuck on environment (happened a lot that my character was glued to some minor texture/pixel), its hard to differentiate all the pickups and even worse, keep track on how much charges you have left over.

Even worse, you have to read what these things do, while being pushed pretty fast by the screen scrolling up.
At my second run i already memorized some cards, so theres a learning factor and thats acceptable.
However it felt like a design attempt on a powerup system that didnt click with me and felt counter intuitive from what i imagined hwo it should actually work.

So frankly, i just dont like it.
Picking up a fireball attack i can use 9 times or a magnet that only works 8 times sounds boring to me and ended up being boring.
Couple that with the fact that combat wasnt as much an important part as i hoped it would be.

Again, i imagined this to be more similar to Vampire Survivors in the sense that i run updwards and kill tons of monsters, picking up powerups that stack and make me more powerful.
This would also have made sense, as i had to make decisions whether i want to grab gold (and achieve my goal), pick up a shard (meta progression) or a powerup.
Cant have it all, risk reward.

But here i didnt get any of that.

The biggest enemy in this game is the environment and trying to not get stuck on a bush or a corner texture as you expect your character to glide along but then moving like wrapped in sandpaper.

The screen also moved to fast to make this any fun.
I kind of expected this to be a major issue when going in but hoped there was some clever design and ideas that made this work.
So i pick up a quest to collect a ticket. 
I spawn, screen moves upwards, ticket is spawned to the right but i need to go upwards a good bit and then back down aaaaaaaaand the screen already ate the quest item, cool.

Thats not fun guys.
Other tasks ordered me to get damaged by bombs on purpose.
Like....why are those starting tasks?

Thers also tiny more nitpick things, but you would assume you could see how much gold you going to pick up when running over it.
Thats just 2 coins laying there and thats 3 (visually), you run over it and one time 2 coins is 4, next time its 3.
The game wants me to take risks to collect gold and doesnt do a good job at providing me proper information.
In other areas this works far better.
Bag of gold is 50. Clean cut, i can work with this.

I made it only to level 5 on first run, because of the mentioned reaper issue of him getting stuck and then hitscan kill me when going unstuck.
Second time i got to like 7 or so.

Theres a handful of characters, like 6 and i guess you need to work a lot for unlocking them.
I liked few things a lot:
The way you can get buffs after each level that felt important.
Meta unlocks are plenty (but omg will this require a ton of grind).
The hybrid design of trying to gain enough gold fast enough and at the same time becoming stronger.

Visuals are ok. Not great, but solid.

A ton of grind and while i am ok with that to a degree, it looked a bit over the top here.
In my two runs of about 20 minutes playing i gathered 16 shards.

I was really hyped for this game, wanting to see Ron Gilbert's take on the exciting genre of Action Roguelites.
I'm a fan of Vampire: Survivors, Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor, Risk of Rain 2, etc so if you also like those games, my opinion could perhaps be of use to you.

Unfortunately, it feels like the developer either declined to look at what other games in the genre do right, or intentionally decided to go a different way. In any case, the results are not at all as interesting as I had hoped.
You see, one thing that these games have in common is that different characters (or weapons), have a one "something" that makes playing with them radically differrent. Either it is a crazy AOE bonus, or an exciting projectile weapon, or an interesting melee mechanic, etc. 
So every time you start a new game or find a new unlocked weapon, it feels like the game is meant to be played in a totally different way, and it keeps it exciting and addictive to keep unlocking stuff. You cannot wait to farm some more coin or some more missions to unlock some other character, some other weapon, some other bonus.
Or, even more exciting, the crazy combination of some character bonus with some combo of weapon or bonuses that makes you a killing machine or something.

Death by Scrolling is the opposite to all of that.
All weapons found during the time I was playing this game were minor variations of the same concept, with upgrades to those weapons or unlocks limiting themselves to lame "+5% damage" or "+2% projectile speed".
The character moves very slowly. Enemies can be defeated, but there is little point to do so other than to get gold to finish the run. That is, the point of killing monster is not to get better and get crazy exciting bonuses or new weapons, which encourage you to risk and try to get the droppable gold they release, no. The point of killing monsters is to reach 5k gold and end the run. 
So, essentially, you are supposed to kill monsters to reach a Game Over screen. This is kinda the opposite of what you would want in one of these games.
It's not like finishing the run gives you crazy unlocks or permanent bonuses for subsequent runs, no. 
Maybe it unlocks some other character that is only different in graphic and in a lame "+5% movement" bonus or something like that.

Weapons and other bonuses or effects are extremely limited. They come with ammo (very little of it, like 18 shots or less), and after you have shot those, your character reverts back to some lame default weapon, or the effect just plainly disappears.
You got a cool crossbow that shoots 3 bolts per attack? Enjoy it will it lasts for a whole lot of 10 shots!
You found cool power up that lets you walk over water? Only for 10 steps, sorry.
It's as if the designer was terrified of giving cool stuff to the player and thought that the best gameplay was to go around with the default boring melee/ranged attack.

You pick up gems that are laying about, which is your usual source of permanent progression. It takes you tons of gems to unlock something.
It wouldn't be a problem if 
- The things to unlock were exciting. They aren't. They are supposed to be equippable buffs, but they are so tame and lame that there is nothing excited about it. "+5% damage" or "+1 extra heart" after having to gather about 50 gems for each of them, or more.
- The gameplay would be riveting, and you just got the gems along the way. If it was the case, you wouldn't mind that gathering gems was slow, and the permanent unlocks were tame, since it would just be a cherry on top of how much fun you are having. 

But it is not the case. The gameplay is extremely straightforward, unrewarding, and uninteresting.
You move up in an autoscrolling level that has a certain length. 
In the time it takes to reach the end, you kill enemies for gold (that they drop but you need to go and get it), find a few gems that you need to reach to pick up (which is not fun with a slow character in an autoscrolling game full with choke points and blocking scenery).

You kill enemies by picking cards that are laying around. The cards have a line of text on top of them describing what they do. But since the text is constantly moving, the screen is full of camera shake, projectiles, and enemies, and you need to be watching for the killing edge of the scrolling screen and for enemies and blocking scenery, there is no real time to read what the text says and decide whether you want or not those cards. So you either ignore them or pick them up almost at random. There is not time for choice for the player, so in that way, you remove choice from the player.

Then these cards have weapons or effects that last for a few auto-uses. Either ammo or steps, or hits. Etc. All in all, in less than a minute since you picked the card, it will be gone or replaced with something totally else.
At the end, you stop caring about what the cards are because they are mostly samey, mostly effimeral, and the entire point of killing enemies goes against your interest of the game itself (why would I want to "win" if I get mostly nothing out of winning?).

There is a quest system, if you can call it that. It is limited to an NPC telling you "Find my X", and then, during a run, you need to find that X item in the autoscrolling level and pick it up. The reward is usually just gold, which pushes you towards the Game Over screen. So, again, it is worth arguing whether you would actually want to do these quests.
Again, the point of the game should be to have fun as you play it, not to "win" the levels, which is just another form of Game Over.

I played the game for 1.5 hours, and in that time it convinced me that I had seen all that the game had to show. If that was not the case, then I apologize, but the game did a very poor job at hinting at the awesome mechanics and gameplay that I perhaps missed by not grinding it for 10 more hours.

You might be thinking why did I bother to write such a wall of text for a game that I hate.
The reason is that I don't hate the game. I was looking forward to it a lot.
And I have loved Ron Gilbert as a developer since he created Maniac Mansion and wrote his "Why Adventure Games Suck" essay.

But I think this game requires a time for introspection and that the developer writes a "Why Death by Scrolling Sucks" while other action roguelites don't suck at all. 
If he does, then he can reshape this game into something very fun and special. It wouldn't be the first game that has had a total comeback and new life after some reworking.

As it is, I cannot recommend it, even for its low price.

It's a good game but it's so obsessed with counting to the extent I can't recommend it.
There's a limit to the number of stealth kills, a limit for turns on objectives, a limit on mission length, a limit on game length, a limit on using characters. Everything is limited to make the situations seem stressful and it's easily the worst aspect of the game.

For example, the limit on stealth kills seems to be a cover for enemies not detecting corpses. Something which is pretty funny when you turn on persistent corpses and watch enemy soldiers stop right in front of one.
The turn limit could easily be replaced with wave mechanics to make the map more dangerous.

Currently I can't enjoy the game as it is because I don't want to speedrun every mission while speedrunning the entire game. I think that's fine to have as a difficulty option or to increase mission rewards but otherwise it's just annoying to be forced into.

A very fun "X-com-like" set in WWII behind enemy lines in occupied France. 
The game lets you make some tough choices, both on the overmap as during battle. 

Just like in X-com the game shows percentages to hit before you shoot, but unlike X-com missing is not as punishing because you can also deplete the enemies moral, pinning them to their spot.

The game haves some optional stealth missions (eighter Ambush where after a set of stealth kills all your soldiers get their action points back for 'the ambush' or missions that let you stealth kill for as far as you can push it). If that is not your cup of tea, you can just start shooting.

There is some jank in the game, like parts of the interface (around the cursor) disappearing (which fixes itself by toggling soldiers) or attacks landing that should not be able to hit (Even got knifed by a pined down soldier who I shot with overwatch from 5 squares away). 

That said, the only complaint I have is that I can't manually position my soldiers before the mission starts. Too many times I had to waste a turn or two repositioning my soldiers because the computer decided that my shotgun wielding medic needed to be in the back and my sniper next to their grenadiers.

Urbek City Builder is a voxel-based city simulation game that emphasizes organic growth over micromanagement. Instead of relying on money or predefined zoning, progress is driven by resource chains and population needs. Every district, building, and industry evolves naturally based on player choices, making the city feel alive and reactive. The minimalist voxel art style is clean and functional, allowing you to focus on systems rather than spectacle.

Gameplay revolves around balancing resources such as food, energy, education, and labor. Each building affects others through proximity bonuses and dependencies, encouraging thoughtful layout planning. The absence of currency changes the usual city-builder rhythm—you think in terms of materials and sustainability, not profit. It rewards efficiency and long-term planning more than short-term expansion.

As your city develops, neighborhoods evolve according to their environment. Working-class districts, high-density housing, and cultural zones all emerge naturally depending on how you manage education and services. This mechanic gives the city a sense of personality and makes experimentation enjoyable. Watching small villages grow into complex, interdependent societies feels satisfying and earned.

Performance is stable even in large cities, and the interface is clear, though it can feel dense at first. The game offers a sandbox mode with adjustable difficulty, letting you tailor the challenge. Tutorials explain the basics, but much of the learning comes from trial and error—an intentional design choice that suits the game’s philosophy of discovery.

While Urbek City Builder lacks the depth and realism of major simulation titles like Cities: Skylines, its strength lies in simplicity and creative freedom. It provides enough complexity to engage strategy enthusiasts without overwhelming casual players.

Overall, Urbek City Builder is a refreshing take on the genre. It replaces economic micromanagement with ecological thinking, turning city building into a puzzle of balance and interconnection. A quiet, thoughtful game for those who enjoy watching systems grow through logic and patience.

I've played the heck out of this game and I love it - and because I love it, I'm at a point where I need to drop it. Here's why:

Like others have said, the English translation for this game is clunky, confusing, and sometimes way too literal (I'm paraphrasing the best I can remember it, but a line was, "although she can't tell salty from sweet, she's good with her hands and has been a big help" - WHAT DOES THAT EVEN MEAN?? Are her taste buds broken?? XD). 

I didn't mind it at first - it still makes sense, especially if you're familiar with eastern culture - but after a certain point the relationship system really opens up and the game gives you a ton of opportunities to bond with every villager. It's amazingly well-done, and I genuinely love each of these characters. They're all written with love and have interesting backstories that you slowly discover as you help them solve their problems.

But that's the issue, isn't it? Because this is such a central part of the gameplay, you want to spend time on it and discover everyone's story. That's really hard to do when they speak in such weird and uncomfortable sentences you need to skim through the dialogue just to get through it. You have to fill in a lot of the blanks because there's hardly any subtext, unique character mannerisms struggle to come through, and the comedic moments land so flat you're probably more confused than amused.

To the developers, I really hope now that the game has launched, you find the time to get proper English localization. For just a two-person team, what you've launched is amazing. It hits all the right cozy notes and manages to balance exploration, foraging, crafting, and character-building in a way that never feels like a grind and is genuinely a delight. I just wish us English-speaking folks could experience the characters and writing the way it was meant to be experienced T_T

Until then, I'm tucking this one into my back pocket and hoping I can come back to it again soon.

Happened to start playing Drova shortly after DA: Veilguard and what a contrast it was: from empty corporate husk of a game to something with an actual soul, that you can tell was made with love and dedication. Within its scope and budget I think Drova succeeds at every aspect: gameplay, presentation, story. Nowadays, you are lucky if a game got two out of those three.

And speaking of presentation, I was never crazy about pixel graphics, but thanks to this game it started growing on me. Simply astonishing how much authors were able to achieve with such limited amount of pixels in terms of expression, depths and detail.

Where Drova might not be everyone's cup of tea is that it follows quite a few old gaming design conventions, such as absence of quest markers or easily missable parts that will prevent you from getting the true ending, making it often nigh to impossible to figure directions on your own without looking stuff up on the internet. So keep your eyes peeled, look under every stone and talk to everyone.

Overall, I think the developer put a great mark on the genre and I am eager to see what they will come up with next.

I will, without any doubt, recommend Drova to anyone checking out this page, especially if you've been gaming for 20+ years. The art style reminds me of SNES titles with a huge map to explore, and the overall vibe is obviously inspired by Gothic, but the combat system feels modern with an early Souls-like feel to it. Enemies are unforgiving, and I-frame dodges are the bread and butter of your defense.

I've been rerolling the hardcore challenge on insane difficulty for hundreds of hours. While resetting is frustrating, the fact that I keep starting over speaks more than words.

In days when shareholder interest has corrupted the favorite brands of our childhood, I truly appreciate the work of the independent devs here, and I'm very much looking forward to their next project.

4/5, because I need some ceiling for masterpieces like Hades 2, Stardew Valley, etc. We're not there, but it's really good. Enjoy!

Remember all those mid to late 90s 3D 3rd person action games? When level designers were still figuring out how to help players not get lost in their creations and hide secrets that will be fun and rewarding to look for? When programmers were experimenting with capabilities of early 3D hardware, coming up with hacks and tricks to get more interesting visuals? 11th Dream is trying to bring back and improve upon those games in the same way as pixel art games today build on ideas from the 80s. It is a very interesting idea, but it is not for everyone.

Pros:
[list]
    [*]Wild visuals! Definitely play in well lit room.
    [*]One hour time limit for story campaign, in the spirit of the original Prince of Persia.
    [*]Difficult situations that require use of terrain, correct choice of weapons, and generally stacking odds in your favor by being clever and skilled.
    [*]Music.
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
    [*]Color palette choice and visuals can make situations hard to understand and get clear picture of. I'm sure I killed about as many allies as enemies.
    [*]Difficulty can be artificial and frustrating at times, just as it was back in 90s. I'm looking at you, 5-minute-long 3rd person platforming level without checkpoints and largely missing visual depth cues!
[/list]

All in all, it is hard to say where issues are deliberate in pursuit of the chosen art and design style, and where it is just an oversight. If you're looking for something unusual, even when it's rough around the edges, this game might be for you.

過去シリーズもほぼ経験済み。
ゲームの新要素等、ネタバレ込みのレビューです。

[h1]良かった点[/h1]

[b]① 過去作に引けを取らない完成度[/b]
[list]
[*]元々完成度が高いシリーズで歴史も長い為、本作のハードルは高かった。
[*]しかし過去作の良い点を踏襲し、悪い点を改善した良作がシレン６。
[*]過去作同様、ゲーム性は相変わらず奥深く、とても完成度の高い新作です。
[/list]
[b]② 過去作の賛否両論点を改善（体力回復の仕様）[/b]
[list]
[*]シレン４で「体力自然回復が最大体力数が増える程、少なくなる」という仕様に変わった。
[*]この仕様変更により、逃げて戦闘を回避するゲームとなり、爽快感が減ってしまった。
[*]育てた装備で敵をなぎ倒していく爽快感もシレンの醍醐味なので、不満の声も多かった。
[*]本作はこの仕様を従来の状態に戻している。（最大体力数が増える程、回復量も増える）
[*]おかげでゲームに爽快感が戻り、苦行感も減った。
[/list]
[b]③ 過去作の賛否両論点を改善（悪ふざけ）[/b]
[list]
[*]シレン４から悪ふざけとも取れるアイテム名や説明文が増えてしまった。
[*]具体的にはシレンの世界観にそぐわないネットスラングを説明文に混ぜる等である。
[*]本作はその要素をほとんど排除。世界観を壊すような文章はほとんど消えた。
[*]アイテム名も従来通り真面目な内容に戻った。
[/list]
[b]④ 過去作の賛否両論点を改善（理不尽なモンスター）[/b]
[list]
[*]過去作に存在した極端に理不尽な能力を持つモンスターは消えた。
[*]具体例を出すとシレン４、５の「ドレッドラビ」というモンスター。
[*]対処アイテムを持っていないと何処に居ても即死が発生し得る理不尽能力持ちであった。
[*]厄介な能力持ちは本作にも沢山存在するが、だいぶ緩和されている。
[/list]
[b]⑤ 過去作の賛否両論点を改善（仲間プレイヤーの使いやすさ）[/b]
[list]
[*]仲間プレイヤーの体力やレベルが常時画面上で確認できるようになった。
[*]ＡＩも賢くなり、不意に離れたり勝手な行動もしないのでストレスは減った。
[*]過去作では使いにくい部分が目立っていたので、良い改善。
[/list]
[b]⑥ 新要素の面白さ[/b]
[list]
[*]新要素は沢山あるが全て面白い。
[*]面白い理由は使い方次第でプレイヤーを有利な状況にする追加要素ばかりの為。
[*]特に「神器」と呼ばれるハクスラ要素は好評価。
[*]落ちている武器や盾にランダムな追加効果があり、拾う度にガチャ感覚を楽しめる。
[*]強い能力が沢山ついた「神器」を拾った時の快感はかなりのもの。
[*]過去作ではプレイヤーを不利にする意地悪い追加要素も多かったので今作は好感触。
[/list]
[b]⑦ ゲーム内の情報がシリーズ一充実している[/b]
[list]
[*]アイテム、モンスター等の情報が細かにまとまっており、いつでも確認ができる。
[*]各ダンジョンにどのモンスターが配置されているかも確認ができる。
[*]アイテム売買の際に値段も簡単にゲーム内で調べられる。
[*]新たに追加された「道場」で、モンスターの能力確認やアイテム使用のデモが行える。
[*]おかげで「このモンスターにこのアイテムを使ったらどうなるのか」等の検証が簡単に。
[/list]
[b]⑧ ボリューム[/b]
[list]
[*]挑戦できるダンジョン数はかなり多い為、やり込み要素は豊富。
[*]ダンジョンはそれぞれ手強い為、全てクリアするとなるとかなりの経験を要求される。
[*]クリア後のイベントも多く、ストーリーのボリュームもそれなりに存在。
[/list]

[h1]悪かった点[/h1]

[b]① 合成の解禁タイミング[/b]
[list]
[*]シレンシリーズの重要な要素として「合成」というものがある。
[*]この「合成」がイベントを進めないと実行できない。
[*]シリーズの面白さを支えている要の１つが、最初から出来ないのは不満要素。
[*]ただ何度かプレイすると勝手に解禁されるので、些細な不満点ではある。
[/list]
[b]② デッ怪と画面サイズの兼ね合い[/b]
[list]
[*]通常より数段体が大きな「デッ怪」という類の敵が存在する。
[*]画面上下が狭い為、上下移動を行うと突如画面に「デッ怪」が現れる形になりやすい。
[*]結果、勢い余って隣接してしまい攻撃を食らってしまう。
[*]「デッ怪」は攻撃力が高く即死する場合も多い為、致命的である。
[*]「デッ怪」に隣接する際は強制的に一歩踏み止まる等のシステム的な配慮が欲しかった。
[*]操作の問題なので、個人で気を付ければ良い些細な問題ではある。
[/list]
[b]③ 一部理不尽なダンジョンが存在する[/b]
[list]
[*]理不尽に感じたダンジョンは「やりくり上手の森」。
[*]各階毎に渡されたアイテムを使用して打開していくダンジョンである。
[*]最終階は高確率で敵に囲まれている為、打開アイテムが無いとそのまま詰んでしまう。
[*]階を進むと所持アイテムは全て没収されるので対処法は無く、完全なる運ゲー。
[*]唯一不満を言いたくなるダンジョンであった。
[/list]

[h1]まとめ[/h1]
　風来のシレンは長いシリーズですが、本作は集大成とも言えるとても良い出来でした。
　シリーズを何から始めれば良いかと聞かれれば、迷いなく本作を勧めます。
　難易度もライトユーザー向けに調整しており、ゲーム内の情報も豊富で初心者に優しいです。
　しかし手強い要素も多く、シリーズファンでも楽しめる内容となっています。

i went into this without knowing much about the Klonoa franchise and it really exceeded any and every expectations i had for it. from the visuals, down to gameplay and story, everything was perfect. even if the visuals can be a bit clumsy, this remaster has so much love put in, that I dont mind. the environmental design is literally lovely, so many times ive just paused to look around. the carefully crafted layouts were fascinating to watch in the original titles, but the remaster gave them a huge glow.
(fyi, i knew about Klonoas existence all the way when i was a kid, its just a shame i was never THAT interested to deep dive into it at my young, full of dreams age.)

Klonoa is a dream traveler, a heroic being that is sent to visit dreamworlds while he sleeps, to fix any problems happening.
the story seems simple at first but as it goes along, it gets a lot deeper, both of the games are set in a colorful world full of friends, Klonoa is tasked with a seemingly simple goal but gradually discovers things are more complicated than he was told.
the first game is relatively easy but the second is more challenging with its creativity and puzzles.
its nothing revolutionary, but its loaded with charm. its definitely going to hit even better for people who grew up on a PS1/PS2 and played the OGs.
the second game felt a little stiff but it wasnt anything i couldnt get used to.
note that the second game isnt exactly a sequel, it isnt connected, actually, none of the games are connected. Lunatea is completely divorced from Phantomile.
if it was a sequel, the moos wouldnt be there, and Lolo wouldnt make sense having the same powers as Huepow + the whole design change? it looks so different it actually hurt me a little, cause ive been fond of the first design more. i liked Klonoa being just a little creature in the first game, as alot of people say, in the second game, he just looks like a Sonic character now :"D. (atleast he wears clothes like a civilized being, unlike some.)
he probably just grew up right? became more mature and stuff, the boring answer is that Namco most likely wanted to redesign aswell.
or the more exciting answer, maybe when he travels to a new dream world, his apperance changes to fit within that world.
but then why does Joka come back in Heroes etc.? maybe these restricted characters to that world arent actually restricted, they could be real things that Klonoa knows in the real world, and dreams do have something to do with reality usually. wish we knew more about where he came from, more about his real world.
i was little bit disappointed to find out the only thing Klonoa "seems to remember" from the first game, besides his name, is the ability to double jump with a moo.
but atleast his emotional experience of sorrow is real.

the main draws are the creative visuals, the beautiful music, and the emotional story. this is a game for those that are looking for an adventure, not challenge. (you can challenge it later.)

Давайте з козирів. Світ гри – неймовірно атмосферний. Я зараз неіронічно скажу: Frogwares вміють творити камерні, затишні, надзвичайно імерсивні локації майже на рівні з Ubisoft із її космічними бюджетами. А вони, на хвилиночку, являються чи не еталоном по творенню красивих віртуальних світів. По місту просто приємно гуляти, вмикаючи фотомод щохвилини. Тут ідеально схоплюється згусток атмосфери американського нуару, переплетеного зі щупальцями Лавкрафтівських жахів. Гра творить настрій і робить це майстерно.

Історія – захоплююча, із багатьма вловимими алюзіями і омажами. Саме сюжет, окремі додаткові історії та оцей неспішний детективний ритм ставали причиною більш тривалих ігрових сесій, ніж це було заплановано. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3591660642

В грі присутні сутички із людьми та монстрами. Вогнепал, гранати, пастки – для серйозного бою. І атака складною лопатою як додаткова опція. Бойова система нагадує старіші ігри Silent Hill: не душна, не супер глибока, але достатня в контексті детективної сутності The Sinking City. Сюди ж додали систему крафту, щоб набої й інші розхідники мали свою ціну.

Відповідно, The Sinking City краще грати так, немов ви читаєте книгу чи граєте у інтерактивне кіно. Роздивляйтеся приміщення, читайте записки, слухайте коментарі Чарльза. В грі є чимало моторошних історій, які не лякають вас прямо, але додають емоцій через усвідомлення трагічної події, чогось незвіданого і несказаного. Власне, як це часто було у оповіданнях самого Лавкрафта. Тоді ви відчуєте доторк холодних щупальців, присутність жахливих істот із паралельних вимірів за сантиметр від вас, запах цвілі, безвиході та марноти. Комбінація візуалу, музики і історії в цій грі працює чудово. 

Окремо виділю наявність складних, неоднозначних виборів. Лише кілька разів я з ходу знав, що хочу обрати згідно власних переконань. Часто ж гра примушувала сидіти багато хвилин, роздумуючи, яке з двох зол є меншим. Після кожного складного рішення ми дізнаємося його наслідки через новини та інтерв’ю в газетах. Класно, таке ми поважаємо. 

[h3]Що можна зробити краще. Типу, побажання розробникам [/h3]

Що мені, як ґеймеру, хотілося б бачити в наступних частинах. Для гравців – можна читати цей розділ як недоліки гри. 

1. Розширення детективної механіки. Щоб ми могли зібрати багато доказів, скласти з них різні висновки (хибні, істинні, напівхибні тощо). Іншими словами, щоб розв’язання справи не було просто збором фіксованої кількості фактів, які ведуть до фіксованого висновку. Натомість, щоб гравець міг пропустити якийсь факт/доказ. Інтерпретувати зв’язки багатьма способами. Так, це складно реалізувати, але якби вийшло збагатити дане ядро гри і впровадити, наприклад, через додаткову «реалістичну» складність, було б прекрасно.
2. Варіативність в діалогах та наслідках. Щоб добре думати, як відповідати, а не просто перебирати всі доступні фрази в діалозі. 
3. Більша різноманітність інтер’єрів. Конкретно в The Sinking City це сильно кидається в очі: приміщення всі під кілька типів, із однаковим розташуванням кімнат, предметів декору тощо. 
4. Більша інтерактивність зі світом. Нічого надкосмічного, фанатам не потрібний рівень GTA. Просто додавати дрібних фішок тут і там: можливість сісти за столик в кафе, можливість перекинутись фразами з перехожими, випадкові події на вулиці тощо. 
5. Кілька разів, коли гра по-справжньому мене лякала, траплялися у моменти багів, які вибивалися із зрозумілого ритму гри. Як от коли NPC, вперше за 20 годин, застряг у вхідних дверях приміщення, просто стоячи там і нагадуючи головного героя. Або труп монстра різко і неприродньо підскакував з підлоги після останнього пострілу. Тому, *підморгую* - вкраплення абсолютної нетиповості, нестандартності, раптовості у зрозумілу розміреність гри працюють чудово.

Більшість з цих пунктів вже в процесі розвитку у The Sinking City: відповіді у деяких діалогах прямо впливають на подальші наслідки. Світ став дещо інтерактивнішим. So, this is the time of the year, when I wanted to play something with the grey atmosphere, maybe spooky or scary. Checking my library I found this game, which I bought some time ago and kept it specifically for this time of the year. And well, I’m glad that I’ve decided to play it and didn’t keep it for too long. 

Frogwares, the developers of “Sherlock Holmes” detectives, did another great job of crafting an incredibly atmospheric and stunning world. The Sinking city is a mix of classic American noir with wet, anxious, cul-de-sac mood of Lawcraft horror. Visuals + music + the story + lore of this world puts you in a very special mood, which I find appealing in a late Autumn period.

The story itself is interesting. It keeps your attention, having this moment of: “Ok, I’ll do one more task and that’s it for today…”, when you want to finish the part of the puzzle and see how it ends. Not only the main story, but those secondary quests as well. I would describe the whole game as a novel, where you’re moving step-by-step through the story, solving mysteries and cases. Just like the novels of Lawcraft themselves, it will not scary you straightly, throwing something disgusting in your face. Instead, for example, you’ll read some notes, observe the corpses and your mind will come with a picture of what happened here some time ago, giving you chills or tragic feelings.

As for gameplay, I hope you don’t expect that open world action or role play experience (if you played “Sherlock” games – then you know 70% of what to expect in this game). The Sinking City is rather linear, story driven game in an open world city with some additional stories (quests), with ability to make your own choice here and there which will leave the mark on the game’s world. Those choices often are tough, with grey moral and concept of “lesser evil”. There is action too: gunfights with a few types of weapons, grenades and traps; and melee fight with only one type of attack. The closest comparison I can think of is the older games of Silent Hill: fights with humans and monsters are not too complex, not annoying, but just ok for adding some action into slow paced detective core. 

There are some moments, that could be done better. Many of the interiors are identical by structure. The detective part is about gathering all evidences, that will lead you to one conclusion or two interpretations, without a chance to miss something on a way. But fairly speaking, there are not much detective games that give you this much of freedom… The remastered version on “Ultra” settings has pretty high requirements to hardware. The world is rather not interactive, but a decoration. Yet compared to “Sherlock” games here you see a progress: you can use weapon anywhere on the streets, people react on it and so on. 

It’s a good game if you know what to expect: a story driven, rather – linear game in a semi-open world with a good story and detective mechanics. What it does, it does well – dives you into the mystery world of horrors, where you’re trying to find your way through and out. So, if this is what you’re looking for – it’s worth buying, especially on sales. I’m looking forward to the sequel, because first game brought me many strong emotions and aftertaste.

What happens when Lovecraft's works collide into one comprehensive universe, then mix with further occult myths like the Golem of Prague and undead Mayan? The Sinking City is exactly that, a rough but charming melting pot of cosmic horror and esotericism by the underfunded AA Ukrainian studio Frogwares.

There are so many problems with its gameplay, especially repetitive combat against the same 4 types of enemy, the over-reliance on the crafting system and the overused repetitive level layouts. Yet despite all that, the city of Oakmont and its eerie but memorable stories carry such a great atmosphere that I'd recommend this game to anyone who loves the weird fiction genre. There's something truly special about being thrown into a bizarre, decaying but fully believable world and stumbling upon its strange characters and moments that make you pause and question things. And that's why The Sinking City is one of the most authentic Lovecraft games for me, an imperfect but truly unforgettable experience.

Loved this game so much that I bought it on Switch and finished it on there as well. While the graphic filtering is a bad choice, you can mostly fix it by tampering with the files and following a steam guide. One of the best stories/combat systems I've ever experienced in a JRPG. This game is much more about how it's characters interact with each other and the world around them, rather than a serious game with a major threat. I only wish I had the opportunity to play this as a child.

The art style is very detailed for being early 3D. I think it looks good. It kind of reminds me of other games from the era. Sadly, it suffers from some of the same issues I have with most of the early 3D games, navigation.
	One of the biggest issues I had with this game was that the camera is pointed down at the ground all game long! I get into a wide open area that I should be able to see a lot in front of me and all I see is the grass at Justin's feet. I get into a dungeon and I'm constantly shifting the camera around obstacles that block my view of my characters to try and see where I'm going, where the items are, and where the enemies are. Since there are obstacles between the camera and the characters, I keep moving the camera to see them and lose place of where I have been and where I'm going. I found navigating so bad that I saw two options. I either spent even longer in the already bloated combat filled sections or I followed a map online. I did the latter. It made navigation a lot more trivial, but it drastically improved my speed at progressing through areas and was absolutely the right choice for me. 
	The music is mixed bag. Some of it I really didn't like and some of it was quite good. Where the game does music well is during the music that is trying to portray an emotion. When it fails is when its trying to evoke the environment that the song plays in. There are a lot of tracks that want to make use of earthy sounds which I usually like. However, the implementation here is more wacky and different than it is the earthy tone I believe that they were going for. It might be limitations of the sound chip for the Sega console it originally released on. I'll include a mention of the voice acting here as well. It's bad. Very bad. I am less bothered by this than I would with a much more current game. This game is from an era where almost all voice acting was pretty bad and so I give it a lot of slack. Just know that it will be bad if you decide to play it. 
	The combat and skill progression systems do not value the player's time. This was a case often enough in the day when the game first released, but it is particularly bad here. Levelling up proficiency with weapons and magic elements requires the use of those specific weapons or spells types in order to level them. This means that in order for combat to feel like efficient use of your time, you will be wasting time casting spells that do not damage enemies and using weaker attacks spells to get more experience for your skills/spells so that you can learn new skills/spells. This makes each battle take longer and this is one of those games where the dungeons are 5 minutes long without battles and 1 hour long with them, so it really drags the game out. The upside for those who always like reaching for new skills/spells will like that you will have a new things to strive for almost all game long even if you treat the game like I did and spend extra time in most battles working on your abilities. It was the primary reason that I felt motivated to keep playing the game in all honesty. But even as I did keep playing, it really dragged the game out to be much longer than it needed to be. Now this is a case of many good ideas and poor implementation because many ideas from this combat system and even from the skill progression where used in subsequent game in the series and done a lot better in those games. 
	The biggest reason why I didn't like the game was the aspect of every game that is most important to me, the characters and the story. I can't stand these characters. They are annoying little brats. They don't grow. They don't change. It's even rare for them to go through challenges that have any effect on them. I've had people tell me that this is a more accurate way to write child characters. That might be true, but it doesn't make for interesting personalities that I have any interest in investing in. Justin, our protagonist, wants to go on an adventure. He is a nice enough kid who wants to do the right thing. That is the extent of his characterization through out the entire game. He never loses that singular motivation all game long, save once. A last moment of doubt gets dropped on him right at the end of the game that wasn't built up to. It just happens and then is resolved in a matter of 15 minutes. Other things happen along the way that he decides to do because its the right thing to do, but that's about it. Any challenges “the player” faces do nothing to change that. I do like how the side characters join and then leave when their part of the story is done. It is often the case for side characters to have a quest you complete upon meeting and recruiting them, only for those characters to basically sit in the background for the rest of the game. This game fixes this by literally taking them out of the party so that it doesn't matter that they have no reason to stick around with the party. I wish more games did this if they don't have anything interesting for side characters to do after their introductions. 
	The reason why I said the player faces challenges is because that's what we get, challenges for the player. We fight through the challenges, even though challenging is not a word I would associate with this game. The final boss had 2 forms and only got one turn when I fought it, which it used to cast a debuff. I also only needed to heal once every 5-10 battles in the first half of the game. Much too easy. Justin never acknowledges that challenges even happen. No one ever talks about what just happened. How about a life altering event that changes the very nature of one of our characters? Our response is, how did we get here? Someone loses someone close to them? Our response is, I don't know what to do now. Not one event in this game has any narrative weight to it because our characters almost never react to anything emotionally. They do react in other ways. Justin has agency when he sees something right in front of him to an annoying degree. He is sure he is right at all times and never falters. But he is 14 and acts like it, so him turning out to be right the vast majority of the time by believing that adventurers can do anything isn't interesting in any sense. If there isn't something directly in front of him, he has no idea what he is doing and so our tasks end up being, “I don't know what to do next, lets talk to someone who will tell us exactly what we need to do next instead of having the story direct us along a naturally story path”. So it often seems like the plot is happening around us and both the characters and the player are just going along for the ride.
	Because of this, I don't really care about the story. There isn't much of an overarching story until 2/3 of the way through the game. Until then, we are running around with one place in mind because we want to adventure and that is as good a place as any. Of course various things will tie together and that place will be important in giving us a task of some importance, but I really needed some motivation for why we felt the need to go there in the first place. At least the NPCs give good background lore on the world and they change dialogue depending on what happened most recently, so there is always a reason to talk to them if you are enjoying the world.
	Review too long. Bad remaster.

TL;DR

I do not like this game. I know I've played a lot of hours on it, but I loved Grandia 2 and heard this one was better so many times that I had to give it an honest try. For me, this game is drastically worse than Grandia 2. I think this is a weak story with weaker characters. It has a good first draft of a combat system that gets drastically improved in subsequent games in the series. It has terrible navigation because of an incomprehensible level of zoom/angle from the camera. If you want a good game with this combat system, then try any other game in the series, but this one isn't a good use of your time.

This is a single-player, linear, lovecraftian, card-based game.  Do I recommend this?  Maybe.  "It depends" on you and what you like.

You will probably like this game if you are into...
Single player card games like: Stacklands, Inscryption, Slay the Spire, and Balatro
 - Puzzle games like: The Witness, Blue Prints
 - Short games.  I completed all achievements in about 10 total hours.  This includes a couple restarts.
 - Games that aren't too hard.  I completed this without making any notes.  This is one way it is unlike Blue Prints.
 - Lovecraftian games like Eldritch Horror, Arkham Horror, and Darkest Dungeon
 - Games you can pause.

You will NOT like this game if...
 - You expect fully acted voice dialog
 - You have no patience for reading (the story depends on you actually reading dialog and card text)
 - You expect action.  This is a reasonably slow-paced game.
 - Memorizing card "recipes" (e.g. This card at this location grants X card reward).

What could make this better?
 - Some roguelike elements (e.g. more like Slay the Spire and Balatro).
 - Some really out-of-the-box story & gameplay like Inscryption.
 - An interface that is easier to read on Steamdeck.

In [i]Unbox the Room[/i] you're an interior designer hired by clients to unbox their belongings and make their new homes into their dream spaces. A sandbox mode is also available for free design.  

[h3][u]Gameplay & Settings[/u][/h3]

This game has the same vibe as Unpacking (another great one to play)! You unpack clients' belongings and put them where they are supposed to go. There is also a sandbox mode where you can get creative and have all the items unlocked to design your own rooms. 

The client’s objectives for the most part are pretty easy to fill and there is a tutorial that starts you off in story mode that does a good job on showing you the basics. Eventually you will be able to recolor items and do larger designs as the story progresses. 

Visually the game is cute with a pixelated cartoony look with some relaxing music in the background.

Settings & extras include; language selection, audio controls, resolution and display options, controller icons and sensitivity. The game also supports mouse & keyboard (which I used). 

[h3][u]Overall Experience[/u][/h3]

I enjoyed the story mode in this game, although a bit on the shorter side. It took me about 2 hours to complete the story mode and get all the achievements. I recommend looking at the achievements while playing so you don’t miss any but overall they are pretty easy to get. A fun little game but maybe wait for a sale unless you're going to spend a lot of time in the sandbox mode. ⭐

As of writing this post, I've put 21 hours into this game, running through multiple variations both beta unstable as well as the stable releases, to which which I have am breaking my review down into the following: The good, the bad, the ugly:
     The Good: I enjoy the new style base building as opposed to the original TerraTech which emphasized more of a factory production facility, base building in TerraTeach Worlds creates better aesthetics while also allowing a more three dimensional build design. Further, I enjoy the concept/idea of local flora acting as antibodies defending the planet from any would be invaders, players included, as it's given me much more to be mindful and aware of.
     The Bad: I'm not too keen on the persistent pop-ups of information I'm already far too well aware of in the midst of my gameplay. Though I don't mind being told when my Tech is heavily damaged, I don't like my controls becoming frozen with a pop-up telling me for the 12th time+ I need to press a certain key to repair my tech. Furthermore, I've found if I skip stages in the "tutorial" the game does not compensate: for example: If I've already taken over an Outlaw base, raided it, then bought the Pioneer Cab before the "tutorial" has instructed me to do so, the mission objective remains fixated on purchasing the cab with no option of doing, even when constructing a new tech with the new cab equipped.
     The Ugly: Fixing or correcting player experiences should not be a low priority when it comes to any development of any project. If gameplay is good, we are willing to wait for additional content, content or corrections to content should not take precedence over how a player is able to interact with the game. Such can be said for any industry: construction for example: what good is building a roof before you've got the walls to place it on? There's been several times I've had to completely restart the game just by trying to swap cabs on my tech only for the entire thing to reject the new cab, fall to pieces, then refuse to recognize any cab I've even picked up, leaving me no ability to even build a new Tech with which to operate. I'm also not keen on the idea of any front mounted turrets I have have this tendency to fire into the air straight up as though I'm shooting at birds when I'm aiming at a target directly in front of me on the ground. Lastly, Before I can honestly recommend this game the sea faring content is in dire need of adjusting, as I put together several variations of sea faring Tech's only for the entire thing to sink to the bottom of the ocean with no means of traversing back to the surface, prompting me to make the trip to the next content on the seafloor, at a snail's crawl while vulnerable to enemy attack yet unable to fire back.
     Should these flaws in development in game as well as in studio become amended, I believe this could be a tremendously popular game, until then, I'm afraid I'll simply have to hold my breath on this title.

Not the greatest game ever made - but it's fun, and better than it has any right to be. "Lovecraft-ian city builder" isn't the most obvious mashup. But it totally works, and there's a surprising amount of depth to it. If you like the cthulhu mythos, and you have even a passing interest in city builders, give it a try. You'll get enough enjoyment out of one side or the other to justify the price.

My only real complaint is that some of your followers' needs are a little out of step with the rest of the game. I haven't yet come across a way to eat fish, shellfish, etc - other than clams. Apparently we're not big into seaweed, either, even though we live on the coast. But I do need not 1 but 3 separate buildings to make.. pasta sauce? I'm not sure the game is really aiming for immersion, but times like that are when it loses me. After you're done carving sigils into your followers' backs, or burning them on pyres, or sacrificing them to summon horrors, you simply must make sure they can get their bottled milk. There was definitely a missed opportunity here to make some of their basic needs a little creepier.

I really enjoyed my time with Worshippers of Cthulhu and would definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys city builders, especially if you’ve played and liked games like Anno or Frostpunk.

[b] What I really liked: [/b]
 · It’s not as intense as some other city builders when it comes to micromanagement or tech trees, so it ended up being a more laid-back, fun experience for me. (For reference, I played the campaign on Normal.)
 · The cult and H.P. Lovecraft vibes are spot-on, and I really enjoyed the narrative across the 4-act campaign.
 · Each act introduced a new mechanic that kept things fresh. Act 3’s burning bones mechanic to manage production inefficiencies was great!
 · I genuinely liked the cult decision pop-ups and always took time to read through them. The art and presentation for these were excellent.
 · The tutorials did a great job introducing new mechanics and pacing out the tech unlocks, so I never felt overwhelmed.

[b] A few ideas for the devs: [/b]
· You probably shouldn’t be able to ascend followers without first unlocking or building the Ascension alter. I managed to skip this tech in Acts 3 and 4, which felt a bit odd.
· I didn’t need to unlock all the techs to finish Act 4, and I only reached level 3 ascension with a few followers before completing the campaign. It felt like a missed opportunity to explore more of the late-game tech.
· A ship trading hub to move goods between islands would be awesome. Instead of global trade, you’d have to set up routes and ferry materials between your settlements. It’d make things more challenging and hands-on, but could add a cool layer of depth.

A reboot that layers modern presentation and audio onto the old philosophy. The tactile feel is strong and the systemic depth is thin. It works well for newcomers while leaving core fans a bit unsatisfied.

An absurd game. I'll explain the mechanics as I understand them, since I couldn't quite glean them from the trailer or description.

You shoot objects with bananas. The game tells you whether it was correct or incorrect. After a few incorrects, you game over, and restart from the beginning. This time, you can remember which objects were which, and get farther.

You can use midair jumps to skip ahead islands and learn objects while in a game over state. And there are checkpoints which help you in this learning process.

I find this game very amusing. There's lots of little touches too, like the sound effects and different level layouts, and other fun things, that add to the ethereal and sarcastic atmosphere.

Early on, I believed that if you encounter the same object twice, then its correct/incorrect status will be the same. And, sometimes it is, by pure chance. But, in fact there is no correlation; you have to memorize each instance of each object by trial-and-error. And, there is a finite size to the game; it doesn't keep generating forever. So, it's a different game than I thought it was, and harder too. But still amusing.

If this game looks like it would make you laugh, I'd recommend buying it and giving it a go.

[h1] The True Future War: Immersion in Terminator's Wasteland  [/h1] 
Terminator: Resistance is a game that understands its source material on a fundamental level. It doesn't aim to be a groundbreaking game, but rather a deeply immersive and authentic simulation of the post-Judgment Day hellscape first shown in the original films.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3542727122
The game's greatest achievement is its incredibly thick, oppressive atmosphere. From the ashen skies and ruined cities to the constant, terrifying presence of Hunter-Killers, the world feels genuinely lethal and desperate. This is amplified by a stellar sound design where the distant, metallic stomp of a T-800 is enough to freeze your blood. The immersion is top-notch, making you feel not like a super-soldier, but like a scared survivor using stealth, scavenging, and makeshift weapons to live another day.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3539662685
The story, while simple, effectively captures the spirit of the human resistance, allowing you to build relationships with a cast of characters who feel like they've stepped right out of James Cameron's universe.
https://youtu.be/gqRrd4_eWNU
However, you must meet the game on its own terms. This is a AA experience with a modest budget clearly on display. The gunplay is functional but unremarkable, the character animations can be stiff, and the RPG systems are relatively light. It's a straightforward, linear adventure.

It's a cool exploration game. It's kind of like if Mario Sunshine, Deadspace, and System Shock were passing the blunt and everyone's gay. The setting is existentially horrific but it's played straight and sincere with a story that is grounded in the human elements of its world. The elements that would be presented as horror are instead treated as just a normal part of living in this world.

Pros:
+ Great music and atmosphere
+ The art direction is pretty and makes the limited resources available to the team go a long way towards actually accomplishing their goals, anything it lacks in terms of fidelity are things which the game wouldn't actually have been meaningfully improved by but would have taken away from its ability to finish its goals elsewhere
+ The movement is solid on its own, but when you get into the Zero-G sections of the game, it's fantastic
+ It has some surprising ImSim elements that are greatly welcomed and very interesting
+ The levels that are here are for the most part very well designed and varied with the limited resources available; most of them revolve around some kind of set piece room that defines your exploration of the zone, with only a couple of the levels feeling like they were treading on a formula
+ Exploration is heavily rewarded with extra lore that helps fill out the cast of characters whose lives (and deaths) drive the narrative
+ The underlying fiction of the world is extremely intriguing and leaves you wanting to learn more about these more fantastic aspects of the world
+ The devs kept their eyes on an experience that's in a scope that they knew they could deliver on, and uses the playtime to work up its strengths without bloat or underbaked attempts at overscoped ambitions; it's a short game, but I like it when a game knows what it can accomplish and aims to deliver on that

Cons:
- While the story, and in particular the worldbuilding, is very interesting, its focus on the humans inside it feels incomplete. There's big questions about how these people lived that feels like there's more to talk about and explore here but which is superficially glossed over in favor of eulogizing them. It makes the treatment of remembering them as an exploration of who they were, and by extension of the world they lived in, seem shallow when you try to interrogate how it made you feel and think afterwards. These are things which could be answered with the subsequent acts, but along with the cliffhanger, leaves me with the sense that I wanted a little bit more out of it.
- There's next to no real threat in the game, which could be a positive for you, but it drives home that when you do die, it's likely due to a strange physics interaction and unpredictable danger more than an actual intended threat
- The game's progression is very quick and simple in a way that will make it possible for you to fill out everything well before the end, and which will trivialize the already very minimal threats you'll face and completely eliminate obstacles that need to be puzzled out, while also removing the incentive for engaging with the most interesting part of its cleaning mechanic and how it ties to your resource gathering
- Some upgrades will make your functionality worse in ways that you'll wish you could toggle off
- Some of your toolkit feels less-than-useful; the tall/wide sprays on the base spray liquid feels like it does nothing, and the most effective and efficient form of cleaning without spending limited resources I found seems like a deeply unintended method of playing the game.
- This is a day 1 review, so these might be fixed, but there were several small bugs that could make 100% completion impossible, with one collectable found being uninteractible and some of the cleaning targets being stuck behind geometry making it impossible to accurately clean them. Also a few typos. These might/likely will be fixed in the future, but it's not something I'll care enough to go back through to try to 100% the game over.

Overall, it's a great first act that gets you invested in the world. I would have personally liked it if there was more of the ImSim DNA in there. There's plenty of room for more mechanics, puzzles, and obstacles, and I want to see how they expand on what's already here.

The only reservation I have to recommending it is that it being only Act One makes it feel more like a proof of concept or expanded demo over a full game, because it's not the full game yet. You might want to wait until all of its Acts are released and see whether they deliver in the end on the full arc before deciding whether it's worth the price point for you. But I personally do think it's worth supporting now to help make sure those other Acts do happen.

If you do seek to fully clean a map, prepare to run through the map 2-3 times, because they spawn more crap after you leave and sometimes the crap spawns outside the map, which means you need to clear what you can, leave, and re-enter a third time so it spawns the remaining chunks in-bounds.
