Grunn is a solid time loop puzzler, but lacks much impact. Using the polaroids as a hint system to help you make consistent progress run over run worked well, as they gave enough information to help without giving up the puzzle. The map is generally small enough that traversal wasn't particularly bad, and I never had any issues with controls or stability. The gardening mechanics are somewhat fun/satisfying, particularly in early runs. The game timer is also very generous, which gives you ample time to explore and experiment each run.

My only meaningful complaint is that I wish it had more shortcuts. The few that I found were definitely useful, but it feels like there should have been more opportunities to take advantage of later knowledge to avoid the early tedious tasks for each run. This doesn't end up being a major issue, but due to the somewhat short runs (the longest run I had was ~45 minutes), I was doing some tasks more often than was fun.

Overall, I did end up kinda bored by Grunn even if I liked it; it didn't do any specific things wrong, but it also failed to excite me. The puzzles had a few "Ah-ha" moments, but were generally very easy. The 100% experience wasn't particularly bad, but almost none of the achievements were much fun either[spoiler]besides the worm stuff, which was admittedly pretty funny to me[/spoiler]. Grunn is obviously a well made game created with care, so I do stand by my positive review, but it wasn't exciting. If you really like time loop mechanics, I think you could do alot worse as it easily stands above others in the genre that I tried.

I don't think the words I could give would properly give the game the justice it deserves, but I'm gonna try my best. Alien Isolation is a modern horror classic plagued by review bombs upon launch. 11 years later at the time of this review, this game holds up extremely well for a game that was released in 2016.

This game, many years later, tackled adapting the Alien franchise into being scary once more, and put aside the "run and gun" and shoot 'em up game style, and opts in for a more tactical and stealth approach. Stealth is a primary focus of the game, trying to avoid humans, the alien, and other nuisances. The game has a huge focus on atmosphere. Every sound of the Nostromo, every sound you make, every sound a human makes, every sound the alien makes, it is all fine tuned to fill you with such dread and anxiety to the point you'll be paranoid about "Where is the alien gonna drop? Oh god what was that sound?! I'm doomed, aren't I." I don't hear the sound design of the game get talked enough, actually. This game immerses you into the character you control, every sound you hear is designed to make it feel as if you, the player, are experiencing the horrors the main character has to face and endure, and it is all delightful. Even the moments where you have to be out in the vacuum of space are such a sweet treat, listening to the metal clash against the Nostromo, the absolute dead air leaving you only to imagine what is happening around the ship.

I would recommend a first timer's play through of this game to be on Hard mode so they always feel pressured by the Alien and the enemies the game throws at you. Alien Isolation is what I like to describe as a game that not only challenges you, but also tests your ability to adapt and find ways to deal with each individual challenge, but the game also, unfortunately, suffers from an issue where if you play on lower difficulties, you will rarely find challenge, and imo, satisfaction. Humans are dumber, the Alien's stalking and aggressiveness tone down alot, and generally the whole balance of the game is thrown to wack on difficulties on anything below Normal. I believe if you wish to truly experience Alien Isolation, then try the game on Nightmare.

Please do give the game a try, for it is, in my honest opinion, one of the best horror games in modern time, and something I believe alot of horror games fail to recreate what truly causes fear and anxiety. That, is Alien Isolation. Fear and anxiety, incarnated.

Very solid and atmospheric Metroidvania stuck in an incredibly janky engine.
In terms of gameplay and presentation - this is truly a gem. The exploration feels great, there are many MANY relics that either give you cool new abilities or open a path forward, or both, sometimes you have to use them in clever way or solve a puzzle to progress, it has everything a good metroidvania should have.
In terms of atmosphere I think it accomplishes it better than any Castlevania ever did - game uses it's 2d graphics, ambient musics, story and voice acting very well to make it feel very oppressive and downright creepy at times.
The gameplay is what you would expect, it's 2d exploration with a lot of combat although the controls feel a bit clunky at times probably due to the engine quirks.
And the engine is sadly the biggest issue of this game. There is barely any options to change, even games from 2000's would feel weird without any sound options, the game will not read controller layouts correctly and display incorrect buttons, and will absolutely freak out during shop visits - change resolution, window size, stutter and sometimes even crash, I never felt comfortable buying any items without saving first.
Couple of less important gripes is that the game likes to slap you with an instant game over trap. Yeah they are usually telegraphed somewhat but it still sucks when you miss the clue and you have to replay chunk of the game because savepoints are not that common, and there are so many of these traps it almost feel like an old Sierra adventure game, but to be honest most of them kill you in a pretty creative ways so I can't be too mad at it.
The other thing is that sometimes the relics feel like they are there just to pad the game time, like there are couple of instances where you defeat a boss an obtain a relics which ONLY function is to let you pass ONE barrier so you can get ONE item behind that barrier. Just give me that item after defeating the boss at this point, what's the purpose of that additional walk I had to do.
All in all - game feels like a free high quality game you would find on the internet during mid-2000's like I Wanna Be The Guy - it's great, it's fun, it's competently made, full of SOVL and it accomplishes what it wants to accomplish - but it's held together by spit, duck tape and prayers. Now of course this game is not free but it's still good and if you can excuse a lot of jank then I think it's worth the asking price.

BLACKTAIL is an action-adventure game developed by The Parasight and published by Focus Entertainment. It reimagines the Slavic legend of Baba Yaga as a coming-of-age story set in a surreal, fairy-tale wilderness.

Players control Yaga, a young girl accused of witchcraft and exiled into an enchanted forest. Armed with a bow and a handful of spells, she must hunt spirits, uncover memories, and choose between becoming a protector or a terror. Morality choices shape the narrative, influencing abilities, dialogue, and how other characters perceive her.

Gameplay mixes first-person archery, exploration, crafting, and light RPG elements. Combat emphasizes movement and precision—using arrows, traps, and magic to defeat spirits and corrupted creatures. Gathering herbs and resources supports crafting new arrows, potions, and upgrades.

The world is open but structured around interconnected zones filled with quests, secrets, and environmental storytelling. Each area blends beauty and decay, creating a dreamlike atmosphere grounded in Eastern European folklore.

Visually, BLACKTAIL uses painterly art direction and strong lighting to create contrast between wonder and menace. The color palette shifts dynamically with player morality, reflecting Yaga’s transformation from innocent to legendary witch.

Sound design is exceptional. Folk-inspired music, ambient forest sounds, and ethereal voices create a haunting yet tranquil tone. Voice acting, particularly Yaga’s internal dialogue, adds personality and emotional nuance.

Overall, BLACKTAIL is a creative and atmospheric retelling of myth through immersive gameplay and moral choice. It stands out for its unique art style, narrative depth, and balance of exploration and combat, appealing to players who enjoy narrative-driven fantasy adventures with philosophical undertones.

Talk about a fall from grace for Frictional Games after the fantastic prior releases, Amnesia: Dark Descent and SOMA. Amnesia: Rebirth is absolutely terrible. Incredibly cliche horror tropes, terrible writing, unbearably bad voice acting, and monster encounters that are so poorly executed that it makes you just want to stop playing the game.

Amnesia: Rebirth breaks the #1 rule of all horror games: DO NOT FRUSTRATE THE PLAYER. Once the player becomes frustrated, the immersion is removed, and everything ceases to be scary. This game frustrates the hell out of you. It makes absolutely no sense that the game would take 2 hours building up to the first monster encounter only to make it the stupidest interaction you could possibly imagine. 

The big problem with monster encounters is: there is only ONE right answer as to how to escape, but the game is incredibly unclear on what that right answer is. Are you supposed to just run? Are you supposed to block the door with heavy objects? Is there some other path entirely? All of these scenarios will come up in one way or another, so the game teaches you that they all in theory should work. But then encounters are designed in such a way that only ONE of these will work. 

Oh you tried blocking the door with heavy bags? Oh sorry that's not how we wanted you to do this encounter, therefore the monster will just 1-shot break the door down and insta-kill you. 

After you experience this time and time again, the game becomes nothing more than an extraordinarily tedious walking simulator with a terrible storyline. And I'm using the term "storyline" pretty loosely-- the writing is ungodly awful.

I will be generous and rate this game a solid 4/10.

A brilliantly atmospheric horror/cyberpunk game with old-school survival horror gameplay. 

Thematically, this is one of my favourite niches - a "mid-apocalypse" dystopia - aka a world where humanity has passed a point of no return and both the world and society are crumbling towards extinction. 

The storytelling and pacing are generally great - I was pleasantly surprised at how much voice acting is in Hollow Body; the standard of acting is good too. It's also interesting to see a dystopian recreation of a British city - a very uncommon sight in the gaming landscape. The dev has done a good job of keeping the setting consistent by using voice actors from the source setting too. 

The gameplay has a few clunky elements, particularly the combat not being the easiest to control - however this issue might even add some "authentic" charm for fans of old tank control horror games, as it's basically problematic in the same way I always found those. 

Overall, I loved exploring this bleak universe and hope Headware develops another game in the same setting!

This is a solid 7/10 survival-horror game. It's short, but sweet, and never overstays its welcome.

Finding out this was a solo developed effort made me appreciate it all the more. Hollowbody isn't a looker, but its dated graphics and grainy visuals lend itself to the psychological horror it strives for.

Guns are cool.  I like that, being set in England, only the revolver is an actual gun. The shotgun, secret flamethrower and the bow and arrow have an improvised, man-made look to them that accentuates the fact that guns aren't legal over here, save for a select few.

The pacing is good. Almost too good, actually. I was around mid-game when suddenly, I was at the end.

I like the enemies, they're rather simplistic but on Hard/Punished you have to burn them ala the Crimson Heads in REmake.

Music is sombre, dream-like, helping to bolster the Silent Hill vibes it desires.

Story is okay, I was more interested in the background lore and their very good vocal performances/writing than I was the overarching narrative. I think the intro would have been better as a cutscene or more mysterious, the game wasn't really better for playing as Sasha in the hazmat suit. If Nath ever wants someone to help write, I would love to. I particularly want to see more of the neo-noir elements as admittedly, that's what sold me on the game initially. 

I enjoy the dual-perspective. I did my first run on third person cam and my second is underway on fixed camera.  The lock-on can be a bit wonky, I would have preferred a reticule. 

As for the negatives:
Enemies can hit you as you transition into new areas, I had this very commonly in the train station near the end and it was frustrating me a lot.

The train station is a little buggy. After turning on the power, I went to look for the C4, and it didn't spawn on the body where it was supposed to even after reloads. A force close of the game and playing back up to that point fixed it.

Pausing during scenes can mess with the camera, leaving you watching the floor.

Enemies sometimes attack you in your inventory, despite no indication it's real-time.

Ending was kind of obscure for the sake of it, which reminds me of how overboard FROMsoft have gotten with their games' lore. 

This was a really good effort and I'd happily buy the next game by Nath, hopefully with this feedback taken into consideration.

It's finally time for me to write a review, which I probably should have done a long time ago.

I had waited patiently for this game for 5 years, and had been a Patreon supporter for STB for multiple of those years, including prior to Slitherine supporting the game as a publisher. I played the earliest alphas that I recall being available to patrons, all the closed and open betas, all of it. I provided feedback and felt that I was not shouting into a void. I at one point spent a couple of hours in a voice chat with one of the devs (FLX, this will have meaning later) helping create ideas for voice lines, and I think I recognize at least one that made it to release as something I helped with. I was asked at multiple points, because I was previously in the military, questions about fairly simple, small things that showed me the depth at which the devs wanted to go to create perhaps not a realistic, but immersive experience. My hope was through the roof.

Thinking back, the warning signs started popping up before the game released. The institution of auto-smoke for vehicles was a red flag. By this point, I had already realized that the feedback I provided post-Slitherine involvement was ignored (not blaming Slitherine, just using it as a time reference), and I can only imagine that providing feedback was an illusion of being involved in something we were all passionate about. The campaign was literally an afterthought because in the games formative years the team intended for it to only be multiplayer PvP. They didn't even think about adding skirmish until some of the later betas and the massive amount of feedback they received on that particular point (and we of course saw that enemy skirmish AI wasn't present at release, and allied ones still aren't).

On release, I had fun in multiplayer because it was a new experience, I could access everything rather than just some (as in the betas), but I quickly learned how frustrating the game was to play. Vehicle survivability was absolutely insane, and infantry felt incredibly weak (spoiler alert: this is still true because the devs refuse to make changes that would actually fix the problem). Many of us went from Wargame Red Dragon, where these devs also came from, which had incredibly strong infantry, to a game where the polar opposite was true. I don't need to belabor how awful the balance is because you can find what I can only assume are thousands of reviews complaining about it. I've seen people make tangible, constructive suggestions, only to be ignored on countless occasions. I've a good, longtime friend who is a popular content creator (>100k subs) who also told me to give up on the game, because he also tried to provide feedback after sinking countless hours into the game and understanding it at a fundamental level and was told he was wrong.

The anticheat, or lack thereof, is of course a core problem.  Most of the actual 'anticheat' was STB/Slitherine relying on Discord mods to read and evaluate cheating reports that were initially set up in the discord then were routed to a specific email address. Even with EAC implemented now, the original anticheat is still in the game. This means that modding the game is nigh impossible, and at this point, that is the only thing that will bring me back to the game: allowing me to not play FLX's version of this game. He is primarily responsible for the squandering of this title's infinite potential.

Here's the kicker: the game's state is completely in line with FLX's vision. If the community didn't have a say (through terrible reviews, diminishing player count, the Discord being full of negativity, PARTICULARLY the patrons, etc), I am 100% confident he would double down and keep things as they are. He completely, and openly, rejects criticism, whether constructive or otherwise. From my understanding, he similarly rejects dissent from within even the dev team itself. I've watched members of the moderator team leave or at least become openly critical of the game, not because they're volunteers/unpaid, but because they also share the cynical view of the game, which exists largely because of FLX. He is, in every sense of the word, the end-all-be-all decisionmaker. Recently, he asked me a question after a rather cynical scathing of the state of the game in the Patreon channel, I spent over an hour compiling what I felt was a constructive, holistic answer (the subject was, in particular not just on the balance but the OPTICS of the balance; i.e. how it looked having the community be the reason that the demonstrable lack of balance only got worse with every single patch since release), and he rejected it outright as a personal attack on the team (read: him). That was the last straw for me. I experienced his good side, but my opinion of him has significantly tanked and probably will never recover. In the words of the same aforementioned friend, "he's [FLX] is not typing a response, he already had all the answers." It was shortly after this that I cancelled my Patreon subscription. Sure, that is largely symbolic, but to go from one of the longest-time supporters at the highest Patreon level before Slitherine was in the picture to joining the cynics after release was never, ever something I expected to do. 

The sad thing is this: I still believe in the potential of Broken Arrow. Somehow, some way, I believe it is possible to salvage. I don't believe they'll ever truly balance the game as long as FLX has any say in the decisionmaking, but I do believe in what I can only assume will be years, the ability to mod the game will make it worth playing again (maybe you shouldn't make a modding channel in the discord if modding the game got people permabans from the in-house anticheat). Modding being added is exactly the answer I gave to the most well-meaning, awesome member of the Slitherine team involved in the game (Sam) when he asked me what would bring me back. 

My review doesn't even touch on some other broader issues, like the network affecting missiles, nor some other, more drama-related issues surrounding the anticheat that the vast majority of the community isn't aware of.

[b]Pompeii: The Legacy[/b] invites players to journey back to one of history’s most tragic yet fascinating events — the eruption of [i]Mount Vesuvius[/i] in 79 AD. Developed as a mix of historical simulation and narrative-driven strategy, the game aims to recreate the final days of Pompeii while exploring the culture, politics, and daily life of the ancient Roman world.

The game’s strongest asset lies in its historical authenticity. The developers have clearly invested significant effort in research, bringing [i]Pompeii[/i] to life with stunning accuracy. The streets bustle with merchants, politicians, and common citizens, each with their own routines and ambitions. As a player, you assume the role of a prominent citizen trying to secure your family’s legacy amid the shadow of an impending catastrophe.

[b]Pompeii: The Legacy[/b] blends city management, social interaction, and survival mechanics. Players must balance wealth, influence, and resources while preparing for the unknown. Managing estates, overseeing trade, and participating in political debates all form part of the experience. Unlike traditional city builders, this isn’t about expanding endlessly but about preserving stability and legacy in a fragile environment.

As the disaster unfolds, the tone shifts dramatically. What begins as a game of prosperity turns into a desperate struggle for survival. The final act — escaping or saving others — depends heavily on the choices you’ve made. This transition from simulation to survival storytelling is one of the game’s most powerful moments, creating emotional weight rarely seen in strategy titles.

Graphically, [b]Pompeii: The Legacy[/b] is breathtaking. The city is richly detailed, from mosaics and frescoes to the grand forum and distant view of [i]Vesuvius[/i] looming over the horizon. As the eruption progresses, the visuals become hauntingly beautiful — ash clouds roll across the sky, lava illuminates the ruins, and panic fills the streets. The sound design complements this perfectly, with authentic ambient noise, Latin-inspired music, and chilling environmental effects that convey both the splendor and terror of the setting.

[b]Pompeii: The Legacy[/b] is a rare and compelling mix of historical realism, emotional storytelling, and strategic gameplay. It captures both the grandeur of [i]Roman[/i] civilization and the human tragedy of [i]Pompeii[/i]’s final hours. Despite some technical imperfections, it stands out as one of the most evocative historical simulations in recent years.

Senran Kagura: Bon Appétit! is an unapologetically eccentric rhythm-game spin-off that takes the extravagant fanservice, humor, and character-driven theatrics of the Senran Kagura series and redirects them into a full-blown cooking competition. Developed by Meteorise and published by XSEED Games and Marvelous, the game abandons the series’ usual ninja brawling to pit its cast of shinobi girls against each other in culinary duels judged by none other than Master Hanzo. The setup is intentionally absurd—the winners vie for a mythical scroll said to grant any wish—and the tone never once pretends to be serious. Instead, it leans playfully into the franchise’s trademark blend of ridiculous stakes, exaggerated reactions, and shameless spectacle.

The visual presentation remains one of the game’s strongest draws. Character models are vibrant, expressive, and animated with the same flair the series is known for, and the PC release benefits from higher resolutions and smoother framerates than the original handheld version. Each cooking battle is framed with over-the-top cutscenes, flashy transitions, and the familiar clothing-damage flourishes that the franchise openly revels in. The game’s art direction embraces its own theatricality so thoroughly that it’s difficult not to smile at the sheer excess of it all. This visual identity, paired with the silly dialogue and tongue-in-cheek story segments, ensures that the game maintains a buoyant, comedic energy throughout.

Where Bon Appétit! diverges from its action-oriented roots is in its rhythm gameplay, but this ambition is met with mixed results. The mechanics are straightforward: hit inputs in time with the beat, build combos, and outperform your opponent across three rounds of musical cooking. While the idea is charming, the execution lacks refinement. Many rhythm-game veterans have criticized the note charts for being stiff or inconsistently mapped, occasionally breaking the natural flow that is crucial to satisfying rhythm gameplay. The soundtrack itself offers a modest lineup of mostly J-pop and character-themed tracks—energetic, upbeat, and fitting the tone, but not particularly memorable or diverse. Once you’ve played through the full list of songs, repetition sets in quickly, especially since the gameplay doesn’t evolve much from track to track.

The narrative and mode structure are similarly compact. Each character has a brief story path filled with playful dialogue and personality-driven moments, but the routes serve more as comedic interludes than meaningful development. For long-time fans, these segments are enjoyable opportunities to see favorite characters in a new context, often poking fun at their established traits. For newcomers, the humor may still land, but the stories offer little depth. Replay value exists mainly through unlocking cosmetic items, viewing new scenes, and trying higher difficulties, but the limited song list makes deep engagement difficult unless you’re heavily invested in the characters and tone.

Despite its shortcomings, the game does succeed on the level it seems most committed to: providing a zany, irreverent, character-focused diversion for fans of the franchise. Bon Appétit! never tries to compete with heavyweight rhythm titles; instead, it positions itself as a comedic side dish for players who appreciate the series’ combination of charm and outrageous fanservice. Its lightheartedness, colorful visuals, and playful sensuality make it a pleasant, if shallow, diversion when taken at face value.

Ultimately, Senran Kagura: Bon Appétit! is not a rhythm game that will win over genre purists, nor is it a narrative showcase for newcomers. But for those already fond of the series’ energetic style, flamboyant characters, and unabashed humor, it offers a compact, entertaining detour filled with personality. It’s a confection—sweet, flashy, and lacking in nutritional value—but enjoyable for exactly what it is.

Wenn man bei den Soulslikes ganz vorne mit dabei sein will, darf man sich kaum bis keine Schnitzer leisten und muss vor allem bei den Bossen und beim Kampfsystem abliefern. Leider überzeugt Lords of the Fallen in keinem der beiden Bereiche vollends. Schwertschläge werden teils mit meterweiten Hechtsprüngen ausgeführt, das Trefferfeedback ist nicht rund genug und die Kamera veranstaltet mitunter wilde Drehungen. Dass die Entwickler Bosskämpfe können, zeigen sie mit einer Handvoll Highlights, plustern das Arsenal dann aber mit belanglosen Bedrohungen auf, um erfolglos die fehlende Feindesvielfalt abzufedern. Mit dem Weltenwechsel zwischen Axiom und Umbral bietet Lords of the Fallen eine interessante Idee, die im festgefahrenen Soulslike-Genre Anerkennung verdient. Auch die Waffenvielfalt, die grandiose Optik und Grafik sowie das stimmige Sounddesign sind bemerkenswerte Pluspunkte. Angesichts mehrerer kleinerer Unstimmigkeiten und der inkonstanten Framerate reicht das aber nicht, um aus Lords of the Fallen mehr als nur ein grundsolides Soulslike zu machen.

Ys: The Oath in Felghana — Review

Ys: The Oath in Felghana is one of those games that reminds you why fast-paced action RPGs are so much fun. It takes everything good about Ys VI: The Ark of Napishtim — the responsive combat, the great music, the sense of adventure — and sharpens it to perfection. It’s leaner, tougher, and more refined, often considered one of the best entries in the entire series.

Originally a full remake of Ys III: Wanderers from Ys, it doesn’t just update an old game — it completely reimagines it. What was once a 2D side-scroller is now a slick 3D action adventure that feels timeless even today.

Story and Setting

As always, you play as Adol Christin, the red-haired hero who can’t stay away from trouble. This time, Adol and his friend Dogi travel to Dogi’s hometown — the peaceful land of Felghana. But, of course, things aren’t peaceful for long. Monsters have started appearing, local lords are acting suspiciously, and an ancient power begins to stir beneath the land.

The story here is simple but surprisingly emotional. There’s no huge world-ending plot, but the personal stakes — protecting Dogi’s people, uncovering the mystery of the cursed statues, and confronting old betrayals — give it real heart.

Unlike many JRPGs of its time, Felghana doesn’t drown you in dialogue. It says just enough, trusts you to care, and lets the gameplay carry the rest.

Gameplay

This is where the game truly shines. The Oath in Felghana is all about speed, precision, and rhythm. Adol moves fast, attacks fast, and dodges even faster. The controls are so responsive that every hit feels crisp and satisfying.

Combat combines sword combos, jumping attacks, and magic spells that you upgrade as you play. Each spell has a clear purpose — from area control to ranged damage — and mastering how to switch between them is key to surviving later boss fights.

Speaking of bosses — Felghana has some of the best in the series. They’re challenging, creative, and always fair. Every battle is a test of reflexes and pattern recognition rather than grinding levels. Beating a tough boss here feels earned.

The progression system is simple: collect ore to enhance weapons, find items that increase stats, and occasionally unlock new movement abilities. It’s streamlined in a way that keeps you focused on what matters — the action.

Presentation

Even years later, Felghana looks great in motion. The 3D models are simple, but the art direction and lighting create a nostalgic charm that hasn’t aged poorly. The environments — ancient ruins, fiery caverns, icy peaks — all feel distinct and full of energy.

But what really stands out is the music. Falcom’s Sound Team JDK absolutely outdid themselves here. The soundtrack mixes metal, synth, and orchestral elements in a way that makes every battle feel epic. Tracks like Chop!! and Valestein Castle are instant classics — pure adrenaline in musical form.

The sound design supports the pace perfectly — fast, punchy, and satisfying.

What I Liked

Tight, responsive combat that feels amazing to play

Incredible boss fights — challenging but fair

Phenomenal soundtrack (one of Falcom’s best)

Streamlined structure with no filler

Emotional but concise story

Perfect length — no grind, just pure action and adventure

What I Didn’t Like

Some difficulty spikes can frustrate newcomers

No real side quests or big world to explore

Limited character interaction outside the main plot

Older graphics might not appeal to everyone

Final Thoughts

Ys: The Oath in Felghana is a near-perfect action RPG. It’s fast, skillful, and focused — every fight, jump, and upgrade feels purposeful. It’s the kind of game that rewards mastery and punishes laziness, but never feels unfair.

It also has that special Falcom energy — a mix of earnest storytelling, great pacing, and unstoppable momentum. You can tell it was made with care and confidence.

If you’ve never played Ys before, this is one of the best places to start. It’s short, exciting, and pure. If you already love the series, you probably know: this one’s a classic for a reason.

My Score: 9/10
An exhilarating, finely-tuned adventure — the essence of what makes action RPGs timeless.

There are those that play Outer Wilds, the Blue Prince and Tunic.

And then there's you, the weirdo, that plays Void Stranger.

This isn't an indictment against your tastes or the aversion to the mainstream.
Instead, it's a welcome into the obscure, the esoteric, and the punishing.

Please allow me to introduce one of my favorite games and why you should play it, even if that recommendation comes with a [i] heavy [/i] asterisk.

[h1] The Comparisons: [/h1] 
The best way that I can describe Void Stranger, is that it's weirdly specific and obtuse like a Lucas Pope game, while having a lot of charms like an old Treasure title. It is filled with the mentally masochistic layers of detail like an in-depth escape room, all while it's delivered in a distinct monochromatic artstyle that makes the entire experience feel like a forbidden, cursed Game Boy cartridge.

[h1] The Warnings: [/h1]
This is a game that's unabashedly honest about what it is: It's a sokoban game, which will already filter a good 95% of Steam players. It isn't a simplistic novelty Sokoban like Helltaker, so don't let the cute girls fool you. (But don't let them deter you, either!) 

This is a long-form game like old Nintendo titles. You WILL get filtered. You WILL get mad. You WILL put it down at some point for one of those two reasons, and that's okay. Don't be afraid to embrace your inner schizophrenic and write down your chicken-scratches of codes, symbols, puzzles and theories. In fact, this game encourages and rewards that behavior, all the way down to a lore standpoint.

[h1] The Advice: [/h1]
If for some reason, you get hardwalled to the point of being seemingly stuck and you need guidance, spoiler-free walkthroughs do exist, but make that a final option because exploration, ah-ha moments of clarity, and story exposition are directly tied to the discovery of mechanics. It's an Outer Wilds scenario where literally the entire game is based on knowledge and learning, where even the most oblique details can alter your entire perception. 

If you rob yourself of that, then you've stripped yourself of an epiphany that you're entirely capable of reaching, only to be cursed with knowledge that wasn't your own to gain.

You can absolutely do this.
It may take you three solid months like it did for me, but don't give up.

After all was said and done, this has become one of the hardest recommendations that I could ever make for my friends, while also becoming one of the hardest recommendations that I could ever make for my friends.

Se você gosta de CRPG e também da temática "Roma Antiga", esse jogo é simplesmente único no mercado!

A parte da história, diálogos, opções de escolhas nas conversas e decisões a se tomar achei muito boas. Muito competente no seu papel de CRPG clássico, tirando uma ou outra missão que fica faltando uma alternativa interessante e diferente das mostradas no game na forma de resolução que ajudasse no role-play.

O jogo se desenvolve por "campanhas", nas quais levamos nossa legião para regiões e temos que resolver conflitos. Lugares como Grécia, Norte da África, Gália e também Roma.

Os diálogos com os NPCs achei bem enxutos e bem escritos, não são textos enormes, tipo Pathfinder: Kingmaker ou WotR. O que obviamente ajuda por conta do jogo ser totalmente voice-acted (dublado), estilo BG3.

Na parte de gameplay, o jogo tem a parte da "Pacificação", em que controlamos nossa legião em um mapa, estilo sandbox, explorando, dominando regiões e nos deparando com eventos aleatórios. Confesso que acabei enjoando da metade para o fim, porque acabam as novidades e fica algo cansativo. Tem como iniciar o game desativando, que acho que deveria ter feito. Vou testar depois como fica.

E o principal, obviamente, é o combate por turnos, em que controlamos nosso "squad" em um mapa, bem ao estilo XCOM ou Divinity: Original Sin. Lidamos com espaços hexagonais, em que os personagens também podem pegar covers (semi ou completo). Posicionar bem seus soldados faz muita diferença. Seja alguém com um escudo bloqueando uma passagem ou se escondendo da mira de arqueiros.

O jogo conta com as classes: Princeps (guerreiro com escudo), Veles (rogue), Arqueiro, Triarius (uma classe mais versátil, tanto suporte como DPS) e a da DLC, Gladiador. Cada uma dela tem 3 variações de builds e skills para escolher, dando uma leque maior de personalização e opções para se usar no combate.

Na parte técnica: graficamente muito bonito para o escopo do game. Cenários lindos como florestas, desertos, casarões em Roma, cavernas ou montanhas com neve na Gália. Encontrei pouquíssimos bugs, mas, como qualquer jogador experiente de CRPG, basta salvar o tempo todo que não é um problema. O próprio jogo faz saves automáticos antes de todos os eventos e batalhas. A parte do som e trilha sonora também muito boas, nada a reclamar.

Zerei com mais ou menos 100 horas na dificuldade normal, apenas setando a IA dos inimigos no Insano (máxima). O que consumiu bastante de tempo foi justamente o microgerenciamento da pacificação, que enjoei do meio para o fim. Desativando o jogo, deve fluir melhor, na minha opinião.

Enfim, recomendo bastante, justamente por conta da minha primeira frase: O jogo é único no mercado.

I was first drawn to [b]SHAFTED[/b] by the cool art style. I found the pictures used for the aliens, for your operators, and for the shadowy cabal to be evocative.

I was also intrigued by the gameplay displayed in some of the screenshots, which reminded me of [b]Pipe Dream[/b]. I've always enjoyed this style of mini-game, from playing [b]Pipe Dream[/b] itself in [b]Microsoft Entertainment Pack 2[/b] to the hacking minigame in the first [b]Bioshock[/b]. 

It's a good thing I enjoy it too, since [i]much[/i] of your time with the game will be spent utilizing this gameplay mechanic to maximize mineral output. Your mineral output is also affected by the arrangement in which you place your structures. Initially I found myself pulled into the puzzle of it all, but after a while I began to get frustrated. 

Every turn, the alien (that is demanding payment from you, no less) destroys certain squares with some sort of orbital laser blast. It feels awful to have carefully considered the placement of a structure and to excel in your [b]Pipe Dream[/b] mini-game, only to have the structure randomly destroyed. To make matters worse, you'll often spend currency to upgrade your structures and begin mining a lower level, and the resources put into this effort are also lost when the building is destroyed.

As the goals for my mining colony continued to increase, my patience with the incessant alien attacks decreased. Eventually, I decided to move on to something else that was more fun. By the way, I thought that [b]SHAFTED[/b] would be a good candidate for Steam Deck play, but it doesn't work all that well - if I recall correctly, you're mostly just using the touchpad as you would a mouse.

Phenomenal. Addictive. I haven't barreled down on a game like this since Kenshi. I was starting to wonder if another experience like this was out there waiting for me. I am grateful. 

If you like open-world, survival, depth, long-playthrough, rewarding gameplay loops ... this is a masterclass in game design. My first playthrough was 155 hours. So, a lot to enjoy here. 

One common critique seem to be:
"The difficulty is excessive, unfair or off-putting."

I made mistakes. Got surprised. Cornered. Mismanaged inventory. Zigged when I should have zagged. Got overwhelmed. Unlucky. Died. But overall, thought the difficulty was beautifully balanced to create tension that was engaging but surmountable. Never felt unfair. But, I can only speak for the build I was kind of nudged into by choosing Dirwin.

Another common critique seems to be:
"The save system disrespects the player's time." 

So, you save by sleeping. You get a "mobile" bed early on. Many POI's have beds. All the towns do. You can pack a bedroll that is somewhat expensive, one-use, and takes up a bunch of your inventory. This all makes sense to me. 

The game gives you a choice: 
- Be risky/cheap
--- Don't pack your bags thoughtfully.
--- Be stingy with consumables. 
--- Go out on long excursions into the unknown, run low on supplies, and maybe get merked near the end losing loot/experience/time.


Or manage risk: 
---- Stay within a few tiles of a bed/safety and head back for supplies/sleep. 
---- Spend money/space on sleeping rolls/fodder/throw-ables/potions/pricey food.
---- Clean out half a dungeon, or see a mini-boss then retreat for sleep/save/loot drop/resupply. The dungeon will stay half-cleared. 


There were times when I was risky/cheap/impatient ... everything worked out ... and I felt clever. 
Then ... there were times when I didn't. 

It's a survival game ... your decisions matter.

This leads to the third most common complaint I saw.
"Hours traveling back to a POI." 

This one I am genuinely confused about.
I don't think I ever traveled more than five minutes to get back to a POI. 
Middle mouse button > Scroll > Click on the other side of a tile > Your character will cross a whole tile in 30 seconds? 
I mean ... How far are ya'll walking to hit a dungeon?
The whole map? ... Never stopping to rest?
Idk ... sounds risky.

These choices though ... they really make Stoneshard an incredible experience. 

Anyways ... Ink Stains! ... Damn ... You guys are awesome. 
Looking at your roadmap ... here's what I am personally most excited for:
- New POIs - yes.
- More tasks/quests/NPCs - Always!
- Random encounters - Sounds fun.
- More enemies - Sure.
- Stealth - yeah - it's needed.
- Story - Not necessary but ... nice extra.
- Alchemy - yeah ... I want to make some of these consumables/throwables and not rely on vendor RNG.
- More regions (DLC?) ... take my money :) 

What I didn't see though is:
- More tilesets for the dungeons - This is where we spend a lot of time. More secret rooms. How about some rope-bridges. Dark rooms. Wet rooms. Banquet halls. Integrating some cave tile-sets ... sewers .. to connect different areas ... maybe we could "free" more hostages ... see more wizard lairs ... more carnage 
- Expanding on the excellent foundation you laid for Brynn - It needs some love.
- Can I make my own character?

Stuff I don't think you really need: 
- More ability trees/weapon types??? - You've already got eleven weapon types with loads of overlapping trees - it's already a lot to take in ... like ... a lot. More weapons/armor = Great ... you don't need many more trees.  
- Lockpicking - Ehhh ... minigames? ... That's not your vibe. Crowbar makes sense. Pass.
- Maladies - uhhhh - I disable these in every game that allows me to. Please don't give me malaria and then force me to find the one plant that cures it. Not fun.

Some constructive feedback:
- Less "pottery" in the crypts please. Gets very tedious in the big ones.
- Dial back the timers for "maladies" in the towns please. I don't mind helping them out but ... too aggressive. 
- Let me open my bag while looking in another inventory - Let the bag take priority. 
- Let arrows in my inventory go into another inventory (when opened) "shift" instead of the quiver.

Ys SEVEN represents a pivotal moment in Nihon Falcom’s long-running action RPG series—a point where the franchise stepped confidently into modern real-time party combat while preserving the spirit of swift, exhilarating adventure that defines Adol Christin’s journeys. Originally released on the PSP and later brought to PC by XSEED Games and Marvelous USA, Inc., the game marks Adol and Dogi’s arrival in the kingdom of Altago, a land recovering from war but shadowed by strange quakes, ancient prophecies, and political strife. What begins as simple exploration quickly escalates into a sweeping conflict involving the Five Great Dragons, dormant forces, and a kingdom struggling between tradition and change. The narrative may follow familiar JRPG contours, but it maintains a momentum and charm that keeps the journey engaging from start to finish.

The most striking departure from earlier entries is the combat system. Ys SEVEN abandons the one-man action style of older titles in favor of a three-character party you can switch between instantly. Each party member embodies one of three attack types—Slash, Strike, and Pierce—and enemies strongly favor or resist one of these categories. This simple but effective weakness triangle adds a constant layer of tactical awareness, encouraging you to swap characters fluidly rather than rely on a favorite. Layered atop this is a growing arsenal of skills, each tied to weapon proficiency, and the Flash Guard mechanic—a precisely timed block that negates damage and rewards you with temporary boosts. The result is a battle system that feels fluid, aggressive, and thrilling, capturing the high-speed DNA of the Ys brand while introducing a degree of tactical depth not present in older titles.

Boss battles are a clear highlight. Many encounters fill the screen with enormous enemies, sweeping attacks, and tight windows of opportunity. These fights showcase Falcom’s knack for designing climactic set pieces that challenge reflexes without feeling unfair. They also benefit from the game’s stellar soundtrack, composed by Falcom Sound Team jdk. Music has always been one of the Ys series’ greatest strengths, and Ys SEVEN continues that legacy with dynamic, guitar-driven tracks during boss battles and warm melodies during exploration. Even players who find the visuals dated often note that the music elevates the experience considerably, lending emotional weight to both quiet and explosive moments.

Ys SEVEN’s visual presentation reflects its origins—its models and textures carry the unmistakable mark of a PSP-era title—but the PC port smooths those edges with higher resolutions, Steamworks support, and improved performance. While the environments are simple, they remain colorful and readable, and the art direction still preserves a sense of scale and atmosphere, particularly in regions like the Shannoa Forest or the ancient Dragon Sanctums. The upgraded framerate enhances the combat’s responsiveness, ensuring that fast, precise movement remains at the heart of the experience.

Structurally, the game is straightforward. Regions unlock at a steady pace, offering new landscapes to explore and a growing roster of party members to train. Side quests, while not elaborate, contribute to the sense of Altago as a living kingdom with its own history and local concerns. These optional tasks build goodwill with townsfolk and sometimes unlock worthwhile equipment or story flavor. The central narrative progresses briskly, rarely pausing for overly long exposition, and this helps maintain the sense of adventure that defines the series. The trade-off is that some themes—political tension, cultural divides, character arcs—are touched on with brevity rather than depth.

Despite its strengths, Ys SEVEN does reveal limitations. The dungeon design can feel formulaic compared to later entries, leaning on straightforward layouts and repetition rather than complex puzzles or multi-layered mechanics. Some mid-game regions require backtracking that momentarily disrupts pacing. The combat, while excellent, does not evolve as dramatically over the course of the game as some players might hope; once you understand the skill system and attack-type triangle, the overarching loop remains familiar. And although the story is functional and occasionally moving, it rarely surprises, adhering closely to archetypal JRPG beats.

Even with these shortcomings, Ys SEVEN remains a standout title in the series and an accessible entry point for newcomers. It offers a generous 20–30 hours of content, a satisfying progression curve, and a combat system that feels both modern for its generation and delightfully responsive by today’s standards. The sense of movement, the rhythm of swapping party members, and the thrill of facing down colossal bosses all contribute to an adventure that captures the heart of what makes Ys enduring.

In the end, Ys SEVEN is a celebration of action-driven RPG design—swift, spirited, and unpretentious. It may not carry the visual grandeur of newer titles, but its mechanical confidence, energetic soundtrack, and engaging combat bring it to life in ways that transcend its handheld roots. It remains one of the most important turning points in the Ys franchise and a memorable journey for anyone who values fast-paced action and classic JRPG atmosphere.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*]Great sound effects
[*]Cool visuals, animations, and overall art style
[*]Beautiful effects artwork
[*]Weapon and relic modifiers are smartly designed
[*]Characters, abilities, and relic swaps feel well-balanced and interesting
[*]Lots of creative enemy designs
[*]Difficulty increases nicely with added curses
[*]Dual-character mechanic is fun (some combos are clearly stronger, but it works)
[*]Excellent Italian translation
[*]Arena layouts with curves and corners make for clever bounce strategies
[*]With hotkeys, you can actually play just with the mouse — it becomes super fast, intuitive, and satisfying

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*]Enemy variety could be better
[*]Too short — few levels and not much randomization
[*]Little incentive to take on harder fights over normal ones
[*]Final boss feels underwhelming
[*]Unlock system is neat but gets repetitive since runs feel very similar

Fallout ist ein Meisterwerk der Spielegeschichte und wahrscheinlich als Widerbelebung des Genres 1997 bis heute eines der einflussreichsten Rollenspiele auf dem Computer aller Zeiten. 
Der Spieler merkt beim genaueren Hinsehen die Nähe zum Pen & Paper Rollenspiel, so wie sie damals auch versucht wurde möglichst detailliert auf die Rechner zu übertragen. Das fängt bei einem der besten Hintergrundsysteme für Charakterwerte und Perks, die es bis heute gibt an – Das S.P.E.C.I.A.L. System auf GURPS Basis- geht weiter bei der Spielerischen Freiheit, die damals wirklich unglaublich war – selbst ein Run mit Int 1 ist möglich und bietet dabei urkomische Konsequenzen- und endet mit einem fordernden, actionpunktbasierten Rundentaktikkampfsystem, dass mit mit jedem besiegten Gegner eine Euphorie ins Blut schießen lässt.
Schon allein das durch Fallout etablierte – wenn auch von Wasteland & Mad Max inspirierte- Universum ist nicht ohne Grund heute noch in Nutzung und mit Brettspielumsetzungen, Prime Serien & co. beliebter denn je. Es bietet neben moralischen Grauzonen, philosophischen Fragen zu Ethik und dem Wesen von Mensch und Gesellschaft auch eine künstlerische Eigenleistung, im Grunde das ATOM- Punk Gesellschaftsfähig gemacht zu haben. Die Welt ist düster, versifft und teils auch gruselig, der grandiose Sound tut dabei sein Übriges und ich will keine Sekunde darin mit seinen tödlichen Skorpionen, absurden Charakteren und skurrilen Humor missen. Und dass, auch wenn ein heutiges Durchspielen schon gewisse Frustresistenz erfordert. Das fängt schon bei der Charaktererstellung an. Ohne wirklichen Plan und Wissen, was die Werte für Auswirkungen haben, ist verskillen beim ersten Run für mich unausweichlich gewesen. (Bei Gott, pumpt euch voll mit Agility). Es folgt ein Spiel mit umständlichen Inventarmanagement, unsteuerbaren Begleitern inkl. Friendly Fire (nehmt denen bloß die Granaten weg) und fiesen Zeitlimit bis zu einem bestimmten Schritt in der Kampagne ( schade, dass hinterlässt bei jeder Erkundungstour ein schuldigen Beigeschmack auf der Zunge)
Dafür funktioniert das Kampfsystem mit seinen Action Points, dem innovativen VATS- System und der taktischen Tiefe – wenn sich der Spieler eine Weile darauf eingelassen hat- unglaublich gut und ist eine Freude, auch heute noch! Kein Wunder, dass dieses Kampfsystem in Fallout: Tactics einen eigenen Ableger bekommen hat.
Gut gefallen hat mir auch neben den vielen Waffen, die es zu erkunden gibt, das leveln, erhöhen der Werte, erlangen von Fähigkeiten und die dadurch deutlich im Spiel Spürbaren Konsequenzen für meinen Charakter und die Spielweise. 
Für mich sollte jeder der Spielhistorisch interessiert ist, zumindest mal in Fallout reingeschaut haben, bei Möglichkeit die englische Version. Mich hat die Postapokalypse mit seiner Story, bei der es doch um mehr geht, als das es auf den ersten Blick scheint von vorn bis hinten in seinen Bann gezogen und ich hatte auch nach heutigen Bewertungsprämissen nach einer kleinen Eingewöhnungsphase wirklich viel viel Spaß.

Это хорошая сессионнка менеджмент-градостроитель с элементами рандома.

Из плюсов:
++ Неплохой визуал и дизайн в целом
+ Неплохой саунддизайн из аудиошума могу назвать только звук дождя в буран, в который иногда не слышишь (не можешь акцентироваться) уведомления.
+ Система на выбор из рандома краевых камней, рецептов зданий и указов, заставляет адаптироваться под условия от местности, с учётом выпавшего. Это плюс в копилку реиграбельности.
+ Есть прокачка от каждой завершённой катки. Она открывает нам новые возможности, фоново облегчая и игру и создавая новые ситуации. Что также плюс в реиграбельность (есть фоновая прогрессия и она ощутима)
+ Есть разные карты, которые не только влияют на ресурсы но и на стиль игры в целом.
+ В отличии от многих инди игр такого типа - тут удобный  UI и есть свои приятности в настройках.

Минусы:
- Во время обучения вышел патч, обучение сбросилось. Дали ресурсы и послали играть. Обидно, т.к. обучение довольно долгое и пришлось разбираться с многими аспектами самому.
- Иногда рандом душит. Не смотря на то что на 40 каток до уровня Наместник (3-4 грейд сложности не помню) у меня 1 поражение, я точно помню как 3 раза подряд выпадал мусор, который блокировал выход на события, т.к. походы туда будут чистым самоубийством без прогрессии.
- Маршруты к печатям зачастую полностью свободны и на них не встретишь ни одного события. А сами события, зачастую не просто челлендж, а стоят с невозможными условиями для их прохождения.

Кому игра подойдёт:
- Вы знаете что это сессионка, в которой вас будут подгонять (катки ограничены условием, а соответственно по времени). 
- На одну катку у вас уйдёт около часа, полтора. 
- Вы готовы к рандому и готовы не гореть, а адаптироваться. И готовы к тому, что это игра не про то где у вас всё хорошо, а наоборот идёт не так как надо.
- Здесь нужно будет думать. Все ваши действия, вплоть до добычи древесины (на определённых локациях), могут сильно влиять на благополучие вашей колонии и победу.

Кому игра не подойдёт:
- Людям которые ожидают от игры затяжной игры как в градостроителях, по 8-20 часов на одну партию
- Людям которые ожидают стабильности от игры, где рандом должен влиять допустим на цены на рынке и на события у людей, но никак не на выбор пути развития и уж тем более строительства, с отсекающим другие выборы.
- Людям которые ожидают что это будет релаксирующая игра. Это не так, мы всю игру пытаемся выбраться из удавки, которая медленно (а иногда и достаточно быстро) пытается нас убить, мы пытаемся одним прогресс баром, опередить заполнение другого.

Я однозначно рекомендую эту игру в том числе без DLC, как уникальный и приятный опыт в формате менеджмент-выживания.

Awaken - Astral Blade (why do so many games insist on sub-headers now?) is a sedate platformer that struggles to be a metroidvania until about a third of the way through. The story begins with voiced dialog that makes the Saturday morning toy commercials of the 80s look Shakespearean by comparison, but, as you progress, you find that only segments of dialog are given even that much attention. This is, perhaps, for the best, as to call the writing middling would be an insult to fan fiction you find in the trash. To be fair, this may be the result of poor translations. For instance, the game uses "talking of which" when the actual phrase is "speaking of which." Also, it cracks me up that the energy sword you wield is called Enginery Sword, so its an engine sword? Alternatively, for those who know Georgian, that means you're running around with an Engineering Sword. Neither one makes sense, but they do both make more sense than the overall story.

The graphics are OK at best. The environments can be lush but also confusing, as background elements can look like a wall that's not hiding a secret area, of which there are plenty. Characters, on the other hand, look like they stepped out of a coloring book. Any beauty in the graphics is marred by their poor animation. Characters look more like stilted marionettes than fluid characters. When this is combined with the voice acting and script as well as still images, the cinematics come off as just bad. All of this makes for a disjointed play experience.

This disconnect is felt starkly in player feedback. Awaken does a good job of trying to teach you weapon combinations as you unlock them, but when it comes to other character mechanics, it fails entirely. Weapons, feats, and other items increases your attack power (or other stat), but the game never tells you what your actual attack power is. That means that when the game says you get a +2, that means nothing. If your base attack power is 2, that's a great increase, but if its 1000, that's nothing. Throwing numbers at you without establishing baseline is less productive than throwing spaghetti at the wall and inventing an alphabet out of what sticks. In further illustration, Awaken does provides a pretty simple item upgrade system where you get so many slots that you can fit things into, but it never actually explains it; you're left to figure it out for yourself.

Awaken does not innovate on the genre. If anything, it regresses a bit. Innovation is not required for a metroidvania, as such games can just polish what has come before, but an attempt at innovation could have elevated and excused the game's many flaws. As a footnote, but do these games insist on the high jump requiring you to face slam into the ground first? Are you a basketball? Such a silly action.

It is important to acknowledge, that the team at Dark Pigeon isn't that big (according to the really short credits). I want to say that a larger team may have been able to deliver a better experience, but I have seen tiny teams deliver good experiences. This simply wasn't one. In the end, if you are looking to scratch that metroidvania itch, you can give this a try, but I suggest exhausting your other options first.

Petit Island, developed by Xelo Games and published by SOEDESCO, is a wholesome and serene adventure that invites players into a pastel-hued world of discovery, memory, and reflection. It tells the story of Lily, a young feline adventurer who journeys to her grandfather’s island to relive his youthful memories and document the places and faces that once defined his life. The game is a gentle blend of exploration and lighthearted interaction, designed to capture the warmth of nostalgia rather than the thrill of challenge. From the moment you set foot on the island, it’s clear that Petit Island wants to soothe rather than excite, offering a peaceful retreat wrapped in soft colors, relaxing music, and an undercurrent of emotional storytelling.

The world of Petit Island is immediately inviting. Its visual presentation is bright and colorful, painted in warm tones that make the island feel like a sunlit dreamscape. Villages, beaches, forests, and mountains flow naturally into one another, creating a sense of organic discovery. Each area feels handcrafted, with cozy cottages, fishing docks, and scattered relics of the past adding texture to the experience. The anthropomorphic characters who inhabit the island are equally charming, with cheerful designs and simple animations that fit the game’s cozy atmosphere. While the visuals are not technically complex, the art direction compensates by creating a comforting sense of place. Accompanied by a tranquil, melodic soundtrack and ambient nature sounds, the game establishes a rhythm that encourages relaxation and quiet contemplation.

Gameplay in Petit Island revolves around exploration and gentle interaction. Players can freely roam the island, taking photographs, catching bugs, fishing, and digging for hidden items that tie into Lily’s quest to preserve her grandfather’s memories. These activities are never rushed or difficult; instead, they function as meditative rituals that let you absorb the world at your own pace. Conversations with the island’s inhabitants reveal fragments of story and personality, though they remain surface-level rather than deeply developed. There are also light progression elements, such as unlocking new areas or completing small tasks for villagers, but these are kept deliberately simple. The result is a game that values presence over pressure, aiming to immerse players in a soothing loop of exploration rather than test their reflexes or problem-solving skills.

The heart of Petit Island lies in its emotional core—the bond between Lily and her grandfather. The story unfolds through journal entries, dialogue, and the objects you find scattered around the island. Each discovery carries with it a touch of nostalgia, hinting at the passage of time and the bittersweet nature of memory. It’s a theme that resonates in subtle ways: old photographs, familiar landmarks, and faded friendships reflect the universal desire to preserve the past while still moving forward. The narrative isn’t overly complex, but its sincerity gives it heart. It’s easy to see the game as a metaphor for reflection and familial love—a small, quiet story told through the act of wandering and remembering.

Despite its charm, Petit Island’s simplicity can also be its biggest limitation. The gameplay mechanics, while relaxing, lack depth and variety. Fishing, bug-catching, and item collection offer little challenge, and after a few hours, the activities begin to feel repetitive. Some features, such as home customization or certain collectibles, appear underdeveloped or lightly implemented, leaving the impression that the game’s scope was scaled back during development. Navigation can also become tedious, as the island’s layout often requires long walks back and forth without a fast-travel option early on. These design choices, though consistent with the game’s leisurely tone, can test the patience of players looking for more dynamic progression. Petit Island is clearly meant for those who find joy in slow pacing rather than momentum.

Where the game shines most consistently is in its atmosphere. Even when its mechanics start to feel repetitive, the mood remains engaging. There’s an undeniable charm in simply wandering the island at sunset, listening to the waves lap at the shore, and capturing the world through Lily’s camera. It evokes the same peaceful escapism found in titles like A Short Hike or Alba: A Wildlife Adventure, yet with its own flavor of gentle Southeast Asian-inspired coastal charm. The developers’ focus on mood and mindfulness ensures that even when little happens mechanically, players still find moments of quiet satisfaction. The inclusion of animal characters and the emphasis on kindness and empathy make it a perfect fit for those seeking a family-friendly or meditative experience.

Petit Island is ultimately a love letter to slow living and personal reflection. It does not aim to surprise or challenge its audience, but to comfort them. Its world feels alive in the way a fond memory does—warm, familiar, and slightly imperfect. For those who appreciate games that allow space to breathe and wander, it offers exactly that: an island of calm amid the noise of modern gaming. It may not satisfy players looking for complex mechanics or narrative twists, but it succeeds wholeheartedly as a relaxing journey through nostalgia and nature. Petit Island is a gentle reminder that sometimes, the greatest adventures are the quiet ones spent in the company of memories, sunlight, and the distant hum of the sea.

Look, a solid half of the enjoyment of this game is nostalgia for all us 80s/90s kids who learned a weird amount of geography from a woman in a red hat.  If you don't have that nostalgia, a lot of this game is going to lack the kind of punch that it does for us.
That said, it's a solid puzzle game.  There are a ton of mini puzzles on each caper that are repeated across the capers but not in their solutions, just that it's the same set on each caper.  And there's pixelized ACME Files for when you're not playing the capers that's a nice nod to the original games.
Some less than great things: the voice acting is wildly inconsistent (every time you move cities, there's repeated affirmations between Sandiego and Player but when you nab the goons, the cut scene with the chief is completely silent).  The chief's animosity seems ridiculous after about two capers because you're doing her job for her but the plot shakily depends her thinking you're still a criminal.  And there are times when you have to stop playing the main caper storylines to go level up in "notoriety" via the ACME Files--which are great little games to themselves but really interrupt the flow (especially since I have no idea if there's a top to the notoriety levels; do you just keep leveling up ad infinitum?).
The 3D animation isn't smooth at all, though bouncing it off the pixels of the Files is a neat go.  I know this is capitalizing on the popularity of the Netflix reboot and again, this is a good little puzzle game.  But I'm not sure I'd like this half as much if I didn't have the memories of singing along to my television as a kid to carry the weak spots.
(I did learn several things about geography, though.  Carmen Sandiego, still teaching me after all these years.  Love that for us.)

It’s fun, ignore the stupid name and try it.

麻枝准的巅峰，KEY的巅峰，「友情」这一题材的巅峰。

就游戏体验而言，个人线虽然质量参差不齐，但是LB的共通和Refrain实在是过于完美，让我不由得想要去称它为神作。

先说个人线，库特比较废萌暂且不谈，小毬线最后关于拯救小毬的情感输稍显逊色以外，来谷线，美鱼线，叶留佳线在我这都留下了深刻的印象。
来谷线中对于校园霸凌的反抗，对于自我的追寻，叶留佳线对于亲情的渴望，对于不幸的思考，还有美鱼线如诗画一般的氛围，我认为都是质量不错的个人线，很大程度上丰富了沉浸感和体验感。

然后是共通。可以说Key的共通一直都是其一大亮点，从罚抄的超自然研究部耍宝日常到SP的鸟白岛大探险，共通线一直都是Key质量最稳定，人物塑造最集中的一个区块。而LB到共通可以说是神中神。有趣的小游戏（战斗排位赛，棒球等等，说到棒球，我天天打猫身上，你猫还跳起来被打，麻枝准真不是略茂区吗（笑）），优秀的人物塑造，以及将所有角色紧密连接在一起的【Little Busters】这一队伍的羁绊，真的是我有史以来玩过最优秀的塑造之一。而且LB的共通真是细的离谱，根据你攻略角色的顺序，共通线内容也会改变，角色性格也会改变。这细致入微的刻画真的会让人感到非常惊喜。而这，其实也是一个最大的伏笔，一个贯穿游戏的最大伏笔。

接下来，Refrain线。RF其实并不长，也就4-5h的流程，甚至感觉不如SP的Alka+Pockets长度长。但是，RF的塑造可谓是完美。五个章节，分别描写了【Little Busters】五人组里每一个人被救赎，成为挚友，再一同前进的过程。最后恭介的落泪更是让人眼泪止不住的流。“我们一起创造了这个世界，一个不断轮回，不断重复的世界，我们假装一无所知的对待你们，引导你们，只为了在这场梦醒的时候，在我们离开的时候，你们能够不再绝望，不再孤独，可以坚强的活下去。”而最终，他们两人也确实做到了，他们成长了，前进了，并且，大家一起。

高く跳べ高く空へ，
高く蹴れ高く声を上げ，
いつか挫けたその日の向こうまで，
きみの声忘れない涙も忘れない，
これから始まる希望という名の未来を，
その足は歩き出すやがて来る過酷も，
乗り越えてくれるよ信じさせてくれるよ！

Если целью было заставить игрока прочувствовать ту же усталость, что испытывает герой, - то у него это, безусловно, получилось. Sucker for Love, or SFL as I will likely call it the rest of this review, is a fantastically written monster dating sim. While the runtime is short for an initial play through, there are branching endings and paths that make replaying a worthwhile option. Each of the three chapters have multiple endings, with chapter 2 in particular having 6 possible outcomes for the story! This was a really fun game to play on Twitch, my viewers had a great time seeing each chapter come to a close and I had a blast being a down bad goober for a few hours.

SFL was a pleasant surprise for me, and it was just the right amount of a subversion of the dating sim genre to get me interested. I'm not usually one to dabble in these types of games but the writing and the surprise gameplay mechanics that presented themselves made this a game worth checking out. Rabi-Ribi, developed by CreSpirit and GemaYue, is one of those rare indie titles that hides extraordinary depth beneath a deceptively cute exterior. At first glance, it appears to be a lighthearted platformer about a bunny-turned-human named Erina exploring a colorful world filled with equally adorable characters. However, a few minutes into the game make it clear that this is much more than a simple cute adventure—it’s a highly refined fusion of Metroidvania exploration and bullet-hell intensity. The combination of tight platforming, fast-paced combat, and overwhelming on-screen chaos gives the game an identity that feels both nostalgic and unique, successfully blending two genres that rarely coexist with such harmony.

The foundation of Rabi-Ribi lies in its intricate world design. The game presents a vast, interconnected map full of secret rooms, collectibles, upgrades, and optional challenges. Like the best Metroidvanias, progress depends on acquiring new abilities that allow Erina to traverse previously inaccessible areas—double jumps, wall climbs, and dashes all come into play as the player gradually learns to navigate every corner of the island. Exploration is highly rewarding, as there’s always a hidden power-up or shortcut waiting to be discovered. Yet, unlike many games of its kind, Rabi-Ribi adds a layer of intensity through its boss encounters, which transform the traditional platforming experience into a barrage of flashing lights, homing bullets, and intricate attack patterns. These moments demand focus and precision, pushing players to learn timing, positioning, and adaptability.

The combat system is deceptively deep for a 2D platformer. Erina’s close-range hammer strikes are complemented by Ribbon’s ranged magical attacks, and together they create a combat flow that balances aggression and evasion. The player must manage spacing carefully, switching between direct hits and ranged bursts while dodging complex bullet formations. Each boss fight becomes a dance of endurance and precision, especially on higher difficulties where the screen fills with deadly patterns reminiscent of classic arcade shooters. What’s remarkable is how the game manages to make these fights feel fair despite their chaos—each projectile follows a predictable rhythm, rewarding observation and practice. The result is a gameplay experience that feels equal parts skill-based and exhilarating, encouraging replay and mastery.

Visually, Rabi-Ribi excels in creating a vibrant world that contrasts its intensity with charm. The pixel art is beautifully detailed, featuring fluid animations, expressive character portraits, and imaginative backgrounds that shift from lush forests to eerie caverns to mechanical labyrinths. The cheerful art style and lively character designs lend a sense of whimsy that never undermines the difficulty, creating a striking tonal balance. The soundtrack deserves particular praise—it’s fast-paced, energetic, and infectious, elevating every boss encounter and exploration sequence. Each track fits the mood of its area perfectly, contributing to the game’s rhythm and reinforcing its sense of momentum.

While Rabi-Ribi succeeds on nearly every mechanical level, its narrative is less pronounced. The story revolves around Erina’s search for her lost master and her gradual understanding of her transformation, accompanied by a growing cast of quirky, friendly, and occasionally eccentric characters. The dialogue is filled with humor and references to anime tropes, giving the game a light and comedic tone. However, the sheer number of side characters and the fast pace of interactions can sometimes make the plot feel secondary to the gameplay. For many players, this won’t be an issue—the story is charming enough to provide context without intruding on the experience—but those looking for a strong emotional narrative may find it somewhat superficial. Still, its playful tone fits perfectly within the game’s energetic spirit and gives personality to its world.

The challenge level in Rabi-Ribi is significant, and that’s part of its appeal. Even at normal difficulty, boss fights can be punishing, requiring patience and pattern recognition to survive. The higher difficulty modes, meanwhile, are designed for veterans who want to test their reflexes to the limit, introducing denser bullet patterns and tougher timing. Yet the game remains accessible due to its fair design—failure feels like a learning opportunity rather than punishment. Players who persevere are rewarded with a deep sense of satisfaction, as each victory feels earned through skill rather than luck. The game also includes post-game content, additional modes, and multiple endings, adding considerable replay value for those who become engrossed in its mechanics.

Despite its many strengths, Rabi-Ribi is not without flaws. The map system can feel cumbersome at times, offering little clarity when it comes to unexplored areas or hidden passages. Navigation can become disorienting, especially for newcomers unfamiliar with the genre. Some players may also find the art style misleading—its pastel visuals and cute characters might give the impression of a casual experience, only to be met with a level of difficulty that rivals hardcore bullet-hell shooters. The contrast between aesthetic charm and mechanical brutality can be jarring for those expecting something simple. However, for those who embrace its challenge, that very contrast becomes one of the game’s defining strengths.

In the end, Rabi-Ribi is a masterful hybrid that defies easy categorization. It’s a game that looks like a cheerful side-scroller but plays like a precision-based challenge of skill and strategy. Its combination of exploration, customization, and frenetic combat makes it a standout in both the Metroidvania and bullet-hell genres, offering something few games dare to attempt. Beneath its bright visuals and playful humor lies a deeply satisfying gameplay loop that rewards patience, mastery, and curiosity. Rabi-Ribi is a testament to how indie developers can blend disparate influences into something cohesive, challenging, and unforgettable—a game that proves that beneath the softest of exteriors can beat the heart of a true hardcore adventure.

Preface this by saying that I played the original Valkyria Chronicles many years ago on PS3, and also played this one on my PS4 a good many years ago. I own it on my PS4, Switch, and on Steam. Just getting around to playing it again and decided to leave a review on it because I feel I have more than enough hours from the years of playing it on and off to make a few quick generalized takes on it. There was little to no thought to how this all flows, and I typed as I thought of things to say, so I'm sorry for any redundancy in advance. I don't usually write these, but I have a real soft spot for this game, so it deserved me wasting a quick ten minutes to type this up.

In a nutshell, this game is anime WW2 with some "modern" twists, like single-man portable mortars, APCs, and other things I won't get into too much. If anime tropes or style of story telling make you roll your eyes, you will have a hard time enjoying the story and majority of its cutscenes. I can't act like this isn't an anime game, because it very much is, and it's not trying to pretend it isn't in the slightest.

VC4 is not ground breaking, as VC1 existed over ten years ago already and literally invented the system this game is based on... Turn based, infantry-focused WW2 with light elements of tactics and decision making. And usually a tank you can control. But VC4 isn't trying to be ground breaking. It's just an easy to enjoy ride, much like VC1, but with a new story and new characters, who are all very lovable for the most part. So long as you don't try to take VC4 too seriously, you're likely to enjoy it.

With all of that said, mechanically, VC4 feels like a much fresher, more streamlined VC1, with some minor quality of life and overall refinement/slight balance changes. That means it took a tried and generally favorable formula, and +1'd it. The game still suffers from some issues that were in VC1 that veteran players will be familiar with, but for the most part, the foundation makes for an enjoyable game all the same, as the formula was always novel and unique.

Like mentioned before, the game tries to tell a serious story, which it sometimes succeeds in, while sprinkling in the usual anime tropes to help ease the tension between story beats. To an extent, this is present in the gameplay mechanics to a degree. Much like how I feel about the story, if you don't try to take the game too seriously, it's a solid gameplay loop, with a familiar mechanics system that can begin to feel very samey, but missions and circumstances around them are always unique, keeping the gameplay loop fresh. The missions usually reflect what is going on in the story well, usually centered around otherwise decent twists and surprises and character growths. Nothing ever seems to get too stale or overstay its welcome, even on some of the longer missions.

With all that said, the game is 100% weeb trash, if I haven't made that clear enough by now. Much like anyone familiar with the life cycle of an anime fan, you will ultimately realize all anime is trash, but it's enjoyable trash, if you choose to enjoy it and not be a total square who can't enjoy things. This game is no different. It's the box mac and cheese of video games. Very much something you can turn on and jump right into with little to understand outside of fundamental mechanics, something that is easy to consume, low effort to play (generally) and not really need to use your head too much to enjoy it, especially if you play on easy.

All and all, a splendid time for those who either played the original Valkyria Chronicles on PS3, or if you enjoy video games with anime aesthetic and think you'll enjoy a turn based strategy game with an action-oriented twist. The game really does climax around the two thirds of the way in, and it's an absolute blast leading up to it and the resolution after. I'll always love this game, even if it's ultimately anime trash by my otherwise much more mature standards these days.

INDIKA — игра, которая заставляет задуматься

Я человек верующий, поэтому проект INDIKA привлёк моё внимание ещё с момента анонса. К сожалению, не смог пройти его при выходе, но теперь, наконец, дошёл — и, честно сказать, я поражён. Эта игра не просто удивила, она потрясла своей атмосферой — давящей, тревожной, но при этом глубоко осмысленной.

INDIKA — это не классическая игра в привычном понимании. Скорее, это интерактивный фильм, где ты не столько управляешь персонажем, сколько наблюдаешь за её внутренним миром, болью, поисками и падениями. Да, ты ведёшь Индику, изучаешь окрестности, иногда оказываешься в странных пиксельных вставках — как будто заглядываешь в её прошлое, в моменты, которые объясняют, почему она стала той, кем является сейчас.

История многослойная, и некоторые ответы игрок должен найти сам. Как жизнь довела её до монастыря? Почему внутри столько противоречий? Эти вопросы остаются с тобой до самых титров.

По атмосфере INDIKA напомнила мне нечто среднее между Deadly Premonition и фильмом «Остров» с Петром Мамоновым. В обоих произведениях чувствуется одна и та же тяжесть вины, попытка обрести веру и искупить прошлое. И Индика с Ильёй — яркие примеры того, о чём говорил Христос:

«Истинно говорю вам, что мытари и блудницы вперед вас идут в Царство Божие» (Евангелие от Матфея 21:31).

Игра показывает, что вера — не о чудесах, а о внутреннем принятии и надежде. Концовка подводит к этому очень точно: не обязательно верить в чудо — важно просто верить.

Да, геймплея здесь немного. Это не шутер, не квест и не экшен. Это пища для души, размышление о грехе, прощении и человеческой слабости.
Рекомендую INDIKA тем, кто хочет не просто поиграть, а подумать. Кто готов провести пару часов в мире, где каждая сцена — как икона, написанная через боль, сомнение и свет.
